PREFACE 

"Our Home State and the New World" | child's own state is a part. The other state groups are then considered in the order that seems best. is devoted to a study of the pupil's home state, country, and continent of North America, and also a similar study of South America. It is part of a new series of geographies which are truly progressive in their content and in the order and method of presenting geographical facts and principles.

In this book an introductory treatment of the early exploration of North America, enough to establish in the pupil's mind the European connections of our people, comes first. This is followed by a brief study of the major political divisions and the chief physical regions of the continent. The children then take up a study of their own state. 

This state treatment is presented in simple language, but it is nevertheless comprehensive enough to make its study basic to all future study of geography. 

It is given its proper place in the text instead of being relegated to a "supplement" of a few pages bound in the back of the book, as has been the almost universal custom for a long time. 

Throughout the study of the home state the emphasis is upon the fundamental geographic factors and relations that influence the lives of people. It is a study of geographic controls, whether physical or economic, rather than a study of facts as such.

The text on the state, after an outline treatment of the natural regions of the United States, is followed by a study of the natural regions and economic conditions of the state group of which the Studies of the parts of the United States, of our outlying possessions, of the other countries in North America north and south of the United States, and of the continent as a whole, follow in order, and then, finally, the natural regions, countries, and continent of South America are likewise studied. 

The story of geography as told in this text is a continuous narrative, and as the area described enlarges, frequent comparisons are made with regions previously studied, for the purpose of making clear to the children common or contrasting conditions and characteristics. 

Care is taken to show how and why relief, climate, and products differ in different parts of our country and as between countries. The work of the ice sheet, briefly referred to in the treatment of the physical regions of North America, is again studied in other parts of our own country in connection with the results of its work. The formation of the Grand 

Canyon of the Colorado River is shown to be but a larger expression of forces whose activities and results may be seen today in other parts of our continent. 

Political divisions, such as states and countries, are recognized and located, but within any political unit the work of the people is largely identified with the chief natural regions within its borders. In this way it is possible to show the children that somewhat similar physical conditions lead to similar human activities

vi 

PREFACE 

and that these may at times extend over | kept in mind the fact that they are to be a large area.

However, the larger natural regions of a great country like our own may cut across many smaller political divisions, such as our states, the location of which, as well as the relation of each to others, should be a matter of common knowledge. Political boundaries, therefore, are given full consideration, and the location of natural resources and great industries is set out in terms of cities, states, and countries. For example, it is not enough that the Blue Grass region should be known as a part of the Central Plains. 

It should also be known as part of the state of Kentucky, within whose borders a rich and fertile soil has made a farming region of remarkable productivity and individuality.

A full equipment of maps is provided. 

The basic maps are of the combined physical-political type, and are conveniently placed for reference throughout the text. The groups of states into which the United States is divided are based upon those used in the reports of the United States census. In addition to the basic maps described above, an abundance of black and white maps have been used to show the natural regions, routes of transportation, the distribution of rainfall, important crops, domestic animals, and mineral products, and other matters of importance. In the preparation of all the maps, the authors have used by young pupils, and have, therefore, deliberately excluded details that would only make for confusion. 

Great care has been taken in the choice of the illustrations, both as to size and as to placement, so that they can be easily studied. Each one was chosen because it helps to interpret the text - not merely or primarily because it is a beautiful picture. However, taken as a whole, they constitute an unusually attractive as well as a valuable body of illustrative material.

The teaching material is one of the special features of the book. This material carefully avoids the formal map and review questions of an earlier day, and likewise avoids the lifeless summaries that frequently tempt children to take a short cut in their study. The interesting exercises here provided furnish abundant review material and emphasize the more important geographic relationships and principles. They have considerable variety in form, and thus avoid the monotony often found in checks and review exercises. Above all, they lead the learner to arrive at many conclusions for himself. 

The authors gratefully acknowledge their indebtedness to the many teachers who have tested teaching material, maps, and illustrations in their class rooms. 

ALBERT PERRY BRIGHAM CHARLES T. MCFARLANE

The Western Hemisphere, including the New World 

The earth on which we live is a great ball or sphere. 

Only half of the earth is shown in the map on this page. "Hemi" means half. That is why half of the earth, a half-sphere, is called a hemisphere. 

The large land mass shown in this map was discovered, explored, and settled by people from Europe. To reach it the European explorers and settlers sailed west across a great ocean. 39 That is why this part of our earth has become known as the Western Hemisphere.

Europe and parts of Asia and Africa had long been known, and when the new lands were found they were called the New World. 

The colors on the map show how the land of the New World has been divided into different countries.

America and South America. There are people living in all five of these continents and in the continent of Australia. map facing this page, and the map on page 394, show how the continents are divided into many different countries. 

What interesting stories have you read about the people of other lands?

The more you learn about the earth on which you live, the more you will find it to be both wonderful and beautiful. 

You already know many interesting things about the earth. Look at a globe. 

You will see that it shows much more water than land. Most of the land is in four large pieces. See how the water curves around them. Do you know the names of the oceans into which this great body of water is divided? The names given to four oceans are shown on the map facing this page. 

The largest land mass is made up of the continents of Asia, Africa, and Europe.

One very cold region is the continent named Antarctica. Find it on the globe.

Most of it is always covered with ice and snow. There are no homes of people there. Only a few kinds of birds and other animals are found along the coast of that continent.

How to Look at a Map. - A globe shows what part of the earth's surface is land and what part is water. It shows the shapes of the continents, but does not show the continents or countries or states as large as we sometimes need to see them. 

Any part of the earth's surface, large or small, can be shown on a map. The "scale of miles " on a map is a measure you can use to find how large is any part shown. Using that scale in the map on page 2, see about how wide North 

America is, in its widest part.

In this book you will find and learn how to use several different kinds of maps. A relief map, such as that of North America on page 2, shows lowlands, highlands, and valleys. The lowlands are shown in green, and the higher lands in buff and yellow. The highest lands are mountains over two miles high. These are in purple or they are left white to show that they are always covered with snow. 

If you could go up and up and up and see all North America at once as you can see a farm or park or city from an airplane, the view might be a little like this map. You would be looking at a land about 3000 miles wide and 5000 miles long. In such a view heights of one or two miles would not amount to much. 

But when you are standing on a plain and looking up at a mountain a mile high, it seems very high indeed. 

Look once more at North America on the globe. See that, except in the northwest, the oceans that separate it from other continents are very wide.

2. Add the name of the continent on which there are no people. 3. Draw a line under the name of our continent.

DISCOVERY AND SETTLEMENT 

You are now to learn about the white people who came to North America in 1492 and a little later, and about the people who were then already here. 

How long ago was the year 1492? It was in that year that Columbus made his first famous voyage across the Atlantic 

Ocean. The only white people in the world at that time were living in or near Europe.

Europe. They knew much about the continent of Europe and a little about the continents of Asia and Africa. They supposed that these were the only continents in all the world. 

The Indians. - When, in 1492, Columbus reached some islands of North America, he did not know that he had found a new world. He thought that he had reached the "Indies," as the mainland and islands of southeastern Asia were called. It was for that reason that he called the people here Indians. This name has been used ever since that time, but they are also called red men, because of the reddish-brown color of their skin.

Painting in the American Museum of Natural History, New York

A.-An Indian village. Notice the bark houses at the left, the baskets, corn, and squashes in the foreground, and the birch-bark canoes, the lake, and the cornfield in the distance. pounding corn, another woman weaving a blanket, and the baby or

In 1492 there were fewer than 500,000 Indians in our whole country; not so many Indians as there are people now living in the one city of Buffalo or Milwaukee. Many of the Indians lived chiefly by hunting wild animals, and so they needed much land to supply food for even a few. North of the Gulf of 

Mexico North America was almost an empty continent, waiting for the white men to come and fill it with people. 

Before the white men came, the Indians of our country had no domestic animals but the dog. On land they traveled on foot. On streams and lakes they used a light birch-bark canoe. This could be easily carried across country from one stream or lake to another. 66 

Notice the men with bow and pipe, the woman papoose" in a crib hung up on a birch tree. picture? 

In the eastern part of our country many of the Indians lived a settled life in villages (A). Some had tents made of skins or mats. Others built houses of bark or of wood, the largest of which were 50 or 60 feet long and were divided into rooms. 

Some of the Indians raised beans, squashes, and corn. They gathered wild berries, and in some parts of the country wild rice. Acorns, sunflower seeds, and potatoes also were used for food. Corn and the potato were not known to the rest of the world until after the discovery of 

America. Now great crops of them are raised in many countries.

In the Southwest there were many Indians who lived by farming. As they had little wood, their houses were made

DISCOVERY AND SETTLEMENT 

5 mostly of dried mud, or adobe. Each building, or pueblo, was large enough for a small village. Some were several stories high, the upper rooms being reached by ladders. 

Along the shores of the continent oysters and clams were found, and fish were caught in all waters. Along the northwest coast the salmon caught in the rivers were the chief food of some tribes. 

The Indians had nothing made of iron. 

Their fishhooks were made of bone. 

They trapped wild animals, or hunted them with bows and arrows. They made good arrowheads, knives, and hammers of stone, and they also used copper that they found near Lake Superior. They made pottery from clay (A), and wove blankets and baskets of many different kinds. 

Dances, ball games, foot races, and contests in throwing and shooting were common Indian sports. The boys played with tops, slings, and stilts, and the girls played "house" and had dolls of buckskin.

Many Indian words are still in use as names of states, cities, islands, rivers, and lakes in North America. Here are some examples: Connecticut, Chicago, Manhattan, Mississippi, and Michigan. English French Spanish

Spanish Explorers. Columbus was an Italian, but his voyage of 1492 was made for Spain. He was trying to find a new way to reach southeastern Asia. 

Trade between western Europe and eastern Asia had been carried on by way of the Indian Ocean, but Columbus thought the western route would be shorter. 

When Columbus reached the Bahama Islands and Cuba, he thought he had found the new way to Asia for which he was looking. He made three later voyages to this part of the world, and other 

Spanish explorers followed him. Spanish settlers soon took possession of the lands about the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea, including Florida, Mexico, and 

Central America (B), and most of South 

America. In what is now the United

States they settled not only Florida but also large parts of the Southwest.

French Explorers. -As early as 1504

French fishermen were catching fish near 

Newfoundland. French explorers soon discovered the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes. It was a French explorer who started the settlement that has become the city of Quebec. The lake between the states of New York and Vermont was named after him (map, page 154). What was his name?

French missionaries and traders followed lakes and streams and pushed through the forests to the central part of the continent. They followed the Mississippi River to its mouth and claimed much land for the French king. Many people living in eastern Canada and in the city of New Orleans still speak the French language. Detroit, St. Louis, and New

Orleans are among the many French names that are still found on the map of 

North America. 

English Explorers. The first of the 

English explorers came as traders and to claim new lands for the English king. 

Later Englishmen came to build homes and live here. Their first successful settlement was at Jamestown, in Virginia, in 1607, and the second was at Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts, in 1620.

Other settlements followed along the middle Atlantic coast. The English also took away from the Dutch a settlement at the mouth of the Hudson River and gave it the name of New York. It is now the largest city in North America.

The map on page 5 shows the parts of 

North America as they were first claimed by the Spanish, French, and English.

COUNTRIES OF NORTH AMERICA 

Look at the map of North America on page 6. You will see that most of it is now divided between two great countries the United States and the Dominion of Canada. South of the United 

States you will see Mexico and a number of smaller countries.

The United States. - Our country, the 

United States, was at first formed by the thirteen colonies which won their independence from England in the American Revolution. Now it is made up of fortyeight states, and stretches across the central part of the continent from the 

Atlantic Ocean on the east to the Pacific

Ocean on the west. It takes in much land that was once held by the English and the French, and part of the land once held by the Spanish.

Alaska belongs to the United States. 

Greenland belongs to Denmark, a small country in Europe. 

Countries South of the United States. 

- Mexico, like Canada and the United

States, extends across the continent. It narrows toward the south and has long coast lines on the Pacific Ocean and on the 

Gulf of Mexico. 

Southeast of Mexico is a group of seven small countries. Across one of these the 

United States built a ship canal to connect the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific 

Ocean. What is its name?

Southeast of the United States is a group of islands called the West Indies. In two boundary between the United States and Canada; that of them, Cuba and Hispaniola, there are on the right, between the United States and Mexico. 

Follow the northern and southern boundaries of our country on the map. 

On the land itself there are no such lines as are used to show the boundaries on a map. Instead, the boundary is marked in places by a stone or a post (A and 9A). 

The boundary markers may be close enough together so that each one can be seen from the one next in line. In a river a boundary is usually in midstream; and in a lake, halfway between the two shores (9B). Through what lakes and what river does the northern boundary of the 

United States go? In what stream is part of the boundary between Mexico and the United States? 

Canada and the Northern Islands. 

Canada is the largest country in North

America. It includes all that part of the continent north of the United States except Alaska and Labrador. Many islands, too, along the coasts of the mainland, are part of Canada. Labrador belongs to Newfoundland, which is a British colony separate from Canada. independent countries. Several of the other islands belong to the United States, and the rest belong to countries in Europe. 

Draw an Outline Map of North America.- 

You should know North America so well that you can draw a map of it from memory. But do not try to do that at first.

Ta Take a large sheet of strong paper, use a pencil, and copy your map from the one on page 6. Sketch in the shore line. Do not try to show the small turns and all the "ins and outs." Show the main shapes in smooth lines. Unless you have practiced much map work or other drawing, you will often need to use your eraser. Do not mind if you have to use several sheets of paper before you get a shape that is like the printed map. Besides the main shore line, put in the shores of great bodies of water such as Hudson Bay, Gulf of St. Lawrence, Gulf of Mexico, and the

Great Lakes. Add the large islands, Greenland, Newfoundland, and Cuba. Do not put in the names, unless you can do it in very small, neatly printed letters. Put in the boundaries of the larger countries, but let the small Central American countries all go in one piece. Do your map with care.

PHYSICAL REGIONS OF NORTH AMERICA 

11 

PHYSICAL REGIONS OF NORTH AMERICA 

You have just been looking at the map on page 6, which shows the countries of North America. Such a map is called a political map. 

You are now to look at another kind of map of North America on page 10, called a physical map. It shows the bordering oceans, the great rivers, and the large lakes. It shows plains and mountains. It shows what parts of the land are high and what parts are low. 

Regions of North America. - The height of land is measured from the level of the sea. Find the color guide in the corner of the map. What color shows lands that are less than 1000 feet above sea level? Trace this region from Florida to Nova Scotia. It is the Atlantic 

Lowland. Some of it is nearly level, and some of it is hilly. It is all less than 

1000 feet above sea level.

Notice that the same color is used to show a very large region reaching a long distance north of the Gulf of Mexico on both sides of the Mississippi River. It extends past the Great Lakes and all the way across Canada from south to north. 

Why is this region colored green? Find two routes by which you could go from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, and never be more than 1000 feet above the sea. 

Between the two lowlands of our country that you have just studied there is a region of highlands. What is its name? Follow with your finger the parts of this highland that are between 

1000 feet and 2000 feet above the sea. 

Find parts that are between 2000 feet and 5000 feet high. Two peaks in these mountains are more than 6000 feet high. 

They are marked by small crosses. Mt. 

Washington is 6279 feet high, and Mt. 

Mitchell is 6711 feet high. Find them.

Mt. Mitchell is the highest mountain in the eastern half of North America.

Find, in the central part of the United States, the three rivers named Missouri, Arkansas, and Red. On each of these rivers, using your ruler to help, find a point that is halfway between the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific. A line extending through these points would divide the United States into an eastern half and a western half. Is this line east or west of the Mississippi River? 

Almost all of the western half of North 

America is highland. This highland region reaches from Central America, through Mexico, across the United States and Canada into Alaska. 

How high are the Great Plains? Find 

Pikes Peak. It is over twice as high as

Mt. Mitchell. The map also gives you the names and locations of other mountain peaks and of several mountain ranges. In its widest part the western highland is more than 1000 miles wide. 

How long would it take you to fly across it in an airplane going 100 miles an hour?

There is not much lowland along the Pacific Ocean. On the map find several small lowland regions in the far West. 

It will be easy for you to remember that North America has an eastern lowland, an eastern highland, a great central lowland, and a great western highland.

You know that the central lowland is much larger than the eastern lowland. 

You will also want to remember that the western highland is much wider, much higher, and much longer than the eastern highland.

You should get the same length on both maps. Do you? Greenland is about one fourth as large as the United States. 

On the map on this page, most of Greenland is shown in black. This part of the island is covered by a great glacier, or sheet of ice, several thousand feet thick. At its edge the ice flows slowly down valleys into the ocean (A). There large masses of ice break off and float away as icebergs. 

If all the snow that falls on Greenland melted, there would be no glacier. But it does not all melt. For a long time there has been more snow each winter than the summer sun can melt. This snow packs together until it makes ice. 

The glacial ice, growing thicker and thicker in the central part, presses out around the edges. This is a little like the way molasses candy will act when a big lump of it is left in a pan. A barrel of asphalt is almost always hard and brittle when it is first opened. If it is

GLACIERS

H. L. Fairchild 

A. - Drumlins, in New York state, near Lake Ontario. The nearer drumlin is seen in nearly its full length. left as a lump on the roadside or street for a time it will spread over the ground or pavement. These two examples will help you to understand how glaciers flow.

There are smaller glaciers on the high mountains and in the mountain valleys of 

Alaska. Why? There are glaciers also in western Canada and in the western part of the United States. There are glaciers in the high mountains of some of the other continents. On the Antarctic continent there is an ice sheet larger than that of Greenland. of the glacier, in a ridge or hill called a moraine.

In some places the melting of an old ice sheet has left earth and stones scattered over large fields. In other places earth and stones are heaped up in oval hills which the ice shaped that way as it passed over them. These are called drumlins (A). 

Glaciers move only a few feet or only a few inches a day. As they move along they scrape up loose earth and stones. 

These are held in the moving ice. They help to wear away the rocks over which the glacier moves. In this way glaciers may wear away the tops of hills, or dig a valley deeper.

As the glacier of a mountain valley moves down, it gets into a region that is not so cold. The ice melts more and more until it is melting faster than it is moving forward. When this happens the earth and stones are left at the end At one time the climate of Canada and the northern part of the United States was colder than it is now. There was much snow. Not all that fell in the winter was melted the next summer. The snow got deeper and deeper until it packed into ice. The ice sheet grew larger and larger until it covered more than half of North America, as shown by the map on page 12. 

Find two places on the map from which the arrows are pointing away in all directions. These two places are where the snow was heaviest. As it packed into ice, the ice moved in the ways the arrows point. Compare this map with the map of North America on page 6. Find three cities that are now near what was once the southern edge of this old ice sheet.

NORTH AMERICA 

The cold and the snow that formed the ice sheet of North America lasted a long time. Just how thick the ice was, no one knows. From the markings left on rocks when the ice melted, it is known that the ice moved as the arrows show. From the moraines left at its southern edge we know about how far into the United 

States it reached. 

Before the time of the ice sheet in 

North America there were hills and valleys and streams. There were also forests and shrubs and animals. Under the ice sheet, the hills and valleys were changed in shape. Streams were turned in new directions or blocked up by material that the glacier left, thus forming many lakes. When the ice at last melted off, plants and animals once more lived on the land that the ice had so long covered. 

A. Waterfall in Enfield Glen State Park, near Ithaca,

New York, as seen in the winter. The hills and valleys in this part of the state were greatly changed in shape by the ice sheet.

EARLY HISTORY 

Explorers. Missouri has had a very interesting history. You may be surprised to learn that the first white men to visit our state were Spaniards. They came here about fifty years after Columbus discovered America, but they did not stay long, for they did not come to establish homes. They were hunting silver and gold.

The next white men to explore Missouri were the French. You have already learned that the French settled in the country along the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes. From these settlements along the Great Lakes, French explorers made long journeys that carried them into the Mississippi Valley. The greatest of these explorers was La Salle. 

He was the first white man to travel from the source of the Mississippi River to its mouth. He made the long and dangerous trip in a small canoe. After he reached the Gulf of Mexico, he claimed the great valley of the Mississippi for France. He wanted to establish French settlements in that part of North America like those already established along the banks of the 

St. Lawrence River, but he was killed before he could establish a permanent settlement in that region. 

After La Salle the French explorers came in larger and larger numbers, and hunters, traders, and miners traveled over

Missouri. La Honton was the first white man to travel up the Missouri River. He traveled as far as the mouth of the Osage River. Find it on the map, page 16. At that point on the Missouri River, La Honton built a settlement of several huts. 

He was the first white man to hunt in the interior part of Missouri. 

Fur Traders. You have so far learned only about the early explorers of Missouri. 

After the French had explored much of our state, they began to make settlements. Many of the earliest settlements did not last long because they simply served as homes for a short time for those who came to work in the lead mines and the salt springs, or for those who came to hunt for the rich furs of our state. The oldest lead mines in North America are located near Potosi.

The first permanent settlement was Ste. 

Genevieve, on the Mississippi River.

Find it on the map, page 17. This settlement was near salt springs because to a pioneer salt was very necessary. He used it to cure his meat and to flavor his food. 

The exact date of the founding of Ste. 

Genevieve is not known, but some people think it was about 1732. If this date is correct, the settlement was established in the year in which George Washington was born.

Soon after the settlement of Ste. Genevieve, a group of thirty French pioneers established a fur-trading post near the mouth of the Missouri River. The settlement was named St. Louis, in honor of 

Louis IX, a famous king of France. A

French fur trader named Laclede chose its location as the most desirable for a trading post on the Missouri River.

From a tiny fur-trading village (19 A) St. 

Louis has grown to be one of the largest cities in the United States. If you should visit St. Louis, you would find that many of its streets have French names. 

The Indians. — As you know, the early settlers found Indians in our state. The most important Indians living in Missouri were the Osages. They were said to be the tallest Indians in North America.

Few of the men were less than six feet tall, | and some were seven feet; and they were well built and graceful. They were excellent hunters. Many of the braves could shoot an arrow so forcefully that it would pierce a buffalo. In the small fields that surrounded their villages the 

Indians raised corn, pumpkins, and beans.

The women did most of the work in the field, while the men hunted. The Osages lived in the valley of the Osage River (map, page 16). At present there are no 

Indians living in our state, and they have left little here to remember them by.

Early Settlers. - About 1770 American colonists from the East and South began to come to Missouri and settle upon farms. 

These Americans became the first farmers in our state. The most famous of these early Missouri pioneers was Daniel Boone, who came from Kentucky. Boone settled on a farm in what is now Warren County (map, page 16), and hunted over a large part of Missouri. With his sons he made much salt in the part of our state now known as Howard County. Locate

Howard County on the map. 

Before Missouri became a part of the United States it was part of the large region called Louisiana Territory. You have already learned how La Salle claimed the Mississippi Valley for France. France continued to own it until 1763, when it was given to Spain. Spain claimed it until 

1800, when it again became French land. 

When the United States bought Louisiana 

Territory from France, in 1803, Missouri for the first time became a part of the 

United States. So you see that our state has been governed by France, Spain, and the United States.

Soon after Missouri became part of the United States it was organized as a territory. In 1821 it became one of the states of our Union. Missouri has continued to grow until it is now a great state. MO.-2

A. Natural regions of Missouri.

NATURAL REGIONS OF MISSOURI 

The best way to study the geography of Missouri is to divide the state into natural regions, as shown on the map on this page. 

There are five natural regions. Their names are printed in large letters. What are they? You will study each region carefully, as each differs in many ways from the other regions of the state in surface, soils, and natural resources. After you have learned many interesting things about each of the natural regions, you will understand more easily what Missouri as a whole is like.

The Ice Sheet in Missouri. - You have already studied about the great ice sheet that covered a large part of North 

America. Turn to the map on page 12, and locate Missouri. You will see that part of our state was covered by the great glacier. The northern half of Missouri was once covered by this vast ice sheet. 38 89° 40 39The glacier was important in making the surface and soil of that part of our state as it is today. Its effect on the soil was especially important. The soil is called glacial soil. The present scenery of northern Missouri is also due to the work of the glacier. As the large ice sheet slowly moved over the surface of the land it deposited gravel, rocks, and clay in the old valleys until many of them were completely filled. It also scraped off the tops of the old hills until this section looked fairly level after the ice melted. This is why we call this region the glacial plains. In some places in northern Missouri we can find large stones which were scattered over the surface of the land by the ice sheet. Many such rocks may be found in the northwestern part of the state.

36The glacier also changed the old drainage system of Missouri in many ways.

It filled up many of the old stream channels and forced the water to cut new ones. 

The channel of the Missouri River from 

Kansas City to St. Louis was largely made by the work of the glacier. 

Soils of Missouri. - Soil is very important to us, because it furnishes the food and water for growing plants. Have you ever heard your father say that the soil in a field is either rich or poor? When he says it is rich, he means that the soil has much plant food in it; when he says it is poor, he means that it has little plant food.

You will probably be interested in knowing how the soils in our state were made. On map A you will see that there are two main classes: (1) transported soil, and (2) residuary soil. By studying the map you will notice that the northern part of Missouri is covered with transported soil. Transported soil was carried to Missouri by the great ice sheet.

Now look at the map again, and you will see that most of the region south of the Missouri River is covered with residuary soil. This soil was made by the crumbling or decay of the native rocks. 

Most of this soil was made from sandstone, limestone, flint, or shale. you seen soils of different colors? colors were they?

The water in many of the streams of our state is muddy. This is especially true of the Missouri River, which is sometimes called "The Big Muddy," and also of the streams north of that river. These streams are muddy because they carry millions of fine particles of soil. When they overflow their banks, they leave behind some of the particles of soil and gradually form river plains. Is this soil transported or residuary? The soil of these river plains is very rich, and large fields of corn are grown in it. What kind of soil do you find in the southeastern part of Missouri?

Some of the soil in Missouri is windblown soil. It has been carried to our state and deposited by the wind, generally along the larger rivers. Wind-blown soil is fine and very rich and excellent for apple orchards.

You now know that our state has several kinds of soil. Many kinds of farm prodducts are grown in Missouri, partly due to the variety of soils. The Missouri farmer A.

All of the rivers you have been tracing have smaller branches. Some of the branches are so tiny that they are not shown on the map. The main stream and its branches are called a river system. 

The Grand, Chariton, Nodaway, and

Platte river systems are a part of the 

Missouri river system. The Missouri river system is a part of the Mississippi river system. If you live in the Glacial 

Plains, what is the name of the stream nearest you? To what river system does it belong? 

The Landscape of the Glacial Plains. 

If you live in the Glacial Plains you already know how pretty and restful the scenery is in this part of our state. The pioneers compared this region of gently rolling or almost level land (A), then covered by tall native grass, to a beautiful sea. Today the landscape is more varied than it appeared to the pioneer, for many kinds of grain and hay crops now grow where the tall grass once grew. 

The highest point of the Glacial Plains is in the northwestern part. The region slopes gently to the south, but this slope is so gradual that one does not notice it in traveling across the region. 

The country is somewhat broken near the streams. The almost level surface gives way to fairly high hills and beautiful bluffs near the large streams. The river bluffs along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers are especially attractive.

Great stretches of flat bottom land may be seen along the main streams. Carroll

County has more acres of fertile bottom land than any other county in Missouri.

Find Carroll County (map, pages 16-17) 

and tell why it has so much bottom land.

Mixed Farming. 

The surface of the Glacial Plains is well suited to farming. 

The land is level enough to be plowed easily, and without the loss of much soil during a rainy season. It has sufficient slope to drain nicely. The soil is deep and fertile in most places. Practically all kinds of grain and hay crops can be grown in this region with the least amount of labor necessary to produce such crops. 

It is not surprising, then, that the Glacial Plains region is the greatest farming section of our state. More of the people living there make their living by farming than by any other occupation. 

The most common type of agriculture in the Glacial Plains is mixed farming. 

In a region of mixed farming, the farmers do not devote all of their time to the production of one kind of crop. Instead, they will raise several different kinds of crops and live stock.

If you should visit a typical farm of the Glacial Plains, one of the first things you would notice would be the cornfield. 

Corn is the most important grain crop in this region. It is especially important in the northwestern and western parts. 

You will probably see a field of either oats or wheat, or perhaps both. The largest wheat crops are grown in the river counties.

On a typical farm, you will usually find a field of hay. This hay crop may be timothy, clover, alfalfa, or wild grass.

More alfalfa (A) is grown in the region drained by the Platte and Nodaway rivers than in any other section in Missouri.

The farm also has a garden in which the farmer raises Irish potatoes and many other kinds of vegetables. The farmer's wife usually cans large quantities of these vegetables during the summer.

WAB 7398 A. A strip-pit mine in Missouri. The coal is hauled away in trucks. are the coal is taken from the mine. There three methods of mining coal: (1) strip pit, (2) shaft, and (3) drift.

Each of these methods is used in the 

Glacial Plains.

Where the coal is near the surface of the earth the strip-pit method often is used. Huge steam shovels scrape the dirt away from the layer of coal (A).

The hole dug by the shovels is called the strip pit. Then the layer of coal is broken up and hauled to the tipple, where it is graded, sorted, and loaded into cars for shipping to the market. The tipple is a 

The tipple is a wooden framework used to sort, grade, and load the coal into cars. Picture B shows cars of coal that have been sorted according to size and grade. You see that some of it is in large lumps, and some of it is in smaller pieces. One car is loaded with very fine coal. 

Where the coal deposit is one hundred feet or more beneath the surface, the shaft method is used. This is the method 

B. Freight cars loaded with coal, ready to be shipped to distant markets. most frequently employed in the Glacial Plains. A large hole similar to a huge well is dug down to the layer of coal. The miners drill holes into the masses of coal with electric drills, and load the holes with dynamite. The dynamite is then exploded and it breaks up the coal, which is loaded into cars and later hoisted to the surface. 

Have you ever seen a layer of coal on a hillside? If so, you have probably seen people dig straight into the hillside and mine coal. Such a mine is called a drift mine, and there are many such mines in the Glacial Plains. However, coal mined in this way is usually sold locally in small quantities.

Railroad. This road enters Missouri from 

Quincy, Illinois, and runs to the western border of Daviess County, where it turns south to Kansas City. 

Another line, the Burlington Railroad, crosses the region, running from Hannibal to St. Joseph. It was the first railroad to cross the state from east to west. 

The main line of the Wabash Railroad runs from St. Louis to Kansas City,

Missouri. It passes through most of the 

Missouri River counties. Point out this road on the map. 

The Chicago and Alton Railroad crosses the Mississippi River and enters the state at the city of Louisiana. It then runs west to Glasgow, where it crosses to the south side of the Missouri River before continuing to Kansas City.

Numerous north-and-south lines connect the main east-and-west lines. Important towns have developed at the points where the trunk lines cross. Why?

Many excellent highways have been built in the Glacial Plains. Several federal as well as state highways cross the plains. By studying the highway map you will see that many of them intersect each other at right angles. It is now 

It is now possible to reach practically all the important cities and towns of the region by a hard-surfaced road. Most of the main highways of travel are made of cement (33 A), although some are built of gravel.

Many farm-to-market roads are now being built throughout the region. These roads are usually made of gravel or crushed rock. They extend into the rural sections not on the main line of travel, and are used as feeders for the main highways. Do you live near a farm-tomarket road?

Begin in the northeast corner of our state and trace the Mississippi River until you come to Canton. This city is a local trading center for the surrounding country. Its business houses are engaged in retail trade. By retail trade we mean the selling of goods, usually in small quantities, to people who will use them.

Canton is a city of pretty homes and wellkept lawns. In the summer its streets are shady and pleasant. Other similar centers in this region are Kahoka, Monticello, Memphis, Palmyra, Paris, Monroe 

City, Bowling Green, and Edina. Find them on the map. 

If you follow the Mississippi River southward, you will soon reach Hannibal.

It is built on the west bank of the river in an especially rich agricultural section.

Hannibal is the fourth largest industrial city in Missouri. It has sixtythree factories, and some of the things manufactured are shoes, clothing, cement, buttons, candy, paint, and stoves.

Cities on the Grand Divide. You have already learned that there are two drainage systems in the Glacial Plains divided by a highland called the "Grand 

Divide." At the southern end of this highland is the city of Mexico. It is located in the famous "blue-grass area of Missouri. Mexico has a few local industries, the most important being the manufacture of brick (35 A). Three railroads serve the city. It is famous as a saddle-horse center. Some of the world's finest saddle horses have been raised there. Mexico conducts frequent saddle-horse sales that attract buyers from all parts of our country.

St. Joseph (37 A) is built on large bluffs overlooking the Missouri River. It was established as a small fur-trading post, and it was not long until the town handled a large fur trade with the Indians who

A. - An airplane view of St. Joseph. In the center background is the beautiful city hall and civic center, surrounded by lawns. At the lower left of the picture, surmounted by a clock tower, is the post office. Notice the many trees. then lived in the northwestern part of Missouri. The completion of the Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad in 1859 made 

St. Joseph the most important city in northwestern Missouri. Trappers of the 

Northwest would send furs down the 

Missouri River as far as St. Joseph, where they would be transferred to the railroad cars for shipment to the eastern markets. 

Goods from the East could be sent by rail as far west as St. Joseph. Those intended for the Far West were loaded into wagons; those intended for the Northwest were transferred from the railroads to boats, which carried them up the Missouri River. 

You can see that all this transfer of goods made St. Joseph an important trade center for a large territory. 

St. Joseph is the third city in size in our state. It is surrounded by broad and rolling prairie lands especially suitable for farming. As farms developed in the northwestern part of the Glacial Plains, St. Joseph became the leading trade center. It soon became the shipping point for the surplus corn, wheat, and live stock produced by the farmers. It now has the largest stockyards lying entirely in our state, and it is the fifth largest livestock market in the United States. 

Meat packing is St. Joseph's leading industry. There are, however, more than four hundred factories in the city that manufacture more than a hundred different kinds of articles. In this city are the largest factories in the United States that produce writing tablets, ice-cream cones, alfalfa feed, winter-wheat flour, and pancake flour. Plants in St. Joseph also manufacture large quantities of candy, breakfast foods, clothing, shoes, bricks, and harnesses. 

Six excellent railroads serve St. Joseph. 

These roads are the Burlington, Santa Fe, Rock Island, Union Pacific, Missouri 

Pacific, and Great Western. Look at

the map, page 31, and see how easily you could ship goods from St. Joseph to 

Kansas City, St. Louis, Chillicothe, Hannibal, and Columbia. Can most of the cities and towns in the Glacial 

Plains be reached from St. Joseph? 

St. Joseph soon will also have barge service on the Missouri River. A barge is a large, flat boat that transports great quantities of goods to and from places on the water. It is cheaper to ship articles for long distances by barge than by railroad.

The highway map (page 32) shows you that St. Joseph is served by many hardsurfaced highways. Like other large cities, St. Joseph has a splendid airport and good air service. By air routes the city is within twelve hours of any point in the United States, southern Canada, or northern Mexico.

The largest city in the extreme northwestern part of the state is Maryville. It is surrounded by some of the best farm land in the world, and it is therefore chiefly a trade center for the rural population of the surrounding territory. The 

Northwest Missouri State Teachers Col lege is located at Maryville.

How the Old Plains Look. The great ice sheet did not extend as far south in our state as the region of the Old Plains. 

Therefore the streams and rivers are very old. For thousands of years these rivers have not been disturbed in their work of carving out broad valleys and wearing down the natural divides between their valleys. Now the region is quite smooth or only gently rolling. On the whole it is smoother than the region of the Glacial 

Plains. Do you know why? (Page 20.)

Plains are the Missouri River hills that soon give way to slightly rolling prairies.

Farming. -Some of the best improved farms in Missouri are in the region of the Old Plains. The surface of the region is so smooth that most of the land can be cultivated. Turn to the map on page 21 and find the kind of soil in the Old Plains.

The leading grain crop of the Old Plains is corn (26 A). Wheat is chiefly grown in the northern and southern parts of this region (A). 

Oats are grown throughout the Old Plains (B). Many of the farmers also have small fields of kafir corn, sorghum cane, or soy beans. 

For what are these three crops used? 

The leading hay crops are timothy and clover. There is also an abundance of wild hay, much of which is cut and cured for winter feed. Hay crops are especially important in the region because of the large number of dairy cows that must be fed. In recent years dairying has been increasing steadily, and today the Old Plains region is one of the leading dairy sections of our state. The dairy farms are most numerous around the three large cities of the region 

Kansas City, Springfield, and Joplin.

These cities, with their large populations, consume much of the dairy products. 

Many of the smaller cities and towns have cheese plants, condensed-milk plants, and creameries that use the milk and cream of their trade territory.

Nearly every farm in the Old Plains has some hogs (26 B), but there are more cattle than hogs in the region (maps A, B). 

The abundance of good pasture land, with the large amounts of hay and corn produced in this region, favor the cattle industry. 

Some of the best apple orchards in

Missouri are in the northwestern part of the Old Plains. The orchards planted in the deep fertile soil along the Missouri River are especially productive. The soil and mild climate of the southern part of this region are adapted to growing strawberries. Each year hundreds of carloads of strawberries are shipped to the St. Louis and Kansas City markets.

Lead and Zinc. The most important minerals mined in the Old Plains are lead and zinc. Lead was the first mineral discovered and mined in this region. In 

1848 lead ore was discovered near the present site of Joplin in Jasper County, and two years later a shaft was sunk and the actual mining of lead was begun. 

The mines caused thousands of people to settle in southwestern Missouri.

Some of these people worked in the mines, while others farmed the fertile lands in the southern part of the Old Plains. More lead mines were opened in Jasper County, and also in the near-by counties of 

Lawrence, Newton, and Greene (map, pages 16-17). For years these counties were the most important lead-producing sections of our state, but today the district ranks second. In 1871 zinc was first mined in Jasper County, and two years later a zinc smelter was built at Webb City. The zinc mines soon became even more important than the lead mines. 

The most important zinc mines of Missouri are in the Joplin district in the southern part of the Old Plains region.

State Chamber of Commerce ore. A jig is a series of boxes that operate with a jerking motion. The crushed ore is carried through the jig by running water. The mineral is heavier than the rock, and as the ore passes through the jig, the lead or zinc settles in the bottom of the jerking boxes while the rocks pass out with the water.

A. — A zinc mine. The elevator at the right carries the chat out to the huge piles after it has passed through the jig.

The zinc deposits in this district extend across the Missouri boundary into the southeastern corner of Kansas and the northeastern corner of Oklahoma. This zinc area, extending into three states, is called the Tri-State Mining 

District. It produces one fourth of the world's zinc.

As soon as the lead or zinc has been jigged, it is shipped to the smelter. There it is melted, poured into molds, and cooled into bars called pigs. The pigs of lead or zinc are then sold to factories. 

Coal. The Old Plains have large deposits of coal (map, page 28). Compare the extent of the coal deposits in this region with that of the Glacial Plains. The coal area of the Old Plains extends from the Missouri River southward along most of the western border of our state.

The leading coal-producing county in 

Missouri is Barton. During a recent year it produced more than one and a quarter million tons of coal. This was more than one third of the total amount of coal mined in our state. Bates, Henry, and Lafayette counties rank next in order in coal production. About two thirds of the coal mined in Missouri comes from the 

Old Plains region.

Many of the best equipped shaft mines in our state are in the Old Plains. Strip mining is frequently used in the Old 

Plains, especially in Barton and other leading coal-producing counties. ____ 

Other Minerals. Missouri is not an important gas and oil-producing region. 

There are, however, a few natural gas wells in the western part of the Old Plains (41 A). The largest tripoli mine in the world is in the extreme southwestern corner of the Old Plains. Tripoli varies from a porous to a hard rock-like material. It is used in the manufacture of polishing powders, dry-cleaning compounds, household cleaners, water filters, and many other articles in daily use. 

About three fourths of the marble quarried in Missouri comes from the southwestern part of the Old Plains.

Railroads and Highways. The Old 

Plains are not served so well with main railroad lines as are the Glacial Plains. 

If you study the railroad map (page 31) carefully you will see that two roads the Missouri Pacific and the Chicago and 

Alton -cross the northern part of the region. These two railroads connect that section of the Old Plains with the markets of Kansas City and St. Louis.

The central part of the Old Plains is served by the Missouri, Kansas, and 

Texas Railroad that runs from Boonville in a southwest direction through Sedalia, Clinton, and Nevada. Another branch of the Missouri Pacific runs north and south between Kansas City and Joplin. 

Now turn to the highway map (32 A).

After looking at this map you will realize that the people of the Old Plains are better served by highways than by railroads. There are two main highways running north and south. One is in the eastern part of the region, while the other is in the western part. In the northern part of the Old Plains there are three eastand-west roads that connect Kansas City and St. Louis. The southern portion is served by a splendid highway that connects the cities of Joplin, Springfield, and St. Louis. Many products are carried by trucks over this road to the St. Louis market.

Cities and Towns of the Old Plains. 

The region of the Old Plains has several important cities and interesting towns. 

If you could travel over the Old Plains and visit these centers, you would be able to learn much about them. Probably the best way to make such a trip would be in an automobile. Let us imagine that you are leaving Kansas City for a visit to the cities and towns in the Old Plains. 

From Kansas City you motor south along Highway 71, passing through Harrisonville, Butler, and Rich Hill. Point out these towns on the map. They are trade centers for prosperous farm communities. Eighteen miles south of Rich 

Hill you will find Nevada, surrounded by rich farming land. Dairying has been developed quite extensively around Nevada. Besides having a large retail trade territory, the city has developed a number of local industries. It is served by two railroads, the Missouri Pacific and the Missouri, Kansas, and Texas. The 

Missouri Pacific has machine shops in the city. Camp Clark, the home of the 

Missouri National Guard, is near Nevada, and every summer the National Guard encamps there for training.

Missouri Agricultural Experiment Station 

If you continue to travel down Highway 71, you will pass within a mile of

Lamar. A concrete road connects the town with the highway. Farther along the route you will come to Carthage. It is in the midst of a farming region that produces large amounts of wheat, oats, and corn. A great variety of hay is also grown near Carthage timothy, clover, alfalfa, wild hay, soy beans, and cow peas. The farmers in this district also give considerable attention to the growing of vegetables, berries, and many kinds of small fruits. Many carloads of strawberries are shipped from Carthage during a season (A). Some of the best dairy herds graze in the near-by pastures. 

Marble quarrying is the most important industry of Carthage, and about 2500 carloads of marble are shipped from the city each year. This marble has been used in some of the finest buildings in our country and in Canada. Marble from this neighborhood was used in building our state capitol at Jefferson City. 

Carthage has several smaller industries, the more important ones being flour milling, poultry packing, and chicken hatcheries.

A. - Cattle on a typical farm in Missouri. 

Creameries and plants that manufacture | zinc industry, but later they encouraged gun powder, clothing, and brooms are also located here. 

Carthage has excellent transportation facilities. Three divisions of the Missouri 

Pacific Railroad and the Frisco serve the city (map, 31 A). Two federal highways also cross here. These avenues of transportation give Carthage access to the markets of Kansas City, Springfield, and St. Louis. Each year the Ozark 

State Fair is held at Carthage. 

A short distance southwest of Carthage is Joplin. It is the trading and shipping center of a region made rich by the largest lead and zinc mines in the world. 

Joplin owes its origin and development to the mines, for it began as a small mining camp. For a number of years there were several such camps close together, but the various camps united later to form the city of Joplin. Today it is the fifth largest city in our state.

For some time the citizens of Joplin were mainly interested in the lead and other industries. Now there are flour mills, creameries, and factories making machines, clothing, candy, and cigars.

These new industries have added stability to the industrial life of Joplin. Poultry farming, dairying, stock-raising (A), and fruit growing are encouraged in the surrounding country, and Joplin is rapidly becoming a live-stock center. It is served by five railroads and several highways that give it easy access to all sections of our state and the important cities of our country.

The Ozark Playgrounds Association was organized by the people of Joplin. The purpose of this organization is to advertise the scenic beauty and recreational advantages and opportunities of the 

Ozark section of Missouri. The city has seven parks, noted for their natural beauty. 

If you drive east from Joplin on 

Highway 66, you reach Springfield, on the eastern border of the Old Plains.

A few miles east and south of Springfield you strike the edge of the Ozark

Plateau. Locate Springfield on the map, pages 16-17. It is the fourth largest city in our state.

Springfield grew very slowly until the railroads reached it about sixty years ago. 

The first railroad to reach Springfield was the Frisco (map, 31 A). With what large cities in our state does it connect 

Springfield? This railroad now has lines that connect Springfield with important cities in many of the other states of our country. The Frisco operates its main repair and car-building shops in Springfield. This furnishes the city with its largest industry, for the shops employ several thousand men. Branch lines of the Missouri Pacific also serve Springfield.

The city has a large overall factory and other factories producing more than a hundred different articles. It is the fifth industrial city of our state.

Springfield is situated in a productive farming region and therefore offers a splendid market for all farm products.

It has numerous poultry houses, meatpacking plants, flour mills, stockyards, and creameries. The city ranks fourth among the cities in the United States in the production of butter. It is the distributing center for manufactured articles over a large region. Since Springfield is the largest city within a radius of one hundred miles, many of the small towns near by send to it for their merchan dise. The Southwestern Missouri State 

Teachers College is located there. 

Leaving Springfield, you travel north on Highway 65 along the eastern border of the Old Plains until you reach Sedalia. 

It is served by two railroads that furnish its leading industry. Both railroads maintain shops and offices in the town and furnish employment to many people. 

Sedalia is a trade center with several small factories. It is a city of many beautiful homes. The Missouri State

Fair Grounds are near Sedalia. Every year in August a large fair is held that attracts people from all sections of our state. They come to see the interesting exhibits of live stock, crops, fruits, and vegetables. The horse races are also an interesting feature of the fair.

Northwest of Boonville are Marshall and Lexington. They are typical trade centers with several small industries, such as shoe and clothing factories, chicken hatcheries, creameries, and flour mills.

KANSAS CITY 

As you studied the regions of the Glacial Plains and the Old Plains you learned that Kansas City was an important marketing point for both. Its location in the bend of the Missouri River has favored its growth, and it is now the second largest city in our state.

Kansas City had a beginning similar to that of St. Joseph. More than a hundred years ago it was established as a furtrading post by traders from St. Louis, who bought the furs which were brought from the Northwest down the Missouri River and from the West down the 

Kansas River. Turn to the map on pages 86-87 and follow the Missouri 

River from Kansas City to its source. 

Now do the same thing with the Kansas 

River. You can see that these rivers and their tributaries furnished Kansas City a wide area for fur trading. After a few years the fur trade declined, but about that time Kansas City was becoming an important landing for steamboat traffic.

Later the city became the starting point for the many traders and travelers who journeyed over the Santa Fé Trail to

New Mexico. During this time the city was called Westport Landing. The completion of the railroads to the Pacific 

Ocean greatly aided the growth of Kansas 

City. Soon many railroads were being built from Kansas City to points in the 

West and Northwest, and the city was able to gain control over the trade of a wide area containing some of the best agricultural land in the world.

Population. -After the building of the railroads, Kansas City grew steadily (A), until it now has a population of almost 400,000. A large portion of the people are 

American-born, and Kansas City claims to be the most American city of its size in our country.

KANSAS CITY 

47 "Greater Kansas City" is composed of 

Kansas City and its suburbs, Kansas City in Kansas, North Kansas City, Independence, and the territory surrounding these centers of population. The number of people living in Greater Kansas City is over 600,000. Railroads. 

Kansas City is one of the largest railroad centers in the United 

States. The railroad map (page 259) shows that the railroads enter the city from many places in the eastern part of our country and that they depart for points in the Northwest, West, and 

Southwest. Sometimes Kansas City is called the "Gateway to the West." 

Fourteen main lines and thirty-two branch lines enter the city. Each day about 300 trains arrive in and leave 

Kansas City. Union Station is one of the largest passenger stations in America. 

Industries. - Kansas City is a leading meat-packing center. It is not only in the midst of the hog and cattle region of the United States, but it is easy to reach. by railroad or by trucks. Its stockyards are the largest in America outside 

Chicago. Each year nearly 10,000,000 animals pass through the stockyards. 

The city's live-stock exchange building is the largest in the world. 

Every year in November the American 

Royal Livestock Show is held in Kansas City. 

Those who attend the show see some of the best beef cattle, dairy cattle, hogs, sheep, horses, mules, ponies, and poultry that our country produces. 

Kansas City ranks high as a grain market. Since the city is the center of the greatest grain and live-stock area of the world, it is naturally a leading market for many kinds of food products. The city's industrial life has been greatly 

A. Cliff Drive, Kansas City. 

influenced by its agricultural environment. This fact is clearly shown in the type of products manufactured in the city. The leading factories produce flour, dairy products, leather goods, groceries, and bakery products. The city also manufactures numerous other articles, such as clothing, furniture, iron and steel products, and hardware. 

Homes and Parks. - Kansas City has many attractive homes and boulevards.

Cliff Drive (A), built in solid limestone bluffs along the Missouri River, is one of the prettiest drives in America. There are many parks and playgrounds, the largest one being Swope Park.

THE SOUTHEASTERN LOWLANDS 

The smallest region of Missouri is the 

Southeastern Lowlands. On the map on page 20 you will see that this region is in the extreme southeastern part of our state. It differs in many ways from the other regions.

Origin of the Southeastern Lowlands. 

The origin of the Southeastern Low lands is an interesting story. More than a hundred years ago one of the most severe earthquakes known in our country occurred in this region. The earth shook frequently for more than seven weeks. 

As the earth shook, there were long and terrific noises that sounded like thunder.

The ground rose and fell in great waves like the billows on an ocean; and often the crust of the earth broke and large amounts of sand and water shot into the air, sometimes to a height of forty feet.

In some places, the earth opened and swallowed houses, trees, and animals.

This great disturbance caused the region to sink many feet, and now it is low, level, and swampy. It is only 280 feet above sea level.

Extent and Surface Features of the Southeastern Lowlands. The South eastern Lowlands are bordered on the east by the Mississippi River and on the north by the Ozark Plateau. The Ozark 

Plateau forms the western boundary and the state of Arkansas forms the southern boundary. Look at the map and see if you can tell why the region is sometimes called the " Missouri Panhandle." 

The Southeastern Lowlands were the first part of our state to be visited by white men. 

When the early French and

Spanish explorers visited the region they found it a land of giant trees, dense brush, and swamps. They thought it very strange and interesting, and they did not dream that one day the swampy wilderness would develop into one of the best farming regions in the world. 

As you travel across the Lowlands in any direction you will find the surface almost as level as a floor. The level surface is occasionally broken by very low and narrow ridges. 

Drainage. The Southeastern Low lands slope very gradually from the north to the south. Because the slope is so small, the natural drainage of the region is extremely poor. The land is so flat that water stands upon much of it throughout the year. The Mississippi

River flows along the eastern side of the region, but only a few shallow, sluggish streams enter it from the Lowlands. The slope of the country is so gentle that the streams cannot flow rapidly enough to cut deep channels that would carry the water off to the Mississippi. The largest and most important of the shallow tributaries of the Mississippi is the Little River.

On the western side of the Lowlands is the St. Francis River, which is also very shallow, and of little help in draining the region. On the map (page 22) trace the 

St. Francis River. You can see that it has very few tributaries from the Southeastern Lowlands. 

The poor drainage of the Southeastern

Lowlands region has been its greatest disadvantage. The first problems that faced early settlers was the draining of the water from their land and finding ways to keep it off. They tried to solve this problem by building levees along the banks of the Mississippi. A levee is a large dam built out of dirt, rocks, or

THE SOUTHEASTERN LOWLANDS 

49 concrete along the banks of a river to keep it from overflowing the land. These levees greatly helped the farmers, but they did not solve all their difficulties.

ago. - A dredge boat in operation. The steam shovel scoops up mud from the bottom of the river to deepen the channel. 

The next problem was finding a way to drain the water from the swamps.

Large drainage canals were dug (A) to carry the water off to lakes in Arkansas or to the Mississippi River.

The first of the canals was made about thirty years Some of them are large enough to float a small steamboat, but most of them are smaller. 

If you should travel over the Southeastern 

Lowlands, you would cross a drainage ditch about every mile. This artificial drainage system consists of over 3000 miles of ditches that drain 2,000,000 acres of the richest soil in our state. This great drainage project was completed without aid from either the federal or state government.

These large forests remained untouched for many years after the rest of our state was well settled. In fact, the trees were not cut in large numbers until after the drainage canals were dug. In recent years, however, men have been rapidly clearing away the forests and planting the ground to crops. It will not be long until all the great cypress forests of the Lowlands are entirely gone. After the trees suitable for making lumber have been cut, the smaller trees and bushes are cleared from the land so that the rich alluvial soil can be used for farming.

Forests. -The early explorers of the 

Southeastern Lowlands found dense forests of big trees. Cypress, elm, hickory, oak, ash, gumwood, sycamore, and cottonwood trees were growing in these forests. Some of the cypress trees were engaged in mixed farming. The rich alluvial soil is the most fertile and productive in our state, and it will produce almost all kinds of crops. The growing season is long. In traveling through the region, you see many well-improved farms where once dense forests and swamps were found.

A. A field of young corn. 

H. Armstrong Roberts

Corn is the leading grain crop in the 

Southeastern Lowlands (A). Map A on page 26 shows that this region is one of the important corn-producing sections of Missouri. After the threshing season, farmers often break up the wheat fields and plant them to corn. Earlier planting of corn will produce from seventyfive to one hundred bushels an acre. 

This is an unusually large yield. 

The wheat crop is about one third the size of the corn crop, and most of it is raised in the northeastern part of the region (map A, page 39). Some millers think that the best winter wheat (51 A) grown in our country comes from the Lowlands. In this section the wheat grows unusually tall, often as high as six feet. 

In recent years the wheat acreage has been reduced, because of an increased cotton acreage.

Most of the cotton produced in our state is grown in the counties that make up the Southeastern Lowlands region. They yield two and a half times as much cotton per acre as any other part of the United States. The quality of the cotton is excellent, and the crop is worth millions of dollars yearly. 

Have you ever been in a cotton field?

The cotton is planted and cultivated with about the same machinery that a farmer uses in growing corn. When the cotton is ripe, the fiber is picked from the cotton pod by hand. During the picking season, one can hear the hum of hundreds of cotton gins throughout the Lowlands, where a few years ago one could have heard the ring of the woodsman's ax and the hum of the sawmills as the forests were being cleared from the land.

Rye is a leading crop in the extreme northeastern part of the Lowlands.

Scott County frequently produces nearly one half of the rye grown in our state. 

About three fourths of all the sunflower seeds grown in our country come from the 

Southeastern Lowlands. The very rich soil of the region is adapted to the growth of sunflowers. The seeds are sold to manufacturers of poultry feeds.

Every year many hundred carloads of melons, watermelons, and cantaloupes are shipped from the Lowlands to the leading city markets of our country. One grower will sometimes ship as many as fifteen carloads. A large portion of the melons are grown in Scott and Dunklin counties.

The growing of alfalfa is increasing in importance. The Lowland farmers can

THE SOUTHEASTERN LOWLANDS 

51 make as many as five cuttings of alfalfa during a season. Clover, soy beans, and cow peas are also grown as forage crops. 

The Southeastern Lowlands are not important as a live-stock section. A few hogs and some cattle, however, are found on most of the farms, and dairying has been given some attention in the northern part of the region. Large numbers of mules are raised in the Lowlands, to be used in cultivating the cotton fields.

Transportation.-On the map, page 31, you will see a network of railroads in the 

Southeastern Lowlands. These numerous lines furnish better transportation service than can be found in any other region of our state. Three of the railroads are the Missouri Pacific, the Cotton 

Belt, and the Frisco.

Many of the roads were formerly used for hauling lumber out of the forests. 

Certain railroad companies realized that the region was developing into an important agricultural section that would demand much transportation. These companies eagerly bought the old roadbeds that had been built by the lumbermen and made them a part of their road system.

The construction of highways in the 

Lowlands is neither easy nor cheap.

Almost all the building material has to be shipped into the region, since nature did not lay even a stone or a pebble in many parts of this area. During the period of cutting the forests and digging the drainage ditches, the roads were about as MO - -4

Most of the roads are concrete. Some of the main roads run north and south, while others cross the land from east to west (32 A). 

Cape Girardeau. Cape Girardeau is not in the Southeastern Lowlands, but it is the leading trade center of the region. 

For this reason you will study it now. 

It is built on the Mississippi River banks a little above the northern boundary of the Lowlands. Nearly one hundred and fifty years ago Cape Girardeau was established as a fur-trading post by a small band of Frenchmen, and it is therefore one of the oldest centers in Missouri.

The city is in a section of our state where three important crops cotton, corn, and wheat-grow side by side and produce unusually large yields. 

Cape Girardeau is the most important industrial city in the southeastern part of 

Missouri. Its leading factories make shoes, cement, tobacco products, and bricks. There are excellent transportation facilities for marketing these products. It is served by two railroads and several highways, and by barges and packets on the Mississippi River (A). 

Cities of the Southeastern Lowlands Region. South of Cape Girardeau is 

Sikeston, a busy trade center. Sikeston is in the heart of a wheat-growing district and its leading industry is the milling of flour. The mills produce flour that is shipped as far east as New York and as far south as New Orleans. Some of it is even shipped to foreign countries.

THE OZARK PLATEAU State Chamber of Commerce 

A scene along the beautiful Gasconade River.

Surface and Drainage. The Ozark 

Plateau is the most rugged region in our state, and it has many narrow valleys (A), small tablelands, rolling prairies, and high hills. The borderland has been so deeply cut by swift-flowing rivers that it has a mountainous appearance. 

The Ozark Plateau that you are now to study is the largest natural region of our state. The Ozark Plateau is a part of a highland region that extends into parts of three states Missouri, Oklahoma, and Arkansas (map, page 10). The map on page 20 shows you just what part of our state lies in this region. 

Extent of the Ozark Plateau. On the north the Ozark Plateau extends a little beyond the Missouri River. On the east, the region extends to the Mississippi River; on the southeast it ends abruptly in high bluffs that separate it from the Lowlands. The east central part, known as the St. Francois Mountains, will be studied later as a separate region. On the south, the Plateau extends across the boundary of Missouri into Arkansas. 

On the west the surface of the region gradually becomes more gentle until it meets the Old Plains region. 

The Plateau resembles an immense saucer that has been turned upside down. 

The center or crest of the region extends from Wright County to the east into Texas County, then to the northeast to the eastern border of Washington County. 

Find the crest or high part of the Plateau (22 A), and notice that the streams flow in all directions from the crest. Three important rivers flow north, two of them into the Missouri River and one into the 

Mississippi River. The largest and most important of the rivers flowing north is the Osage. You have already learned that the Osage River rises in Kansas, but it has many tributaries that rise along the crest of the Plateau.

A. 

Bagnell Dam and a portion of the Lake of the Ozarks. The dam is 2543 feet long. There are six huge generators in the power plant. 

The Gasconade River rises in the high | White River enters our state from Arkanpart of the Ozark Plateau and flows in a northeasterly direction until it reaches the Missouri. The Gasconade is famous for the beautiful scenery along its course, its clear, sparkling waters flowing swiftly through a narrow valley walled in by high limestone bluffs.

The Meramec is the only river of importance in Missouri that flows into the Mississippi south of St. Louis. On the map, page 22, follow the Meramec from its mouth to its source. It flows through a very rough part of our state and so there are many rapids in its channel.

The Meramec River could furnish enough power to generate all the electricity used in St. Louis.

The two important rivers of the Plateau that flow south are the White and the St. Francis. On the map find where the sas. Notice that it makes a big bend in the southern part of the Ozark Plateau before it again turns back into Arkansas.
