The St. Francis River flows through the eastern part of the Plateau (22 A). 

You will notice that the St. Francis has no important tributaries. 

Lakes. The largest man-made lake in America is in the Ozark Plateau. It is called The Lake of the Ozarks. This lake was made by building Bagnell Dam (A) across the Osage River. The dam is made of steel and concrete, and it is nearly 150 feet high. It was built at a cost of over thirty million dollars, and completed in 1931.

The Lake of the Ozarks has an irregular shore line of over 1300 miles. The shore line is so irregular that the lake has the appearance of a huge Chinese dragon.

Along the banks are craggy bluffs, rough wooded hills, and many attractive bays and peninsulas. The lake is about 125 miles long and from one to five miles wide, its waters extending into six counties Miller, Morgan, Camden, 

Benton, Henry, and St. Clair.

In making the Lake of the Ozarks many farms and homes in the valley were destroyed. Beautiful scenery loved by the inhabitants of the region was covered up forever by the water. But the lake was made to store an immense quantity of water to be used in furnishing power to the lead mines in St. Francois County. 

It also furnishes electric power for the city of St. Louis. From that city it is distributed to many parts of the Mississippi Valley. Now the lake is rapidly becoming a recreation center too. 

The second largest artificial lake in our state is Lake Taneycomo, which was made by the construction of a large dam across the White River near Branson.

These stored-up waters are also used to develop electricity. Lake Taneycomo is 

25 miles long, with about 200 miles of shore line. How much less shore line does it have than the Lake of the Ozarks? 

Lake Taneycomo also attracts many people to its shore for their vacation. 

Springs. - Missouri is famous for its large springs. There are about ten thousand springs in the Ozark Plateau region, and an enormous amount of cool, clear, sparkling water flows from them daily.

When it rains, all the water does not run off the surface to the streams and rivers. 

Much of it sinks into the ground and flows A. 

State Chamber of Commerce A scene in Big Spring State Park. 

through the holes of the porous limestone rock of the region. Because the Ozark region is so broken, the edges of the rocks often come to the surface in the side of a valley, and water flows out to form a spring. If the spring is a very large one, it may flow from an underground channel that it has cut out in the limestone far beneath the surface. Spring water is cool and sparkling because it has been filtered of its impurities on its journey through the rocks. If on its underground journey it has passed through mineral deposits and dissolved some of the minerals, it is called a mineral spring. 

Big Spring (A) in Carter County (map, page 22) is the largest spring in our state and the second largest one in North 

America. It discharges over 600 million gallons of water every twenty-four hours.

A. The entrance to Marvel Cave. 

It has as great a flow as a small river, or more than enough to furnish St. Louis with its daily water supply. The spring flows from the foot of a high bluff, and is about 100 feet wide. 

Greer Spring, in Oregon County (map, page 22), is considered the second largest spring in our state. The gorge through which Greer Spring flows is three fourths of a mile long and it is cut out of limestone rock. Many people think that 

Greer Spring is the most beautiful of the

Ozark springs. 

Caves. - Because the Ozark Plateau is a region of much rainfall and soft limestone rock, it has an unusually large number of caves. The water will follow cracks down into the soft limestone, and then gradually dissolve the rock until a great hole called a cave is formed. Most of the caves in our state are in the Ozark 

Plateau. Every year new caverns are discovered and the older ones are more fully explored.

The largest cave in the region, and probably the largest in the world, is 

Marvel Cave in Stone County, about two miles northwest of Branson. The cave has never been completely explored, but it has been explored for a distance of ten miles from its entrance. Many large rooms and narrow, winding halls have been found deep under the ground. The largest room is 700 feet long, 350 feet wide, and 175 feet high.

Instead of having a door-like entrance in the side of a hill, as most caves have, Marvel Cave is entered from a small hole in the ground (A) that resembles a sink hole. A winding path underground leads to the floor of the cave 225 feet below.

Among the many interesting things to see in the cave is the large stalagmite in the throne room. A stalagmite is a rocklike formation made by the deposit of minerals from water that drips down to the floor of a cave. When the water drips through the roof of a cave and clings there, it forms stalactites. They look like huge icicles. Thousands of years are required to form a large stalagmite or stalactite. 

There are several rivers in Marvel

Cave, but their sources and their mouths have never been discovered. One is ten feet deep and twenty feet wide. Salamanders and white rats may be seen in the cave. A salamander is a small land-andwater animal that resembles a lizard.

A. -Pure-bred short-horn cattle on a Missouri stock farm. 

There are long, white crayfish in the rivers, and thousands of bats scurry about the large rooms in the winter months.

Mixed Farming. There is much unimproved wild land in the hills along the 

Gasconade, Osage, and White rivers. It is also found in the eastern portion of the Ozark Plateau, where the whole region is a maze of hills and valleys. This wild land has never been cultivated. 

More corn, wheat, and oats are grown in the borderlands of the Plateau than along its crest. But more rye is grown on the crest. Corn is grown chiefly in the valleys. Most of the wheat is grown on the fairly level land southwest of Springfield, and in the eastern counties along the Mississippi River. 

In the southern part of the Ozark

Plateau cotton and tobacco are important crops. Throughout the region, forage crops are important.

Dairying and Poultry Farming. - Map 

B on page 40 shows you that there are many dairy cows in the Ozark Plateau.

Some of these cows are kept on the farms to furnish milk and butter for home consumption, but there are many farms which specialize in dairying. Much of the land that is unfit for mixed farming is adapted to profitable dairy farming. 

The lands that are too hilly to plow are usually covered with thick green grass. 

Then there are many cool clear streams to furnish water for the cows. Most of the dairy products are shipped to the markets. in Springfield and St. Louis. In addition to these large city markets there are many cheese plants, milk-condensing factories, and creameries.

Poultry farming is important in the Ozark Plateau and it is one of the leading money-making farm industries. The eastern counties lead in poultry production because of their nearness to the 

St. Louis markets. 

The 

Fruit Growing and Gardening.

Ozark Plateau is the leading region of our state in producing fruit. Its importance in fruit growing is due to two factors: (1) the soil is excellent for the growing of fruit; (2) the climate is fairly mild and therefore better adapted to fruit production than the cooler parts of Missouri. 

Then, too, the Ozark Plateau region has access to good markets, for the fruit can easily be shipped to Kansas City or St. 

Louis, where the demand for fruit and vegetables is large.

Thousands of apple trees have been planted on the hillsides and in the valleys of the Plateau (A). It takes much work to keep the apple orchards sprayed and pruned so that they will produce fruit of good quality. In the fall the apples are picked and taken to long packing sheds, where they are graded into sizes and packed. Then the fruit is shipped to the markets in many parts of our country. 

The southeastern section of the Ozark Plateau is the peach-growing center. The

peaches ripen shortly after the Georgia | northeastern part of the Ozark Plateau peach crop is gone and before the more northerly peaches are ripe. The Missouri peach is of excellent quality and highly colored. The peach industry of the

Ozark region centers around Koshkonong, in Oregon County.

In the southwestern section of the 

Plateau you find the largest strawberry region of the world, centering around the towns of Monett and Neosho. 

Buyers from all parts of our country come to Monett during the strawberry season to buy for the northern and eastern markets. After the berries are picked they are taken to long sheds in the fields, where they are graded and packed for the market. They are then shipped in refrigerator cars or trucks to the leading markets of the United States. Each year from 20 million to 25 million quarts of berries are shipped from this region. 

When the strawberries are gone, other berries begin ripening. Blackberries, currants, gooseberries, and raspberries are produced, but on a much smaller scale than strawberries. Recently the Plateau has been growing in importance as a grapegrowing region. Taney and Gasconade are the leading grape-growing counties.

The fruit crops furnish employment to thousands of men, women, and children throughout the year and the orchard owners often make large sums of money in a good fruit year. The income from fruit in our state is about the same each year as that from oats or wheat. Corn, however, brings the Missouri farmer more money than the orchards.

Many acres of tomatoes are grown in the Ozark Plateau. The farmer sells the tomatoes to the canning factories which are scattered throughout the region. The is an important vegetable-growing district, and many truck gardens produce large quantities of spinach, beans, cabbage, cucumbers, and potatoes. Most of the vegetables are shipped to the markets in 

St. Louis.

Minerals. By studying the map on page 41 you will see that there are many kinds of minerals in the Ozark Plateau. 

Iron ore is scattered throughout the region, but little commercial use is made of it because the iron is more difficult to extract than that found in some other places. In the north-central part of the 

Plateau there are deposits of lead, although little use is made of them now. 

In the northeast section of the region are large deposits of glass-sand which is used in the factories of St. Louis to make bottles and heavy plate glass. The glasssand industry centers at Crystal City.

Other minerals in the Ozark Plateau are clay, kaolin, zinc, lime, and stone. Point out the places in this region (map, page 

41) where each of these minerals is found.

Forests. The most extensive forest lands in our state are in the Ozark Plateau region, where they are located in the valleys of the streams and the rough upland sections. On the smoother uplands there are fewer trees. In 

In the southeastern part of the Plateau large pine forests once grew, but most of the large pines have been cut. 

Much of the timber in the Ozark Plateau is made up of white, black, and red oak, and many scrub oaks may be found on the ridges. Along the border, in addition to the various kinds of oak, there are walnut, linden, sugar-maple, hickory, and elm trees, and dense undergrowths of shrubs. Cedars grow along the river bluffs. They are especially numerous along the White and Osage rivers. Much of the timber in the region is used for making railroad ties, although some of it is sawed into lumber.

Two main railroads serve the eastern borders: a branch line of the Frisco following the Mississippi River and another running in the same direction but several miles west of the Frisco. Along the southern border is a branch road of the 

Missouri Pacific, running from Springfield to Memphis, Tennessee. A number of roads that connect Springfield and 

Kansas City run through the western border. 

Only one railroad, the Frisco, crosses the central part of the Plateau, following the Ozark Ridge from St. Louis to Springfield. Many places in the Ozarks are several miles from a railroad. 

The Ozark Plateau has an excellent system of highways (map, page 32). The concrete road that follows the ridge of the Plateau from St. Louis to Springfield is one of the most traveled in our state. 

The construction of good highways has meant the building of many new bridges. 

Bridges over the smaller streams are of concrete, while those crossing the larger streams are usually made of steel.

The most important cities of the 

Ozark Plateau are in its borderlands.

The largest city on the western border is 

Springfield, which you read about in your study of the Old Plains (pages 44-45).

On the eastern border is Cape Girardeau, which you studied in connection with the

Poplar Bluff, built on the banks of the Black River, is in the extreme.southeastern corner of the Ozark Plateau.

A. Jefferson City, as seen from the Missouri River.

On the large map of the United States, pages 82-83, follow the Black River from its mouth to its source. Poplar Bluff is the trade center for the river valley country of the Black and St. Francis rivers, and its business life centers around retail trade. Many of the farmers in the surrounding country are engaged in dairying and poultry raising. Poplar Bluff is therefore a market for dairy and poultry products. The city's leading industries are a shoe factory, several woodworking factories, and the machine shops of the

Missouri Pacific Railroad. Poplar Bluff has good railroad and highway connections.

Jefferson City was laid out in 1822, and four years later became the capital of Missouri. It is the place where the legislature assembles to make the state laws by which we are governed and where the governor and other state officers live.

The State Supreme Court sessions are held here.

The city is built on picturesque bluffs overlooking the Missouri River (A). The most interesting place in the city is the magnificent state capitol building (15 A), which was completed in 1918. As you know, the interior of the building was built out of Missouri marble quarried at Carthage. 

State Chamber of Commerce

Jefferson City is near the center of our state (map, pages 16-17). This is a desirable feature in a state capital, as it can easily be reached from all sections of the state. The city has good railroad and highway service. Three federal highways intersect there. The most important manufactures of Jefferson City are clothing, shoes, and bricks. The repair shops of the Missouri Pacific Railroad are located there.

Other Cities in the Ozark Plateau 

Region. -On the southwestern border of the Ozark Plateau is Neosho, a city of beautiful streets and well-kept homes. 

It is famous as a marketing center for fruit and berries, and for the federal fish hatchery that is located there.

East of Neosho is Monett, situated on the edge of a rich and productive tableland of the plateau. It is in the midst of a farming region that devotes special attention to dairying, poultry raising, and fruit growing. Monett is often called the strawberry capital of our state, for each year hundreds of carloads of strawberries are shipped out of the city in special cars or trains. It is the headquarters of the 

Ozark Fruit Growers Association. The purpose of this progressive association is to assist the fruit growers in marketing their fruit.

Near the center of the crest of the Ozark 

Plateau is Mountain Grove, the home of the Missouri State Poultry Experiment 

Station and the Missouri State Fruit

Experiment Station. These experiment stations try to improve methods of raising poultry and growing fruit.

In the central part of the southern borderland of the plateau is Westplains, a tomato-canning center. It has six 

It has six large canning factories, and several small ones. The peach industry of the region centers around Westplains and Koshkonong, which is near by. 

In the central part of the Ozark Plateau is Rolla, where the Missouri School of Mines is located. The school is a branch of the University of Missouri. Northeast Northeast of Rolla, in Franklin County, is Washington, a small town famous for its cob-pipe industry. The farmers near Washington grow a special variety of corn with cobs large enough for making pipe bowls.

THE ST. FRANCOIS MOUNTAINS 

The St. Francois Mountains region is in the east-central part of the Ozark Plateau (map, page 20). Now turn to the map on pages 16-17 and find the counties lying wholly or partly within the region. 

How the St. Francois Mountains 

Region Looks. The region of the St. 

Francois Mountains is an interesting and beautiful part of our state. It is the roughest section in Missouri and is made up of hills, mountain peaks, and deep valleys. Most of the mountain peaks are less than 1700 feet high. The highest point in our state, Tom Sauk Mountain (63 A), 1800 feet above sea level, is in this region. Other high peaks are Wolf and 

Buzzard mountains. Among the hills and mountains are many pretty valleys, some of which are from 500 to 700 feet below the mountain ridges. Most of the valleys have steep, rocky sides, and in some sections great areas of the surface are almost covered with solid rock.

Mining. -The St. Francois Moun tains are the oldest and most important mining district in our state. More than one third of the population depend upon mining for a living. What minerals are found in this region? (Map, page 41.)

Probably the first white men that settled in our state made their living by mining lead. The earliest known lead mines in Missouri were operated in the 

St. Francois Mountains by the French more than two hundred years ago. One of the first mines was Mine La Motte, which continued to produce lead until recently. Today the region produces one third of the lead mined in the United

States and one sixth of the world's supply. 

Its yearly value is frequently one fourth of the total value of all minerals mined in our state. 

You have already learned that some iron ore is found in almost every county in the Ozark Plateau. The most important iron-ore deposits in the state are in the St. Francois Mountains. Iron was discovered in Missouri as early as lead, but it was not mined until nearly a hundred years later. The earliest iron mines in this region were near Ironton, but later mines were opened at Iron Mountain. 

The deposits in Iron Mountain were the largest that had been found in our state and the veins of ore were almost pure iron. The top of the mountain was taken off and the iron ore dug from its center. Some of the veins were over twenty-five feet thick, and part of them. extended down as far as 280 feet into the earth. The mine was an interesting place to visit, for one could stand on the edge of the great pit and watch the miners dig many feet down in the earth.

Farming. Most of the land in the St.

Francois Mountains is not suitable for cultivation. The few farms in the region are in the small valleys, which range from a few acres in size to thirty or forty square miles. About half of the farm land is used for pasture land, where stock cattle are grazed. The cattle are allowed to graze during the summer and in the fall they are sold to winter feeders in the corn-growing districts, who fatten them for the market. 

The leading grain crops are corn and wheat. In recent years there has been an increased interest shown in dairying and poultry raising, but most of the 

farm products are used by the people living in the immediate neighborhood.

ST. LOUIS 

You have already learned that St.

Louis was founded by the French as a furtrading post (page 18). On a cold February afternoon in 1764 Auguste Chouteau and his band of thirty men landed on the site of the future great city of St. Louis.

The next day the men were busy building log huts to shelter themselves from the cold weather. Soon after the first huts were built, Pierre Laclede came to the young trading post. Under his direction the village was laid out, and within a few years St. Louis became the leading furtrading post in the upper Mississippi Valley. It soon became the leading fur market in the West, and a little later it became the leading fur market of the world. From this small beginning, St. 

Louis has grown to be the largest city in the Mississippi River basin. is largely American-born. There are, nevertheless, many people living there who were born in countries in Europe. 

About one third of the foreign-born are from Germany, while those born in

Russia and Italy tie for second place. 

There are a number from Ireland, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Scotland, and England.

Trade. St. Louis is the center of a large trade area, for there are nearly 5 million people living within a radius of 150 miles of the city. This trade is of two kinds: wholesale and retail. A wholesale house is a business establishment that sells products only to retail stores. A retail store sells products directly to the people who use them. 

St. Louis is one of the largest wholesale centers in the United States. Many of the retail merchants of the small towns and cities near by get their goods from its wholesale houses. St. Louis is often said to be the most accessible of all American cities. Let us find out why the city is so easily reached from all points.

This excellent network of transportation that centers in the city is a great aid to both the city itself and its surrounding rural sections. 

The farmer can ship his stock and grain to the city, and in return receive products that St. Louis manufactures and sells. 

There are few places in our country that cannot easily be reached from St. Louis.

Many of the larger cities may be reached by traveling over night in a comfortable sleeping car. Nineteen trunkline railroads serve the city, carrying many passengers and much freight. 

Every day about 30,000 travelers pass through the great Union Passenger Station.

St. Louis is also at the center of a great inland waterway system that our country is developing in the Mississippi Valley. 

When the system is completed, it will give St. Louis a river connection with many of the other leading cities in the central part of the United States. The business houses can ship their products by water up the Mississippi as far as Minneapolis in Minnesota and down the river as far as

Manufacturing. The manufacturing industries of any city depend upon the following factors: (1) raw materials, such as products from the farms, mines, and forests, (2) laborers to work in the many St. Louis is fortunate in having all the factors that combine to make a great industrial city. The Mississippi Valley, the greatest farming region in the world, sends much of its grain, live stock, and dairy and poultry products to this center. 

It thus furnishes the city with a large amount of raw materials.

The Mississippi Valley also has large supplies of coal and oil that furnish power used in operating the factory machines.

Much of the electricity used in the industrial plants of St. Louis is generated in the power plant at Keokuk Dam in 

Iowa. You have already learned about the large mineral supplies near by, and you have just finished reading about the city's excellent transportation facilities that carry its manufactured products to all parts of the country. You also know

that millions of people live within the trade area of St. Louis and furnish a market for its factory products. These natural advantages have made St. Louis the largest manufacturing center of our state and one of the largest cities in the 

United States. 

There are nearly three hundred different industries in St. Louis. Almost everything that is generally used by most people is made there. The various factories produce articles valued at more than a billion dollars each year. 

The leading manufacturing industry is the making of iron and steel products. 

It includes the manufacture of stoves, furnaces, mill machinery, street cars, hardware, automobiles, railroad cars, airplanes, and electrical equipment. 

The second most important industry in St. Louis is the making of clothing. 

This includes suits, coats, shoes, boots, dresses, hats, fur coats, and neck pieces.

More shoes are made in St. Louis than in any other city in the Mississippi Valley.

The preparation of foods is also an important industry in St. Louis. This industry includes meat packing, the milling of flour, bakery products, and the manufacture of candies. Among the numerous other articles made in St. Louis are paints, glass bottles, furniture, drugs, stock and poultry feeds, and bricks.

THE STATE AS A WHOLE 

Thus far you have studied the various natural regions of our state and you have learned many interesting things about each of the different parts of the state in which you live. Now, you will no doubt be interested in making a study of our state as a whole.

Climate. - What is weather? What is climate? When you talk about the weather you have in mind the wind, temperature, or rainfall over a short period of time. Climate is the average wind condition, temperature, and rainfall over a long period of time.

There are many kinds of climate in the world. Some places near the Equator have a hot climate. Others, for instance those along the Gulf Coast of our country, enjoy a warm climate. Perhaps you have gone to the Rocky Mountains in the summer to enjoy the cool mountain climate. The land where the Lapps live has a cold climate most of the year. can see that, from the standpoint of temperature, climate can be classified as hot, warm, cool, or cold. From the standpoint of rainfall climate may be dry or rainy. You 

Before you can know the kind of climate Missouri has, you will first have to learn something about the temperature and rainfall of the state. Temperature and rainfall are the most important factors that determine the climate of any place. Missouri is about halfway between the North Pole and the Equator, and our climate is neither extremely cold nor extremely hot. But the temperature varies greatly between summer and winter. Missouri has a rather hot summer climate. The average July temperature

The length of the growing season determines the kinds of crops that can be raised in various parts of our state. 

The length of the growing season in Missouri differs in the different parts of the state (B). In most of the northern part, the average date of the last killing frost is April 22, while the average date of the first fall frost is October 12. This gives the northern part of our state a growing season of 172 days. In the central and much of the southern part of Missouri the average date of the last killing first killing frost in the fall is October 18.

This gives those parts of the state a growing season of 188 days.

Occupations. One of the most important problems you have tried to solve in a study of the natural regions of Missouri is how Missourians make a living.

You have already learned about the kinds of occupations that people follow. Now you will be interested in studying those occupations, in order to see how the geographic environment of our state has aided them. 

Mixed Farming. More people earn their living by farming than by any other method in our state. The most important crops which they raise are corn, hay, oats, wheat, and cotton. Corn is the chief crop, and it is grown in every county of our state. Study map A, page 26, and find what sections of Missouri lead in corn production. Most of the corn is fed to hogs and cattle on the farms where it is grown.

Hay ranks next to corn in value, and every county produces some of this important crop. Most of the hay grown in 

Missouri is alfalfa, timothy, and clover. 

The leading small-grain crops are oats and wheat. Oats are largely grown in the regions of the Glacial Plains and Old 

Plains (39 B). Wheat is chiefly grown in the river valleys, where the land is level and fertile (39 A). Some barley is produced in the northeastern counties. state ranks first in the production of Our 2. The cotton produced in our state is of a very high quality. It is chiefly grown in the eight counties of the Southeastern 

Lowlands. Practically every farmer in

Missouri grows a crop of potatoes for his family's use, and some raise larger fields of potatoes for sale.

Gardening and Fruit Raising. -There are many small vegetable farms or truck farms near the large cities of our state, where lettuce, radishes, onions, spinach, cabbage, cucumbers, beans, tomatoes, peas, and rhubarb are grown. Some of the best vegetable farms are in the valley bottoms of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers. Nearly all the farmers and many people living in small towns cultivate a garden for home use. 

The southwestern corner of our state is one of the important strawberry districts of our country. Each year many million quarts of berries are shipped from Missouri to all parts of the United 

States and Canada.

Apple orchards are found in all parts of our state, but most of the large commercial orchards are along the Missouri River. The deep soil near the river is especially fine for apple orchards. In recent years many apple orchards have been set out in the southwestern part of the Ozark Plateau, where the soil, climate, and long growing season are ideal for fruit growing.

There are large peach orchards in southcentral Missouri, centering around Koshkonong in Oregon County. The peaches ripen shortly after the Georgia peach crop is gone and before the Michigan peaches are ripe enough for market. Most of the orchards are planted on the upper slopes of valleys, where they are not so likely to be injured by late frosts. 

Cherries, plums, pears, grapes, blackberries, and raspberries grow in nearly all parts of our state. There are many grape vineyards in the Ozark Plateau, particularly in Gasconade County. Cherries are chiefly grown north of the Missouri River. Watermelons grow in all parts of the state. Because of its rich alluvial soil and long growing season, southeastern Missouri is one of the leading melon districts of our country. 

Stock Raising, Dairying, and Poultry 

Farming. Missouri is one of the leading live-stock states and there are more hogs than any other kind of live stock. Since the hogs are fattened for market on corn, the greatest numbers of hogs are usually found in the leading corn-producing counties. In numbers, cattle rank next to hogs and they are fairly evenly distributed over the state. Most of the sheep are in the counties north of the 

Missouri River. The Ozark Plateau is perhaps best suited to sheep raising (75 A) because of its rolling grassy uplands and abundant water supply. Missouri has more horses than mules, but the state is famous for its mules. They are used for heavy farm work.

During recent years interest in dairying has been increasing steadily in every part of Missouri. It is especially profitable near large cities, where there is a market for butter, milk, and cheese. Many small towns have creameries and cheese plants that use the dairy products of the surrounding country. In some parts of the state there are also milk condenseries and milk-powder factories. Dairy farms are most numerous in the Old Plains, where there are excellent grasslands for pasture and near-by marketing centers. 

Greene County is the leading dairying county in our state.

Missouri now ranks high as a leading state in poultry raising. Nearly all the farmers keep some poultry, and many have flocks of several hundred hens.

Almost every town has poultry houses that buy poultry and eggs for the market.

A. 

- Sheep pasturing on the uplands.

Many towns have one or more hatcheries that sell hundreds of day-old baby chicks that are hatched in enormous incubators. 

The leading poultry-raising counties are those where a large amount of grain is grown and those near large centers of population.

Lumbering. When white men first came to our state, they found about two 

Much thirds of it covered with forests. of the timber was large and valuable, and lumbering became an important industry. 

Today only about one twelfth of the state is in forests. Most of the present timber is in the Ozark Plateau, and in the 

Southeastern Lowlands. At the present rate of consumption, the forests of Missouri would last us only about 8 years if we did not import any lumber into the state. Most of the timber that is cut is used for making lumber or railroad ties. 

Each year 15,000,000 ties are made in our state, enough to construct a railroad 

2000 miles long.

Missouri needs to adopt a definite program for the restoration of the forests that have been needlessly and carelessly destroyed. Forest reserves should be set aside and planted in valuable timber. In this way timber would be provided for the use of future citizens of our state.

Farmers should be encouraged to plant small plots of ground in trees, especially land that cannot be used in raising farm crops.

Transportation. You now know that our state produces large amounts of both agricultural and mineral products. 

These materials are valuable because there are many places in our country that need them, especially the great industrial centers that require a large amount of raw material for their factories. 

We send our raw materials to the places that want them by means of the railroads (A) and highways. For this reason transportation is very necessary to both the producer of raw materials and to the factory owner.

The first railroad in our state started from St. Louis in 1851; by 1859 there was a road running from Quincy to St. 

Joseph. Today there are 8000 miles of

railroads that connect most of the trading centers of Missouri. On the map on page 31 you will see that many railroads enter our state at St. Louis and run west to Kansas City. North and south of these lines you will see several other roads that cross our state from east to west.

These east-and-west lines give us direct connection with the great industrial centers of the East and the valuable markets of the Far West. There are also many railroads that run north and south, and connect with the main lines running from east to west. Find the names of some of the cities where the north-andsouth lines cross the main east-and-west railroads.

Besides the railroads as a means of travel, Missouri has built many fine highways. As recently as 1920 Missouri had very few good roads, but today we have thousands of miles of them. The roads have been built by selling bonds, by taxing gasoline, and by requiring a license fee for all automobiles. The United 

States government also helps our state in its road-building program. 

Most of the highways are concrete, gravel, crushed rock, or chat. In some places deep cuts have been made through hills, and in low places huge fills have been necessary to make our roads fairly level. 

Look at the map on page 32 and you will see that the highways, like the railroads, connect with one another. The main highways are almost complete, and the Road Department is now building numerous farm-to-market roads.

Many trucks use the highways to haul goods to all parts of our state. They pick up the grain, vegetables, fruit, and live stock of the farmer and haul them to city markets. Then they haul back to A.

Population. - The population of Mis souri is nearly 3,650,000, an average of about 53 persons to a square mile.

About half of the people live in towns. and cities, and half on farms. More than 

95 per cent are native-born Americans.

The map on this page shows the average number of people living in each county, or the density of population in each county. What is the density of population in your county? 

Missouri has sixteen cities with a population of 10,000 or more. Three cities - Kansas City, St. Louis, and St. 

Joseph - have more than 75,000 people.

The most densely populated counties are in the Missouri and Mississippi valleys and in the southwestern part of the state.

The most sparsely settled counties are in the southeastern and south central part of the Ozark Plateau. 

Recreation. Missouri has purchased several large tracts of land that have been developed into playgrounds for its citizens. These playgrounds are known as state parks, and they are ideal places for fishing, camping, and hunting. Most of the state parks are in the Ozark Plateau region (map, page 32). You have learned that this region has beautiful springs, caves, and interesting scenery. Missouri is trying to preserve the beauty spots for the enjoyment of all its people. 

Indian Trail State Park in Dent County is the largest of the parks, and it is maintained as a game preserve. A game preserve is a place set aside as a refuge for wild animals and fowls, where they are safe from hunters and can increase in numbers. The deer (A) in the park are allowed a run of 2500 acres. A pen of 

20 acres is used for wild turkeys. 

Deer Run State Park in Reynolds

County is devoted to raising deer and wild turkeys. Many young pine trees have been set out to grow in the park under the protection of a forester.

Several of the state parks have fish hatcheries. One of the largest hatcheries is in Bennet Spring State Park in Dallas and Laclede counties.

NATURAL REGIONS OF THE UNITED STATES 

Do you remember the lowlands and | much above sea level. highlands of North America? Turn to page 11 and read again what is said there about them. Notice that the United 

States stretches east and west across the continent. See the maps on pages 6 and 

10. Notice also that the great highland area in the western part of the continent has a northwest-southeast direction. The smaller eastern highland has a northeastsouthwest direction, as does the lowland between it and the Atlantic Ocean.

The central lowland of the continent, with a varying width, stretches north and south between the Gulf of Mexico and the Arctic Ocean. 

The land slopes gently toward the ocean. The water in the rivers that cross it moves so slowly toward the ocean that these rivers are called sluggish. Railroads built on the plain run for long distances in straight lines or with very gentle curves.

There are parts of all these great physical regions of the continent in the United States. The map on pages 82-83 shows them on a larger scale. This is a physical map, like that on page 10, which uses colors to show the height of the lands above sea level. The black and white map on page 80 shows clearly the natural regions into which the country is divided. 

Read the names of the natural regions on that map. 

Atlantic Coastal Plain. - Find the lowland bordering the Atlantic Ocean known as the Atlantic Coastal Plain. It stretches along the coast from New York to the southern end of Florida and includes at the north Staten Island, Long Island, and Cape Cod. At the south it joins the lowland region north of the Gulf of Mexico called the Gulf Coastal Plain. 

The Atlantic Coastal Plain was at one time a part of the sea bottom. The rocks under its surface are soft and in them there are shells like those found on the seashore. No part of the plain is very 

Piedmont Plateau. - West of the 

Atlantic Coastal Plain the land is higher and the rocks are older and harder. This region is called the Piedmont Plateau. 

The boundary between the coastal plain and the Piedmont Plateau is the Fall 

Line. Where rivers cross the Fall Line there are usually rapids or waterfalls which furnish power, and at many such points cities have grown up. 

Find the Piedmont Plateau on the map, page 80. The word piedmont means "foot of the mountain." The plateau is given this name because it is the foothill region of the Appalachian 

Mountains. Continuous with the Piedmont Plateau there is a lower region to the north and east of New York City.

In many places it is rough and rocky. 

The hills were once much higher but they have been worn away.

Appalachian Mountains. - - West of the 

Piedmont Plateau are the Appalachian

Mountains and Valleys. They extend from central Alabama (map, page 87) northeast until they cross the northern boun dary of New Hampshire and Vermont. 

The rock layers out of which these mountains are formed were once horizontal. 

Long ages ago they were crumpled into ridges and valleys. Out of these the present mountain ranges and valleys were carved by the work of rain and rivers, sunshine and frost, heat and cold. 81

NATURAL REGIONS OF THE UNITED STATES 

85 

The Appalachian Mountains may once have been much higher. Now they vary in height from less than 2000 feet to a little over a mile. Only a few of the peaks are rocky. Their steeper slopes are covered with forests. There are heavy winter snows in the northern part and in the higher regions, but these all melt in the summer, so there are no glaciers. 

Different parts of this mountain region have been given special names in several of the states. One very wide and beautiful valley is the Great Appalachian Valley. It extends from Alabama through a number of states to the northeast. 

Appalachian Plateau. West of the 

Appalachian Mountains is a highland region called the Appalachian Plateau. 

It is nearly as high as the mountains, but the rock layers are horizontal instead of being folded. At one time its surface was nearly level, but many streams have cut through it, so it is now a region of hills with deep valleys between them.

By climbing to the top of one of the hills, and imagining all of the valleys filled again, you would get a good idea of its former surface. In general the northern part of the Appalachian Plateau is known as the Allegheny Plateau, and the southern part is called the Cumberland Plateau. 

Lake Plains. On the northwest the highlands decrease in elevation and slope down to the plains of the Great Lakes.

Notice the extent of the Lake Plains as shown on the map, page 80. 

Through four of the five Great Lakes, trace the boundary line between the 

United States and Canada. Which one of the five lakes is entirely in the United 

States? You have already learned how large bodies of water make the summer and winter temperatures of the bordering lands more moderate. In what regions would you expect these differences in temperature to increase the length of the growing season? (Map 84 A.) 

Central Regions. West from the 

Great Lakes region and the southern part of the Appalachian Plateau are wide lowlands on both sides of the Mississippi River. They are gently rolling and nowhere more than a few hundred feet above sea level. On the south they join the plains that stretch from Florida to 

Texas north of the Gulf of Mexico. 

What are these two lowland regions called? (Map, page 80.) 

Within the great lowland area of central United States there is a small highland region called the Interior Highlands.

It is made up of a mountain region and a plateau region, much like the Appalachian 

Highlands. Find it on the map. 

Western Highlands. Several of the natural regions of our country are included wholly or mostly in the Western Highlands. 

Just west of the Central Plains is the natural region known as the Great Plains. 

Find it on the maps, pages 80 and 82.

Its elevation increases gradually from east to west. The western part of the

Great Plains is a region of scanty rainfall whose grasslands furnish food for grazing cattle and sheep, and where few crops can be raised without irrigation. 

The Rocky Mountains are high and rugged, and some of the higher slopes and peaks are snow-covered throughout the year. Some other slopes and peaks, too, are so high that trees will not grow on them. The belt along the slopes where the trees thin out until there are no more is known as the timber line.

Rain falls on the Rocky Mountains in summer, and snow in winter, especially on the western slopes. Much of the winter snow melts in the summer time, and many great rivers flow out of these mountains (A). Most of them flow toward the east across the Great Plains. 

Find some of them on the map, page 82.

West of the Rocky Mountains are vast plateaus that vary in height from 2000 to 10,000 feet above sea level. Find the two regions called the Columbia Plateau and the Colorado Plateau. You will learn more about these when you study the Western States. 

West of the Colorado Plateau is a

On the western side of the great highland about which you have been reading are other great mountains. To the north the mountains are called the Cascade 

Range. West of the Great Basin the mountains are called the Sierra Nevada.

Several of the high peaks in these two mountain ranges have small glaciers. 

How were they formed? (Pages 12-13.) high range called the Wasatch Mountains. Find it on the map, page 82.

Beyond the western base of the Wasatch range is the Great Basin. It is called the Great Basin because it is bordered on the east and on the west by high mountains, and because its rivers do not reach the sea.

Some of the streams flow into lakes that have no outlets. Evaporation from them takes away as much water as the streams bring in. The streams are small, because there is not much rain in the Great Basin. See map 84 B. 

Close to the Pacific Ocean are some rugged Coast Ranges. They are not so high as the Cascades or Sierra Nevada, from which they are separated by wide valleys.

 NORTH CENTRAL STATES 

You have made a careful study of your own state. You have learned about its hills and plains, and about its climate, its products, its people and their industries. 

You have learned, also, that our country is divided into great natural regions and you have located these natural regions on the maps. 

There are many reasons why you should know about the different states that make up our country. One reason is that in sending goods or letters from one place to another you must give the address to which they are to go. The name of the state is always a part of that address. 

Another reason is that every ten years our government gathers many facts about our people and their industries. This is called taking a census. After these facts are gathered they are published, so they may be of use to our people. In printing the results of the census, the government gives the facts by states and by groups of states. It does not give these facts by natural regions.

Many facts and relations that you study in geography are based upon the census. 

In this book the states of our country are divided according to census groupings (map, page 88). The natural regions in each state group will be studied also. 

You will learn how surface, climate, soil, and other conditions influence the products of different regions. You will see how some or all of these conditions extend beyond the borders of one state group into other state groups. 

Your state is one of the North Central

States. This is the group of states you are now to study. They are shown on the map on pages 90-91.

NORTH CAROLINA

The Coming of Settlers. It was not until much of the best land of New York, Pennsylvania, and other Atlantic states was occupied that the real settlement of the North Central States began. 

Many people in the East had heard stories about the fertile plains south of the Great Lakes and beyond the Appalachian Mountains. Except for the Indians it was an empty land. Those who went there to make new homes faced great A. Bronze statue of the Pioneer Woman, in Kansas hardships. They had to depend upon 

City, Missouri. 

Canada to the Arctic Ocean (map, page 

10). In the northern part of our country these Central Plains (page 80) are occupied by the North Central States, shown on the map on pages 90-91. This is the group of states you are now to study. 

Early Exploration. Turn to page 7 and read again what is said about French explorers. Then turn back to the map of the North Central States. Notice the rivers that flow into the Great Lakes. 

From several points on the Great Lakes French explorers made their way to the west and south along streams flowing into the lakes. From some of these streams they crossed low divides to eastern tributaries of the Mississippi, and followed these until they reached the Mississippi itself. One of the French explorers, La

Salle, made his way along the great river to its mouth in the Gulf of Mexico.

Some of the explorers were missionaries who wished to convert the Indians to Christianity. Others were traders who bought furs from the Indians, and set up trading posts or places for trade. There were not many of these posts and they were widely scattered. They did not help much in the settling of this part of our country. supplies they took with them and upon what they found in the new land. 

To leave the older settlements behind and seek new homes farther west was to establish a new front of settlement a new frontier. Only men and women of courage would do this. But there were those who were willing to try because they could find fertile lands that would be all their own, and that is what they wanted. 

From many places in the East brave men and women with their children and household goods and farm animals set out on the great journey. The march of settlement toward the West did not end until it pushed beyond the Western Highlands to the shores of the Pacific Ocean.

In the north the early settlers followed the south shore of Lake Erie. Others made their way across the highlands of 

Pennsylvania to Pittsburgh. From that place they floated down the Ohio River to some point in Ohio, Indiana, or

Illinois. Somewhere they would land and make a home. Settlers from the South 

Atlantic States and from Kentucky likewise made their way to the Ohio River and the states north of it. 

Some of the new settlers traveled by wagons drawn by horses or oxen, some rode horseback, and others walked (A).

EARLY HISTORY 

93 

Most of the women and younger children rode in the wagons with the household goods. The farm animals were led or driven along with the wagons. There were no roads for these first settlers to follow through the wilderness. None were built until much later. They waded through small streams and built flatboats to cross or to float down the larger ones.

Michigan and Wisconsin were easily reached by way of the Great Lakes, or across the plains that lay about them. 

Missouri was settled by men from both 

North and South. In the other North 

Central States west of the Mississippi most of the early settlers were from the North. Many of the later settlers came directly from Europe. 

How the Land Was Brought under Cultivation.— In southern Ohio there are hilly uplands that are a part of the Appalachian Plateau (page 80). There are also some hill lands in southern Indiana.

This hill country varies in elevation from about 1000 feet above sea level in parts of Ohio to a few hundred feet in Indiana. There are likewise upland areas in northern Michigan and in northern and southwestern Wisconsin. These upland areas and the larger part of the lowlands of Ohio and Indiana were originally covered with forests. Even in the treeless regions called prairies there were some trees along the rivers and on their bordering bluffs.

The first settlers selected their homes where there were trees even if it meant much hard work to clear the fields. They needed logs and lumber for their houses and furniture and for shelter for their animals. Another reason why the first settlers did not like the prairies was that they were afraid that no crops would

A. 

Sod house built by early settlers on the prairie. grow where trees were not growing. 

Some time later they learned that the treeless plains had a rich deep soil and they began to cultivate it. They put up buildings the walls of which were made of sods piled on top of one another (A). 

The early years of settlement were years of hardship, great danger, and loneliness. They were years of hardship because of the lack of many things needed, and because of the hard work necessary to clear the soil and to cultivate it with the poor tools of that day. They were years of great danger because of fights and wars with the Indians, who wanted to stop the white settlers from turning the hunting grounds into farms. 

They were years of loneliness because in this new land the settlers were far away from their friends. They could see them only by taking the long, long journey back to the place from which they had come. Even their nearest neighbors might be miles away too far to travel, except when it was necessary. 

With the passing of the years things grew better. More settlers came. Settlements grew larger and there were more farms. farms. Roads were built, though they

had no hard surface like the macadam or concrete roads of today. When the winter snows were melting, or after heavy rains, the roads were very muddy. Where a road crossed a boggy place, however, it was covered with logs laid down side by side so that the horses and wagons would not sink into it. Later some canals were built, and finally the railroads. People were friendly and lived close enough to each other so they were able to visit back and forth. After the railroads were built (maps, pages 116, 259), the farmers could sell their surplus produce in the cities or ship it to eastern markets. The people became prosperous. 

In the North Central States you now find a large population and ten or more cities of great size. Millions of people have come there from foreign lands. 

Other millions have been born there. 

There are many farms, mines, oil wells, mills, factories, and packing houses.

The farms are large and are cultivated by the use of the most modern machinery. 

These states have become one of the great food-producing regions of the world.

2. The first settlers of this region required a great deal of courage. 

3. Settlers, at first, selected lands on which there were trees. 

4. The first roads built were very different from those of the present day.

THE LAND AND ITS CLIMATE

THE LAND AND ITS CLIMATE 

When settlers first began moving into the region you are now studying, the land belonged to the national government. 

Later it was divided into one-mile squares, called sections, and these into quarter sections, each having 160 acres. When the states were formed many of the boundaries followed the straight lines between squares. It was natural that when roads were laid out in such regions, many followed these boundary lines. 

At first the government sold the land to the settlers for $2 an acre, later for $1.25 an acre. Still later the government B. gave a quarter section to a settler who would make a home on it and farm the land for five years. As a result most farms were larger than those in the East. 

The Highlands. You have read about the forested uplands in Ohio, Indiana, Michigan, and Wisconsin. In northern

Michigan there are places that are more than 2000 feet above sea level, but the highest elevation in Wisconsin is some- 

Grain drill, drawn by a tractor. This machine plants the seed in rows close together. what less. The same hilly upland extends into central and northern Minnesota. It is a region of very old rocks like those in the northern Appalachians. It is covered with glacial material, and dotted with thousands of lakes. 

Much of the southern half of Missouri, south of the Missouri River, belongs to the Ozark Plateau. Its surface is from 

800 to 1800 feet above the sea, and it is largely a region of forests and mines, although there are also many small farms. 

The Prairies. - The prairies, or treeless parts of the Central Plains, are usually free from stones, and are covered with a black, rich soil which is in places ten feet in depth. As the land is nearly level, or only gently rolling, large fields may be laid out and planting and harvesting machinery can be used. Where single crops such as corn or wheat are grown the most modern machinery will be found in use. Gang plows, harrows (A), grain drills (B), reapers (89 A), headers, A. — Harrows, drawn by a tractor. Can you tell why har- threshing machines, and great tractors rowing is done? are part of the equipment of these farms. NCS-6

Climate of the North Central States. 

The North Central States are far from the sea, and have hot summers and cold winters. The annual rainfall varies from about 45 inches in the southeast to less than 20 inches in the west (84 B). Winds from the west and storms from the Gulf of

Mexico pass over this part of our country. 

The average length of the growing season is 200 days in the very southern parts of Illinois and Missouri, on the lowland along the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. It is 110 days in the northern parts of Minnesota and North Dakota.

In the heart of the prairie country it varies from 140 to 170 days, allowing enough time to mature or ripen the chief crops of temperate latitudes. It must be remembered, also, that crops get most of their growth by daylight, and that the summer days are longer in the north than in the south. The 110 crop-growing days in northern Minnesota have more daylight hours than 120 days in southern Illinois.

The water of the Great Lakes is warmed during the summer and stores up heat. 

As water does not cool so quickly as land, the autumn winds are warmed in passing across the lakes. As a result the growing season is longer on the side of a lake toward which the wind is blowing than in regions in the same latitude that are not near large bodies of water.

In general, therefore, the 

North Central States have warm summers for the growth of crops. The winters are cold but clear, and very bracing. The soils are rich, many of the rivers and lakes are navigable, and the plains are level so that railroads have been easily constructed. 

These facts help to explain the rapid increase of population and the growth of many cities. 

The Corn Belt and the Wheat Belt. 

Study the wheat map (A). A great deal of wheat is grown in central Kansas, and much wheat in the far West, especially in 

Washington and Oregon. Turn to the corn map (97 A). Very little corn is grown west of the central region of the 

United States. Much of the West is either mountainous or dry, and corn needs rain and warm days.

Notice that corn grows south to the Gulf Coast and is found all through the cotton-growing region, while there is hardly any wheat in the cotton belt. 

Corn grows well in the heat and moisture of the South; wheat grows best in the dry, clear air of higher and cooler places.

Farming in the Corn Belt. You must not get the idea that corn and wheat are the only crops grown in the corn belt or that the whole farm is used for crops. 

Oats and hay are raised chiefly for the horses used on the farm, although some of each may be sold if there is a surplus. 

Oats will ripen where it is quite cool, so they are raised chiefly in the northern part of the region and in the highlands. 

However, most farmers grow some. Hay, including timothy, clover, and alfalfa, can be grown throughout the North Central 

States wherever there is enough rain.

This means that a part of the land must be used for pasture. Farming in such regions as this where many crops and farm animals are raised is called mixed farming. 

Usually mixed farming is much safer for the farmer than the raising of a single crop would be. If a farmer raises only

A. Cultivating young corn, four rows at a time, with an auto-driven cultivator. one crop to sell and that crop is a failure he has done his work for nothing. If he raises several crops, one may fail and he will still have something to show for his work. A wise farmer, in most places, does not limit himself to one crop. or early in July. When dried it is stored in the barns or in large stacks. 

In mixed farming the crops are rotated. 

That means that the same crop is not always planted in the same field. This is because different crops use different plant foods or different amounts of the same plant food. By changing the crops every year or every two or three years no single plant food in the soil will all be used up. 

Another advantage in mixed farming is that the farmer can spread his work through the year. His plowing may be done in the fall if he is planting winter wheat, or in the early spring if he is planting oats. During the growing season the wheat and oats do not need cultivating, but the corn must be kept free from weeds (A). The hay is cut late in June 

After the hay has been gathered the wheat and oats are cut, tied into bundles, and allowed to stand in shocks in the field so the seeds can dry. When the grain is dry enough it is threshed and the grain stored or sold.

Even after the ears of corn are ripe they are left on the stalks until the kernels are dry. The ears are then pulled from the stalks, husked, and stored in large cribs. 

The Corn Crop. Corn is also known as maize and is often called Indian corn, because the Indians raised it. It is a native of the Western Hemisphere, but was introduced into Europe soon after the discovery of America. Although it is now raised in many parts of the world that have a suitable climate, the crop in the United States is far larger than the crops of all other countries together.

STOCK RAISING AND MEAT PACKING 

99 

Nearly 3,000,000,000 bushels of corn are raised each year in our country.

This is about two thirds of the number of bushels of corn raised in all the countries of the world.

Some of the corn is ground for corn meal and is used for making cornstarch and breakfast foods, sirup, oil, and other corn products.

The greater part of the corn, however, is fed to hogs and cattle. This is the reason why the corn belt is also the chief live-stock region in the United States.

Meat Packing. - In former times the people of a city were supplied with meat by farmers near at hand, who drove in their cattle, sheep, or hogs and sold them to the local butcher. Today, beef and pork enough to supply New York or

Philadelphia or any other large city cannot be raised near these cities. They must often be brought from a great distance. Modern trains and ships make this possible. Some animals are shipped alive, but the greater number are slaughtered in cities that are not far from the stock farms and ranges. 

Such cities are known as packing centers. Chicago is the greatest of these. 

It is not only in the midst of the prairie stock farms, but is easily reached by railroads from the stock ranges west and southwest. Still nearer the ranges are the packing houses of Omaha in Nebraska, Kansas City (101 A) and Wichita in Kansas, Sioux City in Iowa, St. Joseph and St. Louis in Missouri, and East St. 

Louis in Illinois.

STOCK RAISING AND MEAT PACKING 

101 A. Stockyards at Kansas City, Kansas. The animals are kept in different pens, so that those of one owner may be kept separated from those of other owners. These yards can hold 70,000 cattle, 50,000 hogs, and 50,000 sheep. 

The stockyards receive the animals as they come from the trains. Thousands of cattle and hogs and sheep are butchered every day, and the families of those who work in the packing houses would people a good-sized city. Most of the meat is sent in halves or in whole carcasses, by refrigerator cars, to cities and towns in all parts of the country; and in stores there it is cut up and sold in the form of steaks, roasts, or other "cuts." Some of the meat goes abroad in cold storage. Some is frozen, salted, smoked, or cooked and sealed in air-tight cans. Meats prepared in these ways will keep for a long time and can be shipped to distant markets. 

The horns and bones are turned into buttons, hairpins, combs, brushbacks, and handles of many kinds. Other parts serve for making glue, soap, glycerin, poultry food, gelatin, and for various medical preparations. Nothing is wasted.

THE WHEAT BELT 

Now, what about the wheat belt?

Look again at the map, page 96. The winter wheat is grown in the corn area, only there is more, much more, wheat in 

Kansas, and very much less in Iowa.

Wheat grows well in Iowa soil, but it pays better to raise corn there. Notice that wheat grows also in northern Texas.

Follow the chief regions of wheat production to the north and east through the North Central States and on through 

Pennsylvania to Maryland and Virginia. 

The Red River of the North. When the glacial ice was melting in the region that is now Minnesota and North Dakota, there was a very large lake where these states join each other. Much fine mud settled in the bottom of the lake. When the water finally drained away a very flat lake plain was left. A sluggish stream, the Red River of the North, flows across this plain. Here are some of the richest wheat lands in the whole world. 

Spring wheat is sown in the spring as soon as the soil can be worked. It is harvested in the late summer of the same year. The spring-wheat-growing region extends into Saskatchewan, Alberta, and 

Manitoba in Canada (map, page 284).

Winnipeg is the trading center of the Canadian wheat region. The growing season in this wheat area is short compared with the growing season of the cotton or corn belts. However, the springwheat region has very long days, and the long period of sunlight makes up for the shorter length of growing period. 

Wheat requires less rain than corn. 

It grows best in a region having about 

20 inches of rain a year. The great wheat states in the northern part of the central farming region have dry summers. This helps the ripening and the harvesting of the crop. Threshing can be done out of doors, and large barns to house the harvested wheat are not needed. cattle.

The 

Spring and Winter Wheat. The northern part of the wheat belt is suited to growing spring wheat. In Minnesota and the Dakotas and some other northern states the winters are cold and dry. 

These conditions are poorly suited to the growth of winter wheat. Winter wheat 

Winter wheat must be sown in the autumn of one year and harvested in the early summer of the following year. After it is planted in the autumn it grows to several inches in height before cold weather stops its growth. It will live through the winter under a light blanket of snow. It will live also in regions where there is no snow if the winter cold is not severe.

With the warm weather of spring it begins to grow again.

Many of the spring-wheat farmers keep cattle. The manure from the cattle barns helps to keep up the fertility of the soil, and caring for the cattle keeps the men busy when there is little other work to do. The climate and soil of the springwheat-growing region is suited to the raising of potatoes. They are not a large crop, however, because the demand at home is small and the cost of shipping the potatoes long distances to market is too great.

By these simple means wheat bread could be produced only for the few. Now gang plows turn over the soil, and used for seeding (95 B). drills are

OTHER FARM PRODUCTS 

Special crops are raised where soil and climate favor them or where great markets call for them. Some of these special crops, especially vegetables and fruits, are raised for city markets in near-by gardens. Others may be crops for which the soil or climate of a region may be particularly suited. So in parts of the 

North Central States, as markets and transportation have improved, the farmers have raised more special crops. Students of farming often tell farmers of special crops suited to their land. 

Special Crops of the North Central 

States. Much flax is grown in North 

Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota.

It is not grown for its fiber, but for the seed, which is used for making linseed oil. After the oil has been pressed out, the cake that remains is a valuable food for stock. The oil is used in mixing paints. Most of the flax fiber used for making linen is raised in Europe. 

Other special crops are celery, beans, and sugar beets. Kalamazoo, Michigan, is the shipping center of one of the districts where fine celery is grown. Michigan and Wisconsin raise more sugar beets than any other states east of the Mississippi River, and have a number of factories for making the sugar. Tobacco is raised in parts of Ohio and Wisconsin. 

Grains. Three fourths of the oats 

raised in the United States are produced in this group of states. Illinois and Iowa, which have the largest proportion of prairie land, are the leaders in raising this grain. Most of the oats are fed to horses and poultry, but some are used for the food of man. Rye and barley are raised in some parts of this region. 

Forage Crops. - Hay is a very important crop of the North Central States.

Besides hay, the forage plants include corn, sorghum, and kafir corn. This lastnamed forage plant grows well in dry regions.

Fruit. The North Central States pro duce much fruit. Many grapes are grown in southern Michigan, near Lake Michigan; and in northern Ohio, near Lake 

Erie. You will find few grapes on the

Wisconsin side of Lake Michigan because the prevailing, or most frequent, winds blow from west to east. In autumn, frosts come early in Wisconsin, but the wind passing over the lake to the Michigan side warms the air over the vineyards and keeps off the frosts till later. 

Apples, peaches, and other orchard fruits are grown in abundance in Michigan and 

Ohio and also in Missouri, Illinois, Kansas, and other states.

MINING AND LUMBERING 

The North Central States are well provided with useful minerals. Most of these states have coal beds (map, page 

141). Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Missouri have deposits of iron ore. 

Copper is found in northern Michigan, and lead and zinc in Missouri, Kansas, and Wisconsin. Petroleum and natural gas, building stones, and clays are found in many states of the group. 

Iron. - Minnesota produces more iron ore than any other state. Most of the ore which is used in the Pittsburgh district comes from the three states of the Lake Superior region. Much of it is an earthy ore that is easily dug in open pits. Trains of ore cars are run into these broad pits, and the cars are filled by steam shovels. 

When filled, the ore cars go to Duluth, Superior, or other ports on Lake Superior or Lake Michigan. They are run out on long piers, and the ore is dumped into great pockets and from these into the holds of ore vessels, to be taken down the lakes. Most of the ore is unloaded (A) at Detroit, or at Toledo, Cleveland, Erie, Buffalo, or some other port of Lake Erie, or at Chicago or Gary on Lake Michigan.

Some of it is smelted in these cities, but much goes on to Pittsburgh. 

Thus in most cases the iron ore is brought near the coal beds, or near large markets. But the big freight steamers that bring iron ore from Lake Superior to the lower lake ports do not have enough freight to carry on the return trip.

Therefore, they can afford to carry coal very cheaply. Some of the coal is shipped to cities farther west. A steel plant at Superior, Wisconsin, uses coal brought from the lower lakes in this way. 

In the North Central group the manufacture of iron and steel, and of iron and steel castings and machinery, is important not only in the cities already mentioned, but also in many others. It is, for example, the chief industry of Youngstown and 

Canton in Ohio; and of Joliet in Illinois.

Sawmill. The band saw passes around two large wheels, one above and one below. A slab or a board is cut from the log on each trip of the car past the saw. 

Coal. In this group of states there are extensive beds of soft or bituminous coal, especially in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and Missouri. There are coal beds under about two thirds of the state of Illinois. With so much coal to supply power, manufacturing has grown very rapidly in many of the cities in the 

North Central States. 

Copper. Michigan is one of the four leading states of our country in the production of copper; the other three are Arizona, Utah, and Montana. The

Michigan copper is found on the Keweenaw Peninsula, and has been longest known. Pieces of the metal were broken from ledges of rock and carried southward by the ice sheet. The Indians sometimes picked them up and hammered them into implements. Now the copper ore, consisting of small particles of metal scattered through the rock, is mined far below the surface.

The United States produces about half of the world's supply of copper. This

Much copper is exported.

Other Mineral Products.- Much pe troleum and natural gas are found in 

Kansas, and smaller amounts in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Michigan.

The limestone and clay needed in the manufacture of cement are found in many places in the North Central States.

There are large cement factories in Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, and Kansas.

Missouri ranks first among the states in the production of lead and zinc. Gold is mined in the Black Hills in South 

Dakota, and Michigan produces more salt than any other state in the country. 

Lumbering. Lumbering (A) is still carried on in the forests of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, though most of the white pine and much of the other

timber have been cut. The industry is no longer so important as it once was in the North Central States, or as it is now in some states of the South and on the 

Pacific coast.

Duluth and Superior, at the head of Lake Superior, are large lumber markets, as is also Minneapolis in Minnesota. The cities of Grand Rapids, Michigan, and 

Rockford, Illinois, are especially known as furniture-manufacturing centers (A). The making of farming implements has become a very important industry in this group of states, for here are found (1) supplies of lumber, (2) supplies of iron, and (3) farms that offer a market A.- In a furniture factory in Grand Rapids. Chicago is near the lumber and iron of the Lake Superior region, and has supplies of coal for her factories, and a ready market in all the prairie states. Among the many other centers of this manufacture are Moline, Peoria, and Rock Island, Illinois; Springfield, Ohio; and South Bend, Indiana.

CITIES AND TRANSPORTATION 

The population of the North Central States has grown rapidly in recent years, especially in the states bordering the 

Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. Only a few of the many cities of the North Central States have so far been mentioned. You should know more about the chief cities of this region and about the transportation routes that serve them.

The Ohio Basin.The Ohio River basin reaches from New York to Alabama (map, page 87). Find two streams that come together at Pittsburgh. One of these comes from New York. Find the

Tennessee River where it flows out of Alabama. A large part of the Ohio basin is in the great Appalachian Plateau. 

Much of Ohio and parts of Kentucky and Tennessee belong to the plateau. In the lowlands of the Ohio basin in Kentucky is the rich Blue Grass region, and in the lowlands of Tennessee is the Nashville basin.

A. 

Making automobile tires in Akron.

The Ohio River, as you know, was a great gateway for the early settlers. 

They came from the East to the place where Pittsburgh is, and went down the 

Ohio in rough houseboats called "arks."

They also came through the Great Valley from Virginia and through the rough plateau to settle the Ohio lands on both sides of the river. The river is now a great freight route for coal and other products, and has three very large cities on its banks - Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, and Louisville (pages 90-91). 

Cities in and near the Ohio Basin. - 

Cincinnati is the largest port on the 

Ohio River except Pittsburgh, and is an important railroad center. It is a gateway to the South, the city having built its own railroad to Chattanooga. It is a manufacturing center for boots and shoes, clothing, pottery, machinery, tools, and ornamental iron. It is a large market for fruits and vegetables, as well as for hardwood lumber. Many residents of near-by cities in Ohio and Kentucky carry on business in Cincinnati.

On the Ohio River in Indiana is Evansville, a hardwood lumber market. It has flour and grist mills and furniture factories.

In Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois there are many important cities not on lakes or on navigable rivers. Among these the largest is Indianapolis. It is an important railroad center, and is the center of trade for the state. It has large pork-packing establishments, machine shops, and automobile and other factories. In Indiana, also, Fort Wayne has large machine shops and other factories; and South Bend makes automobiles, wagons, and plows.

Columbus, the capital of Ohio, is near the coal fields of the state, and has many manufactures, especially of machinery, cars, and shoes. At Dayton, another city of Ohio, are manufactured railroad cars, airplanes, and most of the world's supply of cash registers. Akron makes more rubber goods than any other city in the world. This industry was established there long before automobiles were made. 

But when the cities of the North Central

States began the manufacture of automobiles and trucks it was natural that the Akron rubber factories should manufacture tires and tubes (A). It leads all other cities in this work.

United States. The main stream crosses almost the entire width of our country, from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico.

It is a very sluggish stream and is useful for power only in the upper part of its course. The elevation at its source is
