Cities of the Mississippi River. 

-St.

Louis, the chief city of Missouri, is the largest city in the basin of the Mississippi

River. It is on the west side of the 

Mississippi, a little below the mouth of the Missouri River. It is midway between the traffic of the upper and that of the lower Mississippi. Railroads from 

Chicago, Pittsburgh, New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore center here. 

St. Louis handles a great variety of products (A), including tobacco and cotton from the South, meat from the West, wheat from the North, coal from Illinois, and the lead, zinc, coal, glass, and iron of Missouri. It was one of the early trading posts in the Mississippi Valley and is still a great fur market. It is a great lumber market, and its manufactures include shoes, clothing, tobacco, chemicals, and railroad and street cars. 

It is also a meat-packing center. 

Several bridges cross the Mississippi

River at St. Louis. On the Illinois side of the river is East St. Louis, with flour mills and other factories (A), besides some large meat-packing establishments just outside the city limits. 

At Keokuk, Iowa, 140 miles northwest of St. Louis, is a concrete dam across the 

Mississippi River, 31 feet high and nearly a mile long, one of the greatest power dams in the world. In the power house the water turns immense water wheels, called turbines, and generates electricity.

Most of this power is used in driving machinery and street cars in St. Louis and other cities. Steamboats on the river pass the dam by means of a lock. 

At the head of navigation on the Mississippi River are St. Paul and Minneapolis in Minnesota. St. Paul is the capital of the state, and Minneapolis is the largest city. The two cities are so close to each other as to be one center of population, having together more than 700,000 people. They are often called the Twin 

Cities. Minneapolis owes its development as a manufacturing city to the water power of the Falls of St. Anthony in the 

Mississippi River. The great fields of the spring-wheat belt are near, and 

Minneapolis has become the largest center in the world for making flour (A). It also has large linseed oil mills. St. Paul has a large wholesale and retail trade, and is a printing and publishing center. Many railroads center in the two cities, with lines running eastward to Milwaukee and 

Chicago, northward to Winnipeg, westward to Seattle and Portland, and southward to St. Louis.

In central Iowa, on a tributary of the 

Mississippi, is Des Moines, the capital, largest city, and chief trading center of that state. It is a manufacturing and railroad center.

Missouri River in Missouri is Kansas

City, with a large trade in live stock, grain, and agricultural implements.

Cities of the Great Lakes. Of the thirteen largest cities in the United States, five are counted as cities of the Great 

Lakes. They are Chicago and Milwaukee on Lake Michigan, Cleveland and

Many of the shops and markets of the prairie states are in these seven cities, which are railroad centers as well as lake ports. Here the grain, cattle, and hogs are sold. From these cities supplies are sent to the homes and farms in the rich agricultural regions. —- 

Chicago. Chicago is second in size among the cities of our country and fourth in size among the cities of the world. It has a population of about 

3,500,000. It is near the head of Lake

Michigan, the only one of the Great Lakes that lies wholly within the United States.

The rich fields, mines, and forests of 

Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Illinois are not far from Chicago, and the city has naturally become the center of great business activity. The Central

Plains are so nearly level over large areas that many railroads have been easily built from the city. These railroads, the shipping on the lakes, the vast and rich prairies, and the coal, iron, copper, and lumber that are not far away, have all helped to make Chicago the chief city of the central lowland of North America.

The University of Chicago is one of the great universities of our country. 

A small stream called the Chicago

River has been deepened and forms part of the harbor of the city. The outer harbor is protected by long breakwaters.

The water supply of Chicago comes from Lake Michigan. It is taken from the bottom of the lake at a point some miles out from the shore. To avoid the pollution of the water with sewage the city dug the Drainage Canal. This canal is nearly 30 miles long and not less than 22 feet deep. It conducts the waste of the city, mingled with water from Lake Michigan, to the Illinois River. This canal is designed for use as the connecting link between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River system and therefore as part of an important route for commerce when the channel of the Mississippi is deepened enough to permit the use of larger vessels.

Chicago has many lofty business buildings, wide boulevards (112 A) and parks, and the means of transportation common to great cities, such as surface and elevated railroads. There are also subways for carrying freight from one part of the city to another. Iron, coal, and grain are the chief products carried by its ships. 

Its stockyards and meat-packing business (A) are the largest in the world.

In the making of agricultural implements, as you have learned (page 107), it is the first city in the world, and in the manufacture of clothing it is second only to 

New York. It has the leading grain exchange of the country, and its elevators have a capacity of many millions of bushels. It manufactures much iron and steel. The parlor, sleeping, and dining cars on many of the American railroads are made in Pullman, a part of Chicago, and many street and freight cars also are built there. 

Other Lake Cities. Milwaukee is on the shore of Lake Michigan, about 85 miles north of Chicago, and is the chief city of Wisconsin. Like Chicago, it has the advantage of sending and receiving goods both by lake and by railroad. Its manufactures include leather, machinery, iron and steel, flour, knit goods, packed meats, and shoes. Milwaukee is an important grain-shipping port and has enormous grain elevators. It is also a distributing point for the coal brought in by lake steamers from Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania, and shipped throughout the Northwest.

Among other cities on Lake Michigan are Racine in Wisconsin, a manufacturing center for agricultural implements, automobiles, and carriages; and Gary in Indiana, with immense steel works, tin-plate mills, and cement works. A. In an automobile factory near Detroit. Here the engines are tested.

At the head of Lake Superior are Du luth in Minnesota and Superior in Wisconsin, which have iron furnaces, steel mills, and large grain elevators and ore docks. These cities ship iron ore, lumber, and grain eastward, and coal to the west.

All traffic from the upper to the lower lakes passes the city of Detroit. This city is an important railroad center. It is connected with Canada by a bridge and by railroad and vehicular tunnels under the Detroit River. Detroit is fourth in size among the cities of the

Among its many other manufactures are automobiles and clothing. 

Toledo, at the west end of Lake Erie, on a river harbor, has a large trade by lake and rail. Among its manufactures are iron and steel goods, automobiles, ships, electrical machinery, glass, and clothing.

A.-Manufacturing districts and chief lines of transportation in the United States. 

Transportation in the North Central | was much traffic down the Ohio and Mis- 

States. No other part of the United

States is so well adapted to the development of transportation routes to all parts of the country as the North Central region. The country is nearly level, or at least is not so hilly as to interfere with the making of good roads. Plenty of stone suitable for making excellent roads can generally be supplied from quarries near at hand.

It costs less to build railroads in a level country than in a mountainous region, because there are no expensive cuts and embankments. Several railroads join 

Cleveland, Detroit, and Cincinnati with 

Chicago, Milwaukee, and Indianapolis.

Others have been built westward to 

St. Paul, Minneapolis, St. Louis, Kansas 

City, Denver, and other cities farther west and south. In the older days there sissippi rivers from Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, Louisville, and St. Louis, to Memphis and New Orleans. In later years railroads have been built from north to south along the Mississippi Valley, and there is not so much traffic on the rivers, except that vast amounts of coal are carried down the Ohio River from Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

Thus in the North Central region transportation is easy. The region is mainly a lowland. It has a network of roads, many of which follow boundaries between sections (page 95). It is crossed by great rivers, and has on the north the greatest system of fresh-water navigation in the world. 

There are many motor busses and trucks in use for carrying passengers and freight for short distances within the cities or for longer distances between cities.

THE INTERIOR HIGHLANDS 

117 A business man of Chicago can go to and from his suburban home by rail, by motor bus, or in his own automobile. 

By means of the telephone he can carry on business with men in Milwaukee, Minneapolis, St. Louis, or, if he wishes, with business men in Europe or South America. He can go by train to New Orleans or 

New York in a day, and in less than three days to San Francisco, without missing meals or sleep. By using an airplane he can make any of these journeys in less than half the time taken by fast trains (map, page 259).

Great educational institutions have helped him and his children to business success and to a knowledge of the world and its affairs. Every state in this group supports a university. All but three of these universities have more than 5000 students each, and some as many as 

13,000 or 14,000.

THE INTERIOR HIGHLANDS 

Find the Interior Highlands on the map, page 80. This region, surrounded by the lowlands of central United States, lies partly in the North Central States and partly in the South Central States.

It occupies a large part of Missouri, the northwestern half of Arkansas, and a part of eastern Oklahoma. These highlands have folded mountains and a plateau region like those of the Appalachians and are sometimes spoken of as a western extension of the Appalachian Highlands.

The Ozark Plateau in Missouri and northern Arkansas is a true plateau only in the west. In its eastern part the rivers of the region have cut deeply into the underlying limestone rocks, and the whole region is a maze of hills and valleys. 

Farming. - In the hill-and-valley region of the Ozark Plateau much of the soil is stony and poorly suited to ordinary farming. The stones are flinty material once included in the limestone rock but left on the surface when the limestone was dissolved or worn away. Some crops can be raised with profit even in such soils as these. Orchard trees grow well, and this region has become famous for its fine.

Some of the land that cannot be cultivated is used for pastures for cattle and sheep. The farmers depend upon corn for a part of their own food as well as food for their live stock and poultry. Corn-fattened beef cattle and hogs are raised for sale. 

Lumbering. Highlands that cannot be cultivated or used as pasture are covered with a growth of oak, ash, hickory, and other hardwoods. Many a farmer in Missouri or Arkansas makes money in winter by lumbering on his own land or for some company. - Among the mineral resources of the Interior Highlands are lead, zinc, bauxite, and coal. While lead and zinc are found in several parts of this area, the chief region of production is 

Mineral Wealth. 

near Joplin, Missouri, where there are large smelters. Most of the bauxite comes from Arkansas. The mines are along the southeastern edge of the Interior Highland, not far from Little Rock.

Coal is found in widely scattered mines in both Oklahoma and Arkansas. Little

Rock is the capital of Arkansas, and a trading and manufacturing center. The mining of bauxite, the clay-like ore from which aluminum is made, has become a very large industry. As a result of the growth of this industry, Little Rock has increased rapidly in size. 

Southwest of Little Rock in the Ouachita Mountains is a region of mineral springs that has been made into a national park. The springs of this region have been found helpful in the treatment of certain forms of illness, and Hot Springs has become a famous resort for health and pleasure.

A Buffalo Country. Look at one of the five-cent pieces now in most common use in our country. On one side you will find the head of an Indian. On the other side you see a humpbacked animal called a buffalo. When the first white men pushed their way into the Great Plains they found both Indians and vast herds of buffaloes. There were so many buffaloes that much later, when railroads had been built across the plains, trains sometimes had to stop and wait when a herd was crossing the track.

The hides of buffaloes were cured and made into robes that people could wrap up in so as to keep warm during a winter ride. Buffaloes were hunted until almost all of them were killed. Finally our government and that of Canada set 

National Park Service A. Buffaloes in the Yellowstone National Park. 

aside certain areas as reservations where small herds are kept. If the buffaloes had not been protected in this way there would be none living now.

Grazing on the Great Plains. what did these vast herds of buffaloes on the Great Plains live? They ate the native bunch grass. This grass grows green and fresh in the time of the spring rains, and is dried up and cured like hay by the summer sun. The buffalo therefore found food on the open plains in winter as well as in summer. The first settlers in this region naturally turned to grazing and farming. The grazing industry was successful and grew rapidly. 

Farming was less successful and many of the early farms were soon abandoned. 

Farming methods, however, were SO changed and improved in later years that there are now many fine farms in the Great Plains.

In the early years the cattle were allowed to roam the plains in the care of cowboys. They were left out of doors

A. Cattle on the Great Plains, in northern Montana. mothers, and thus it is easy to pick them out also. The other calves are divided among the owners according to the number of cattle each one owns. Each calf is then branded by a hot iron with its owner's mark. the year round, even in the cold northern | Most of the young calves will follow their part of our country. They fed on the native bunch grass as the buffaloes had before them. Better methods are now in use in the north, where fierce winter snowstorms called blizzards sometimes cover the ground with snow. In the old days when this happened the cattle often died from cold and hunger. Now they are sheltered and fed during the winter. 

Their increase in value more than pays for the cost of the shelter and food provided, and for the necessary extra labor. 

The Round-Up. - Pasture lands in the Great Plains are now being fenced in, and the unfenced ranges are rapidly disappearing. Where they still remain the cattle are brought together in a round-up twice a year. The cowboys of various ranches work together. They spread out in lines or parties and drive the cattle scattered over a large area into one small area. Day after day they take a different section of the country. When the cattle have been rounded up, they are found to belong to many different owners. 

Each grown animal has its owner's brand. 

In the autumn round-up the animals that are ready for market, or to be shipped to the prairie states for "finishing off," are separated from the herd by the cowboys. The rest of the herd is allowed to wander back on the range. 

Ranchmen. Much of the old range land has now been fenced in as large ranches. The ranchman's house usually is built by a stream or spring, and near it are smaller houses for the helpers, corrals and barns, a garage, a blacksmith shop, and a pasture for horses. The helpers may still, as in the old days, be called cowboys, but their work is very different. Instead of herding the cattle and protecting them from cattle thieves, they help the ranch owner in keeping the fences in repair and in watering the cattle. In the more northern states where

A single ranch may include hundreds of acres or even many square miles. One or two acres of corn or grass land in 

Iowa will keep a beef animal. To keep one in the dry plains where the wild bunch grass furnishes most of the pasture, from fifteen to twenty-five acres are necessary for each animal. 

Ranchmen today use every effort to raise the kind of beef animal that can be sold for most in the market. The longhorned scrawny animals of the early open-range days are no longer seen. In their place you find heavy-bodied, shortlegged beef animals of the finest grade. 

They are no longer driven hundreds of miles to market as they once were. Instead they are sent by fast freight trains and are carefully fed and watered and given time to rest on the way. — - 

Sheep on the Great Plains. In the days of the open range, sheep as well as cattle were pastured on the Great Plains, but the sheep herders and cattle men had many bitter quarrels. There were several reasons for this: (1) The cattle 

B.Shearing sheep. men were there first and did not want any sheep to come into their pastures. (2) Sheep eat the grass much closer than cattle do, sometimes even pulling up the roots to eat them. (3) Sheep leave an odor on grass over which they pasture.

This odor is at times offensive to cattle, and they are said to avoid pastures where sheep have been recently grazing. Now that much of the pasture land is fenced, cattle and sheep can easily be kept in different pastures. On the map, notice particularly the sheep-raising region of 

Texas. More than half the goats raised in our country are found in this region.

Rainfall on the Great Plains and

Farther West. Over most of the Great 

Plains the rainfall is less than 20 inches a year (84 B). The same thing is true for much of our country that lies west of the Great Plains. The map shows two regions of heavy rainfall running north and south in Washington, Oregon, and California. It also shows several areas of rainfall of from 20 to 40 inches in the region of the Rocky Mountain ranges. 

The amount and seasonal distribution of rainfall in any region has an important effect on agriculture. Before taking up the study of farming on the Great Plains it will be well to stop for an explanation of the rainfall in the western part of our country.

Over most of the eastern and central part of the United States the rain-bearing winds are from the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. In the western part the rain-bearing winds are chiefly from the Pacific Ocean. They are called westerly winds and come for the most part from the southwest. 

Blowing from the Pacific toward the western coast they bring much moisture to the land. It is in the form of invisible water vapor that the wind picked up from the surface of the sea as it blew across it. 

A warm wind can contain more of these invisible water particles than a cooler wind. If, therefore, a wind from the

Pacific Ocean has all of the moisture it can contain, it must drop some of this moisture when it cools. In crossing mountains the winds are forced to greater elevations, and are cooled as they rise. 

Rain is therefore left on the western slopes of the Coast Ranges, the Sierra Nevada and the Cascade Range, the ranges of the plateaus, and those of the Rocky 

Mountains (pages 80, 82, 84 B).

After crossing any one of these ranges the wind moves downward over its eastern slope. As it does so its temperature is raised. It can pick up more moisture as invisible vapor. There will be very little rainfall. For this reason, even when the western mountain slopes have heavy rains or snows, the eastern slopes, the interior valleys, and the plateaus between ranges are much drier. 

From what has been said you will understand that the westerly winds that blow down the eastern slope of the Rockies and across the Great Plains leave but little rain. Not only is there but little rainfall in the Great Plains region, but violent storms sometimes sweep across the country. These are twisting storms that follow a narrow path and cause a great deal of damage. They are called tornadoes. Once in a while cold northern winds called northers sweep south even as far as Texas, causing much damage and distress. 

Farming on the Great Plains. In the eastern part of the United States and on the prairies, the farmer depends on the rains to water his crops and to supply the wells and springs. When no rain falls for a time, he may wish that he could water his potatoes or his corn, but it very rarely happens that any of his crops fail for lack of rain.

In the western part of the Great Plains, and in many parts of the Plateau and Pacific States, the annual rainfall is small, as you have just learned. Frequently the rain that does fall comes down in fierce storms and runs quickly away or soaks into the porous soils of the plains, beyond the reach of roots.

A.-Irrigation ditches. The field shown in this picture slopes gently from the foreground to the background.

Irrigation. There are parts of the 

Great Plains where water from mountain streams and from deep wells is used to water the fields for crops. This is called irrigation. Farmers have used irrigation since ancient times in the dry regions of Egypt and in many other countries where the rainfall is scanty. Even the 

Indians of our Southwest used irrigation, in a small way, long before the Spanish explorers came to that region.

The large rivers of the Great Plains come from beyond the crest of the Rocky Mountains and are fed by the rains and snows at their sources. They furnish much water to the plains. The waters of the South Platte and Arkansas rivers in Colorado (map, page 226) have long been used for irrigation. Find Denver in 

Colorado, east of the Rockies. Large ditches near this city take water out of the South Platte River. Each ditch is tapped at many points and the water carried in smaller ditches to the fields below it. If necessary, the fields are leveled and still smaller channels and furrows lead the water to the seeds and roots (A). In villages or parks the small ditches are so arranged as to water the roots of flowers, shrubs, and shade trees. 

In the early days of irrigation in the western part of our country a man might dig a ditch of his own to bring the river water to his farm. When population increased so many farmers needed water that it was best and most satisfactory for them to work together. Companies were formed to build dams to hold back the water of streams and form reservoirs or artificial lakes. The companies dug

The Reclamation Service. In 1902 

the government of the United States organized the Reclamation Service. It was to reclaim, or make useful for agriculture, more of the dry or arid lands. Under this plan the government finds a good location, or site, on a large river and builds a great dam. A site is a good one (1) if the valley is narrow with a bottom solid enough to carry the weight of the dam; (2) if the subsoil or rock is not so porous as to let the water seep through under the dam; (3) if the land back of the dam is so shaped that a large lake or reservoir can be formed; and (4) if the lands below the dam have such R. You must not think that citizens of all the states are taxed to furnish water to western farmers. The money for this work was raised from the sale of public lands in the states where it is now spent for irrigation. The farmers who buy the land and use the water must pay back to the government, in several installments, the cost of the improvements. The money is then used to make similar improvements in other dry regions.

Life in Irrigated Regions. As a usual thing farmers who make use of irrigation do not have large farms. All of a man's time is taken up in work on a few acres. 

He finds that it pays him to cultivate his land with great care, because irrigated farms can be made to yield large crops. 

Where many small farms get their water from the same canal the farmers live as near neighbors, almost as in a village. Schools, churches, and stores can be built near all the people. Life in irrigated regions has many comforts and advantages that cannot be had by those who are scattered on the large farms of the prairies and on the ranches of the 

Great Plains.

Dry Farming. In some parts of the

Great Plains and in other parts of the West where there was not enough rain, farmers at first tried to raise crops in the usual way. Too often, however, their crops failed, and the farms were given up. 

In dry farming there are four important things to do: (1) The ground is plowed before the rainy season so that as much rain as possible will soak into the soil, and as little rain as possible will flow off the surface. (2) The surface or top layer of the soil is cultivated frequently. 

This is to prevent the loss of much moisture from the soil by evaporation. (3) Such crops are raised as need the least moisture for their successful growth. 

An example is found in some kinds of wheat, first grown in this country from seed that was brought here from dry countries. (4) Sometimes it is best to grow only one crop in two years, but to keep the soil cultivated so as to prevent much evaporation. Thus the farmer has what is left of two years' rainfall for the use of the plants in one year. 

Do not think that the Great Plains region is the only one in our country where farming by irrigation and dry farming are carried on. As you study the 

Plateau and Pacific States, you will learn of other very large regions where one or both of these methods are in use. They are described here because you need to know about them if you are to understand how the industries of the Great Plains are changing.

The Black Hills. The Black Hills are a group of rugged mountains in the western part of South Dakota. Part of the region is covered with a forest which has been made a forest reserve by the government of the United States. Gold and other minerals are mined, but the region as a whole is thinly settled. 

Other Minerals of the Great Plains.

Both oil and coal are found in the Great Plains (map, page 141). The chief oil fields are in Wyoming in a district north of Casper. The largest of these fields has been named the Teapot 

Dome district. Other deposits are found along a small river called Salt Creek.

THE COTTON BELT 

Turn to the map on page 88. Find the two state groups called the South 

Atlantic States and the South Central

States. Larger maps of these groups will be found on pages 128-129 and 131.

They include that part of our country where one crop has been so important for many years that people speak of it as the land where "Cotton is King."

Where Cotton Is Grown. - Map A 

shows where cotton is grown in the United 

States. You will see that it is raised chiefly in the southeastern part of our country. It is the chief crop, or one of the chief crops, over a broad stretch of country from Virginia to Texas. It is grown in the drier parts of the Coastal Plain, and it is a great crop in the Piedmont region in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. The cottongrowing region includes most of Alabama and Mississippi, large parts of Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, and some of Louisiana and Tennessee.

The map shows that very little cotton is grown in Florida or in the hot and 

2.000 bales swampy lowlands of other South Atlantic

States. It grows well in the Mississippi lowlands, except in the swamps of Louisiana. It is not grown in the dry highlands of Oklahoma and western Texas or in the cool highlands of Tennessee. 

Cotton needs a warm climate but not great heat. It needs a growing season of about 200 to 240 days. During its growing season it needs rain every few days, and it must have an annual rainfall of not less than 23 inches if the fields are not watered by irrigation. What is the annual rainfall in the different parts of the cotton-growing region? (Map B, page 84.) While the cotton is ripening and being harvested, it needs weather that is bright and sunny. If there is too much rain at that time, the bolls decay. 

For its best growth cotton needs a fine, rich, well-drained soil that can be easily worked. Such soils are found in the coastal plains and in the Mississippi lowlands. A region of rich black loam in Alabama and Mississippi, called the "black belt," and another region in Texas, called the "black waxy prairie," are especially fine cotton soils. Texas raises more cotton than any other state. 

A. Cotton-producing regions of the United States.

Cotton Growers. Cotton is raised on large farms or plantations whose owners are called planters.

Many planters rent parts of their plantation to farmers who wish to raise cotton but have no land of their own. 

Farmers who rent land may own tools and farm animals or they may not. 

If they do not, they depend

THE COTTON BELT 

133 A.- Cotton field in Oklahoma. Notice the large white bolls of cotton, ready to be picked. Cotton is the chief crop of this farm, although in the adjoining field there are farm animals. on the planter for mules and tools and for whatever else is necessary. In each case the rent to be paid is agreed upon and it is usually paid in cotton when the cotton is picked. Some part of the rented land is generally planted to food crops for the farmer and his family and for any farm animals he may have. 

Among these renting farmers there are both white men and Negroes.

There are many farmers who own small farms on which cotton is the chief crop. 

They also grow food crops and keep some farm animals. 

How Cotton Is Grown. Cotton is grown each year from seed. In the southern part of the cotton-growing region planting begins as early as February. In the northern part the seeds may not be planted until early April. Why is the planting done later there? 

About three months after the seeds are planted, the plant has grown and is covered with blossoms. As the blossoms drop off, seed pods, called bolls, are formed. The fine white fiber or lint that we call cotton grows on the seeds inside these bolls. As the bolls ripen they open, and fluffy masses of white fiber burst out (B). B. Cotton bolls, nearly the actual size. The fibers are from inch to 14 inches long.

PRESS & BARGES CYPRESS Courtesy Mobile Chamber of Commerce 

A. - Bargeloads of cotton brought down a river of Alabama to the port of Mobile for export. Barges of this size will each carry hundreds of bales of cotton. How much does a bale weigh? 

Every year great damage is done to the cotton crop of our country by the boll weevil. This is a beetle that punctures the flower buds and the young bolls and lays its eggs in them. The grubs that develop from the eggs cause the buds to drop from the plant and ruin the fiber in the bolls. No way of completely preventing this damage has yet been found. 

How Cotton Is Harvested. The bolls do not all open at the same time. For this reason cotton pickers must go over the field several times. In southern 

Texas the picking may be kept up until late into December if the bolls continue to ripen. Most cotton picking is still done by hand, although some cottonpicking machines are now being used.

The cotton is then taken to a gin house, where it is run through a machine called a cotton gin, which separates the lint from the seeds. The cotton gin was invented by Eli Whitney in 1793. Before that time the lint was pulled from the seed by hand. It was a very slow and expensive way of doing this work, and the result was that no very great amount of cotton was grown. Now, by using the gin, the cost of preparing the crop for market is so much less that cotton is grown in great quantities. It is the fiber most used in the making of cloth. Our country grows more than half of all the world crop. 

More than half of the workers in this industry are Negroes. 

Marketing the Cotton. After the lint is separated from the seeds it is pressed into bales of about 500 pounds each and in this form it is sent to market. It may go to cotton mills in or near the state in which it was raised. It may go to England or some other foreign country. It may be sent north to mills in the northern part of our own country. Savannah and Charleston on the Atlantic coast, and 

Galveston, Houston, New Orleans, and

Mobile on the Gulf coast, are ports from which cotton is shipped.

THE COTTON BELT 

135 A. 

Cotton mill on the Fall Line near Columbus, Georgia. Notice the great size of both buildings. This mill employs nearly 3000 people.

Formerly cotton growers saved only enough seeds for the next year's crop and threw the rest away. Then it was found that if the seeds were hulled and crushed they could be used as a fertilizer or as a food for cattle. Today the seeds are hulled, ground, and then pressed to get the oil that they contain. The hulls and the seed cake or meal that is left are sold as cattle food in our own country, Canada, and several European countries. 

Cottonseed oil has many uses. It is made into a substance like lard much used in cooking. It is used as a substitute for olive oil, it is burned in miners' lamps, and it is used in making fine soaps. 

For a long time the southern states were growers of cotton, but had no mills for making cotton cloth. The cotton was used in the mills of New England and other northern states or sold to foreign buyers. In recent years many cotton factories have been built in the South. 

These modern mills are among the finest in our country (A). The southern mills now use more bales of cotton than are sent to the New England factories.

There are many of these great cotton factories in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. They have been built in the Piedmont and along the Fall Line, partly because the falls in the rivers furnish water power.

The cotton grower has a great advantage in marketing his crop because it does not spoil quickly. The grower of small fruits and vegetables in Florida and elsewhere must market his crops at once. Crops of that kind spoil quickly after they ripen and must be sold even if the selling price is less than the cost of raising the crop.

What becomes of all the cotton goods that are made in the factories of our own and other countries? In the hot parts of the world most of the clothing of millions of people is made from cotton cloth. 

Even in cooler countries such as our own, cotton cloth is used for much of the clothing worn. Clothing factories use fine cotton cloth in the manufacture of men's shirts and underclothing and for dainty dresses and trimmings. Men's overalls and working dresses for women are made of the heavier kinds of cotton goods. 

Cotton is used also for window hangings, for bed sheets, and for many other things.

A. Cultivating young cotton plants. For best results, much cultivation is needed.

In the days when our country was first settled the colonists were forced to make much of their own cloth, and their own and their own clothing. At first there was no cotton. 

Linen and wool were the fibers chiefly used. 

These were twisted into threads by using a spinning wheel, and the threads were woven into cloth on hand looms. Every housewife was kept busy making cloth and clothing to meet the household needs. 

Modern methods of manufacture have made it possible for much of this work to be done in great factories.

OTHER CROPS OF THE COTTON 

BELT For many years most southern farmers raised nothing to sell but cotton and a little corn. Cotton was king. Year after year the same crops were planted in the same fields (A). Little by little these plants took from the soil the plant food that they needed. It finally was necessary to return food to the soil by using fertilizers. This made it more expensive to raise the cotton, but the farmers could sell their cotton for money and they needed a money crop. For that reason they continued to raise cotton. In recent years, however, they have also raised other important crops to sell. 

Mixed Farming. When the boll weevil began to damage the cotton crop, many of the southern farmers turned to mixed farming. In mixed farming the land is not used every year for the same crop. One crop may be planted for a year or more, and then followed by a different crop that does not use the same kind and amount of plant food. With this changing or rotation of crops the soil does not wear out so quickly and it is not necessary to use so much fertilizer.

Many southern farmers who still raise cotton and corn also raise hogs and beef cattle and the crops needed for their food. 

On many dairy farms in the northern part of our country the farmers raise corn and cut up the ears and stalks for the silo. This gives the cattle a good winter food when the pastures are covered with snow. The southern farmers also raise corn for their live stock, but the growing season is longer and most of the crop is left standing until the ears have ripened.

OTHER CROPS OF THE COTTON BELT 

137 The ripe corn is fed to the poultry, beef cattle, horses, and mules, and is used to fatten hogs. Sometimes the whole ear is given to the animal. At other times the kernels of corn are taken from the ear and fed as shelled corn, or the shelled corn is ground before it is fed. 

Other crops used as food for farm animals are peanuts, cow peas, velvet beans, soy beans, and sweet potatoes. Some farmers feed both the nuts and the vines of the peanut plants to their farm animals. 

Others sell the peanuts and feed the animals the vines. On many farms the vines are cut as hay. On other farms the farmers turn their animals into the field to eat the vines or the cornstalks, after the peanuts or ears of corn have been gathered. Sweet potatoes are used chiefly as food by people, but they are also used to feed hogs that are to be fattened. 

Dairying is not one of the most important industries on southern farms. Usually a farmer will keep cows to supply his family with milk and cream, and there are dairies near southern cities. It is in the northern parts of our country that dairying is carried on most extensively. 

There you find the green pastures, clear spring water, and cool climate that are most favorable for this industry. 

Orchards. - Peaches are grown in many parts of the South. They ripen early and are ready for market long before those grown in northern orchards. The best of the southern peaches are famous for their size and quality. More peaches are grown in Georgia than in any other southern state. The raising of pecans has become an important industry in the South. Groves of pecan trees are under cultivation along the Gulf coast and as far north as South Carolina.

A.-Packing peaches for shipment in central Georgia. 

In the extreme southern part of Texas there is a subtropical region in which vegetables, oranges, and grapefruit are raised in large quantities for sale in northern markets. 

Special Crops. - Tobacco is one of the valuable crops raised in several southern states. There is a wheat-growing region in western Texas and Oklahoma, and in some of the higher and drier parts of Texas and Oklahoma kafir corn is raised as a cattle food. The chief wheatgrowing section of the United States is in the states of the Mississippi Valley, but some wheat is raised in many other states. Sugar cane and rice are important crops in certain states drained by the Mississippi; but before studying them you should read something about the great Mississippi lowland. 

The Mississippi River. Starting at the mouth of the Mississippi River (map, page 83) follow it north to its source in 

Lake Itasca. As you go up the stream notice where it is joined by the Ohio River on the east and the Missouri River on the west. These two streams are the largest tributaries of the Mississippi. On the east the Ohio and its branches drain a large part of the Appalachian Highlands.

On the west the Missouri and its tribu- | flows rapidly it can carry along the rock waste that its tributaries bring to it. As the slope of its bed decreases and it moves less swiftly, it must drop a part of its load. taries drain parts of the Western Highlands. Through these and other tributaries the Mississippi receives also the drainage of much of the central lowlands. 

The lower Mississippi River is a very muddy stream. The "mud" in the water is really very, very fine particles of rock material or earth. Some of it comes from streams whose waters flow so swiftly that the stones in their beds are bumped or rubbed against each other.

In this way large stones are broken into smaller pieces. The rough and broken edges are worn off, and after a long, long time the stones themselves are worn away. Much of this rock material is washed into the rivers from the valley slopes that border them. This happens when there are heavy rains in the valley, or when the snow that covered the hillsides in the winter melts in the spring. 

At these times every gully in the fields and on the hillsides and every gutter by the roadside will be filled with muddy water rushing toward the nearest river.

From stream to stream this muddy water passes until at last it reaches the Mississippi, the "Father of Waters."

In thinking of the rock waste that the 

Mississippi carries, keep these facts in mind: (1) It comes from all parts of the 

Mississippi drainage basin. It is made up of particles of many kinds of rocks and should make a fine and fertile soil. (2) Streams that flow swiftly can carry a greater amount, or load, than streams that flow slowly. A stream moving swiftly among the hills can carry more than one of the same size winding a lazy way through the plains. (3) Large streams can carry a greater load than small streams. So long as the Mississippi 

Floods. Over most of the region drained by the Ohio River the average annual rainfall varies from 40 to 60 inches. 

Sometimes large parts of this drainage area will have unusually heavy or longcontinued rains. When this happens, the smaller highland streams change suddenly from pleasant brooks into rushing, roaring torrents. They pour their water into the larger branches. These increase suddenly in size, flooding the lowlands and hurrying on to the Ohio itself. 

The same thing may happen when heavy winter snows in the higher or more northerly parts of the Ohio drainage area melt suddenly in the spring. In either case the lower lands along the Ohio are flooded. These flood waters flow on to join the Mississippi and cause it to overflow its banks also. Heavy rains or melting snow in other parts of the Mississippi drainage area may cause floods, but it is from the Ohio that the great river receives most of its flood waters. 

Lowlands border the Mississippi from the mouth of the Ohio to the Gulf. In times of very high water hundreds of square miles may be flooded and great damage done. Buildings and live stock are swept away and crops ruined, and even some of the people may be drowned. 

The United States Weather Bureau has flood stations on the Ohio, the Mississippi, and many other rivers. Men at these stations send out flood warnings when the rivers begin to rise. This usually gives the people time to do what they can to save their property.

A.-Levee on the Mississippi River, in Louisiana. Notice how low the water is. At times of high water the river will rise almost as high as the levee. The pipes crossing the levee carry water for irrigation. 

Levees. - During floods the rivers are large, they flow swiftly, and they carry much rock waste. As soon as the rain 

As soon as the rain stops and the snow is melted, the flood waters begin to go down. The water in the river moves more slowly. It can no longer carry its load of rock waste. The larger and heavier particles are dropped first, and then, as the water moves more and more slowly, finer particles also are dropped. 

When rivers overflow their banks more of the rock waste is dropped on the part of the flood plain that borders the river than in any other part. Because of this the banks of the river are built higher than those parts of the flood plain farther away from the stream. This means that when a stream overflows these built-up banks, the lower country beyond them is sure to be flooded. 

To keep rivers from overflowing their bordering lowlands in times of high water men sometimes build high embankments called levees (A). Many levees have been built along the banks of the lower Mississippi. It is only when there is a break in a levee, or when the water rises above it, that the land protected by levees is flooded. flooded. But these floods are the worst of all. 

The Delta Lands. When a river flows into a lake or an ocean it is lost in the larger body of quiet water. It then drops the remaining rock waste it has been carrying. This is true of the Mississippi where it enters the Gulf of Mexico. 

A long, long time ago the Gulf of

Mexico reached far up the Mississippi Valley. During all of the years since that time rock waste that reached the mouth of the river has been filling this ancient bay. It has now been completely filled and the land made from the rock waste is pushing forward into the Gulf.

The river deposits so much of this rock waste that it almost blocks itself, and divides into smaller streams. streams. These smaller streams are building their banks into the Gulf. Notice them on the map (page 129). They are like the fingers of a great hand. This river-made land of the lower Mississippi is its delta. Perhaps you were in the class that last year took

an imaginary journey to the hot sunny land of Egypt in Africa. If you were, you will remember that the great river of Egypt also has a delta at its mouth. 

Can you give the name of this river?

The Mississippi delta lands are low and so far south that they have a hot climate. 

In parts of these delta lands there are swamps. In other parts there are forests. In still other parts the land is dry enough so crops can be grown. The hot climate, the fertile delta soils, and the long growing season make it possible to raise both sugar cane and rice. 

Sugar. Nearly all the sugar cane in the United States is raised in Louisiana, although a small amount is grown in Georgia and other states of the far South. 

Sugar cane needs a growing season of eight months or longer. What parts of the United States have a growing season of that length? (Map A, page 84.) The cane grows like a very large and very tall grass (A). 

The stems are from 10 to 16 feet high and from a half inch to over two inches thick.

A.-Young sugar cane.

When the cane is ripe, the leaves are stripped off and the cane is cut close to the ground. Then it is taken to a mill where it is crushed between rollers to squeeze out the sweet juice from which sugar is made.

Nearly all the sugar of the world was at one time made from cane, and much of our present supply still comes from the same source. Some years ago it was found that sugar can be made from certain kinds of beets. You will learn later about the sugar-beet-growing sections of our country. You will learn also about a kind of sugar that is made from the sap of maple trees. 

Rice. Louisiana leads all the states in raising rice, as it does in growing sugar cane. Nearly half of the rice grown in our country comes from this state. 

The best kinds of rice are grown on flat lands. During a part of the growing period the rice fields must be flooded.

This is usually done two or three times after the rice is planted. There is much level land in Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas that can be flooded by pumping water into ditches that will carry it over the fields. These lands are excellent for growing rice. The soil is fine and fertile. 

The fields can be flooded when necessary, and it is easy to drain them so they will be dry during the harvesting of the crop. 

When rice is ripe, it is harvested and threshed in much the same way as other grains. The rice grain has a clinging hull or outside coat which is then removed by a machine before the grain is ready for use. In our country most people like rice that has also been polished. The polishing removes a brownish coating of great food value, and gives the rice grain the dull white look of a pearl.

MINERAL AND OTHER PRODUCTS OF THE SOUTHLAND 

On the map on pages 128-129 find the states of Louisiana, Texas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas. In addition to the great crops grown there, these states have also some very valuable mineral resources about which you should learn. Among them are petroleum, sulphur, and salt. The map on this page shows where the chief deposits are located. 

Petroleum and Natural Gas. Notice on the map two of the regions producing petroleum. One of these borders the 

Gulf of Mexico in Texas and Louisiana.

The other, by far the largest and most productive, stretches from central Texas eastward into Louisiana and Arkansas, and northward through Oklahoma into Kansas. This region is known as the mid-continent field.

A. - Oil wells in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. The skeleton towers are called derricks. One is built over each well, for use in drilling the well. You will see from the number of derricks that a great many wells have been drilled. 

They are so close together because each land owner has the right to drill wells. In the open country the wells would be farther apart. Notice also the many round tanks for storing the oil. 

Deep in the earth, underneath the fields and the cities, are layers of rock in which the petroleum is found. This rock is usually a sandstone in which there are very small openings between the fine particles of sand. It is in these spaces and in any larger openings in the rock that petroleum and natural gas gather.

When natural gas is present, it is at the top because it is lighter than the oil. 

Petroleum is a thick, heavy oil of a very dark brown color. To get it holes are 

To get it holes are | drilled down to the rock containing the oil, and pipes are pushed into the holes. 

Through these the oil may be pumped in much the same way that water is pumped from deep wells (A). Many oil wells do not need to be pumped at first. In those wells as soon as the drilling is finished the gas and oil come out with a rush that carries them many feet into the air. Such a well is a "gusher," and sometimes a great deal of oil is lost before the well is capped and brought under control. 

B.-Tank cars in Oklahoma, used for shipping oil.

Both natural gas and petroleum are very valuable. The gas is sent from the wells through pipes buried in the ground to homes and business places in many parts of our country where it is used for heating and lighting. The petroleum is sent to refineries where it is purified and made into many products, including fuel oil, gasoline, kerosene, and oils and greases for all kinds of machinery. 

Some of the crude oil is shipped by rail to refineries or to seaports in great tank cars (142 B). At one time this was the usual way of shipping the oil. Now there are many pipes reaching over our country from the wells to refining centers, markets, and ports on the Gulf of Mexico, the 

Great Lakes, and the Atlantic Ocean (A).

The oil is pumped through these pipes from one pumping station to another until it reaches the refinery or port. 

Courtesy Natural Gas Pipelines of America B.-Laying a pipe line. 

put together so well that there is rarely any loss of oil through leaks or breaks. 

Refining and Distributing. The refining is done by heating the oil in tanks or stills so as to separate it into its different products. From the refineries the petroleum products go by train to large wholesale centers for distribution to retailers. Such fluid products as fuel oil, road oil, kerosene, and gasoline go to wholesalers in tank cars, but some of the gasoline is pumped through pipe lines.

These pipes, like the pipes carrying natural gas, are usually buried a few feet in the ground so they will be out of the way (B). They cross plains for long distances in almost straight lines. They cross hills and wind their way along valleys. Wherever they go, the pipes Casper Kansas Chicago

Growth of Population in the Petroleum 

Fields. The discovery of oil usually means wealth for those who own the land and for many of the producers. It also means growth and prosperity for the villages and cities in an oil district.

They are no longer mere trading centers for the farming region around them. As workmen connected with the oil industry move in, it becomes necessary to meet their needs for food, clothing, and homes. 

More houses are built. More and larger stores are needed. Population increases as the oil and other industries prosper.

Among the oil-refining cities in the 

South Central States are Beaumont and 

Port Arthur. These cities have also become ports from which much oil is shipped. Tulsa in Oklahoma is the chief oil center in the mid-continent field. 

Other centers of the oil industry include Muskogee and Oklahoma City in Oklahoma, Fort Worth in Texas (A), and 

Shreveport and Baton Rouge in Louisiana. Find all these cities on the map, pages 128-129. 

Oklahoma City owes its growth and importance chiefly to the prosperity of the state of Oklahoma, which is largely due to the oil industry. This city is the capital of the state and its chief railroad and trading center. 

Sulphur. Along the Gulf coast of

Texas there is a region of lowland where there are beds of sulphur at depths of 

500 to 1500 feet. Sulphur is a yellow rocklike mineral for which there are many uses. Among these are its use in the manufacture of wood pulp, in making rubber goods, as a bleach for whitening cloth and other materials, in the manufacture of some medicines, and in making sprays to kill insects on trees and plants.

Most of the sulphur that the world now uses comes from Texas. In mining it wells are drilled and pipes are sunk to the sulphur beds. Four pipes are put down in a well, each one of the smaller pipes being inside the one next in size. The largest pipe is usually 10 inches in diameter. This rests on top of the sulphur deposit. The first inside pipe is 6 inches in diameter; it is used for forcing hot water into the sulphur deposit. The next pipe, of 3 inches, is to carry melted sulphur up, and the smallest pipe, 1 inch, is to carry compressed air down.

Water, hot enough to melt the sulphur, is pumped down into the sulphur bed. 

The melted sulphur is forced up to the surface by means of compressed air. 

There it is run off into large wooden tanks to cool and harden. A great block of almost pure sulphur is built up inside the

tank. This block of sulphur can then be broken into small pieces for shipment (A). 

Salt. There are vast deposits of salt underneath the surface of Louisiana and Texas. No one knows just how large these deposits are, but it is known that they are of great size. They have been found below the sulphur beds and elsewhere. 

This rock salt is very pure and white. 

It is taken out in blocks that are brought to the surface and crushed. Whenever it becomes necessary, wooden supports are put in the mines, or pillars of salt are left to hold up the roof (B). The white ceilings, walls, and floors of the great rooms that are left when the salt has been partly removed are very beautiful to see. 

Salt is prepared in different forms for different uses. You all know about the fine white salt that we use to season our food. Salt is used also in packing meat and fish to keep them from spoiling, and in curing hides. It is used in the manufacture of washing soda, bleaching powders, and many chemical preparations.

It is used in the glass and soap industries and in making glaze and enamels.

Other Minerals of the Region. 

number of other minerals are found in the 

South Atlantic and South Central States. 

The more important ones will be taken up for study when you come to the natural regions in which they are found. 

Among them are coal, iron ore, and limestone in West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Alabama.

In Georgia and Tennessee there are quarries (C) from which beautiful marble is taken. The blocks of marble are shaped and polished and sent to different parts of our country to be used in fine buildings.

A.-A bauxite deposit in Arkansas. How large are the cars in the train shown here? 

Bauxite, the clay mineral from which aluminum is made, is found in central 

Arkansas and in Tennessee. Arkansas has in some years produced half of the world's supply of bauxite (A). A loose and crumbly rock material called phosphate rock is found in Tennessee and in 

Florida. The Florida deposits are the largest in the world. The rock is dug with a steam shovel, after the surface soil has been removed. It is then washed and ground. It is used alone, or with nitrate and potash, as a fertilizer. 

The The Forests of the Southland. 

southern pine grows on the coastal plains all the way from North Carolina to Texas.

It furnishes an excellent building lumber much used for interior woodwork and for other purposes.

Many of the pine trees are tapped to get their sap. From this sap turpentine, pitch, tar, and rosin are made. 

These are called naval stores. Years ago, when nearly all ships were made of wood, the pitch and tar were used to make them water-tight. Since that time they have been used for many other purposes, but the name naval stores is still used. 

The cypress is another southern softwood tree. It grows chiefly in swampy regions (B). Its lumber has a straight grain and is very easily worked. It is used in the construction of wooden or frame buildings for shingles and outside walls, and for doors, window frames, and other purposes on the inside of buildings. Cypress will not quickly decay in contact with the earth, and is therefore used for fence posts. Some of the finer wood is used for musical instruments and chests. 

In addition to the pine and cypress forests of the South there are large areas where most of the trees are hardwoods. 

These areas include the southern Appalachians; northern Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi; most of Kentucky and

Tennessee; and parts of Oklahoma and 

Texas. These regions are higher than the Atlantic and Gulf lowlands and have a cooler climate and better drainage. 

In the pine forests railroads are built into the region where the trees are to be cut down. Machines pile the logs on flat cars, which are then hauled to the larger mills. Sometimes portable mills are used; that is, mills that can be moved.

In the cypress swamps many of the largest and best trees grow where there are no railroads to handle them. Cypress logs are therefore bound together and floated to some place where there is a mill or a railroad leading to a mill. 

Memphis in Tennessee is on a high bluff overlooking the Mississippi River. Across the river is Arkansas, and just to the south is Mississippi. These states have extensive forests. Ships can reach Memphis from the Gulf, and the city has many railroads. It has become one of the chief lumber markets of our country, especially for hardwoods. Its factories make many articles of wood, including such products as doors, window sashes and frames, window blinds, floor boards, and stairs.

The manufacture of articles made from wood is carried on in so many of the cities and villages in the South that they cannot all be named here. Shreveport in Louisiana and Fort Smith in Arkansas are lumber-manufacturing centers.

Lumber is shipped from many ports on the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. Among the more important are Mobile, Alabama; 

Savannah, Georgia; Jacksonville and 

Tampa, Florida; Charleston, South 

Carolina; and Wilmington, North Carolina. Much lumber is sent to market by railroad.

Furs in Louisiana. One other industry in the South must be mentioned because it is so unexpected. When you think of furs it is natural to think of the cold countries, for many fur-bearing animals live only in such countries. some fur animals, chiefly muskrats, live along the marshlands and in the network of waters through the delta lowlands of 

Louisiana. Besides muskrats there are minks, skunks, otters, foxes, raccoons, and opossums. Thousands of men make their living by trapping. The furs taken each year are worth millions of dollars.

CITIES OF THE SOUTH CENTRAL STATES 

The rapid growth of industry in the South has increased the importance of a large number of cities in the South Central States. Among the factors that have helped in this increase are the shipping of cotton, the development of the oil areas of Texas and adjoining states, the development of water power, and the increase in manufacturing. 

New Orleans, the Gateway to the 

South. New Orleans, the largest city of the South Central States, is a most interesting city. It is on the Mississippi 

River about 100 miles from its mouth. 

It is often called the "Crescent City' because its southern part lies in a bend of the river (A). There is one part of the old city where descendants of the early 

Spanish and French settlers still live.

There the houses, the narrow streets, the languages that you hear spoken, and the quaint customs make you feel almost as if you were in a foreign city. 

New Orleans has more than fifty miles of water front for shipping. Most of the wharves are on the river, but the city also fronts on Lake Pontchartrain. A canal and an inner harbor join the Mississippi and Lake Pontchartrain. This inner harbor is large enough for ocean-going vessels. The city stands on low ground, while levees more than twenty feet high keep back the flood waters of the river.

149 YO A. - Unloading bananas. The belt conveyer is lifting the bananas from the ship's hold. Many bananas are brought into the country through New Orleans. 

New Orleans carries on a river trade with cities on the Mississippi as far north as St. Paul, with cities on the Ohio as far as Pittsburgh, and up the Missouri as far as Kansas City (map, page 87). The rivers are not much used by passenger steamers now. Railroads, motor busses, and airplanes give much faster service.

Some kinds of heavy freight are sent by the river route because they can be carried much more cheaply by boat. Coal barges from the Pittsburgh district are tied together and pushed by a "towboat all the way to New Orleans. Cargoes of wheat, cotton, lumber, and tobacco form part of the freight carried by these river steamboats (B). 99 Since the great ship canal was cut across the Isthmus of Panama a ship can go from New Orleans to ports on the Pacific Ocean as easily as it can to ports on the Atlantic. Because of this,

New Orleans has become an even more important shipping center for the products of the Gulf lowlands and for those of the Mississippi Valley. 

B. Towboat with freight barges on the Mississippi 

River, near Memphis, Tennessee. A railroad train to carry this amount of freight would be about a mile long. 

From New Orleans railroads lead north over the plains to great cities and railroad centers. Other railroads from New Orleans run eastward to the Atlantic and westward to the Pacific coast. Because of the river and ocean trade and the railroads, New Orleans has become the southern gateway of the United States, as New York is the eastern gateway.

Other Cities of Louisiana. - About 100 

miles up the Mississippi from New Orleans is Baton Rouge, the capital of Louisiana.

One of the greatest oil refineries of the world is in this city. In northwestern 

Louisiana is Shreveport, second in size among the cities of the state. It has oil refineries, lumber mills, and a large glass factory. Sand for the glass is found in

Arkansas, not far away, and close by is natural gas, the best fuel for making glass.

Galveston is one of the leading seaports of the United States. It stands on a low island at the mouth of Galveston Bay.

In the year 1900 a storm wave from the 

Gulf swept over the city and did terrible damage. Since that time the city has built a sea wall seventeen feet high and more than seven miles long to protect it from other storm waves in the future (A). 

You will remember that Texas raises more cotton than any other state. Much of this cotton is exported from Galveston. 

No other port in any land sends so much cotton to the mills of the world. Galveston also carries on an immense trade in other products. It ships an enormous amount of petroleum and petroleum products. It has great grain elevators and ships much wheat, because wheat from the great fields to the north can reach Galveston by rail more easily and cheaply than other ports. Several steamship lines run between Galveston and 

European ports.

About fifty miles northwest of Galveston is the city of Houston. It is on a small river that flows into Galveston Bay. 

This river has been enlarged into a ship canal wide enough and deep enough for ocean-going ships. Houston is the largest city in Texas, and since the ship canal was built it has become an important port. 

Pipe lines from the oil fields bring crude oil to its refineries. Other raw materials for its mills and factories come from Texas and near-by states. These raw materials include rice that must be hulled and polished, cotton seed from which the oil is to be pressed, and lumber for planing mills and woodworking shops. Railroads run into Houston like spokes to the hub of a wheel, and there are large car shops in the city. 

Galveston and Houston are twin ports.

So are Port Arthur and Beaumont. The 

Gulf oil field is not far away, and these cities form a natural center for the shipment of petroleum and its products.

Interior Cities of Texas. - Austin is the capital of Texas and the trade center for the southwestern and south-central parts of the state. It is a live-stock, wool, and cotton market. San Antonio, the oldest city in the state, is the center of a farming and live-stock region with growing manufactures and a large trade. 

Dallas is the principal shipping and financial center of Texas. It has a large trade in wheat, cotton, live stock, and meats. It manufactures leather goods, cotton gins, cottonseed oil, and agricultural tools. At Fort Worth, not far west of Dallas, there are stockyards and meatpacking establishments, car shops, and oil refineries (144 A).

El Paso is a health resort and a center of trade with Mexico. It is on the Rio 

Grande in the western part of the state. 

One hundred miles up the Rio Grande from El Paso is a great dam built by the 

United States government. The water held behind this dam is used for watering fields down the valley, where vegetables and tropical fruits are raised. 

Cities of Alabama. Near Florence, a small city in northwestern Alabama, the United States government has built a great hydroelectric power plant (A). 

This is on the Tennessee River, at a place where the river drops rapidly enough to give much water power. 

Mobile and Birmingham are the two chief cities of Alabama. Mobile (134 A) is a seaport and a place of trade and commerce; and Birmingham is a great city of iron works.

As Alabama has a share of the lumbering industry of the South, you may be sure that lumber will find its way to the wharves of Mobile. From this port cotton and lumber are sent to our Atlantic ports and to Europe.

Birmingham is close to the Great Appalachian Valley, where, at its southern end, it opens on the coastal plain. Birmingham is one of the cities in the Appalachian

Cities in the Lowlands of Tennessee and Kentucky. In central Tennessee there is a lowland region known as the "Nashville basin.' To the east, south, and west of it there are forested hill lands called the "Highland Rim." Underneath the basin lands the rocks are of limestone. As limestone decays it forms very fertile soil, and so the Nashville basin is a very rich farming country. It is a region of mixed farming, producing wheat, corn, and tobacco, and raising dairy cows, beef cattle, and hogs. 

The chief city of the Nashville basin is Nashville, the capital of the state and a railroad and trading center. Among its manufactures are furniture and other lumber products, flour and other food products, clothing, and knit goods.

Find Louisville, Lexington, and Frankfort on the map. These cities are in the Kentucky lowland that is bordered on the southeast by the Cumberland Plateau. This lowland has a rich soil because of the decay of the underlying limestone. It is an excellent agricultural district called the "Blue Grass" region from a kind of grass that grows in the pastures and meadows (A).

In this region you find fat cattle, sheep, and fine horses. It is also one of the great tobacco-growing regions in our country. 

Much corn is grown, and some wheat also, for the Blue Grass region is a region of mixed farming.

Louisville is the chief city of Kentucky. It was at first a very small settlement on the south bank of the Ohio River. At this point there were some rapids in the river. Boats could not pass these rapids, called the "Falls of the Ohio," and both passengers and freight were landed and transported around the falls. The navigation of the river has since been greatly improved. 

A canal has been built around the falls, and the transfer of goods and passengers is no longer necessary. Louisville early became a railroad center and, because of its manufacturing industries, it is of constantly increasing importance. It is now the marketing and manufacturing center for a large tobacco region. 

Because Louisville is a great railroad center it has shops in which railroad engines and cars are repaired. As you would expect in a region where many beef cattle, sheep, and hogs are raised or brought in from the west to be fattened, there are meat-packing plants. There are petroleum refineries using crude oil from near-by and more distant fields.

There are woodworking plants using lumber from near-by forests as well as other timber supplies. There are factories in which a variety of agricultural tools are manufactured and there are many machine shops and foundries.

One of the wonders of central Kentucky is the Mammoth Cave, one of the largest in the world. It was formed by waters from the earth's surface that made their way to underlying limestone rock and dissolved it. There are 150 miles of underground passages. There are subterranean (under the earth) rivers, many waterfalls, and great rooms with high ceilings.
