Atlantic Coastal Plain. - The Atlantic 

Coastal Plain includes a small part of 

New York, nearly two thirds of New

Jersey, a narrow strip in southeastern Pennsylvania, and a large part of the 

South Atlantic group. The plain is very flat, and is bordered on the ocean side by a gently sloping beach (A). The river valleys are not deep. From the coast the plain extends westward as far as the Fall Line. This long belt of lowland is called the Tidewater Country.

The lower parts of the rivers are tidal, and many of them flow into broad bays due to the sinking of the coast. Of such bays, the Chesapeake is the greatest. 

The Susquehanna, Potomac, and James rivers flow into it. The water at the entrance of the bay, in its main channels, and in its harbors is deep enough for ocean ships. 

Northeast of Chesapeake Bay, between 

New Jersey and Delaware, is Delaware 

Bay. Ocean-going ships use it and the tidal waters of the Delaware River to reach the port of Philadelphia. From the deep water of the bay to Philadelphia a channel 32 feet deep and 600 feet wide has been dredged, at a cost of many millions of dollars. Smaller boats are able to use the river as far as Trenton, New Jersey. 

South of Chesapeake Bay, indenting the mainland of North Carolina, are two large sounds, Albemarle and Pamlico (map, page 131). They are shallow and can be safely used only by small vessels. 

They are partly shut off from the ocean by a long chain of narrow, sandy barrier beaches, or outer shore lands, built up by the waves and winds. From these beaches a number of capes extend into the ocean. Near them the water is shallow and they are dangerous to large ships.

Farther to the south the bays are smaller, but they too are due to the sinking of the land. The rivers, such as the Savannah, allow the tides to come to the inner edge of the coastal plain. 

In a 

Swamps and Their Drainage. country so flat and so close to sea level as the part of the coastal plain bordering the 

Atlantic, there will usually be many swamps. The South Atlantic States have several that are very large. One of them is the famous Dismal Swamp (A), 30 miles long and 10 miles broad, in Virginia and North Carolina. A part of it has been drained, cleared, and used for farming.

A canal through the Dismal Swamp is one of several canals that join a number of natural water bodies into an inland waterway 2500 miles in length. This waterway is used by small ships trading along the Atlantic coast, for it is protected from the storms on the Atlantic. 

Another one of the great swamps of the 

Atlantic Coastal Plain is in Florida. This state has also many lakes, and because the lakes and swamps are both caused by the same conditions they are studied together.

The rainfall map on page 84 shows you that the rainfall of Florida is very heavy. 

As most of the state is only a few feet above sea level, the rain does not run off the surface of the land quickly. As a result there are over 30,000 lakes in 

Florida, and a larger number of swamps.

The underlying rocks of much of the 

Florida peninsula are limestone. Water soaks through the soil and dissolves the limestone in some places. The surface soil sinks into these limestone pockets or sink holes. Water fills them and forms a lake. Some of the lakes are connected by underground streams that flow through 

A.-In the Dismal Swamp, Virginia. the limestone rocks. Some underground streams come to the surface as springs. 

The largest lake in Florida is Lake Okeechobee, a shallow body of water, in which there are few places with a greater depth than 15 feet. Connecting with this lake on the south and southeast is the great swamp region known as the Everglades. Over some parts of the Everglades the water is almost deep enough to be called a lake. In the shallow waters there are many islands. They are covered with a dense growth of grass, underbrush, and trees. There is much saw grass, so named because of the sawlike teeth on its edges. In this region along the border of 

Lake Okeechobee, are some of the finest cypress trees in Florida. 

Part of the Everglades has been drained by a large canal cut to the sea, and smaller canals that connect with it. The work is very expensive. Land that has been drained has been settled, and crops of fruit, vegetables, and sugar cane are being grown on it. The raising of sugar on the drained lands of the Everglades may become a very important industry.

From Florida to New York along the

Atlantic Coast. At the southern end of 

Florida and extending in a great sweeping curve south and west are the Florida 

Keys. They are islands of coral rock and of sand made from the broken rock. 

Coral rock is made by the hard skeletons of tiny coral animals that live and die in warm ocean waters. Each living coral fastens itself to the rock, and when it dies, its skeleton is added to those of the corals that have lived and died before it. It took a long, long period of time for the skeletons of these coral animals to make the rocks of these islands. Part of the peninsula is made of the same kind of coral rock.

Sponge Fisheries. - Around the Flor ida Keys, at the southern end of the peninsula, and on the west coast, many men are engaged in the sponge fisheries. 

Sponges are the soft skeletons of small animals that live in warm salt water, where they fasten themselves to rocks on the bottom of the sea. In shallow water men gather them by using a pole with a hook on the end with which to tear the sponges loose from the rocks where they grow in clusters. In deeper waters men go down in diving suits and cut the sponges from the rocks. Each wears a water-tight suit and helmet, and air is pumped to him through a rubber tube. 

From what you have just read you know that coral animals and sponges only grow in warm ocean waters. You know, therefore, that the waters around Florida must be warm at all seasons of the year. To understand why this is so you should know why there is such a difference in the climate of countries that are near the poles, and that of countries that are near the Equator. 

Climate. When you think about the climate of a place you should have three things in mind: (1) the temperature, (2) the rainfall, and (3) the prevailing or usual winds.

In the northern parts of our country the winter is the cold season. It is then that the snow comes and people stay indoors more than at other seasons of the year. 

Spring follows and, especially in the lowlands, it begins to get warmer. If there is enough rain, the grass starts to grow, leaves come on the trees and shrubs, fruit trees and flowering shrubs put out their blossoms, and crops are planted. Summer is the hot season. mer is the hot season. Crops are growing and must be cultivated. This is the time for many picnics, hikes, and outdoor sports, and many kinds of outdoor work. 

In the fall it begins to get colder. The late crops are gathered. The leaves of the hardwoods change their color and are later blown from their branches. Winter comes on once more.

In the far south, and especially in southern Florida, the seasons are different. The summers are hot, but the winters are also warm. One reason for this is that Florida is much nearer the Equator than the states in the northern part of our country. There is, for example, a difference of 20 degrees of latitude between northern New York and southern Florida (map, page 87). 

At sea level, as you go north or south from the Equator, the temperature is usually about one degree less for each degree of latitude. This is not true for all places and at all times, for there are many things that may influence the temperature of a place. It is, however, usually about true and it is a fact worth remembering in your study of geography.

Why should a difference in latitude make a difference in temperature? You must have noticed, wherever you live, that the higher the sun is in the sky the warmer it usually gets. The sun is higher in the sky at noon than it is early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

Usually it is warmer near noontime than it is in the morning or evening.

The sun is higher in the sky at noon in the summer time than it is at noon in the winter time. Usually midday in summer is much warmer than midday in winter.

So you can say that the higher the sun is in the sky the warmer it usually is. In 

Florida on any day in the year the sun is higher in the sky at noon than it is at the same time in places to the north. This is because of the difference in latitude.

On the map, just a little south of Florida, find an east-and-west line named the Tropic of Cancer. This tropic is 23 degrees north of the Equator. There is another tropic the same distance south of the Equator; it is named the Tropic of Capricorn. The part of our earth between these two tropics is called the tropical region or the Torrid Zone. The word torrid means "hot." Every place in the Torrid Zone has the sun directly overhead at noon sometime during the year.

Every place on the Tropic of Cancer has the sun directly overhead at noon on 

June 21. North of the Tropic of Cancer and south of the Tropic of Capricorn the sun is never directly overhead. Florida is so near the Tropic of Cancer that on 

June 21 the sun is nearly overhead at noon, and on every day in the year it is high in the sky. The climate of Florida is subtropical, which means "almost tropical." 

A second reason for difference in temperature between any two places may be because one place is higher above sea level than the other. Temperature usually decreases about one degree for each 

300 feet of increase in height. Most of Florida is level and only a little above the sea. There are no mountains in that state where people can go to get cool in the summer time as they can in other parts of our country.

Florida has a more even temperature throughout the year than places that are not near the ocean or some other large body of water. This is because winds blowing over land from the bordering waters are usually much warmer than the land in winter and cooler than the land in summer. Florida is so nearly surrounded by water that winds from almost any direction will modify its temperature in these ways.

Sometimes, but not often, there are severe frosts in northern and central Florida, when a cold wind drives into the state from the north. During most of the winter, when high mountains and the northern parts of our country are covered with snow, southern Florida is a land of sunshine and flowers. For this reason many people who do not like the cold northern winter spend that season in Florida.

Florida is a region of heavy rainfall. 

The heaviest rainfall comes during the months from June to mid-September. 

Once in a while violent windstorms called hurricanes sweep in from the ocean and cause considerable damage. They generally come in late summer or early fall. 

Some parts of the state have more than 60 inches of rainfall in a year, and every part has more than 50 inches.

more. 

Crops. - Because there are not many frosts, even in winter, the growing season in Florida is much longer than it is in the northern part of our country (84 A).

In central Florida it lasts for 300 days or In most parts of New York state, for example, it lasts from 120 to 190 days. 

Because of the high temperature, heavy rainfall, and long growing season, the trees and some of the crops of Florida are different from those that grow in cooler or less rainy regions. 

Notice the size of the fruit, and the size of the trees. 

Among the forest trees the southern pine is cut for its rather coarse-grained lumber, much used for floors and interior trim. It is very different from the finegrained white pine of northern forests.

Other Florida trees are the live oak, cy- A.-Picking grapefruit in Florida. press, and palmetto. Among the trees of 

Florida are some that grow in regions that are nearly frost-free. The palm trees are beautiful and graceful. The cabbage palms are found in the central and southern parts of the state, but the splendid royal palm and the coconut palm are found only in the south. 

Florida raises oranges, lemons, limes, and grapefruit (A). These citrus fruits, as they are called, cannot be successfully grown in the northern states because a hard frost kills citrus fruit trees. Even in Florida orchards of this kind are planted only where there are few frosts. 

When frosts threaten, oil or coal fires are kept burning in the orchards until the danger is past. They can raise the temperature of the air four or five degrees.

The pineapple is another warm-country fruit that is grown in Florida. 

Truck Farming on the Atlantic Coast. - One of the large industries of the coastal region is truck farming. In most of the truck-growing regions the farmers plant their first crop after the frosts of spring and gather their last crop before the frosts of the fall. The land is under cultivation during almost all of the growing season and the truck farmers are able to raise two or more crops on the same land in one season. 

Most of the vegetables and fruits raised by truck farmers are for sale in the larger cities, especially in the northern cities.

There they bring high prices during the winter months. The first to reach these markets come from southern Florida, a subtropical region usually free from frost during the whole year. Some vegetables and fruits from Florida will be found on sale in northern cities before the end of 

February or early in March. 

Along the Atlantic coast the length of the growing season decreases toward the north. The farther north you go the later it will be in the year that the first crops ripen. Vegetables and fruits of Georgia follow those from Florida.

U.S. Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Plant Industry 

A. A well-tended strawberry field in Florida. There are several hundred plants in each row. 

These are followed by the crops of South Carolina, North Carolina, and so on north to New Jersey and Long Island. Before the last of the northern crops have been gathered, the second crops from the far 

South will be coming into the market.

As a result people in the North may have some fresh vegetables and fruits at any season of the year.

This succession of crops from south to north and back to the south again includes peas, beans, celery, lettuce, cabbages, melons, tomatoes, strawberries (A), and many others. When the crops are being harvested, every available worker is kept busy, young and old alike. Many of these crops are so perishable that they must be rushed to market. Fast trains with cars kept at a proper temperature, or ships which make a quick voyage, are used. There are times when loading platforms of railroad freight houses and steamship piers are crowded with crates and baskets of vegetables waiting to be shipped.

The sandy soils of the coastal plain are easily worked, but they are not suited to all crops. 

Grass, corn, and wheat will not grow well on them. They are much better for raising vegetables. That is why this long stretch of sandy soils from Florida to Long Island has become a vast truck-raising region. Even in raising vegetables it is necessary to use fertilizers to furnish the plants a part of their food. 

Each truck farmer selects the crops that he believes will grow best on his land. In some regions most of the truck farmers raise the same crops and very few of them raise more than one or two kinds. This is because they have learned to specialize in the crops for which there will be a demand when they are ripe. Strawberries are grown all along the coast, especially from Virginia to New Jersey. A famous tomato-growing region extends along the shores of Chesapeake 

Bay. Melons are grown at their best in 

Delaware and southern New Jersey.

One of the best of the truck-farming regions is the peninsula between Delaware

Bay and Chesapeake Bay. The waters by which it is almost surrounded help to give it an even temperature and to keep it free from frosts until late in the fall. 

This is a region in which tomatoes, potatoes, and sweet potatoes are largely grown. The sweet potato is raised as far north as New Jersey, but it grows best in the South, where the climate is warm and sunny, with a long growing season. 

Much of the crop is used in the South, but a part is sent to northern markets.

In different parts of the truck-growing region so many vegetables are raised that they cannot all be sold as fresh vegetables in city markets. They are, instead, sent to factories to be canned. There are more canning factories in Delaware and Maryland than elsewhere in the truckfarming regions. Baltimore, Maryland, is the chief center of this industry.

A.-Truck farm in eastern Long Island. 

Near every large city there are market gardens which supply the city people with fresh vegetables for home use. 

They are called market gardens because they are small, like gardens, and are as carefully cultivated as gardens are. For example, there are large areas on Long 

Island (A) where market gardeners raise vegetables and small fruits for the markets of New York City. They are near enough to the city so that, during the growing season, the gardeners can load trucks in the late afternoon, or at night, and make their runs during the night. In this way fresh vegetables reach the city markets so they can be sold in the morning when the people come to buy them. The truck-farming region of the island is toward the eastern end.

There the farms are larger, and most of the potatoes, lettuce, cabbages, cauliflower, and tomatoes grown are sent to market by boat or train. 

Tree Fruits. Among the tree fruits raised on the Atlantic Coastal Plain the oranges and grapefruit of Florida, and the peaches of Georgia, have already been mentioned (page 159 and page 137). 

Peaches, apples, pears, and cherries are raised farther north on the coastal plain. 

The peninsula between Delaware and

Chesapeake bays (map, page 83) is famous for the orchard fruits that grow there, and there are fine orchards of all these fruits in New Jersey.

Tobacco. Study the map on this page.

Carolina, and South Carolina. Tobacco is grown in the Piedmont as well as in the 

Atlantic Coastal Plain, and some of the large tobacco factories are in the Piedmont. 

The tobacco plant is a native of the 

New World, and it was not known in 

Europe or Asia until America was discovered. The raising of tobacco as an industry began in the colonies of Virginia and Maryland.

In the early days tobacco was used in place of money in these colonies. For a long time it was one of the largest exports to Europe. The ships of those days sailed up the tidal rivers to the farmer's wharf and took his crop of tobacco to London. In time, the growing of tobacco spread into the Carolinas and across the mountains to Kentucky and 

Tennessee. Although mainly cultivated in these southern states, it also grows farther north.

Almost all the tobacco in this country is raised east of the Mississippi River.

North Carolina grows the largest crop, (A) and Kentucky ranks second. These states are followed by Tennessee and 

Virginia in the amount raised. The fine quality of much of the North Carolina tobacco gives it specially high value. 

Some tobacco is grown in western Florida and is used in the manufacture of cigars; but most of the tobacco used in

Peanuts. The chief peanut-raising region is in North Carolina and Virginia, but this crop is raised also in Alabama and in other parts of the coastal plain. 

The use of peanuts and peanut vines in feeding stock has already been mentioned (page 137). Many peanuts are roasted and eaten out of hand, plain or salted. 

Peanut butter, made from the roasted and ground nuts, is a spread for sandwiches. Peanut oil is used in the manufacture of soap and in cooking. 66 

Oyster Fisheries. - One of the inter esting and important industries carried on in the Chesapeake and Delaware bays is the raising of oysters, sometimes called oyster farming." The most extensive oyster beds in the United States are those of Chesapeake Bay. A few oysters are still taken from natural beds, but most of them are now raised in places that have been prepared on the bottom of shallow seas. Young "seed oysters can move about in the water. Each one soon fastens its shell to some other object, such 99

as another shell or a pebble. In preparing a bed for the young seed oysters it is important that the shells or other objects to which they are to fasten should be clean. In our country old oyster shells are chiefly used. In other countries such things as tiles, bundles of sticks, stones, and branches of trees are used. 

Some of the oystermen go out in small boats and gather the oysters from the sea bed with long-handled tongs. In other cases the oysters are scooped off the bed by dredging machines that use a large bucket or a wire netting.

The oysters are then washed and graded for shipment. Some of the oysters are "shucked" (that is, taken from the shell) and canned. A great part of the catch is packed in ice or in refrigerator cars to be sent to near-by markets or to cities that are distant. Baltimore,

Maryland, is the chief center of the oyster industry (A).

The Long Island beaches, especially those that can be quickly reached from New York, are crowded with people whenever the water is warm enough for bathing. Those who like surf bathing will go where the ocean waves come in upon a sandy shore. Others will go to resorts on the more quiet waters north of the barrier beach.

As they can be reached easily and cheaply by bus or railroad, many thousands of people visit them during the summer, especially on hot days and evenings.

On the map (page 154), follow the shore line from New York to Delaware 

Bay. Along this shore you will notice that there are long, low, barrier beaches like those along the shore of Long Island. 

At the northern end of this line of beaches is Sandy Hook, which reaches out into the Lower Bay of New York. Along the New Jersey coast the water behind these beaches forms lagoons. Little by little the lagoons fill with mud as the tide goes in and out and the water plants grow and decay.

Atlantic City. These and many smaller places (A) are pleasure resorts to which people go to enjoy the cool breezes from the sea and the pleasures of surf bathing. The greatest of these is Atlantic

City. The lagoon which was west of it has been nearly all filled, and the railroad leads to the city without crossing any large body of water. Most of the visitors to Atlantic City and to the other pleasure resorts along the New Jersey shore are there for rest and recreation. There are more than a thousand hotels in Atlantic City. Some of them, built where they look out over the open Atlantic, are very large and very luxurious. Others are much smaller and less expensive. 

Great piers, used for exhibits and other entertainments, run out into the ocean.

There are ten miles of board walk along the beach (155 A). It is built above the level of the sands so it can be used even when the winds drive the waves far up on the shore.

On the land side of the board walk are shops, restaurants, and the entrances to the great hotels. The board walk itself on a sunny day is filled with a happy crowd of people on a holiday. Many walk, but others hire wheeled chairs, each with a man to push it about. 

Atlantic City is but one hour by railroad from Philadelphia, and three hours from New York. From these two cities with their many millions of people, and from other places all over the United States, people come to Atlantic City and other resorts on the New Jersey shore.

Some Famous Winter Resorts. In contrast with the summer resorts along the northern coast of the Atlantic Coastal 

Plain, Florida is a winter playground.

The larger and more famous winter resorts are on or near the coast. Winter residents of southern Florida have the choice of many fine hotels, and can enjoy many outdoor sports, including boating, ocean bathing, and deep-sea fishing.

Jacksonville, in the northeast, is on the wide, deep inlet from the sea called St. 

Johns River. It is a railroad center and the chief seaport on the Atlantic side of 

Florida (A). 

South of Jacksonville, about an hour by train, is St. Augustine. It was founded by Spaniards in 1565, and is the oldest city in the United States. It has many visitors who enjoy the narrow streets, the interesting old buildings, and the lovely flower gardens of this fine old city. 

Farther south is Palm Beach, one of the more fashionable of the Florida resorts.

It has miles of streets along which you can see the homes of people who live there only during the winter season.

Still farther south on the east coast are 

Miami and Miami Beach.

Transportation. The visitor to Florida has the choice of several ways of making the trip. From New York City and other Atlantic ports the trip may be made on fine ocean-going steamers. Those who go by automobile may travel over splendid roads from almost any part of our country. Airplanes may be used; there are excellent landing fields in several 

Florida cities. At Miami the airplanes carrying mail to South America and 

Central America take off. Fast express trains with sleeping cars, dining car, and observation car may be taken from any of the larger northern cities to all important points in Florida. 

One railroad runs the entire length of the peninsula not far from the eastern coast. At the southern end it continues along the line of the Florida Keys to Key

West, crossing the water between the islands over low bridges. 

From Key West ships and airplanes make trips to Havana in Cuba.

It is interesting to notice that in many parts of Florida the houses have been built in a Spanish style. This is partly because that style of building is suitable for hot countries. Many of them, especially in the south, have no heating stoves or furnaces, for it is seldom cold enough to make heating necessary.

Other Cities of the Coastal Plain. 

Locate, on the map, Savannah, Georgia; 

Charleston, South Carolina; and Wilmington, North Carolina. All three of these cities are ports. Each one ships much cotton and lumber, and Savannah ships naval stores. Among the industries of Wilmington are the canning of vegetables and the pressing of oil from cotton seed. In each of these cities there are beautiful old southern homes on lovely shaded streets. Many of these homes, with their wide porches, their hanging balconies, and their large rooms and great staircases, really deserve the name of mansions. 

On Hampton Roads, formed by the broad mouth of the James River where it joins Chesapeake Bay, are the cities and harbors of Norfolk, Newport News, and 

Portsmouth. Norfolk and Newport News are visited by many steamers trading along our coast, and by steamships from many foreign countries. From these NCS

These are used in the factories of Portsmouth in the manufacture of fertilizers. At Portsmouth there is a very large United States navy yard. Newport News has a large shipbuilding industry (A). All three cities have good railroad connections.

Line from New York to northern Ala-Atlantic Coastal Plain and the Piedmont. bama. Notice on page 131 the large cities that are located along this line. 

Do not think of the Fall Line as a sharp line dividing two natural regions that are very different from each other. It is instead a belt of country of varying width. In crossing it there are places where you would go gradually from the flat land of the Coastal Plain into the hilly land of the Piedmont. Where the rivers have dug valleys across the Fall Line, the change from the sands and clays of the Coastal Plain to the hard rocks under the Piedmont may be very sudden.

In most of the rivers there are rapids or waterfalls at this point. The power furnished by these falls, and their situation at the head of tidewater, led to the early location of settlements along the Fall 

Line. A number of these settlements have grown into important manufacturing and trading centers.

Fall Line Cities in the South. Three cities on the Fall Line in Georgia are 

Columbus, Macon, and Augusta. All of these cities have large cotton mills. 

Columbia, the capital of South Carolina, and Raleigh, the capital of North Carolina, are two other Fall Line cities engaged in manufacturing cotton. Columbia also manufactures fertilizer. 

Richmond, the capital of Virginia, is at the head of navigation on the James

River. It was first settled at a time when ocean ships were small, and it carried on an important trade with Europe. The larger ships of today cannot reach the city, but some freight is still carried over the river route by small boats. Rich- 

Because of the nearness of Richmond to some of the tobacco-growing regions, the manufacture of tobacco has long been an important industry there.

Washington. -Turn to the map on page 131 and find the District of Columbia. It is between Virginia and Maryland. The boundaries of the District of 

Columbia and of the city of Washington are the same. This place was selected for the capital of our country in 1790, and became the capital ten years later. 

It is not a part of any state. It is governed under the authority of the Congress of the United States. 

Washington is so near the Fall Line that it is usually thought of as a Fall 

Line city. The Falls of the Potomac are really a short distance northwest of the city. When the city was planned and the places for the public buildings were chosen, they were some distance from one another. For that reason the city was called "the city of magnificent distances." Since that time the spaces between these first public buildings have been filled in by other government buildings and private ones. Washington is now a city of a half million people. 

Thousands of visitors also come on business or to see the national capital and enjoy its beauties.

Among its great buildings and monuments are the Capitol and the White 

House. The Capitol is the large build ing with the great dome (169 A) where

Congress meets to make the laws for our country. The White House is the home of our President, and his offices are

Washington does not owe its growth to its location, to its trade, or to its manufacturing. facturing. It has few manufactures, and its trade meets only the daily needs of its people. It is very different in this way from other large cities.

Washington has grown because it is the capital of a great country. Many officers of the government and many thousand workers in the different government departments make their homes in Washington. in Washington. Most foreign countries have representatives living in Washington to look after the interests of their governments and their people.

A little farther down the Potomac River is the old home of George Washington, called Mount Vernon. Thousands of people visit it every year. The house is furnished and kept up much as it was when Washington lived there.

Baltimore and Wilmington. 

One of the great Fall Line cities is Baltimore, a seaport on a tidal river near the head of Chesapeake Bay (map, page 131). It is one of the leading commercial and manufacturing cities of our country. In this city live nearly half of the people of Maryland, and it is the largest city in the South Atlantic group of states. 

The harbor of Baltimore is large and the water is deep enough for ocean steamships to dock. Railroad connections reach all parts of our country. To Baltimore come articles for shipment to other ports on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts and to many foreign countries. 

Goods received by steamship are distributed over the railroads to trading centers in the different parts of the United States. 

The chief manufactures of Baltimore are clothing, metal goods, and fertilizers. 

Shipbuilding and the canning of fruit, vegetables, and oysters are also important (163 A). Where do the canning factories get their raw materials? (Pages 

160 and 163.) 

Johns Hopkins University, one of the great universities of our country, is in Baltimore.

Delaware has one large city, Wilmington (map, page 154). About half the people of the state live there. Its industries include shipbuilding and the manufacture of heavy machinery, paints, and such explosives as dynamite and gunpowder and all kinds of ammunition. 

Philadelphia. Philadelphia is on the tidal part of the Delaware River and can be reached by large ocean steamships (map, page 154). It has a population of about 2,000,000. It is larger than any other city in our country except 

New York and Chicago. 

Independence Hall is in Philadelphia.

It was in this small red brick building that the Congress of 1776 met to declare the colonies free from British rule. Here is preserved the "Liberty Bell," which rang loud and long when the Declaration of Independence was first read to the people of Philadelphia. When the war of the Revolution was over, it was in 

Philadelphia that the Constitution of the

United States was written. This city was the capital of the United States from 1790 to 1800. The University of 

Pennsylvania is in Philadelphia.

Among the many industries of Philadelphia are manufactures of wool, cotton, leather, and iron, and the refining of sugar and petroleum. The crude oil is brought by pipe lines from the oil regions (143 B). Raw sugar comes from Cuba (A). Hides and skins, from which leather is made, come from many countries. 

Wool brought from distant lands is made into carpets and rugs. Cloth, clothing, and knit goods are made.

Coal and iron come from the mountain and plateau regions not far away. 

At Philadelphia there are shipyards, plants where steel for bridge building is prepared, and the largest plant in the world for building cars and locomotives. A.

The location of Philadelphia gives it many commercial advantages. As a seaport it takes part in the coastwise trade with cities of the Atlantic and Gulf ports.

Trenton. - Trenton (map, page 154) is the capital of the state of New Jersey. 

It has water power, large pottery works, and rubber factories. More pottery is made in New Jersey than in any other state in our country except Ohio.

Of that made in New Jersey, Trenton makes over half. It has factories in which earthenware, white granite ware, and very fine and delicate china are made.

Much of the clay and other raw materials used in this industry are brought from other states.

NEW YORK CITY 

The first settlement on Manhattan 

Island at the mouth of the Hudson River was made by the Dutch. They called it 

New Amsterdam. Later it was taken from the Dutch by the English and was renamed New York. At that time it was only a small village at the southern end of Manhattan Island. Now it is the largest city in the world, except London in England.

Size and Population. The city of 

New York includes five of the counties of the state, with an area of about 308 square miles. It includes Manhattan

Island, Staten Island, the western end of Long Island, and a part of the mainland south of Yonkers. In 1930 there were about 7,000,000 people living in the city. 

Manhattan Island is more densely settled than other parts of the city.

In visiting the city there are two things that you can do to help you to understand how large it is and how important it is to the people of the world. 

One thing to do is to go to the top of some very high building (A) on a clear day and study the city that lies spread out below you. The other is to take a ride around Manhattan Island in a sightseeing boat. 

Piers and Docks. - Starting from the southern end of the island, most visitors take boats that begin the trip by turning east. You will find it more interesting, however, to go north first, up the Hudson 

River. Soon after starting you will see the piers that have been built out into the river from both its banks. Heavy supports or piles are driven into the river bottom. The tops of these are left standing several feet above the water so that they will not be covered even at high tide. On them a floor is laid down to make the pier, and on most piers a building has been put up - a warehouse in which to store goods that have been shipped to the city.

Between the piers there is open water reaching to the river bank. These water spaces between the piers are the docks

Ships coming to New York to load or unload usually enter one of the docks and tie up alongside one of the piers. As your boat goes on up the river you will see ships in the docks, for there are always many ships in the docks of New York. 

Ships and Boats. You may be fortunate enough to see a great passenger steamer starting for Europe. The passengers will be standing on the decks waving good-by to friends who are waving to them from the pier. Slowly the steamer backs out into the stream.

Powerful little tugboats push at its sides to keep it going right. At last it is out of the dock and away from the piers. The tugs swing it around so that it heads down the river toward the ocean. A journey across the Atlantic Ocean has begun. 

Or you may see a great steamship dock-

At last by pulling on the ropes, and with the help of the tugs, the steamer is worked into its dock and its passengers are landed. 

As your little boat continues on its way you see ferryboats crossing the river carrying passengers, trucks, and automobiles between New York and the cities on the New Jersey side of the river. You see barges loaded with brick, crushed stone, coal, or wheat. There may be flatboats carrying freight cars from the railroads on one side of the river to railroads on the other side. You will pass many docks where freight steamers from all parts of the world are loading or unloading their cargoes. 66 

Bridges and Boroughs. Toward the northern end of Manhattan Island your boat will pass under the George Washington Bridge (174 A). Shortly after that you reach the place where the Harlem

River connects with the Hudson. It is this narrow winding body of water, really a strait, that separates Manhattan Island from the mainland part of New York state. It is crossed by many bridges. 

At its eastern end the Harlem joins the East River, which is a broader strait connecting Long Island Sound with New 

York Bay. On the map, page 175, the course of the Harlem River is shown by the boundary between Manhattan and the Bronx.

The city of New York is made up of five counties. Counties are divisions of a state for purposes of government.

A. The city of New York and vicinity. The dashed lines (---) mark the boundaries separating the five boroughs. 

Metropolitan District. Several thickly settled regions are near the city of New 

York. One of them is beyond the western boundary of New York City, in New Jersey, where there is a large group of cities and villages with a combined population of about two million. Another of these regions is north and northeast of the Bronx. It includes Yonkers, Mt. 

Vernon, New Rochelle, and a number of other places in near-by New York and 

Connecticut. A third thickly settled region near New York City is east of 

Queens in Long Island. Adding all these regions together, you get an area of 2541 square miles, called the Metropolitan

District, with a population of about 11,000,000. 

Why should 11,000,000 people gather together at or near the mouth of the Hudson River? One reason is that New York

City is a great trading center. It carries on trade not only with all parts of our own country but with all parts of the world. A second reason is that New 

York is a great manufacturing city. 

Trade. The people of our country buy many things that come from other parts of the world. Our people also have or make things that the people of other countries want. Goods brought into our country are imports. Goods sent out of our country are exports. More than a third of all the imports and about a third of the exports of our country enter or leave the country through the port of New York.

It takes a great many ships to carry all of these imports and exports across the ocean. When you took the trip around 

Manhattan Island you saw ships from all parts of the world loading or unloading. 

The imports that they bring will be distributed to all our larger cities, and from them to smaller villages and country stores. The exports that these same ships will take away must be gathered from all parts of our country. 

Over what routes are the imports distributed and the goods to be exported gathered together? Railroads from New

England and from the central, western, and southern parts of our country center in New York (maps, pages 116, 259).

Freight boats sail to and from ports on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Even the barges on the Barge Canal have some part of this work to do. The greatest of all these trade routes is the one from the interior of our country that reaches New York through the valleys of the Mohawk and Hudson rivers. This is the route of the New York Central Railroad. 

The New York Central passenger sta tion is at 42nd Street in midtown New York. Its freight lines and stations are on the west side of Manhattan Island along the Hudson. The passenger station at 42nd Street is used also by the 

New York, New Haven, and Hartford 

Railroad, one of the great railroads of

New England. The Pennsylvania Rail road enters New York by a tunnel under the Hudson River. Its station is on the western side of Manhattan between 31st

Street and 33rd Street. This station is used also by the trains of the Lehigh Valley Railroad, and by trains of the Long Island Railroad which come through a tunnel under the East River. 

Several other railroads from the west and south end on the New Jersey side of the Hudson. Their passengers may reach 

New York by ferry, or by motor busses or electric trains through tunnels under the river. 

Manufactures. No other city in our country equals New York in the value and variety of its manufactures. You will remember that manufacturing calls for (1) raw materials, (2) power, (3) labor, and (4) markets. By rail and steamer any raw materials needed can be brought to New York for use in its factories.

Coal from the mines of Pennsylvania, fuel oil and gasoline from tanks and refineries in New Jersey, and electric generating stations all furnish power. The population is large enough to furnish the needed labor and a great market. By rail and steamer the manufactures can be sent to markets in all parts of the world. 

The chief manufacturing industry is the making of clothing. New York makes far more clothing than any other city in our country. The industry in 

New York City includes the making of suits, overcoats, dresses, hats, underclothing, and fur coats and neckpieces.

The industry second in importance in 

New York City is the preparation of foodstuffs. This includes the refining of sugar; the making of flour, bakery products, and candy; the slaughtering of animals and the preparation of meats; the grinding of spices; and the roasting of coffee.

Printing is another great industry of New York. More books, magazines, and newspapers are printed there than in any other city. Among the many other manufactures of New York are cigars, cigarettes, and sheet metal work.

Underwood & Underwood

A.-Fifth Avenue, New York, looking north toward Central Park. This avenue is nearly always crowded with taxicabs, busses, and other automobiles. 

Business and Buildings. Two other facts should be kept in mind as helping to explain why there are so many people in New York. (1) Nearly every great business in the world has an office or agent in New York to look after the distribution of its products or the purchase of supplies. (2) Where many people are gathered together there must be stores, office buildings, schools and colleges, churches, theaters, and hotels. There must be ways for people to travel quickly.

There must be banks where money can be deposited and borrowed.

To carry on any business there must be managers, clerks, salesmen, stenographers, and bookkeepers. For the larger buildings there must be renting agents, elevator men, machinists, and cleaners.

Schools and colleges must have teachers and caretakers. There must be men to operate taxicabs, busses, street cars, and the electric trains that run on tracks above the street or in the tunnels, or subways, under the streets and under the rivers. 

There must be firemen, policemen, postmen, doctors, lawyers, and engineers. 

As the business of the great city grows, so does its population. In former days many workers came from foreign countries as immigrants and settled in the city near others who spoke their language.

There are parts of New York City where nearly all the buildings are occupied by groups of foreign people. As the population of the city grows, land becomes more and more valuable and small buildings are torn down and larger ones put in their places.

Many great office buildings more than twenty stories in height have been built. 

Some are more than forty stories high.

The largest of these are in the southern and midtown sections of Manhattan (174 A). The great banks also have their main offices in southern Manhattan, but several of them have branches scattered throughout the city.

PE

New York is a center of education and culture. It has famous museums, art galleries, and many colleges. Here, too, are Columbia University, New York 

University, and Fordham University. 

Where do the millions who work in the city live? Many thousands live in the suburbs that is, in the smaller cities and villages in or near the Metropolitan District. They go to the city each workday morning and back to their homes at night. Traveling for so long a distance between home and work is called commuting. Those who do so are commuters.

Those who live in the city may live in large or small apartment houses. Apartment buildings are usually from five to thirty or more stories high. An apartment may have from one to twenty or more rooms, and the rooms may be large or small. In the larger buildings (A) there are usually several separate apartments on each floor. Each apartment opens on a public hall, but it is entirely separated from all the others.

Bring Galloway Many apartment houses, especially the poorer ones, are called tenement houses. 

A.-Looking north from Washington Square, New York.

At the left is the Washington Arch, at the southern end of Fifth Avenue. At the right are several old residences, contrasting with the modern apartment hotel behind them. 

There are stores and warehouses in New 

York where goods are sold wholesale; that is, to dealers, and usually in large quantities at a time. There are thousands of small stores, especially in residential districts, where goods are sold at retail; that is, to consumers, usually in small quantities. Other retail stores are very much larger in size, some of the largest and finest being in the midtown district of Manhattan. Each of these department stores, as they are called, is really many separate stores under one roof and under one management. 

In the high apartments, hotels, and office buildings, elevators take people up and down, and leave them or take them on at any floor. In the very tall buildings the higher floors are reached by express elevators that do not stop at any of the lower floors except the ground floor.

THE PIEDMONT 

Turn again to the map on page 80, and trace the boundaries of the Piedmont Plateau. Make a list of the states, from 

New York to Alabama, through which this region extends. 

The Piedmont is higher toward the south and lower toward the north. On the east is the Fall Line about which you have been reading. On the west is the Appalachian Mountain and Valley region which you are soon to study. 

Your map shows the Piedmont extending into New England; but you will study New England as a separate region. 

The Piedmont of the Middle Atlantic States. North of Manhattan Island is the part of New York City called the 

Bronx (page 174). Much of the Bronx and a small part of New York state to the north is a region of low, well-rounded hills. It is a part of the Piedmont 

Plateau (map, page 80) which extends south across northern New Jersey and southeastern Pennsylvania. In both of these states the country is higher and more hilly than the Atlantic Coastal 

Plain. One of the New Jersey ridges forms a high rocky wall on the west side of the Hudson River. The ridge is called the Palisades (183 A). 

Cities of the Northern Piedmont. 

Just north of New York is the large city of Yonkers. Many people who live there work in the city of New York, but many others work in their own city. Among the goods manufactured in Yonkers are carpets and rugs, felt hats, elevators, and rubber goods. There are also sugar refineries and machine shops. The New 

Jersey cities nearest New York City are 

Hoboken, Jersey City, and Bayonne 

National Jewelers Publicity Ass'n, Newark, N. J.

A.-In a factory where watch cases are made. Each case is carefully inspected before shipment. (map, page 175). They lie along the lower southern part of the Palisades ridge. 

Here, on the west bank of the Hudson 

River, most of the railroads from the southern, western, and northern parts of our country have their Atlantic coast terminals. Several of the great Atlantic steamship lines have their docks, piers, and storage warehouses on the New 

Jersey side of the Hudson. 

More crude oil, or petroleum, is refined in Bayonne than in any other place in the world. The oil comes to it through pipe lines from most of the principal oil fields of the United States and by tank ships from other oil regions. Jersey City has slaughtering and meat-packing plants and soap factories. At Hoboken ships and ships' engines are built and repaired. 

Newark, the largest city in New Jersey, is a great manufacturing center with many different industries. Among its important manufactures are electrical machinery and supplies, paints and varnishes, leather, jewelry, chemicals, and meat products.

It is a railroad center, and is one of the great airports of the eastern United

States. Newark is developing as a seaport by deepening and widening a channel to the sea and building piers. 

Paterson's great industry is the manufacture of silk, including the steps of weaving, dyeing, and finishing. Passaic also manufactures textiles. Perth Amboy has a good harbor and shipyards. There are drydocks where ships can be cleaned or repaired. Elizabeth manufactures half of the sewing machines made in this country, and other articles of iron and steel, including wire. Both Elizabeth and Perth Amboy smelt and refine copper, and through these cities much coal from Pennsylvania is shipped. In the forested upland region of northern New 

Jersey the cities of the Piedmont find a source of pure water. 

On the 

Southeastern Pennsylvania. map (page 80) find the Piedmont region of southeastern Pennsylvania. Locate the same region on the larger map on page 154. The country is quite hilly, but it has an excellent soil and is one of the richest farm regions in the United States.

Some of the farmers there are descendants of the early Quaker settlers, and many are descendants of Germans who first settled in that region. They are noted for their industry and thrift, and for their good houses and barns, well-cultivated fields, and fine herds of cattle.

Among the crops grown are wheat, corn, vegetables, fruits, and tobacco.

Most of the corn is used as food for hogs and cattle. Some fruits and vegetables are sold fresh in the markets, and others are sold to canneries. There are many dairy farms, especially near the large cities, and on other farms tobacco is the one great crop. Most of the farmers, however, carry on mixed farming. 

Lancaster, west of Philadelphia and almost in the center of this Pennsylvania section of the Piedmont, is one of the chief trading centers. It has stockyards that are among the largest in the country. Its many factories get electric power from a great power plant on the 

Susquehanna River, 25 miles to the south. 

Farming from Maryland to Georgia.

The mixed-farming region of southeastern Pennsylvania is continued through the Piedmont in other states southward to Georgia; but the farms are not all as productive, the farmers are not always as prosperous, and the crops are not always the same. As in other mixedfarming regions, there are usually several market crops, and other crops for home use and farm animals. In the Piedmont region of Maryland and Virginia, as well as in Pennsylvania, there are large, wellkept apple orchards from which fine fruit is sent to our own and foreign markets.

The tobacco district of Pennsylvania is continued southward through Maryland, southern Virginia, and the Carolinas.

Tobacco is a crop that takes from the soil a large amount of plant food that must be put back again by the use of fertilizers. In the southern part of the 

Piedmont the money crop is cotton. 

Farming as a Business. You have learned much about the crops grown in different parts of our country, and there is much more to learn. This is a good time for you to think of farming as farmers think of it as a business. 

To be successful, the farmer must know many things about his farm and about the crops and live stock that he raises. He must choose the crops that will grow well on the soils of his farm. 

They must be the kind that will ripen

THE PIEDMONT 

181 

A.-Plowing with a tractor-drawn plow that turns two furrows at once. Many farmers use a single plow drawn by a team of horses. during the growing season. There must be enough but not too much rainfall, and it must come at the right time of the year. 

In planning and caring for the crops the farmer must know the kind of fertilizer to use, how much to use, and when to use it. He must know when fruit trees or crops must be sprayed, and what sprays to use. In selecting his crops he will take those that are planted at different times and harvested at different times so as to spread his work as much as possible. 

He must know what foods his farm animals need, when they should be fed, and how to care for them.

When there is no work to be done in the fields, there will be roads, buildings, and fences to repair, and trees to cut for lumber, fence posts, and firewood. The housewife is as busy in the house as the farmer in his fields. Farming is not a life for the idler.

The farmer has his rewards. In the more prosperous farming regions many of the homes are fine old mansions. They are set in the midst of great trees whose spreading branches give a welcome shade when the summer sun is high and hot. 

There are outbuildings and barns for housing the animals and farm machinery, and for the storage of crops. All about are the meadows, the pastures, and the cultivated fields.

In the spring time there is the fresh green of trees and meadows and pastures, the brown earth of plowed fields (A), and the pink and white of blossoming orchards. Later each growing crop will take on its own color and over all there will rest the haze of the summer. Then comes autumn, when the crops are gathered. Once more the fields are bare and, with the frost, the foliage becomes golden and russet and red.

There are also smaller, less stately homes, with smaller farms and fewer outbuildings. But there also you will find the patterns of the fields and the same beauty of coloring. For every one, rich and poor alike, there are the beautiful views from high places and the lovely streams winding among the hills.

Cities of the Southern Piedmont. 

All of the Piedmont cities are trading centers in which the farmers of the surrounding country can buy their supplies and sell their farm products. For many years the cities of the Piedmont from

Appalachian Mountains. Because it is had little manufacturing. The tobacco and cotton crops furnished some raw materials, but these were sent to factories in cities more favorably located, especially to those along the Fall Line at the head of tidewater.

In recent years manufacturing in the Piedmont cities has been increasing.

Throughout this region there are many waterfalls, large and small. Plants for generating electricity have been built at a number of the larger falls. As you know, electrical power can be sent over wires from the generating stations to places many miles away. In the Piedmont cities it is used for electric lighting, transportation, and running the machinery of cotton mills, aluminum plants, furniture factories, and ice-making plants. 

Great power lines unite these generating stations with each other, and the combined flow of power can be distributed to cities and factories as needed. 

One of the interesting new industries that is developing in the Piedmont is the use of electricity to get aluminum from its ore. 

Some bauxite (page 146) is found in Georgia, Alabama, and Tennessee, but most of the aluminum is made from the bauxite from Arkansas. 

The manufacture of tobacco is carried on in Winston-Salem and Durham, North

Carolina. There are cotton mills in 

Charlotte and other Piedmont cities, especially in the Carolinas and Georgia. 

The great Piedmont city of the South is Atlanta, the capital of Georgia. It is sometimes called the "Gate City." Let us see why. It is located where the railroads from the northeastern, southern, and central parts of our country meet as they swing round the southern end of the so well located to control the trade of the eastern section of our southern states, many northern business houses have offices in Atlanta. To Atlanta come such raw materials as cotton and lumber, and among its manufactures are cotton goods, furniture, fertilizers, paper, and machinery. Coal from mines in the southern Appalachians, and electricity from a great power plant only 15 miles from the city, furnish light and power.

THE APPALACHIAN HIGHLANDS 

Turn to the map on page 80 and notice the position, size, and direction of the two natural regions there called the Appalachian Mountains and Valleys and the 

Appalachian Plateau. Taken together these two regions are called the Appalachian Highlands, but each of the two parts is also made up of parts that must be studied separately. After this has been done you will study the industries of the two regions combined. That is because several of the great industries are carried on in different parts of the highland and it is easier to study them all at the same time. This is especially true of coal and iron mining and the manufacture of iron and steel.

The Eastern Appalachians. On the map, page 80, trace the Appalachian 

Mountain and Valley region from Maine to Alabama. Of what states does it form a part? As the New England region is to be studied separately you will begin the study of this natural region in the Middle Atlantic States (map, page 154). North of the Piedmont Plateau, in New York state, the Hudson

River (A) has cut a gorge fifteen miles long across part of the Appalachian Highlands. On the eastern side of the river this region extends northward and into New England. On the western side of the river it extends southwest into northern

Alabama. In the Middle Atlantic States this highland area is a region of hills.

Conservation Department, State of New York 

A.-Mount Marcy, the highest peak in the state of New York. It is 5344 feet high- just a little over a mile. 

Mt. Mitchell in North Carolina is considerably higher. 

The hills were once much higher, but they have been worn down by the work of heat and cold, and the work of winds, and rains, and running water. They are a very old part of the Appalachians. 

From Carlisle, Pennsylvania, a single low mountain range, called South Mountain, extends southward into Maryland. fore studying the higher mountains in 

Maryland, Virginia, and farther south, some mention should be made of the 

Adirondack Mountains of northern New York.

Be- The Adirondacks. - This mass of highlands is a region of many peaks but with no ranges. The rivers flow out from the central and higher parts to the surrounding lowlands, and across these to lakes and larger streams. This kind of drainage is called radial drainage.

The rocks that form the Adirondacks are among the oldest of our continent, and they are very hard. The rock layers are not horizontal as you will find them in some parts of the Appalachian Highlands. They have been twisted and crumpled and broken. The highest peak is Mt. Marcy (A), 5344 feet high. The slopes of this and other peaks are steep and rough and covered with forests. 

There are hundreds of lakes in the

Adirondacks, many of which are not shown on the map (page 154). You will remember that the ice sheet covered most of New York state. It ground off the tops of the hills, making them lower and more smoothly rounded. When the ice melted, some of the valleys were partly filled with sand, gravel, and clay, washed into them from the melting ice.

At the same time many stones called bowlders were left scattered over the fields. 

Lake basins were formed because the moving ice dug parts of some old valleys deeper, and blocked other valleys with earth and stones. After the ice melted

away, many old stream valleys were so blocked that the streams flowed in new channels. In doing so they cut gorges and formed waterfalls. 

Most of the lakes of the Adirondacks are there because of the hollows dug by the ice sheet and because the material left by the melting ice made dams across the many stream channels. 

You have read about the summer and winter resorts of the Atlantic Coastal

Plain (pages 163-166). Many people like to go to the mountains instead of to the seashore. There are a large number of resorts in the Adirondacks as well as in other parts of the Appalachian Highlands.

From the tops of the higher mountains you can get wonderful views. On a clear day you can look down into near-by valleys, or a long, long way across the forestcovered peaks and slopes.

A climb to the top of a mountain may take hours of hard work. The state of 

New York is building a road to the top of "Whiteface," one of the Adirondack peaks (A), as a memorial to the men of the state who died in the World War. On this road those who have never been able to climb mountains may ride to the top to see the views. Hunters and campers make their way deep into the forests or to the shores of some small lake hidden away far from road or trail. There, where the air is cool and sweet, they find delight in boating, swimming, fishing, and hunting; and they get restful sleep. 

One reason why the Adirondack Mountains are a delightful region in which to spend a vacation is because they are cool even in the summer. This is largely because of their height. You have learned that there is a decrease in tem- 

Courtesy New York Central Lines 

A. Whiteface Mountain, as seen from Lake Placid. This mountain is almost entirely covered by forest. perature of about one degree for every 

300 feet increase in elevation (page 158).

When people in the lowlands are suffering from heat those in the mountains are comfortably cool. 

The short, heavy rains of the summer help to keep the air fresh, the trees growing, the streams flowing, and the lakes full. But there are long dry periods, so that much of the time the climate is not only cool, but dry. This has led many people who have lung trouble to go to the 

Adirondacks to recover their strength and health.

In the winter time, snow gathers on the mountains and in the valleys. More and more people are going to these mountains each winter to enjoy such sports as skating, snowshoeing, tobogganing, bobsledding, and skiing. Winter temperatures often go to zero or below zero. 

Waterfalls furnish power for the development of electricity. There is some lumbering, and a little mining of iron ore. 

There are large mills in several places engaged in the manufacture of wood pulp and paper.

Blue Ridge. After this study of the 

Adirondacks turn to the map on page 131 and find the mountain range called the Blue Ridge. It is 1000 feet high in 

Maryland and rises to 4000 feet as it crosses the northern boundary of North

Carolina. It gets its name from the color it has when seen from a distance. 

For much of its length this ridge of mountains is a barrier to trade between the Piedmont on the southeast and the Great Valley to the northwest. The 

Potomac River has cut a gap across the ridge at Harpers Ferry, which is just west of the point where the states of Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia meet.

Farther south other rivers have cut gaps across the Blue Ridge near Lynchburg and near Roanoke. These gaps are used by the railroads and the highways which connect the coastal plain with the Valley of Virginia.

It is in North Carolina that these old mountains have their greatest height and width, and their finest forests and mountain peaks. Find Mt. Mitchell, and compare its height with that of Mt. 

Marcy in New York (184 A). Here the 

Blue Ridge widens out into several ranges (A). Among these are the Great Smoky 

Mountains, the Unakas, and the mountains surrounding the Asheville basin, of which Mt. Mitchell is one of the peaks.

The hardwood forests are most extensive in North Carolina, but are found in all the states that reach into the mountains. The common kinds of trees in these forests are oak, ash, maple, chestnut, hickory, black walnut, and birch.

A large amount of lumber is produced. 

In some places the forests have been entirely cut away. On the slopes thus left bare, the heavy rains have cut gullies and washed away much soil (187 B).

In the valley there are thick beds of limestone. Water slowly dissolves them, and this is one reason why there is a valley. Water follows cracks down into this underground limestone, where it dissolves the rock and forms great caverns.

You learned about one of these in Kentucky (page 153). In Virginia also there are such caverns at Luray and many other places. Water with lime in it dripping from the roof of a cavern may evaporate and leave the lime as a stalactite. 

In places a stream may flow for some distance underground in a cavern, wearing away the bottom and sides. When most of the roof falls in, leaving only a little standing, there is a natural bridge.

The best-known bridge of this kind in our country is the Natural Bridge in the 

Great Valley of Virginia (A).

Allegheny Plateau. - 

The Allegheny

Plateau occupies much of northern Pennsylvania and of southern New York. It extends eastward in New York to the Hudson River where a higher and rougher part of the plateau is called the Catskill 

Mountains. The average elevation in southwestern New York and in neighboring parts of Pennsylvania is about 2000 feet, but it is a little higher in West Virginia.

The plateau was once an almost horizontal surface underlain by nearly horizontal rocks. It has been cut by a network of streams into a maze of hills and valleys. Most of the travel across it, both by roads and by railroads (B), follows the river valleys, and passes from one valley to another through cuts or gaps. 

On the north a part of the plateau ends in the steep slopes that form the southern side of the Mohawk River Valley. The 

Mohawk is an important tributary of the 

Hudson River and flows into the Hudson from the west, a short distance north of 

Albany. Find it on the map, page 154. 

In the western part of New York state, and in northwestern Pennsylvania, the northern edge of the plateau slopes more gently to the Lake Plains. B. Railroad in a valley of the Allegheny Plateau the Chemung Valley. Notice the ridge at the right.

A.-Looking across the tops of ridges in the Allegheny Plateau. See how even they are.

How the Plateau Landscape Looks. 

From the picture (A) on this page you can get a good idea of how some parts of the Allegheny Plateau look. Imagine that you have climbed to the top of one of the ridges. From it you can look across the top of other ridges and see that they are all nearly the same height. 

If the valleys between them were filled in again, the country across which you are looking would seem to be a gently rolling plain.

The tops of the ridges are about 2000 feet above sea level. The bottoms of the larger valleys are from 800 to 1200 feet above the level of the sea. There are flat lands close beside the main rivers. 

These valley bottoms are, in many places, a half mile or even a mile wide. When you are looking from a valley bottom, the ridges on each side seem high and rugged. It is only when you are on top of a ridge that you see how even the top of the Allegheny Plateau is.

Effect of Land Forms on Man's Work. 

- Most of the people whose homes are in the Allegheny Plateau live on the flat lands of the valley bottoms. That is partly because the soils there are deeper, better, and easier to plow, and grow better crops. It is also because roads and railroads are built more easily along the valley bottoms from one place to another (189 B). It is in the valley bottoms and on the flood plains of the streams that villages and cities have grown up. 

On the tops of the ridges and on their steeper slopes there is not much soil. 

Some of it was scraped away by the ice sheet, and some is washed away by rains and melting snow. If these ridge tops and steep slopes were plowed, the rain might wash away more and more of the soil. Many regions of thin soils and steep slopes have been left as forests. 

On hill lands of gentler slope many farms are to be found. Each farm generally has a part where trees have been left

to grow. This wood lot, as it is called, furnishes the farmer each year with some timber, fence posts, and firewood. Other parts of the farm have been cleared and are used as pasture land for cattle, horses, and sheep, or as fields for crops.

Among the crops that these hillside farmers grow are hay, oats, corn, wheat, and garden vegetables. The hay and oats and much of the corn are used to feed the animals in the winter time. 

Most of the vegetables and wheat are for use on the farm.

On the hillside farms of the Allegheny Plateau the climate is cool and moist. 

The grass of the pasture lands and fields is not killed by the late frosts in spring or the early frosts in autumn. The cool A. - Chopping corn. The pieces chopped by the machine nights in the plateau do not stop its growth. Cattle can get much food from pasture land that is too steep to be cultivated. 

Dairy Farming. Many of the farms of the Allegheny Plateau are dairy farms; that is, their chief product is milk. Dairy farming has become a great industry because the people in cities need so much milk and cream and butter.

A farmer must do much hard work to make a success of dairy farming or any other farming. He is busy with his crops in the spring, summer, and fall; and all the year round he must care for his animals and keep his buildings and fences in repair.

Think of the important things that must be done on one of the large dairy farms. Hay must be raised. It is needed for both horses and cattle, and some, too, may be sold to get money to buy other things. Corn must be grown. 

Corn must be grown and much of it must be stored in a silo to feed the cattle in the winter time. are blown up the pipe into the silo.

Corn for the silo is cut in September. 

The whole plants - stalks, leaves, and green ears are chopped into small pieces by a machine, and packed into the silo (A). Here this food keeps green and juicy. In the winter it takes the place of the green grass of the pasture. In addition many farmers buy ground corn and other feed for their herds in the winter.

On the better dairy farms the stock barns are well built. Fresh, pure water is supplied for the cattle to drink. The barn and the cows are kept clean. Milk and cream to be sold in cities must be pure and pass certain tests.

In the old days the women on the farm made butter to sell. They had to let the milk stand in open pans a long time while the cream was rising to the top. The cream was then skimmed from the milk, put into a churn, and stirred or beaten until the small particles of butter-fat collected together.

Now on many farms the cream is quickly separated from the milk by a machine (the separator) and is sent to a creamery to be made into butter. From some farms, too, the milk is taken to factories where it is used for making cheese. 

Other Farm Products in the Allegheny

Plateau. - Poultry raising is an important branch of farming in the plateau region; for a supply of eggs and fowls, as well as of milk, is needed both for home use and for sale in the great cities. 

Potatoes and other vegetables are grown on the farms for home use; but on many farms they are grown also for sale. 

Some tobacco is raised and there are fine vineyards and apple orchards along the shores of the lakes in central New York. 

These lakes (map, page 154) are called the "Finger Lakes." Can you tell why?

The Catskill Mountains. The part of New York that has been given the name of the Catskill Mountains is really the eastern part of the great Allegheny Plateau. Its hills are higher, the valleys 

are deeper, and the slopes steeper than in most other parts of the plateau. There are also fewer farms and people, more forests, and more wild life. 

Not far from the Catskills are the millions of people in and near the city of New York. In the summertime when city people take their vacations, many of them think of the cool air and shade of the Catskills. There they know that they will find hotels, boarding houses, or camping places, whichever they may prefer. A large part of the Catskill forest, with its cool valleys, springs of fresh water, lakes, and waterfalls, has been purchased by the state of New York, and is now the Catskill State Park.

Many small villages have grown up in the valleys at points where it is convenient for farmers to come and trade. Some of the larger villages are important trade centers and

Cumberland Plateau. The southwestern continuation of the region you have been studying as the Allegheny Plateau is the Cumberland Plateau (page 189). In the higher parts of eastern 

Kentucky, western Virginia, and Tennessee the Cumberland Plateau in some places reaches heights of from 3000 to 4000 feet. It is even more cut up by 

streams into hills and valleys than is the Allegheny Plateau. The large streams flow through deep gorges. The smaller ones flow in narrow, steep-sided valleys. 

There is little or no flat land on the hill tops or in the valley bottoms along the streams. Railroads, roads, and trails follow the valleys. There are but few bridges in the higher regions. The roads are poor, and the trails are steep and winding. After a heavy rainstorm the streams fill quickly and sometimes they wash away the roads and destroy what few bridges there are.

The Cumberland Plateau is a region of great forests, but because of the few railroads through this part of the country, many of the forest areas cannot be profitably cut. Where lumbering is carried on, streams are used to float the logs to the lowlands or to the railroads.

What about its people? There are some farms and orchards whose owners can get to villages to sell their produce and buy what they need and can afford. 

There are other regions in the higher valleys and among the hills where life is very difficult. 

The people who live there have few things that they can sell and they are a long way from any market. 

Their roads are poor and they cannot take long journeys. There are no near-by villages where the people can go to school or church or where they can find libraries, museums, or theaters. Yet, in spite of all difficulties, with the help of friends and by their own efforts, some of them are able to get some education themselves and to send their children to school.

Daniel Boone and other early explorers and hunters climbed out of the Great Valley through this notch in the highlands and followed an Indian trail to the Ohio River. There they settled what became the state of Kentucky. This gap is important because for many years it was the only easy route to the west out of the Great Valley for many miles along the plateau front.
