MINERAL PRODUCTS OF THE APPA- LACHIAN HIGHLANDS 

In all the mountain belt of Pennsylvania the most important product is coal. There is coal in many states in our country, but Pennsylvania has more than any other. No other coal beds are so near the great manufacturing centers as are the coal beds of Pennsylvania. 

How Coal Was Formed. Years and years ago in the history of the earth there was much swamp land. Forests grew in these swamps and on their borders. The trunks, branches, and leaves of the trees fell into the swamps, and mosses grew there. The water kept this woody material from decaying. From time to time the level of the land would change. The swamp would sink and be covered with water. Sand and dirt would be deposited on top of the woody material. Once again the region would be lifted above sea level and become a swamp in which trees would begin to grow. With other changes of level, layers of sand and mud and layers of woody material would be piled on top of one another. This would take a long, long time.

At last the land remained below sea level so long that great layers of earthy material were piled on top of all the materials that had been accumulating for so long a time. Their weight was enormous and under this pressure the woody material began to change into coal. The land was again lifted above sea level and in some places it was wrinkled into great folds. The earthy material was changed into rock, and the woody material into coal. One proof of this is the fact that fossils of leaves, roots, fruits, and trunks of trees have been found in coal beds. 

Ewing Galloway

A.-Loading a car with hard coal or anthracite in the mine. 

At the right you see one of the supports of the roof. 

Fossils are deposits of stone that have taken the place of leaves, tree trunks, and other remains of plants and animals, but have kept their shape. 

Where the rocks were folded and the pressure was greatest the coal gave off part of its gas and became a hard coal called anthracite. Where the rock layers and coal layers were not folded but remained horizontal not so much gas was driven off. The coal is not so hard and is called soft or bituminous coal. 

Coal Regions. Almost all the hard coal in this country is found in eastern Pennsylvania. Much of the soft coal is found in western Pennsylvania and elsewhere in the Appalachian Plateau. 

In mining the anthracite, holes called shafts are dug into the earth through layers of coal and rock. The coal in each layer, if it is thick enough, is dug out by miners. These miners drill holes into the mass of coal with electric drills. 

The drill holes are loaded with dynamite and the dynamite exploded to break up the coal. The miners then loosen it with picks and load it on little cars (A) that take it to the shaft. There it is loaded into buckets and lifted to the surface.

Keystone-Underwood

A. Coal breaker. Here the coal is sorted and graded after being brought in from the mine. The slate and other waste material is run off up the incline at the right. See the huge pile it has made. 

Not all of the coal can be taken out of each layer. Enough must be left in pillars to hold up the roof, or other supports must be used. In some coal regions so much coal has been taken out that the surface of the earth has begun to sink. 

When the miners are at work water that gets into the mine must be pumped out, or the mine would be flooded. The mine must also be ventilated so that gases will not gather and explode, injuring the miners or shutting them off from the shaft so they cannot get out of the mine. 

When the anthracite is brought to the surface, it goes to the breakers. These are buildings in which the coal is washed, broken into pieces, sorted into different sizes, and loaded into railroad cars (A). 

A number of cities have grown up about the anthracite mines. The largest of these are Scranton and Wilkes-Barre. 

When anthracite was discovered, over a hundred and twenty-five years ago, people thought it had no value, because they did not know how to make it burn. Today there is an enormous demand for anthracite, especially for heating and cooking. 

The railroads that run into the anthracite regions have a great business in hauling the coal. The cities of New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore are the chief markets on the eastern seaboard. Great quantities of coal are taken in barges from the railroad terminals to many Atlantic seaports. 

Several railroads distribute the coal through New York state and New England. Large amounts go to the ports of the Great Lakes and the cities of Canada. 

Other railroads carry it to the west beyond the Mississippi.

In the plateau region of western Pennsylvania there are great beds of bituminous coal. Remember that the rocks of this region are almost flat, so that the coal layers between the rocks will be flat. It is for this reason that it is easier to mine the bituminous coal than it is to mine the anthracite. The rivers in the plateau region, in cutting their deep valleys, cut through rock layers and coal layers near the surface. The edges of some of the coal layers show along the sides of the valleys. In such places it

197 is not necessary to sink a shaft down through the earth to reach the coal. 

It can be mined by digging back into the coal layers from the valleys.

From some of the West Virginia mines coal loaded on barges is sent down the rivers to the Ohio. There the barges are bound together and pushed down the river to supply western and southern markets (page 149).

The beds of soft coal extend south along the plateau to Alabama. This coal is much used in the smelting of iron ore and the manufacture of iron and steel. 

Petroleum and Natural Gas. You have already learned much about the great petroleum industry of our country and about natural gas (pages 141-144). 

For many years western Pennsylvania and southwestern New York were leading petroleum-producing regions and natural gas was abundant and cheap. 

Some oil and much natural gas are still found there. Pipe lines have been built so that the natural gas can be supplied to many of the cities of western New York as well as those in Pennsylvania.

Iron Ore. Iron is mined in the 

Adirondacks, in the highlands of New

Jersey, and in various parts of Pennsylvania. Large deposits are found also in other parts of the Appalachian 

Highlands, especially near Birmingham, Alabama. In recent years most of the ores used in the iron furnaces in western 

New York and Pennsylvania have come from the large deposits that are found in the Lake Superior region. 

Pittsburgh and the Iron Industry. 

The point of land lying between the Monongahela and Allegheny rivers, where their waters join to form the Ohio, was once in the possession of France. To protect this territory, the French had built Fort Duquesne. It was taken by the English in 1758 and renamed Fort

Pitt. The city that grew up around this fort was called Pittsburgh. The iron and steel industry developed at Pittsburgh because it was near great deposits of bituminous coal and near beds of iron ore and limestone rock. All of these are necessary in the manufacture of iron and steel. 

The iron deposits of Pennsylvania no longer furnish enough ore for the mills of 

Pittsburgh and other cities. A part must come from other states. Vast deposits are found not far from Lake Superior in Minnesota, Michigan, and Wisconsin (map, page 141). This ore is mined and taken to the near-by lake ports. It is then brought down the lakes in ore boats to Cleveland, Erie, and Lackawanna, or to other ports on Lake Erie. From these ports some of the ore is carried by rail to 

Pittsburgh and other cities for smelting and manufacture. At the smelting cen-

A. 

- Steel mill at Pittsburgh. At the left of the center are seen the rounded tops of three ovens for heating the air used in blast furnaces. 

Iron ore is a mixture of iron with other | matter. The coal used for fuel is first turned into coke. To make coke, coal is heated in large ovens until some of its gases are driven off. Coke, iron ore, and broken limestone are put together into great furnaces. The furnace has a tall stack or chimney, and a blast of very hot air (A) is forced through the burning mass to increase the heat. The limestone is put in to make the impurities separate from the iron. 

When ready, the melted iron is run off from the furnace into molds in sand, making pig iron, or it may be run directly into another furnace called a converter or into an open basin or hearth. Here it is purified still more and certain other materials are added to it, so that it becomes steel (B). 

Pig iron is brittle, and so are many objects made from it, such as stoves. B. 

Society for Visual Education 

- One step in steel making-pouring ingots. 

Steel is tougher and harder, and can be used for many different things, such as tools, rails, boiler plates, steel for tall buildings, and watch springs. Wrought iron, made by a different process, can be bent or hammered into any desired form. 

The making of glass has become an important industry of Pittsburgh, because of the supplies of cheap fuel and of glass sand near at hand. Much of the American plate glass is manufactured here.

The manufacture of iron and steel and of many articles made from them is carried on in other Pennsylvania cities. 

Each one of these cities usually has other manufactures as well. In eastern Pennsylvania, Bethlehem, Reading, and Lebanon manufacture iron and steel. Bethlehem and Allentown make use of the limestone of the Great Valley in manufacturing cement. 

Roanoke in Virginia and Chattanooga and Knoxville in Tennessee are near deposits of coal, iron, and limestone rock. 

All three cities manufacture iron and steel, but the great iron and steel center of the 

South is Birmingham, Alabama.

Birmingham is close to the southern end of the great Appalachian Valley. 

Here and to the north there is more iron ore left underground than there is in the whole Lake Superior region. Close to 

Birmingham are beds of coal and beds of limestone. There is one place where you can see an iron mine, a coal mine, and a limestone quarry all at once- all the things needed to make iron. Birmingham is sometimes called the "Pittsburgh of the South." It has grown very rapidly. Before 1870 there was no blast furnace and there was no city. Now many thousands of people in Birmingham are at work in the steel, cement, and other manufacturing industries.

NORTHERN LOWLANDS 

were at one time the bed of a large glacial lake. You know that a great ice sheet once covered a large part of North 

America (page 12). It was very thick at one time, but the time finally came when it began to melt so rapidly that its southern edge retreated toward the north. 

With this retreat of the ice front the 

Allegheny Plateau was at last free from ice. The front of the ice sheet, its southern edge, was then somewhere over the Lake Plains in western New York.

Water from the melting ice made a lake between the ice front and the highlands to the south. This glacial lake slowly increased in size and depth until it found a low point on the shore where it could overflow.

As the ice kept on melting, one after another lower places were uncovered where the waters of the lake could escape. For a long time they flowed to the Hudson River and helped to cut the 

Mohawk Valley. At last, when the ice was melted, Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, and the other Great Lakes farther west (map, page 10) came to have their present size.

The glacial lake built beaches much as our Great Lakes are now building beaches. There are such old lake beaches to be seen on the Lake Plains of New York state and in other states farther west. The early settlers used them as roadways, and some of them, much improved, are still in use.

The Soils and Farming on the Lake Plains. The soils of the Lake Plains are fine and fertile and much of the land is under cultivation. The cities and villages of the Lake Plains furnish a market for much of the farm products, and the surplus is sent to more distant markets. In the southwestern corner of the state, bordering Lake Erie, is a grape-growing region from which grapes are shipped to many city markets. Some are used, however, in the manufacture of grape juice. Peaches, apples, pears, and cherries are grown in the region south of Lake Ontario.

A Great Trade Route. One of the most important trade routes in our country is the one connecting New York City with the Middle West by way of the Hudson and Mohawk valleys and the Lake 

Plains. Railroads, highways, and the canal that connects the Great Lakes with the Hudson River follow this route. 

Along this route there are many cities and important manufacturing industries. 

Find Albany on the Hudson River (map, page 154). It is the state capital and is now a port that can be reached by ocean-going freight steamers. A deep channel has been dredged in the Hudson for thirty miles below the city so steamers can reach the wharves of the port. 

North of Albany is Troy, famous as a center for the manufacture of shirts and collars. A short distance west of 

Albany is the manufacturing city of 

Schenectady. There you will find great factories engaged in the making of all kinds of electrical machinery and powerful locomotives. Farther west along this great trade route are the cities of 

Utica, Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo.

Utica is the trade center of a rich farming country, and has large textile mills. 

Syracuse manufactures electric lighting apparatus, typewriters, and automobiles. Rochester leads the world in the manufacture of cameras and other photographic materials. Here also are made fine optical glass, men's clothing, and scientific instruments.

Buffalo is a port at the eastern end of 

Lake Erie, and there are only twelve larger cities in the United States. It is at the western end of the Barge Canal, and at Buffalo much of the freight that comes east by steamers on the Great 

Lakes is landed. 

There are grain elevators, stock yards, and smelters. Flour and cereal foods are made, meat-packing establishments prepare meats for market, and there are many metal industries in or near the city. A modern industry that is increasing in size and importance is the manufacture of airplanes. 

Niagara Escarpment and the Falls. 

In the western part of New York state a high bluff called the Niagara Escarpment separates the part of the Lake Plains bordering Lake Erie from the part bordering Lake Ontario. North of 

Buffalo, where this bluff crosses the 

Niagara River into Canada, the land on one side of the bluff is over 300 feet higher than on the other side. 

The Niagara River connects the two lakes of Erie and Ontario. Between them there is a drop of 327 feet, half of which is where the river tumbles over a cliff 160 feet high to form Niagara Falls.

Niagara Falls are famous all over the world for their beauty and grandeur.

They are visited by many thousands of people every year. You know that falling water is used to turn machinery to generate electricity (page 185). Think of the electricity that might be generated if all the power of falling water at Niagara could be used in that way. But to do this would destroy the beauty of the falls. 

The American and Canadian governments have made an agreement upon the amount of water that can be taken by each country. 

Much of the electricity generated at

Niagara Falls on the American side is used in the city of Niagara Falls for the manufacture of aluminum and other products. Some is sent over wires to other cities, to be used for light and power. 

Lowlands of Northern New York. 

The lowlands that surround the Adirondacks in northern New York are narrow, but they are important as trade routes.

The Mohawk Valley has already been mentioned. North of Albany a lowland route follows the Hudson River for a short distance, then crosses a low divide into the valley of Lake Champlain. This is a direct route from New York City to 

Canada and the city of Montreal. West of the Adirondacks another route follows a river valley north of Utica to the lowlands bordering the St. Lawrence River. 

Railroads and highways follow both of these routes and a branch of the Barge 

Canal connects the Hudson with Lake

Champlain. In these valleys and in that of the St. Lawrence there are some fine farms and large dairies.

Natural Regions of New England. 

Southern Connecticut, eastern Massachusetts, southeastern New Hampshire, and most of Maine are hilly lands. On the map, page 80, this region is shown as a part of the Piedmont Plateau. It is not very high above sea level, and you might almost think of it as a lowland, but you must not think of it as a coastal plain.

Long, long ago, there were mountains where these hill lands are now. These old mountains were worn away by wind and rain, by frost and sunshine, by the slow grinding of ice, and by the work of running water and dashing waves. The average width of this hilly region is about 60 miles, and, except in Maine, it is one of the most densely settled parts of the

Between them is the Connecticut River Valley. The two highlands are parts of the natural region called Appalachian Mountains and Valleys (map, page 80). 

In northern Connecticut and western

Massachusetts this highland region is a hilly plateau with a surface from 900 to 2000 feet above sea level. In it the streams have cut deep valleys. One of these is the valley of the Connecticut River, the bottom of which is only a little above sea level.

East of the Green Mountains, and separated from them by the valley of the Connecticut River, are the White Mountains of New Hampshire. Some of the peaks of the White Mountains have been named after Presidents of the United States. They are in the ridge or range called the Presidential Range. The highest peak is Mt. Washington (203 A). Its top stands out as a rocky summit above the timber line. It can be reached by a cogwheel railroad. From it, on a clear day, you can see the Atlantic Ocean and look into Canada and Vermont.

Climate of New England. 

Northern

New England and southern New England differ in climate because of differences in altitude, in latitude, and in nearness to the sea.

The southern part is warmer because it is low and near the ocean. 

The northern part is colder because it is mountainous and a long way from the ocean. What other reason is there?

In the woods of Maine and in the uplands of New Hampshire and Vermont the winters are long and there is a heavy cover of snow. Thick ice is formed on lakes and streams. In regions with heavy winter snows, vehicles with runners instead of wheels are used during the winter (A). These sleds, as they are called, slide over the snow as it packs in the roads. Along the coast, especially in the south, there is far less snow. 

Winter winds from the southeast come from the warmer sea and usually bring much moisture that falls as rain or snow. 

A winter storm from the northeast, called northeaster," is dreaded because it comes from colder seas and has crossed the cold ocean current flowing south along the coast of Labrador. 

Work of the Ice Sheet. Your study of the work of the ice sheet will help you to understand many things about New England. The ice sheet covered all of 

New England (map, page 12). The moving ice ground off the tops of the hills and lower mountains over which it passed, and left them smoothly rounded (page 

14). It swept away the loose material from hill tops and steeper slopes, leaving bare rock or a thin layer of rocky soil. It deepened some valleys and filled others.

When the ice sheet melted away it left a new surface. a new surface. Some of the old stream channels were blocked so that the water gathered into lakes, many of which later became swamps. Rivers were forced to find new courses where they have since cut gorges and formed waterfalls and rapids. Glacial waste was left in many places as deposits of clay, sand, or gravel, and as moraines, drumlins, and scattered bowlders. All of these things happened in New England as they did in other regions covered by the ice, and they have greatly influenced the lives of the people.

EARLY HISTORY 

207 

Early Settlements in New England. 

Notice that New England has a long coast line. It was natural that when our country was being explored and settled some of the explorers and later some of the settlers would land on these shores. One of the early explorers was an 

Englishman who made a map of this part of our country and gave it the name New England.

On the map, page 204, find the state of 

Massachusetts. Notice the long arm of land extending into the Atlantic Ocean from the southeastern part of the state. 

Find Cape Cod Bay. On the western shore of that bay find Plymouth.

It was at Plymouth (A) that a shipload of men, women, and children landed late in December, 1620. How many years ago was that? They had come from England on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean. 

They had faced the dangers of the voyage across a stormy sea to make new homes in a new land. The ships of that time were small.

There were only a hundred in the little band of people who landed at Plymouth that winter day. But they were full of courage, and faced the future with high hopes.

Most of the land round about was covered with forest. Winter had already come. Nothing could be planted until the next warm season. They could and did cut down trees for the logs with which to build homes. 

For food during that first winter they had to depend upon the supplies they had brought with them and the fish and game they were able to catch. There were 

Indians not far away, but not all of them were friendly. Once in a while, however, the settlers were able to get some food from them.

A. 

Keystone View Co. 

- Plymouth harbor today. The monument marks the spot where the first settlers landed. 

That first winter was a time of terrible hardship, but the story is too long to tell here. The thing for you to remember now is that Plymouth was the first permanent settlement in this part of our country.

As the years went by, more people came to Plymouth, and settlements were made also at other points along the New England coast. To live in this new land it was necessary for the settlers to have homes in which to live, food to eat, and clothing to wear. How did they get these things?

The raw materials for their buildings came from the forest and the cleared fields or rocky shore. The trees furnished logs for houses and lumber for furniture. 

The stones from the fields or shore were used for foundations and fireplaces and chimneys. In the building of the first homes many of the men joined together to help each other. Some were more skillful in shaping the logs for use, others were more skillful in laying the foundation walls or in building a fireplace or oven.

NEW ENGLAND 

In those early days every one learned to there were lowlands where the soil was work with his hands.

For food the settlers had fish and game, and from the Indians they learned how to grow corn and how to use it as food. The settlers wanted to raise larger crops of corn, and to raise other kinds of grain. 

They wanted to grow vegetables and fruits that could be stored for winter use. 

They wanted also to keep such domestic animals as sheep, hogs, cattle, and horses.

The clearing of the land for crops went on as the settlers made their way inland. 

Trees were cut down and their stumps pulled up or burned. Stony lands were cleared and the larger stones piled into fences between the fields. Even when all of these things had been done there were many places where the soil was thin, stony, and hard to work (A). 

 fine and fertile. It was because of the level fields and fertile soil that the Connecticut River Valley was settled early. 

It is still one of the best farming regions in New England.

All through the early years the growth of population away from the coast was slow. On many of the hill farms the thin stony soils yielded only poor crops, and the farmers were barely able to get along. 

When the fertile lands of the Lake Plains of New York and farther west were opened for settlement many New England farmers left their hillside farms and moved west. There they made new homes where the land was rich and easily worked. 

All during the time New England was being settled there were other settlements being made farther south along the Atlantic coast. Those who settled in 

Virginia found a milder climate than that of New England, and finer and more fertile soils. In each of the new settlements there was at first more or less trouble with the Indians. After these troubles were over the Virginia settlers spread out over the land and cultivated large farms or plantations. They found a good market for their tobacco in England and became prosperous. They were able to live well with less labor and with fewer worries than the farmers and fishermen of New England.

EARLY MANUFACTURES 

209 A. 

Whaling ship built in New England. 

Men learned to build ships, using lumber from trees in the New England forests. Shipbuilding soon became an important industry at many points along the coast. As the fishing industry increased, more and larger ships were built. 

The New England fishermen became very brave and skillful sailors. Later when they began to hunt for whales and when trade with China developed, they would be away from home for months or years at a time. It was not long before the shipbuilders of New England were building the swiftest sailing ships of the world (A). Salt fish, lumber, and furs were carried across the ocean to England, and lumber to the West Indies.

The Beginnings of Manufacture. 

Among the things that the settlers in this new land needed were shoes and clothing. 

At first these were made by the settlers themselves. The women spun the wool from sheep into yarn. This they wove into cloth or knit into stockings or other garments. The hides of cattle were tanned as leather, and during the winter or at night this was made into boots and shoes for the family or into harness for the horses. Furs bought from the Indians, or taken from animals that the settlers killed, were made into caps and coats.

After a time the more skillful dressmakers and shoemakers traveled from farm to farm or set up shops in the villages.

AGRICULTURE OF TODAY 

You have learned that for many years after the settlement of New England began, its population increased slowly (page 208). This was because the chief industry was agriculture. The land was hard to clear and hard to cultivate. 

You have also learned that some of the

New England farmers left their stony hillside farms and moved to the more fertile regions in western New York and beyond (page 208). Because of this a number of the poorer farms of New England were left to grow up to forest again. 

When people began to invent machines that would spin, weave, and do other work, they needed power to run them. 

They found this power in the waterfalls of New England streams. Factories and mills were built. Workers were needed, and the population began to increase rapidly. You will soon learn more about these great manufacturing industries.

Just now it is important for you to know that southern New England is one of the most densely settled parts of our country. How did the farmers of New 

England profit from its increase in population?

Farming in New England. -When the rich soil of our western states was brought under cultivation general farming in 

New England was no longer profitable.

This does not mean that there was no longer any farming at all, but it does mean that the New England farmers turned to special kinds of agriculture. 

In doing this they had to select their crops with care. This was true not only because of the thin and stony soil but also because of the climate. The climate is even more important than the soil in determining what crops will grow.

AGRICULTURE OF TODAY 

211 The growing season in the southern lowland is only about six months long. 

There the last killing frost in the spring may come in late April, and the first killing frost in the fall in the middle of 

November. Along the Canadian border the growing season may be only four months long. The last frost in the spring usually comes late in May; the first frost in the fall, in the middle of September. 

Turn back to page 157 and read again about the climate of Florida. Why are the winters in Florida so much warmer than those in New England? Compare the length of the growing season in southern Florida with that in southern 

New England. Explain the difference. 

As the population of the New England cities and villages increased with the growth of manufacturing, there was need of more vegetables and fruit. Market gardening and truck farming became important industries and are carried on near all the larger villages and cities.

Many of the hillside farms where it is too cool or too moist for raising many food crops have become dairy farms as in the Appalachian Plateau. Railroads and trucks bring milk and cream every day to Boston and other cities from nearly all parts of New England. It is distributed to stores and homes by wagons and automobiles. Some of the milk and cream from the fine dairy farms of 

Vermont is sent by fast train to New York

City. In New England, as in other dairying regions, vegetables are raised for home use, and such crops as hay, oats, and corn are raised for the animals. Some farmers raise poultry for city markets, and also raise a part of the food for the poultry.

In gathering the crop a scoop is used with fingers through which the vines but not the berries will slip. At times a single sweep of the scoop will gather a quart or more of the berries. A machine may be used for doing this work (A).

THE FORESTS AND LUMBERING 

The early settlers found forests almost everywhere. Naturally they cleared the lowlands, the smoother and gentler slopes, and the lower hilltops. The rougher and higher lands were left in forest, and form the wood lots of today. You will still find large forested areas in the Green Mountains, the White Mountains, and stretching across Maine.

Why Forests Are Valuable. - The people are now learning the value of the forests, not only for lumber, but also for preventing floods and for keeping a steady flow in streams used for water power. 

The leaves, mosses, and black soil of the woodlands hold much rain water and allow it to flow slowly into the lakes and streams. If the trees were all cut away, the rains and melting snows would rush down the steep slopes. There would be 

There would be floods in the lower river valleys, causing great damage, and in dry spells there would be a failure of the water supply. 

Pine, spruce, and hemlock are important kinds of soft wood found in northern New England. Among the hardwoods are oak, ash, maple, and birch. Lumbering is much less important here than in former times. It is, however, still an active industry in Maine and in parts of 

New Hampshire and Vermont. With care the New England forests will always furnish lumber for local use, supplies of firewood, and some pulp wood. Part of the White Mountain forest has been made a national forest reserve. 

The forests furnish raw material for many small manufactures in New England. Among these are bobbins, spools, crates and boxes, pails, rakes, clothespins, toys, and many novelties. Large amounts of lumber are used for building or made into furniture.

In the lumbering district, most of the trees are cut in the winter time (206 A). 

The lumber camp in the deep snow is a place of hard toil and rough and ready fun. fun. When the snows melt and the logs are driven down the flooded streams of spring (A) the work is both hard and dangerous. Downstream at some good place the logs are collected in a pond. 

One by one they are pulled into a mill to be cut into lumber or made into wood pulp.

NEW ENGLAND 

By a waterfall on some small stream a factory may be built to make spools or clothespins. In some large town or city the lumber may be worked up into moldings, window frames, doors, or flooring. 

These will be sent to Boston or some other city for sale. Bangor and Augusta in

Maine are downstream from great forests and have water power for sawmills and factories. They can ship lumber and its products both by water and by railroad. 

Maple Sugar. - More maple sugar is made in Vermont than in any other state. During March the sap of the maples begins to flow through the trees. 

The farmers bore small holes in the trees and put spouts into them. The sap comes through the spouts and drips slowly into buckets that hang from the spouts. The sap, collected once or twice a day, is boiled in large kettles or pans until it forms sirup or sugar.

MANUFACTURING 

Several causes have combined to make 

New England a great manufacturing region. (1) There is much water power, the cheapest kind of power that man uses. (2) New England is on the sea border.

It has many fine harbors and an extensive railroad system. These help in the collection of raw materials and their distribution to factories, as well as in the marketing of the manufactured goods. (3) Labor-saving machinery came into use early in New England and led to the building of mills and factories and to the training of skillful workers. (4) The industries that prospered grew larger, and other industries of the same kind were started in New England. (5) Because of the success of industries already there, new industries using other raw materials located in located in New England.

There they were sure to find trained factory workers. More workers came, some from the farms, others from more distant places, and in time they also became skillful. (6) Factories making the same kinds but not always the same quality of goods began to locate in the same city. This made it possible for buyers to visit many factories in a short time.

An excellent example of this concentration of an industry in a city is found in Troy, New York (page 200), where many shirts and collars are made. The felt hat industry at Danbury, Connecticut, is an example in New England. 

In any large city the wholesale, retail, and factory districts are usually in different parts of the city. The larger and 

Uses made of the finer houses and apartments are near each other on a few of the better streets.

Where the Raw Materials Come From. 

Very few of the raw materials used in the mills and factories of New England are found or grown in New England itself. Chief among the manufacturing industries of New England are the weaving of cotton and woolen cloth (A), the tanning of hides and the manufacture of shoes, the making of small metal goods and jewelry, and paper making.

Most of the cotton used in New England is raised in our southern states. The wool and hides come from our western states and from foreign countries. The metals and jewels used in New England factories come from other places. Pulp wood for paper making is the only one of the chief raw materials of which New 

England produces a large quantity. 

The Cotton Industry. More than a hundred years ago skillful men in England had invented machinery for spinning and weaving cotton. England did not allow any of these machines, or even any patterns of them, to be taken out of the country. She wished to keep the business for herself. In 1789 Samuel Slater came to this country and settled in Rhode 

Island. Remembering how the English machines were made, he built some new ones. In 1790 he began to make cotton goods in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, a town which now has great cotton mills. In this way our cotton manufacture began.

NEW ENGLAND 

Cotton, pressed into bales of about 

500 pounds each, comes to New England ports by ship from Savannah, Mobile, New Orleans, and Galveston. Some of the New England ports where it is received are also cotton-manufacturing centers. This is true of New Bedford and Fall River, and in those cities many of the bales are unloaded close to the mills. When cotton is sent to inland mills, it must be carried a short distance by rail.

Many people are employed in the cotton industry. A single mill may employ several thousand workers. People from Canada and people from various European countries have come in large numbers to work in the mills. Schools in New Bedford, Fall River, and Lowell train workers for this industry. 

Calicoes, ginghams, and other cotton fabrics are made; also knit underwear, stockings, towels, handkerchiefs, and thread. From the mills the finished goods are sent to the wholesale and retail merchants in all parts of the United States, and to many foreign countries. 

Among the great cotton-manufacturing centers of New England are New Bedford, Fall River, and Lowell in Massachusetts; Manchester in New Hampshire; and Pawtucket in Rhode Island. There are large mills also in Taunton, Massachusetts; in Nashua, New Hampshire; in 

Lewiston, Maine; and in many other cities and towns. In recent years cotton manufacturing has developed largely in the South (pages 134-135), and New

England factories find themselves in competition with southern mills. 

The Woolen Industry. -The manu facture of woolen goods in New England began long ago on the home farms. Later small mills were built in villages along the streams. Now much of the industry is centered in great mills in a few cities. 

Lawrence in Massachusetts, and Providence and Woonsocket in Rhode Island, are large centers of woolen manufacture. 

Many of the cities that make cotton goods make woolen goods also. The weaving of carpets is an important branch of the woolen industry, and special attention is given to making the finer kinds, such as Brussels, Axminster, and Wilton.

Boots and Shoes. The tanning of skins is an old industry in eastern Massachusetts. Men who knew how to make leather were among the first settlers who came from England. Tanning is still done in towns near Boston, but much leather is brought to New England from other states. Boston is the principal 

New England market for hides and leather.

Many common articles, such as traveling bags, pocketbooks, and harnesses, are made from leather. The greatest use of leather, however, is for boots and shoes.

In early days these were all made by hand, but now they are turned out very rapidly by machinery. The region about 

Boston is the leading part of the United States for shoe manufacturing. This region extends to southern Maine and 

New Hampshire, notably in Manchester.

The more important centers of the shoe industry in Massachusetts are Brockton, Lynn, Haverhill, and Boston. This industry alone is more than three fourths of all the business of Brockton and 

Haverhill. Shoes are made also in New 

York, Rochester, and many other cities. in our country. Because of the excellence of American shoes, they are sold all over the world.

Wood Pulp and Paper. In the old days paper was made from rags gathered from homes and factories. 

For more than fifty years, however, much paper has been made from wood, and now newspapers and most books and magazines are printed on such paper. The softer kinds of wood are used, especially spruce. 

Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and 

New York have much spruce, and these states have become important in the wood-pulp industries. Much pulp wood is also imported from Canada.

The trees are cut down, the bark removed, and the trunks cut into blocks about two feet long. The mills, which often make both the wood pulp and the paper, are in or near the forests, usually where a waterfall supplies power. The pieces of wood are ground by heavy machinery or boiled in acid to make the pulp. The acid process leaves the fibers longer and makes the paper stronger than the method of grinding the wood. The city is not near the forests, and the best grades of Holyoke paper are made from rags. Some of the rags come from

THE FISHING INDUSTRY 

Some of the New England ports have sent men and ships to sea to fish ever since the days of their first settlement. Fish are to be found in great numbers in the waters along the coast and in shallow waters a few hundred miles to the northeast. Europeans have fished in the shallow sea to the south and east of Newfoundland (map, page 6) for more than four hundred years. 

Since the trade between our country and Europe is now so large, fishing on these "Grand Banks" of Newfoundland is at times very dangerous. This region is crossed by the great Atlantic steamers.

Although fishing is still an important New England industry, some shore towns have changed their business from catching and packing fish to manufacturing.

Sailors from New Bedford and Nantucket 

Island at one time went out on sailing voyages of three or four years to distant oceans to catch whales. Now New Bedford is best known for cotton mills, and Nantucket as a summer resort. 

How the Fish Are Caught. Boston and Gloucester are the great fishing centers of New England, and are among the greatest in the world. Hundreds of schooners sail from New England ports to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, where cod and halibut are found. The fishing is done from small boats called dories that put off from the schooner with one or two men in each. The fish are dressed and packed in ice, or salted, and the schooner, when loaded, returns to 

Boston, Gloucester (A), or it may be to

Portland or some other fishing center. 

Cod and halibut live in waters of some depth and must be caught with hooks.

Mackerel swim in schools through the surface waters and are caught with huge nets. nets. Lobsters are caught in traps near the shore, especially along the coast of 

Maine. Oysters are common on the south shores, and many are shipped from shore towns. Along the shores of Maine many small herring are canned and sold as sardines. The canning of fish and other sea foods is an important industry at several of the fishing ports. 

QUARRYING 

In all settled countries where good building stones are found, many public buildings and fine homes are built of stone or of brick with stone trimmings. 

Many of the rocks of New England are so hard that they can be cut into blocks and slabs for building and other purposes. 

Granite. The most widespread and important rock in this region is granite.

NEW ENGLAND 

It is hard and is used for buildings, for monuments and tombstones, and for paving blocks and curbstones. New 

England granites are usually of a gray color. There are large granite quarries in Quincy, Massachusetts; Barre, Vermont; Concord, New Hampshire; and in Maine. 

Marble. Marble is quarried in the 

Green Mountains in Vermont, in the 

Berkshire Hills in western Massachusetts, and in Connecticut. The industry is largest in Vermont, which ranks first among the states in this product. Rutland and Proctor are the chief centers. 

Here great pits have been made where the marble has been taken out, and yards and sheds are filled with the blocks and slabs to be made ready for shipment. Marble is used for the walls of buildings, for interior decoration, and for monuments. 

Slate and Other Stones. Slate is a fine-grained rock that splits into thin sheets or slabs, and is used in roofing, for school blackboards, and for floors, stair treads, and other uses in building. Slate is quarried in Vermont and in Maine.

Red and brown sandstones are found in the Connecticut Valley.

The granite, marble, and slate are shipped not only to towns and cities in New England, but also to other states. 

Much of the granite is quarried near the sea and goes by ship. This is usually the cheapest way for any freight that is as heavy and bulky as stone. Nearness to large markets and good transportation facilities make quarrying a large industry in New England. As in other states, beds of sand and gravel furnish materials for concrete which is used in roads and buildings.

SUMMER VACATION LANDS 

Many people who are able to do so take a vacation during all or a part of the summer. Popular vacation places in

New England are to be found along its seashore, among its hills and mountains, deep in its forests, and along the shores of its lakes.

Resorts in Mountains and Forests. — 

Mountains are cooler than lowlands (page 185), and the New England mountains have forests and clear air far away from the smoke of villages and cities.

They also offer wonderful views of woods, fields, lakes, and sky. Hence, in summer, thousands of people go to these mountains for rest and pleasure.

In the wide forests of Maine are many lakes, joined by streams. Here the tourist can canoe for long distances, and can camp, hunt, and fish.

The growth of manufacturing and trade has led to the growth of many large cities in New England. It will not be possible to mention all of them here, and it is not necessary to know exactly what is made in each of these cities. Some cities have been named already in connection with great industries. A few others are mentioned here because of their size and general importance. 

Boston. -The chief port and largest city of New England is Boston. Many other large cities and towns are within a few miles of Boston, and "greater Boston," or the Metropolitan District, as the region is sometimes called, has more than two million people. At Cambridge, just north of Boston, is Harvard, the oldest of American universities. It was founded in 1636, by John Harvard, and

Boston is the capital of Massachusetts and one of the most important seaports of the United States. Coasting steamers run to all points on the New England coast, to the ports of Canada, and to 

New York, the West Indies, and the 

Gulf of Mexico. Several lines have regular sailings to Great Britain and other foreign countries. Cotton from the southern states, fruit from the tropics, and hides from many countries are among the products landed on Boston wharves. 

From Boston are sent many of the manufactured products of New England. 

The city is also a shipping point for grain from the western states. 

Salem, like Boston, is an old seaport, and many years ago ships from all parts of the world brought rich cargoes to its wharves. Boston grew faster and gained more suitable for modern ocean steamships. Boston is also at the most western point on Massachusetts Bay, and from

Boston railroads were built across the 

Berkshire Hills to Albany and the West. 

Railroads run from Boston to the city of New York, and to all important points in New England and eastern Canada.

Southern New England is covered by a close network of railroads. One of the roads passes through the Hoosac Mountain, a part of the Berkshires, by a tunnel about five miles long.

The canal across Cape Cod from 

Buzzards Bay to Cape Cod Bay shortens by several hours the sea route from 

Boston to southern points. 

Boston is the business and banking center of New England. center of New England. Many companies that own mills and factories in the smaller cities have their main offices in Boston. Through these offices they buy their raw materials, such as wool, cotton, or leather, and also make sales of cotton cloth, worsteds, shoes, and other products.

Other Seaports of New England. 

Look at your map and see how the shore curves in and out in deep bays and many headlands. On some of the rivers in drowned valleys boats can sail far inland. Bangor, Providence, and Hartford can trade on water routes, yet notice how far each is from the sea.

Portland is not a large city, but it is a great seaport. It is the chief city of

Maine. It is a trade center for the manufacturing cities of the state, has an excellent harbor, and sends steamships to 

Boston, to other American ports, and to

Liverpool. The Grand Trunk Railway of Canada reaches the sea at Portland, and thus has an outlet in the winter months, when most of the Canadian ports are closed by ice. Thus Portland is a seaport for the country to the north, sending across the Atlantic some of the grain and live-stock products of Canada. 

Other New England coast cities have much coastal trade, but they have grown. partly from other causes. Providence has a large trade by water, but it has become the second city of New England largely by reason of many manufactures. 

It is the capital of the state of Rhode 

Island, and is also the seat of Brown 

University. New Haven and Bridgeport (A), in Connecticut, are large cities on the sea. Because the sea road was open to them, they could get the raw

NEW ENGLAND 

materials of manufacture, including coal, and have become towns of many factories. 

Yale University, founded in 1701, is at 

New Haven.

A Few Inland Cities. Many cities are where they are chiefly because of the things they make. They are places of one or two kinds of factories. But some of the large cities have more than one reason for their growth. Worcester is next in size to Boston and Providence. 

It is not on the sea, but has long had a railroad from Boston and its wharves.

This railroad also extends west to Albany. 

Worcester has a great number of mills and factories of many kinds, especially in iron work and machinery. 

Springfield is a crossroads city, with railroads running north and south in the 

Connecticut Valley, and between Boston and the West. Several smaller cities, many towns, and a large, rich farming region depend on Springfield for their chief trade. 

Hartford is another great city of the 

Connecticut Valley, a center of trade and of many kinds of manufactures. It is the home of large insurance companies. 

There are smaller inland cities which, like the "big three " just named, are well known. Pittsfield has factories, railroads extending in four directions, beautiful homes, and is the chief trading center of the Berkshire region. Bennington, in

Vermont, is an old town, near a battlefield of the Revolution. Burlington, which looks out across Lake Champlain to the Adirondack Mountains, is the chief city of Vermont, and the seat of the state university.

Population: Its Density and Distribu tion. - Table 2 near the end of the book gives the population of the different states. Make a list of the New England states and the population of each. You will find that the total population of New England is more than 8,000,000. An interesting comparison can be made with

Texas, as that state is four times as large as all New England and has only about three fourths as many people. The distribution of the New England people is also interesting. In the northern parts of Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont there are no more people than you would find in other woodland and mountain regions. It is in southern New England, as you have learned, that most of the great manufacturing and trading centers are found. That region has become one of the most densely settled parts of the 

United States. 

Commerce. Before leaving the study of New England, think again of some of the things you have learned as they influence the commerce of this part of our country. You will remember that most of the raw materials used in New England factories must be imported. Some of these come from distant parts of our own country by railroad and by sea. Others are imported from foreign lands in nearly every continent.

To pay for these imports, manufactured goods must be sent to market and sold. Again the railroads and ships are called into use. This means, of course, that more cloth, shoes, paper, and metal goods are manufactured in New England than can be used in those states. It is one of the great manufacturing centers of our country and of the world. Other manufacturing centers, however, have grown up in many parts of the United States, and the industries of New England must today meet great competition.

WESTERN HIGHLANDS 

Toward the west, beyond the central lowlands of our country, are the Western

Highlands. This part of our country is a vast region of mountains, plateaus, and valleys, and most of it is usually divided between two state groups (map, page 88). 

The larger group is called the Plateau 

States (page 226), and the other, including three states, is called the Pacific 

States (page 246).

Taken as a whole, these Western States are divided into a number of natural regions (map, page 80). One of these, the 

Great Plains, is shared with other states to the east, and this region you have already studied. West of the Great 

Plains, towering above them like a great wall, are the Rocky Mountains. Beyond the Rockies are the Great Basin and the 

Columbia and Colorado plateaus. Next beyond the plateau and basin regions is the lofty region made up of the Cascade Range and the Sierra Nevada.

Between these and the Coast Ranges that front the Pacific Ocean are the Willamette-Puget Sound Valley and the Valley of California. All of these natural regions are shown on the map, page 80. 

In studying these Western States you will want to know how people who live there have made use of the natural advantages and resources of each. 

Climate and Scenery of the West and the East. The climate of the Western 

Highlands shows a wide variation between its northern and its southern parts. In

In this western region, where there is enough moisture, there are forests on the western slopes of the The eastern and western parts of the United States are very different in several other ways. In the East the fields are generally green and most of the mountains are low enough so that they are covered with forest. In the drier parts of the West there are scattered grasses and shrubs and the landscape is gray, except where there are trees bordering the streams and where irrigation has covered the fields with green. In other parts the land is high and rugged.

In the East the rain storms are seldom very severe. In the drier parts of the 

West there may be no rain for months, but there are sometimes violent storms called cloudbursts. Then torrents of water rush along the beds of streams while the storm lasts, only to leave them dry again until another storm comes.

CLIMATE AND SCENERY 

229 In the East the air is often humid, or full of moisture. That is why so many summer days are said to be sultry. In the West there is usually much less moisture in the air. When this is true the air is clear and bracing. In the Plateau

States the general elevation of the land is about a mile above sea level. The air is so thin, or rare, that people breathe more rapidly and deeply. Because of this rareness of the air and its dryness, the region has become a noted health resort. Those who come from the dense air of the lowlands are sometimes made very uncomfortable by the rare air of these higher lands. They are unable to run or to work as they have usually done, until they get used to it. The clearness of the air makes the sun and the stars seem to rise and set very suddenly. At night the stars are more brilliant, and more stars can be seen, than in the East.

There is a difference also in the natural scenery of the West and the East. The western mountains are higher and more majestic. Mt. Marcy in the Adirondacks is 5344 feet high, and Mt. Mitchell, the highest of the Eastern mountain peaks,

In some places in the West, as in the East, the waterfalls and rapids of mountain streams have been used to generate electricity (A). The electricity furnishes power and light in mines and villages and for the homes of farmers. But only a small fraction of the water power of these streams has yet been put to work. 

A long time ago many of the mountain. peaks were active volcanoes, from which at times came melted rock or lava and fine dust, steam, and gases that looked like smoke. Lassen Peak in northern

California is the only volcano in our country that is now active (B). Other old volcanic peaks such as Mt. Shasta in 

California, Mt. Hood in Oregon, and

Mt. Rainier in Washington (map, page 

246) now have snow fields that last throughout the year. From the snow fields of Mt. Shasta small glaciers form and move down its sides until they melt. 

On the desert plains the winds blow with great force, for there are few barriers to hinder their movement. There is little cover of grass and there are few roots to bind the earth and sand. Enormous quantities of dust are sometimes blown into the air. Such storms may be somewhat like the blinding snows of a winter blizzard. In some places the winds pile the sand into hills, forming sand dunes. 

Explorers and Pioneers. The first white explorers to visit the western part of our country entered it from the south. 

The southern part of this region belonged to Mexico until about 1848, and Spanish explorers had visited the western coast as early as the sixteenth century. In 1579 

Sir Francis Drake, an Englishman, sailed along the Pacific coast line as far north as 48° north latitude. But no settlements were made as a result of these early ex plorations. 

In 1792, over two hundred years after 

Drake's voyage, the English navigator 

George Vancouver visited the western coast of our country, and discovered 

Puget Sound. He returned again in 1793 and in 1794, and made careful and extensive surveys of the coast. Vancouver 

Island at the opening of Puget Sound (map, page 246) is named after him. 

In 1793 Robert Gray of Boston sailed his ship, the "Columbia," into a large river to which he gave the same name as that of his ship. The Columbia is the chief river in the northwestern part of our country, and one of the great rivers of North America. 

The western part of the Mississippi basin, extending far into the northwest, became part of the United States in 1803, by purchase from France. Captains Lewis and Clark were then sent into the northwestern wilderness to learn more about it. 

They started at St. Louis, went up the 

Missouri River, found a way across the 

Rocky Mountains and the Columbia 

Plateau, and followed the Columbia River to the Pacific. On the map, page 86, trace their route. As you do so remember that these men were making their way through an unknown wilderness.

There were no roads or railroads and few trails to guide them. It was a long, difficult, and dangerous trip that called for great courage and great endurance.

In 1806 a young army officer, Captain 

Zebulon Pike, started westward on a more southern trail. He explored part of the 

Rocky Mountains and his name was given to a great peak that overlooks the plains of Colorado (231 A). About thirty years later Captain Bonneville carried on explorations in what are now the states of 

Idaho, Washington, Utah, and Nevada.

These are a few of the daring men who "broke the wilderness" and made known the wonders of its snow-clad mountains, its sandy deserts, its deep canyons, and its mighty waterfalls. The far Northwest, beyond the Mississippi basin, was claimed by both England and the United States until 1846. In that year these two countries agreed that the western part of the boundary between our country and Canada should be the parallel of 49° north latitude.

As the central part of our country began to fill up, some of the more restless of the pioneers moved to the West. 

In 1844 Captain John C. Frémont, a

EXPLORERS AND PIONEERS 

231 

A. Cogwheel railroad on Pikes Peak. famous American explorer of those days, made his way overland to California.

He made a trail that many others were to follow in the days of the great gold rush. In 1848, only four years later, gold was discovered in California river gravels, and the next year people set out for the gold fields from all parts of the East. Many went by ship around South 

America, a long and dangerous voyage, or went by way of the Isthmus of 

Panama. Others followed the trails that hardy pioneers had marked out across the mountains of our own country. 

It was thus that the life of the West began. Railroads and well-built highways now follow the trails along which covered wagons once slowly wound their way. Homes and comfortable hotels have taken the place of tents. The Indians, with whom the pioneers and early settlers fought, have been conquered after many fierce wars and much wrongdoing on both sides. Many of them now live on reservations -land that the government has set aside for their use. They have farms or ranches, or carry on some of their native industries, such as weaving blankets, rugs, and baskets.

In the years that have passed since that first great rush for gold, the West has made wonderful progress. There are stores of coal, iron, copper, and precious metals to be mined. There are lands that can be profitably farmed by the newer agricultural methods. There are great cities, fine roadways, and magnificent scenery, and those who live there enjoy also the same advantages as those who live in the older East.

THE ROCKY MOUNTAINS 

The early explorers and pioneers who made their way westward across the 

Great Plains found themselves facing snow-clad mountains. From a distance they saw no way of crossing them. It almost seemed as if they had come in their covered wagons to the "end of the trail." Later they were to find the actual end of the trail on the shores of the Pacific Ocean nearly a thousand miles farther west. 

The most promising routes across the mountain wall before them seemed to be the valleys of the rivers. But these often led into steep-walled canyons where roaring waters filled their beds from wall to wall. Later some of the pioneers climbed up the slope to a notch or pass. 

To reach even the lowest of the passes was a long, hard climb, with a steep descent on the western side. 

Today some railroads make use of canyons that the rivers have cut through the mountains from the plateaus farther west. But this was not possible until railroad men had made places for the tracks and for necessary bridges. The 

Royal Gorge route through the canyon of the Arkansas River is a wonderful engineering work (A).

Farms and Pastures in the Rockies. 

Hidden in the mountains are many valleys. Some of them receive enough moisture during the year and are warm enough in summer for the growing of crops. Others get little or no moisture because they are shut in by mountains, but there are mountain streams whose water can be used for irrigation. Still others are too cold to permit the growing of any crop except grass.

A. 

Royal Gorge, on the Arkansas River, in Colorado.

Among the forests that cover the lower mountain slopes there are pasture lands where cattle or sheep can graze during the summer. On higher slopes, even above the timber line, there are pasture lands for sheep that can be used from the time the snow melts in the spring until the fall. A sheep herder and a camp tender, with a number of sheep dogs, are usually in charge of two or three thousand sheep. Each year the herder and his camp tender live alone for months at a time with a covered wagon for a home. 

Much of the pasture land in the mountains forms a part of some national forest reserve (245 A). Before sheep or cattle can be grazed on these lands the owner must get permission from the officer in charge, and must pay a small sum for each animal. 

Mines and Mining. -The mineral resources of the Rocky Mountains are

THE ROCKY MOUNTAINS 

233 

State of Calif. Div. of Mines 

A. Hydraulic mining of gold. 

rich and varied. They include iron, copper, lead, zinc, silver, and gold. All of these metals are usually found in ores, mixed or combined with other minerals. 

In addition to the metals named above, coal and petroleum are also found. The chief regions where each of these minerals is produced are shown on the map, page 141. You will notice that the same minerals are found in many other parts of the Western Highlands. 

Precious Metals. Gold and silver are called precious metals because small amounts of them have a high value.

They are used in making coins, ornaments, and many artistic as well as useful things. These metals are most commonly found in mountain regions. The reason for this is that the rocks in such regions have been folded, cracked, or crushed, and sometimes heated. In some places the metals have been dissolved by water in the rocks and deposited in pockets or cracks with other substances. 

When these pockets and cracks are filled in this way they are called mineral veins.

During the long, long time that has passed since the mountains were formed their tops have been worn away by glaciers, frosts, and streams. Rocks containing gold have been worn away with the other rocks. Many particles of gold were mixed with the sand and gravel carried down the mountains and deposited by the streams. This kind of gold-bearing earth is called a placer. 

Mining Methods. - In getting the gold from placers, the miners put the sand and gravel in a pan with water and shake the pan. The gold particles are heavier than the sand and sink to the bottom. When the other material is washed away the gold can be gathered from the bottom of the pan. Large pieces, called nuggets, are sometimes found.

In order to get the gold more rapidly, a powerful stream of water is turned upon a bank of gold-bearing gravel, through a large hose (A). The gravel may be washed through a trough or sluice having crossbars on the bottom. The gold, being heavy, sinks behind the crossbars and is gathered. This process is called hydraulic mining. 

When metal-bearing rock is found in veins, it is dug out. The mines may be at a depth of hundreds or thousands of feet beneath the surface. Shafts are sunk and tunnels, called drifts, are dug from the shaft to reach the vein. Sometimes the drifts are dug into a mountain side if the vein can be reached in this way. 

The vein may be several inches or several feet thick, and this is followed and blasted out. In many of the great mines there is a network of shafts and tunnels, with every help for drilling, blasting, and hoisting the ore. Pumping is often necessary to keep the mines from being flooded with ground water. The roofs of large openings must be supported by timbers or concrete posts. crete posts. The drills may be driven and the mines lighted by electricity.

Some ores are put through a blast furnace or smelter, as in the case of iron (page 198), to separate the metal from the other materials in the ore. There are smelters at Pueblo and Denver in 

Colorado; at Butte, Great Falls, and 

Anaconda in Montana; near Salt Lake 

City in Utah, and at many other places. 

Some ore is shipped as far east as Omaha to be smelted.

Many of the richest mineral regions are on lands owned by the government. 

A man who searches for ores is called a prospector. When he finds good ore he files a claim on the land and is then given the right to work his claim. 

Rich finds of the precious metals often cause great excitement. Men rush in, it may be by thousands, hoping to gain sudden wealth. Tents are set up, rude cabins are built, mining machinery is brought in, and stores are quickly fitted out with all kinds of supplies. If the region remains productive for a number of years, better buildings are put up and streets are laid out and improved. If the supply of ore is very large, or if the place becomes a center of trade for surrounding regions, a permanent city is established. If the ore is all removed and the place has no other advantages, it may be abandoned after a few years. 

The Great Metal-Mining States. — All the states of the Plateau group produce gold and silver. Utah and Montana lead in silver mining, and rank next after 

Arizona in the mining of copper. Butte, in western Montana, is the center of a mining region that has produced much copper for many years. 

Great quantities of silver and lead are produced in the Coeur d'Alene district in northern Idaho. Much of the trade of this region goes to the important city of Spokane in Washington. 

There are many mining regions in various parts of the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. From these much gold, silver, zinc, and lead, and some tungsten, radium, and other metals are obtained. 

Lumbering. There are very large evergreen forests in the Rockies, especially in Idaho and Montana. They are chiefly on the western slopes of the mountains and in the north where the rainfall is heaviest. Lumbering is carried on (235 A), but this is not one of the great lumbering regions of our country. One reason is the difficulty of getting the lumber to market. Logs cut on the mountain slopes must be lowered by cables or allowed to slide down the mountains in wooden troughs or chutes. The sawmills are usually in the valleys.

THE GREAT BASIN 

Read again what is said on page 88 

about the Great Basin. Why is this part of the plateau country called the Great Basin? Study this region on the maps, pages 80 and 226. Notice that it has, except at the south, a surface several thousand feet above sea level, and that it is bordered, east and west, by very high mountains.

Great Salt Lake. - Streams from the 

Wasatch Mountains dissolve salt and other materials from the rocks and flow into lakes and mud flats whose waters do not reach the sea. The largest lake of this region is Great Salt Lake. If there were enough rain, the level of this lake would rise until it overflowed at some point and its waters would then reach the ocean. But now the water evaporates from the surface of the lake, and is carried away in the air in the form of invisible vapor, about as fast as water flows into it. The salts are left behind, and the lake water has become a brine so dense that bathers float in it without any effort.

There 

Where the Mormons Settled. 

are many short ranges of steep mountains running north and south through the 

Great Basin. Waste from these mountains has spread over the land below them, and sagebrush and other desert plants are almost the only natural vegetation. There are not many people in the Great Basin, except near the Wasatch

Mountains. They are there because the rainfall on the western slopes of the Wasatch is heavy enough to furnish water for irrigation of the farm lands near by. 

In 1847 a company of Mormons came from Illinois, across the Great Plains, through the Rocky Mountains, over the 

Colorado Plateau and through the passes of the Wasatch range. Between the

Wasatch Mountains and Great Salt Lake they found flat land, with a soil so good that it needed only that it needed only water to make it fertile. They built ditches to irrigate the fields and made their new home into a great garden. 

Their leader told them to plow deep and plant alfalfa.” As you know, much alfalfa is grown on irrigated lands. It makes a fine hay or forage crop and gathers nitrogen from the air. The nitrogen makes the soil richer. The roots of this plant go deep into the earth. 

In irrigated regions it grows rapidly and can be cut several times a year. The alfalfa pastures are rich, and grazing is carried on in parts of the Great Basin. 

After 1848 the main route to California crossed this Mormon territory, and the population there steadily increased. 

When, later, a railroad was built through this region it brought more people. The territory of Utah was admitted as a state in 1896. It was found that this is also a region of great mineral wealth, for there are vast deposits of copper, lead, silver, gold, and zinc. The ores of these metals are usually found combined, and it is only in recent times that it has become possible to separate them profitably.

THE COLUMBIA PLATEAU 

The plateau region in southeastern 

Washington, eastern Oregon, and in much of Idaho is called the Columbia Plateau.

It is named after the Columbia River, the chief stream in the northwestern part of our country. The Columbia and its principal tributary, the Snake River, flow across the plateau in deep canyons. 

Those of the Snake River vary in depth from 400 to 6000 feet, and those of the 

Columbia River from 100 to 1000 feet.

Turn to the maps on pages 80, 226, and 

246 and see just where this plateau is before you read about it and about the industries carried on within its borders. 

How the Plateau Was Formed. This great plateau was formed largely from flows of lava over a very long period of time. There was so much of this lava that it filled in valleys and flowed over

the tops of some of the mountains that were there before these flows began. In the Snake River region the lava was very liquid and flowed so easily that it covered large areas before it cooled. It came from many volcanoes that were close together over most of the area. In 

Washington and Oregon the lava and other volcanic material came to the surface through long cracks or fissures in the earth. 

Climate. Because the plateau is shut in so completely by mountains its average temperature is higher than it would otherwise be. The rainfall is largely shut out by the Cascade Range on the west of the plateau region because the chief winds are the westerlies. They leave their moisture as either rain or snow on the western slopes of the mountains. The rainfall of the Columbia Plateau varies from 8 inches a year in eastern Oregon and on the plains along the lower Snake, to 25 inches in higher areas. There is enough rainfall in southeastern Washington to permit dry farming (page 223).

Throughout most of this region the winters are very cold, and there is heavy snowfall in some of the surrounding mountains. This snow melts slowly in the spring and helps to keep up the flow of the rivers. 

Soil and Crops. The topmost layers of lava, especially in Washington and

Oregon, have decayed to form a rich and fertile soil. In some places it has a thickness of over 60 feet. Other soils are the fine rock waste that was deposited over the bottoms of old lakes once found in this region. There are also soils made up of fine wind-blown rock materials that have been left by the winds that have swept across this region. 

The natural vegetation is sagebrush and bunch grass, but wheat is grown by dry farming in eastern Washington and 

Oregon. This is one of the great wheatgrowing regions of our country. Can you name any others? As in other dryfarming regions, there is of course some rainfall. It comes usually in winter or spring and is enough to grow the crop if the seed is planted at the right time. 

When the wheat is ready for the harvest the days are usually bright and sunny, and the grain ripens before it is cut. 

Combined harvesters and threshing machines are used (239 A). The harvester knives (on a cut bar) move back and forth very quickly and cut off the standing stalks at any desired height.

These are carried to the thresher and the grain is threshed at once and bagged or run off into an open wagon that moves along beside the thresher. There is so little rainfall at this time of the year that the bags of wheat may be piled in the fields and left until the farmer is ready to ship or store them.

In the plateau section of central Washington and Oregon there are several valleys where irrigation has made it possible to raise all the fruits and vegetables of temperate latitudes. One of the best of these fruit-growing regions is the Yakima

Valley in Washington, famous for its wonderful orchards and hop yards. Other equally famous orchards are in a valley in northern Oregon near Mt. Hood.

In Idaho dry farming is carried on along the borders of the Snake River plains. There are irrigated regions in many places where the water from smaller streams can be used. Cattle and sheep are raised and mountain pastures are used in the summer.

Cities. Spokane in eastern Wash ington is the only large city of the Columbia Plateau. Several railroads that cross the continent gather here as if in a knot. 

Railroads run south on the Columbia 

Plateau, north into Canada, and east and west to connect the city with other parts of our country. Spokane is a great trading center, collecting the products of the surrounding region to be manufactured or shipped out, and distributing such articles as the people of the region need. Its manufactures include meat packing, flour, and lumber, and products made from lumber.

Walla Walla and Yakima in Washing ton, and Boise, the capital of Idaho, are also important trading centers of the plateau.

THE COLORADO PLATEAU 

The Colorado Plateau is one of the wonderlands of our country. Before beginning its study turn to the map on page 80 and be sure that you know just where it is. High, rocky, and for the most part arid, it is a region of painted splendor. 

Some parts of it are so desolate that you can think of them only as deserts. Many of the rocks are gorgeously colored. You almost believe that some mad painter, with a giant paint brush, has splashed them with all the colors of the rainbow.

Industries. Within the Colorado 

Plateau there are irrigated regions and places where dry farming is carried on. 

There are sections where the sagebrush and bunch grass furnish natural pastures for sheep and cattle. There is a small forest area and there are oil wells and deposits of coal, copper, lead, and zinc.

The map 124 A shows the irrigated lands in this region. Some of the irrigation projects include the making of large reservoirs or lakes that add to the beauty as well as to the usefulness of a region. 

Some are the result of great feats of engineering; for example, the digging of a tunnel through a mountain from the canyon of the Gunnison River in western

Colorado to water the flat lands bordering its tributary the Uncompahgre. In the one valley there was water but little land that could be irrigated. In the other there were broad fields but very little water. The irrigated lands along the Rio Grande border that stream from 

Colorado into Texas.

Population. -The population of the 

Colorado Plateau region is not large. 

There are settlements where mining is carried on, there are cattle and sheep ranches, and some irrigated districts. 

A few hotels provide food and shelter for visitors who come to see the wonders of the plateau, but as a whole this region has only a sparse population.

Some Indians are still to be found in this region. They usually farm small patches of land, look after their sheep or cattle, and work at such native industries as rug and basket weaving and making pottery. Many years ago the Indians who lived in this region were frequently at war with other tribes. To protect themselves from their enemies they built their homes on shelves of rock high up on the steep cliffs that border the canyons.

The ruins of their villages may still be seen. Other villages were built on the flat tops of great masses of rocks to which the early Spanish explorers gave the name of mesa, meaning "table." Their crops were grown on the surrounding plains. 

The methods that they followed were in many ways much like those used in irrigated regions or in dry farming today. 

The Grand Canyon. The Colorado 

River rises in the lofty Rocky Mountains of northern Colorado and flows southwest across Utah. On its way it passes through deep gorges that it has cut into the rocks of the plateau. In Utah it is joined by the Green River, a large tributary which rises in Wyoming. When the river enters Arizona, it bends to the westward and flows in a canyon which in some parts is more than a mile deep. This is the Grand Canyon, the most wonderful gorge in the world (241 A). Its width varies from 5 to 15 miles and it has a length of nearly 280 miles, of which 105 miles are within the boundaries of the Grand Canyon National Park. At the bottom of the canyon the river flows
