THE COLORADO PLATEAU 

241 A. -A small part of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River, in Arizona. You are looking into the inner canyon, with its steep walls. The broad, swiftly flowing river reaches from wall to wall. Most of the rocks are bare, and many of them are brightly colored. as a swift, muddy torrent, with many | over the bottom of this body of water. dangerous rapids. The walls rise in places almost straight up from the water for half a mile or more before the canyon begins to widen out.

In ages past, probably a million or more years ago, the region you are now studying was below the level of the sea. The water that covered it may have been a huge lake or it may have been a bay or an arm of the ocean. From ancient mountains the rivers of that long ago carried rock waste into this lake or sea as the Mississippi is now carrying it to the Gulf. The mud and sand were spread 

Through the years and the ages it accumulated, growing thicker and thicker and slowly changing to rock.

At last the long period of accumulation ended. Slowly the land began to rise. 

Rivers were formed and found their way to the ocean. How many there were no one knows, but the Colorado was one, and with its tributaries it has done most of the work of cutting the famous canyons of this region. As the land rose the rivers cut through the rock layers deeper and deeper like a great saw eating its way through a log that is pushed against it.

The tools with which each river worked were the sand and gravel from its tributaries and the rocks from its bed and the canyon walls. The Grand Canyon was formed by the slow wearing of waterborne sand and stones on rock, just as today the river is still cutting away at its bed and widening its walls and valley. 

It is still carrying seaward, as it has for untold ages in the past, rock waste to enlarge the great plain that it has formed at its mouth by filling in the sea. 

It is well to remember that what rivers and winds, rains and frosts, and snow and moving ice did in the ages past they are still doing today. It is also just as true that what we see them doing today they did in the past. Always they have worked slowly, as it seems to us, but through the long ages they accomplish mighty tasks. The waters of a melting ice sheet carve a Mohawk Valley and provide a great trade route. The falling waters of Niagara carve a great gorge and furnish water power for electric generators. The waste carried by a Mississippi fills a great bay with fertile soil on which millions of people earn their living. 

A river, coming from the mountains, flows across rising land, but holds its course and cuts a canyon that is one of the wonders of the world.

There are many side canyons that join the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River.

In the Grand Canyon the layers of rocks have been cut into wonderful shapes. 

There are rock masses that, seen at a distance or in the evening shadows, look like the towers and temples of a city of Asia, or a great European cathedral. The layers of rock are of many different colors. 

There are reds, grays, yellows, and browns in shades without number. Seen in sunlight or shadow they make a wonderland of great beauty. 

A railroad and an excellent highway reach the south rim of the canyon, where there are hotels to care for visitors.

Those who wish to go down to the level of the river can use a trail down the side of the canyon. The trip down and up this "Bright Angel Trail" is usually made on the backs of donkeys or horses, as the way is steep. Every year thousands of travelers from all parts of the earth visit the Grand Canyon.

The Lower Colorado Region. — The national government is national government is building the 

Boulder Dam (or Hoover Dam) at the lower end of the Grand Canyon. It will provide power, furnish water for irrigation, and prevent floods in the plain below. The lower part of the Colorado 

River flows through a desert plain in which the heat is often very great. This plain is made of the earth and rock waste brought by the river from the canyon and from the highlands far to the north, and spread out in old deltas. 

Find Phoenix (map, page 226) in southwestern Arizona. It is the capital of the state and a trading center in the midst of a rich agricultural region and not far from many mines and smelters. To the northeast of Phoenix a highland area, known as the Arizona Highlands, crosses the state from northwest to southeast and extends into Mexico. In these highlands, on the Salt River, a tributary of the Gila River, the Roosevelt Dam was built. The water from this reservoir has been used to generate electricity for light and power and to irrigate thousands of acres of former desert (map, page 124). 

On these irrigated lands that have an almost tropical climate are grown long-

NATIONAL PARKS AND NATIONAL FORESTS 

Before leaving the Plateau States to take up the study of the Pacific States, you should know something more about the national parks and forests within their boundaries. — - 

The Yellowstone National Park. In the high mountain region where the three states, Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho, come together, is the Yellowstone National Park. Most of it is in the state of Wyoming.

Wyoming. The continental divide crosses the park, so that a part of it lies in the basin of the Missouri River and another part in the basin of the Snake River. 

The canyon and falls of the Yellowstone River, and hot springs and geysers to the number of a thousand or more, furnished the chief reasons for laying out a national park here. Hot springs are found also in some other parts of the United States. Their waters have been heated by hot rocks not far below the surface of the earth. 

The Yellowstone Park is one of the few places in the world where there are geysers, or springs that spout hot water.

A. The geyser Old Faithful in eruption. 

Old Faithful" is so called because once in a little over an hour, with great regularity, a column of steaming water rises from it 120 or 150 feet into the air (A).

Other geysers spout every few hours, or days, or irregularly, but the cause is the same in all. At some distance below the surface of the earth the water in the geyser becomes so hot that some of it is changed to steam. When the pressure of the steam becomes too great, it forces its way out through the water above, pushing some of the water out with it. 

The column of steam and water rushes out of the opening and rises high into the air just as steam comes out of the spout of a teakettle. When the steam 

When the steam has escaped, water collects again and is heated until the spouting is repeated. 

Hot water dissolves many things out of the rocks. When it reaches the surface, the water becomes cooler and drops much of the dissolved material at the mouth of the spring. In this way terraces of wonderful colors and forms have been slowly built up about some of the hot springs in the park. 

Hunting in the park is forbidden, and the elk, bear, and other animals there lose their fear of man and become less wild. 

There are excellent roadways and hotels in the park. The clear air, and the geysers, springs, lakes, rivers, waterfalls, and canyons attract thousands of visitors every year. 

Glacier National Park. In 1910 the government set aside an area of about 

1500 square miles in northwestern Montana as a national park. It is a region of great natural beauty, with towering peaks, lovely valleys, and gem-like mountain lakes. As there are many glaciers within its borders, it has been named the 

Glacier National Park. 

National Forests. In the Plateau 

States, and also in some other states, the government has established a number of forest reserves (245 A). They are mainly in mountain districts where there is enough moisture for trees to grow. It is expected that these forest lands will always be kept under government control. 

The preservation of the forests will prevent the washing away of the soil and the destruction of property in the valleys.

Men trained in forestry, which is the science of caring for trees, have charge of these reserves. Under their direction are many forest rangers, who lead a lonely but a very busy life, constantly moving about on horseback or on foot. Among their many duties they look out for forest fires, put them out when started, and prevent the stealing of timber.

THE PACIFIC STATES 

The map facing this page shows the three states of our country that border the Pacific Ocean. Within the boundaries of these states you will find the 

Sierra Nevada, the Cascade Range, the 

Coast Ranges, the Valley of California, and the Willamette Puget Sound Valley (map, page 80). 

The Sierra Nevada. - California is the largest state in the Pacific group and has the highest mountains. These mountains, the Sierra Nevada, extend nearly north and south through eastern California. The name means "snowy mountain range." Much of the Sierra has an altitude of 13,000 feet, or almost two and one half miles. Find Mt. Whitney on the map. What do you know about this and other mountains in the Pacific States? (Pages 229-230.) The range has a gentle 

National Park Service big tree." slope to the west, but is steep on the east, where it overlooks the Great Basin in Nevada. The lower western slopes of these mountains are covered by forests or have been cleared to form fertile fields. 

The upper slopes are above the timber line, and consist of bare rocks and rock waste. You will remember that the timber line is the belt above which trees cannot grow because of cold.

The streams that flowed down these long slopes cut into the rocks, sawed across veins of gold, and carried the dust and nuggets of the gold to the valley. 

It was the finding of this gold that started the gold rush of 1849 (page 231).

In California there are several kinds of trees unknown in other parts of the world. 

They grow to heights of 200 or 300 feet.

Many have diameters of ten, twenty, or even thirty feet. Among the greatest are the "big trees" (A) that grow on the

slopes of the Sierra Nevada and Coast

Ranges. Both the nation and the state have set apart reserves containing the big trees in order to save them from the lumberman and from destruction by fire. 

Some of these trees are believed to be at least four thousand years old. In the 

Coast Ranges of northwestern California there are extensive forests of the very large trees called redwoods. Picture to yourself a tree so big that if it were hollow at the base you could hold a goodsized class in it!

The Yosemite Valley is a deep canyon in the Sierra Nevada. The Merced River and some of its branches enter the canyon by falls from 300 to 1600 feet high (A).

The Yosemite Valley is as well known, though not so large, as the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. It has been set apart as a national park. 

Cascade Range. The lofty mountain range of eastern California continues northward through central Oregon and Washington, but in those states it is called the Cascade Range. The Cascade 

Range is not so high as the Sierra Nevada, but is broader and is nearly all covered with great forests. Above it rise several volcanic cones, to the region of glaciers and perpetual snow. Seen in the sunlight they are like bright jewels rising above the setting of the dark-green forest. 

Among these peaks are Mt. Hood in 

Oregon, and Mt. Rainier and Mt. Baker in Washington. Mt. Rainier is 14,363 feet in altitude, and is one of the noblest mountain peaks in the United States.

In the heart of a low, broad, volcanic mountain in the Cascade Range is a pit six miles across and 4000 feet deep, half filled with water, called Crater Lake. 

The basin was formed by the sinking of

the central part of the mountain. This place, like the Yosemite Valley, has been reserved by the government as a national park. The banks which you see in the picture (249 A) are 1500 feet high. 

Coast Ranges. Like the Sierra 

Nevada and Cascade Range, the Coast

Ranges extend north and south through the three states. The northern Coast 

Range in Washington, between Puget

Sound and the ocean, is known as the 

Olympic Mountains. The Coast Ranges are rugged in many places, but are not nearly so high as the Sierra Nevada.

These mountains are almost on the very edge of the continent. Between them and the sea there is no such coastal plain as you found in the eastern part of our country.

On the Atlantic side of the United States there are many rivers such as the Hudson and the Potomac whose deep waters provide safe harbors. Look on your map for openings into the land in the Pacific States. California has one in 

San Francisco Bay. Oregon has one in the lower part of the Columbia River. 

Washington has one in the Strait of

Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound, south of 

Vancouver Island. 

The Valley of California. West of the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Range is a series of wide, open valleys, with a fertile soil and a large population. 

One of these is the great valley of central 

California, shut in by the Sierra Nevada on the east and the Coast Ranges on the west. It is four hundred miles long and fifty miles wide. The southern part is drained by the San Joaquin River, which flows northwest. The northern part is

A. 

Part of Crater Lake, Oregon. The island was built up by an outburst of melted rock after the basin had been formed. drained by the Sacramento River, which flows southward. Both rivers receive many tributaries, and they unite before entering San Francisco Bay. The bay connects with the ocean through the 

Golden Gate. The eastern tributaries of both rivers are fed by the rains and melting snows of the Sierra Nevada.

Many of them are small during the dry season. The western tributaries, coming from the eastern slope of the Coast Ranges, are much less important. This slope gets but little rain. For this reason it is scantily covered with forest. There is little or no flow of water in the streams from this region during the dry season. 

The Willamette Puget Sound Valley. 

West of the Cascade Range in Oregon is the fertile Willamette Valley, a region about the size of Massachusetts. Through this valley the Willamette River flows northward and joins the Columbia River.

On the Willamette, a short distance from its mouth, is the city of Portland. West of the Cascade Range in Washington is a broad, fertile valley whose northern part is deeply indented by Puget Sound.

Climate. The climate of the Pacific | Puget Sound and Willamette valleys 

States shows sharp contrasts. The climate of western Washington is temperate, while that of Death Valley and some other parts of southern California is very hot. In each state the temperature of the great valleys is moderate, while the high mountains have frost, snow, and ice.

The lowlands near the Pacific Ocean have a mild climate, being cooled in summer and warmed in winter by the prevailing westerly winds blowing from the sea.

There are also great contrasts in rainfall in this region. Here are the wettest, and some of the driest, lands in the 

United States. Except in high mountains, the winter season is wet rather than snowy. The summers are dry - so dry on some of the lowlands that bags of wheat and trays of fruit can be left out of doors for many weeks without injury from moisture.

The average annual rainfall in western Washington is about 65 inches. In some parts of the mountains it is even more than this, and is the heaviest in the 

United States. Eastern Washington, on the other hand, is east of the mountains and has but about 20 inches of rainfall. 

Oregon shows a like difference between its western and its eastern parts. Northern California, and the high mountains toward the south, have plentiful rains, while the southern parts of the great valley are so dry as to need irrigation. 

Parts of southeastern California are among the driest of deserts. The range of annual rainfall in this state is from 3 inches in some southern parts to 80 inches on the lofty mountains of the northwest (map, page 84). 

Agriculture. The leading industry of the Pacific States is agriculture. In the and in the northern part of the Valley of California, rainfall is sufficient for crops. Even where the rainfall is scanty, as is the case in much of eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, and the southern and south-central parts of California. either dry farming is possible or irrigation works may bring the water of the mountain streams to the fertile lands of the valleys.

In the early days of farming in these states, wheat was a leading crop, and it is still an important crop in eastern Washington and Oregon (page 238). In California the large wheat farms of the early years have disappeared. They have been divided into smaller farms which are more carefully cultivated and on which products in great variety are now raised. The 

Willamette Valley also is a most prosperous agricultural region. In many parts of the Valley of California the land has high value, the farms are small, and fruits and garden crops are raised. Some agriculture also is carried on in the valleys of the west slope of the Coast Ranges. 

The recent agricultural development of California has been in the raising of fruits, vegetables, and nuts. 

It is now the greatest fruit state in our country. 

It is best known for fruits of warm climates, such as oranges and lemons. 

However, three fourths of all its fruit crop is in fruits of temperate latitudes, such as apples, peaches, apricots, and pears. California leads all other states in raising grapes, from which grape juice and raisins are made. In recent years

California has become even more important than Spain as a raisin-producing region. Many of the vineyards are in the valley of the San Joaquin River, in the

Forests and Lumbering. One of the largest and most important of the lumbering regions of the United States is in the three states of the Pacific coast. The great forests there are in part due to the heavy rainfall (map, page 84). Both 

Oregon and Washington have a very large amount of timber still standing, and Washington cuts more lumber than any other state of the Union. The manufacture of lumber products (A) is carried on at Seattle, Tacoma, Everett, Bellingham, and other Puget Sound ports, and at Portland in Oregon. From these places some of the lumber is sent to such distant points as Alaska, Hawaii, Japan, China, Australia, and South America.

Fisheries. Salmon live in salt water, but every year, at the spawning or breeding season, the full-grown salmon swim up the rivers into fresh waters. 

They may be seen hundreds of miles from the ocean as they swim up the headwaters and branches of the Columbia 

River, and of the Fraser River, in western

Canada. In the mountain streams the young salmon are hatched, and swim down to the ocean to make their growth.

After about four years they are fully grown; then they move up the rivers to spawn, and vast numbers are caught on A. Machine for cutting salmon into slices, in a canning the way. factory.

There is a large demand for lumber also in the growing cities and the many mines of the Pacific States. As the lumbermen do not depend upon snow on which to sled the logs, the work can be carried on at all seasons. To prevent careless lumbering and destructive fires, the national government has set apart vast tracts, as national forests, in the mountains of the three states (map, page 245).

When Lewis and Clark and other explorers came to the region (page 230), they found the Indians living mainly on these fish. For many years the white man has made a business of catching and canning them (A). Cans of salmon from the Columbia River or from Puget 

Sound are seen in almost every provision store. If properly put up in air-tight cans, the fish can be kept a long time. 

Fresh salmon also are shipped long distances in refrigerator cars.

One of the canning centers is Astoria, a small city in Oregon at the mouth of the Columbia River. This city was named for John Jacob Astor, who made the place a station for the fur trade of the Northwest. The fur trade has now become unimportant, and the fishing industry has taken its place. Canning is also done at Bellingham and elsewhere on Puget Sound. This industry is important also along the shores of western 

Canada and southern Alaska.

The state governments restrict fishing so that many fish can escape the nets and other fishing apparatus, and make their way up to the spawning grounds.

Mining. Much that is said about mining in the Plateau States is true for the Pacific States also. The discovery of gold in California in 1848 caused mining to become very important in the West. 

Ever since then California has been a great producer of gold, and it now ranks first among the states. There is not so much placer mining as formerly, but the larger veins in the mountains are worked, and the gold is separated by crushing and other processes. California produces also much of the liquid metal called metal called quicksilver or mercury. All the Pacific 

States are producers of gold, silver, lead, and copper. 

One of the largest smelters is at 

Tacoma, Washington, where silver, gold, Washington is the chief Pacific state in the production of coal, and California is one of the leading states of the country in the production of petroleum. The desert areas of southeastern California yield salt, soda, and borax.

San Francisco and the Valley of Cali fornia. - San Francisco stands upon a peninsula between the Pacific Ocean and 

San Francisco Bay. Its harbor is reached through the strait called the Golden 

Gate. The wharves and business streets of the city are on the east side, toward the bay (A), while the residence part is on NCS-15

Groves of orange trees in southern California. Notice how very large these groves are. The San Bernardino 

Mountains are shown in the background. the ocean side. San Francisco Bay and the Golden Gate furnish the natural outlet for the Valley of California. On the map, find Fresno, the center of the raisin district, and Bakersfield, the center of a great petroleum district. Both the raisins and the oil go naturally to San 

Francisco, on the way to more distant markets. There are rich vegetable gardens where the Sacramento and San

Joaquin rivers come together, and there are rice fields and fruit orchards farther north in the Sacramento Valley. 

San Francisco was the first Pacific

Coast city to develop trade across the continent and across the Pacific Ocean. 

Railroads lead also southward to Los 

Angeles, and northward through the 

Pacific valleys in Oregon and Washington to Vancouver, the great western port of Canada. 

The harbor of San Francisco is one of the best in North America, and ships go from it to ports of all nations on the 

Pacific and to many on the Atlantic.

All about the bay are cities and large towns which are suburbs of San Francisco. The largest is Oakland, directly across the bay, where some railroads from the east come to an end. Berkeley is the seat of the University of California. 

Stockton is at the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River and is a market for fruit, grain, and flour. 

Sacramento, on the Sacramento River, is the capital of California. It is one of the oldest cities of the state, is at the head of navigation for large boats, and is a market for fruit. 

Los Angeles and Southern California. 

There is great variety in the scenery of southern California. Go 200 miles north of Los Angeles and you come to Mt. Whitney, the highest point in the United 

States. Go down the western slope of this mountain region and you are under the largest trees in the world. Go down the eastern slope, and you come to Death 

Valley, below sea level, the hottest and most barren desert in North America.

On the coast in the southwest corner of the United States, is San Diego, on a fine harbor. It is a center for fishing and canning, but better known as a winter

San Diego and you come into the warm Imperial Valley, a part of which is below sea level. There flood waters from the 

Colorado River have made the Salton 

Sea. Today waters from that river help the farmers of the Imperial Valley to raise crops of winter vegetables, oranges, olives, dates, and cotton with long fibers. 

Farmers in this region have found that, with industry, they can make their living even on one of the smaller irrigated farms. They can live in a mild climate with plenty of sunshine, seeing snows on the mountains but not having to wade through snowy roads.

It is the outlet of the rich farm and fruit country of the Willamette Valley, and is the chief market and manufacturing center of the state of Oregon. The Cities of Washington. Go north from Portland and cross the Columbia

River. You will still be in a broad lowland of fields and great forests. Two or three hours after crossing the Columbia you will reach a seaport, Olympia, at the head of Puget Sound. Follow the east shore and you will find a chain of cities: 

Tacoma, Seattle, Everett, and Bellingham. From Tacoma, Seattle, or Everett you could take a train across the Cascade Range through a tunnel almost eight miles long, the longest railroad tunnel in the United States.

Seattle is the center of trade with Alaska. This is mainly a summer trade, but all the year ships go between this port and the Orient. Seattle is a city built on hills. Some hills that were too steep for building were washed down by streams of water driven against them with great force. Among the industries of Seattle is shipbuilding. 

At Tacoma much smelting is done (page 253) and there are also sawmills where huge logs from the forests of the 

Northwest are made into lumber. 

Manufacturing and Commercial Ad vantages. Manufacturing is developing rapidly in the Pacific States. Already it stands next to agriculture in importance. 

To a large extent the other industries already studied furnish the raw materials for the leading manufactures, which include: (1) the cutting of timber and its manufacture into boards, shingles, boxes, and furniture; (2) the manufacture of flour; (3) slaughtering and meat packing; (4) the canning of fish, fruit, and vegetables (A); (5) the refining of petroleum; (6) the manufacture of butter, cheese, and condensed milk; and (7) the smelting of ores.

The manufacture of lumber and lumber products is highest in value in all three states. The manufacture of flour is carried on in Portland, Seattle, and Tacoma, from which points it can easily be shipped to Pacific coast, South American, or Asiatic markets. Some flour is made at Spokane, in the wheat-growing region of eastern Washington. The falls in the Spokane River at this point are capable of furnishing an enormous amount of power.

The manufactures of the Pacific States are helped by railroads and water routes. 

Railroads have been built through the great farming and mining regions, and they bring the products of the fields and mines to the cities. Every year the transcontinental railroads carry many trainloads of fresh fruit across the mountains to eastern markets. The fine harbors of the greater seaports are easily reached from the ocean, and to them come ships from China, Japan, and many other distant lands. Commerce with our Pa- 

Commerce with our Pacific possessions Alaska, Hawaii, and the Philippines is increasing, as it is also with Australia, New Zealand, and 

South American and Asiatic countries.

The Panama Canal has increased the water traffic with New York and other Atlantic ports, and also with European countries.

THE PREVAILING WINDS 

or snow on the mountain slopes and on the plain. Some winds blow inland from the Atlantic Ocean, but these are not the prevailing winds.

When you were studying the geography | eastern coastal lowlands, and there is rain of the United States you learned about the winds that cross our country (page 122) and about the distribution of rainfall (map, page 84). The winds that blow across the country are usually from the southwest. These southwest winds, therefore, are the prevailing winds and are called westerlies. In the western part of our country they blow from the Pacific Ocean, where they have picked up moisture as water vapor, and move toward the land as moisture-bearing winds. In crossing the mountains the wind is cooled and the moisture falls as rain or snow on the western slopes.

In the eastern part of the country the winds blow inland from the Gulf of

Mexico and move toward the northeast. 

Even in the central lowland they are moving from the warm southland toward the cooler north, and so rain or snow falls on the plains. The mountains in this part of our country also run southwest and northeast. The winds blow northeast in the Great Valley and along the In the southern part of North America the prevailing winds are from the northeast. These winds grow warmer as they blow over the ocean, and they pick up more and more moisture. This moisture falls as rain on the lands when mountain slopes or plateaus force these winds from the northeast into higher and higher altitudes. This happens where the northeast winds cross Mexico and Central

America, and they leave much rain and some snow on the eastern slopes and on mountain peaks.

The map on page 263 shows the prevailing wind belts that girdle our earth, and the calms between them. There is some shifting of these wind and calm belts toward the north in our summer and toward the south in our winter. On the average, however, they are as shown on the map.

NATURAL REGIONS OF NORTH AMERICA 

263 Between each wind belt and the one next to it there is a belt of calms where there is hardly any wind blowing across the sea or land. The calm belt between the two belts of trade winds is called the equatorial calms or doldrums. The calm belts at and near 30° north and 30° south are the horse latitudes. 

You will notice that north of the horse latitudes in the northern part of the map the winds are from the southwest. South of the horse latitudes in the southern part of the earth the prevailing winds are from the northwest. They are the westerlies. 

South of the horse latitudes in the north the winds blow toward the Equator from the northeast and are called the northeast trade winds. North of the horse latitudes in the south the winds blow toward the Equator from the southeast and are the southeast trade winds.

In the equatorial calms the air is moving upward, but you cannot feel it. At the surface of the earth the northeast and southeast trade winds are blowing into this belt along its edges. In the horse latitudes the air is settling. It is moving downward, and from the outer edges of this calm belt the air is blowing outward over the surface of the earth.

ALASKA 

Many years ago Alaska belonged to Russia, one of the countries of Europe. 

In 1867 it was purchased from Russia by the United States for $7,200,000. Some of our people thought at that time that our government was paying more for 

Alaska than it was worth. Because the purchase had been arranged by William 

H. Seward, then Secretary of State, people spoke of it as "Seward's Folly."

Later you will be able to decide for yourself whether the money was wisely or foolishly spent. Alaska has been made a territory of the United States, with its own laws. It elects a legislature and has a delegate in Congress.

Position and Size. On the facing page you will find a map of Alaska. Before studying it, learn something about the position of Alaska as it is shown on a globe. You will remember that the lines drawn on the surface of the globe from the 

North Pole to the South Pole are meridians. They are north-and-south lines. 

The lines on the globe crossing the meridians at right angles are parallels and are east-and-west lines. Look on the globe at the map of the United States. You will see that many of the state boundary lines are meridians or parallels. 

On the globe find the boundary between 

Alaska and Canada. Notice that the northern part of this boundary is a meridian and therefore a north-and-south line. Follow with your eye the irregular and winding southern part of this boundary until it turns toward the Pacific 

Ocean at Dixon Entrance. This southern part of Alaska along the Pacific coast is sometimes called the "Panhandle.”

Study the map on page 264. On this map trace the boundaries that you traced on the globe. You will notice that the meridian lines on the map are straight. 

They get nearer to each other at the north and if they were made longer they would all meet at the North Pole. They get farther away from each other toward the south and would keep on getting farther apart as far south as the Equator. 

From there toward the south they would get closer to each other until they met at the South Pole. 

Notice that the parallels curve. They are drawn in that way on the map so they will cross all meridians at right angles as they do on the globe. It is not possible to show any large part of the earth's curved surface on a flat map without making some parts larger and other parts smaller than they ought to be. Remember in studying any map that meridians are north-and-south lines and parallels are east-and-west lines. 

You will see on your map a long narrow strip of land with some islands beyond it extending in a curving line southwest into the Pacific Ocean. The narrow land strip is the Alaska Peninsula, and the islands are the Aleutian Islands. All of these are part of Alaska and so belong to the United

States. North of the Alaska Peninsula and the Aleutian Islands is Bering Sea. 

It connects with the Arctic Ocean through 

Bering Strait, where Alaska is only 36 miles from the continent of Asia. The northern shores of Alaska border the cold waters of the Arctic Ocean. About one 265

third of the main part of Alaska is north | there is much rain, with heavy snowfall in of the Arctic Circle. 

Alaska is twelve times as large as New York state, and about one fifth as large as the main part of the United States. 

Point Barrow, its most northerly point, is in almost the same latitude as the most northerly point of Europe. Notice this on the globe. The most southerly island in the Aleutian chain is in almost the same latitude as London, the largest city in the world. The difference in latitude between Point Barrow and the southernmost of the Aleutians is about 20°. This is nearly the same as the difference in latitude between Galveston on the Gulf of Mexico and the western part of the boundary between Canada and the 

United States. 

Although Alaska is much smaller than the main or continental part of the United States, the distance through which it stretches east and west is about the same. 

The distance from its southern point at 

Dixon Entrance to the westernmost of the

Aleutians is about the same as from 

Plattsburg in New York state to Portland in Oregon. 

Climate. Alaska has a great variety of climate. This is due to the difference in latitude between its northern and southern parts, to differences in elevation above sea level, and to the effect of winds from bordering oceans. In the Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula and south along the Panhandle the winds are from the Pacific and have been warmed by its warm currents. Farther north the winds are from colder waters.

The Aleutians have a moderate temperature throughout the year, with heavy rains and almost continuous fogs. Along the Panhandle the weather is cloudy and the mountains. The warm winds from the Pacific are cooled by the mountains and part with their moisture, as on the 

Pacific coast farther south (page 122).

This part of the coast has the heaviest rainfall of all Alaska. In some places in the mountains 100 feet of snow may fall in a single year. This heavy snowfall helps to account for the large number of glaciers in this part of Alaska. Summer temperatures at sea level are high and winter temperatures are moderate. The thermometer has been known to show 87° at Sitka in August, and the lowest temperature recorded there in winter is 4° below zero. Our northern states all show lower temperatures than this. at In the interior the rainfall and snowfall are much lighter. The summers are short and hot and the winters long and cold. 

Such a climate is called continental. 

Winter temperatures of 75° to 80° below zero have been known. 

At Point Barrow the sun cannot be seen for about forty days during the winter. The temperature averages below zero from November to April. East and west along this Arctic shore the average annual rainfall is less than 7 inches.

A. Mt. McKinley, the highest peak in North America. Its summit is always covered with snow many feet deep. 

The land about it has been set aside as a national park in which much wild life is protected. 

Natural Regions. 

On the map showing the natural regions of North America (page 262) find what ones extend north and west from Canada into Alaska. Going inland from the Pacific you will find a region of mountains bordering the coast for more than 1200 miles and extending inland for 200 miles. Next inland is a region of plateaus, bordered on the north and east by an extension of the Rocky Mountains. Beyond them, at the north, is the Arctic Coastal Plain. 

Pacific Region. The Pacific region of Alaska is a continuation of the western mountains of the United States and 

Canada. The Coast Range of the Pan handle is rather uniform in elevation, with no well-marked crest. The mountains slope down steeply to the sea. Many long and deep inlets, or fiords, extend from the Pacific Ocean into these mountains of southern Alaska. Great glaciers move slowly down the valleys into the sea at the heads and along the sides of the fiords. 

Many other glaciers are found farther back in the mountain valleys. There are more than a hundred large glaciers and several thousand small ones in Alaska.

Mt. St. Elias is the highest of the mountains near the ocean, and Mt. McKinley, in the interior, is the highest peak in North America (A). It has a height of almost four miles.

Notice the many islands lying off shore from the Panhandle country. They are the tops of a mountain range most of which is below sea level. Between these islands and the coast are deep quiet waters forming an inland passage, the route of steamers for the north. Along the mountains that look down upon these protected waters you can see some beautiful forests, snow-covered peaks, and cascades and waterfalls without number.

It is this part of Alaska that is most visited by tourists. Its beauty and grandeur can never be forgotten by those who have been fortunate enough to see it.

Alaska from east to west, is useful for transportation in the summer. In winter, travel is by dog sled. Airplanes are now being used frequently. Juneau is the capital of Alaska and the leading mining center of this part of the territory. It is built partly on the side of a mountain (A). 

Central Region. Middle Alaska, along the Yukon and its branches, is a rolling country with no high mountains. 

The mountains to the south are a barrier to transportation because it is difficult to build roads through such a region. The 

Fairbanks is the chief trading center of this region. It is connected by railroad with the coast and by a government-built highway across the Alaska Range to 

Chitina on the Copper River and on to 

Valdez. Fairbanks is at the head of navigation on the Tanana River, a tributary of the Yukon. 

Polar Alaska. Northern Alaska, along the Arctic Ocean, is a low and treeless plain. On its southern boundary are the Brooks Mountains, an extension of

ALASKA 

269 the Rockies of Canada. They are largely unexplored and little is known about them. Much of northern Alaska is a region in which the ground is always frozen to great depths. The surface 

The surface thaws out during the brief summer and produces a growth of plants. Such regions are called tundras and are common on the northern plains of North 

America, Europe, and Asia. Few people live in this region because the extreme cold and the limited resources make it hard to earn a living there. Farming is not possible. Reindeer usually can find food, but raising reindeer so far away from any place where the meat can be sold is not profitable. 

Population. None of the towns or villages of Alaska are large. Juneau, the capital and largest town, has a population of only 4000. The total population of Alaska is about 60,000, much less than that of such cities as Niagara Falls or Binghamton, New York. Less than half of the population are white people, the rest being made up of Eskimos (A) 

Ewing Galloway and Indians. Most of the white population is in the towns and villages along the Pacific coast and is employed chiefly in the mining and fish-canning and fishsalting industries. The Indians are hunters and fishermen and are scattered along the Yukon River Valley. The

Eskimos live along the coast of Bering 

Sea and the Arctic Ocean.

Mining. Since the year 1867 about $700,000,000 worth of minerals have been taken from Alaskan mines. Chief in value among these are gold, copper, and silver. Copper mining did not begin until 1901, but by 1927 its annual value was greater than the combined value of all other Alaskan minerals. The most productive copper mines are in southern and southeastern Alaska.

Since 1880, gold to the value of about $400,000,000 has been taken from Alaskan mines, and silver to the value of over $12,000,000. There are large deposits of coal in Alaska, but little of it is mined, as most of the deposits are so located that transportation costs would be high. Tin, lead, and petroleum are also found.

Fisheries and Furs. The fishing industry is the most valuable of all Alaskan industries. Among the fish taken are salmon, halibut, cod, and herring, but the salmon are of far greater value than all of the others combined. Many kinds of salmon live in the waters of Alaska.

Read again what was said about this industry on page 252. Most of the salmon are canned, and the canneries may be seen all along the Pacific coast. The canned salmon is sent to the United

States and may be found on the shelves of nearly every grocery store in our country. 

In addition to the canneries there are plants where these fish where these fish are salted. 

Hatcheries have been established to keep the waters well stocked with fish. 

Cod are found on "banks" in Bering

Sea in great numbers, but cod fishing has not been developed into as important an industry as it has on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland.

Many fur seals are taken in Alaskan waters. Laws are now in force to regulate the number of seals to be taken each year and to prevent the killing of the mother seals. Since these laws were put in force, and especially in recent years, seals have greatly increased in number. 

The Pribilof Islands in Bering Sea are the breeding ground of the seals. Walruses and whales also are taken in the seas about Alaska. 

Wild foxes and those raised on fox farms furnish valuable furs for export to the United States. These include the red, white, blue, and black foxes. Minks, beavers, otters, and muskrats also are trapped for their skins.

Part of the 371-mile Richardson Highway between Valdez and Fairbanks. Here it winds through an evergreen forest at the foot of a mountain range. 

The trees are, as a rule, not large. They are chiefly poplar, spruce, and hemlock, and will be more useful for wood pulp than for timber. Timber for building is brought in from the Puget Sound ports. 

Because of the cool climate and the frozen and rocky soils, Alaska is not a good agricultural country. Some hardy grains will grow, but much of the grain is cut green for forage. Potatoes (270 A) and some other vegetables are successfully grown. Some dairy cattle are kept and are pastured on native grasses during the summer. They must be fed during a winter of about eight months. 

Years ago reindeer were imported from 

Siberia in northern Asia. Because of the similarity of the climates these useful animals have done well in their new home and their numbers have increased greatly. 

There are now many large herds in the territory. Many people believe that reindeer and moose raised on the tundra lands of Alaska and Canada will furnish a valuable meat supply in future years. 

Transportation. - A good road (A) runs from the seaport Valdez to Fairbanks on a branch of the Yukon River. The

United States government has built and operates the principal railroad of Alaska, reaching 467 miles from Seward, on the south coast, to Fairbanks. Passengers and freight can thus be transported to the heart of the territory, and various mining regions are opened to traffic. Another railroad leads from the seaport Skagway to White Horse on the Yukon; from there one may travel by steamboat down the Yukon to the sea. Coast steamers run along the south shore, and northward to Seward Peninsula and Nome. 

Along winter trails, small flags are placed every few hundred feet to guide and save the traveler during the dreadful storms. Travel is difficult and dangerous also because streams that must be crossed are without bridges.

THE PANAMA CANAL ZONE

THE PANAMA CANAL ZONE 

Turn to the map on page 10 and find the narrow neck of land that connects the continents of North America and South

America. It is the Isthmus of Panama. 

The map shows you that there is a part of the isthmus which is not very high above sea level. One of the lowest routes across it is followed by a railroad. The 

United States has built also a canal across the isthmus, following about the same route. Is this canal of much value to our country or to other countries?

Discovery of the Pacific Ocean. It was in 1513 that Balboa, a Spanish explorer then living in a colony not far away, crossed the isthmus. There were with him a small company of Spaniards and many natives. He had learned from a native chief that there was a large body of water beyond the land. The expedition made its way through forests and swamps until it came to the ocean that we now call the Pacific. Balboa called it the "Great 

South Sea" and claimed it for Spain. 

The Panama Canal. Although some earlier explorations and settlements had been made, the Spaniards now extended their explorations in the western part of 

South America and in southern North 

America. To make it easier to get from

Spain to the western parts of the two continents it was planned to dig a canal across the isthmus. The Spanish government at first did not want such a canal, but many years later the government favored the plan. No work was done by the Spanish, and the canal was not completed until nearly 400 years after it was first talked about.

In 1881 the canal was begun by a French company with a famous French NCS 

- 16 engineer in charge. It was planned to dig a sea-level canal so that ships could pass through without being lifted or lowered in locks. The French companies spent about $250,000,000 in the work and lost the lives of many hundreds of their workmen. They 

They finally gave up the attempt and sold their property and all their rights to the United States for $40,000,000. In 1903 the Republic of 

Panama sold to the United States a strip of land ten miles wide across the isthmus. 

The canal was to run through the middle of this strip. After the United States began work the canal was completed in about ten years.

Getting Ready to Build the Canal. 

While the French were working on the canal many of their workmen died of fever, especially of yellow fever, a very dangerous disease. Before the United

States started to build the canal, Dr. 

Gorgas and many helpers were sent to the Canal Zone to clean up the region so that it would be healthful. Swamps were drained. The breeding places of the mosquitoes that carry yellow fever were covered with oil to kill the larvae hatched from the mosquito eggs. Houses, screened to keep out insects, were built. Pure drinking water was provided. After all this was done to protect the health and furnish the necessary comforts for the workers, the canal work was begun. Its construction was not interrupted by fever or illness of any serious kind among the workers. Today the Canal Zone is a very healthful region in which to live.

Building the Canal. The American plan called for the use of locks. It meant that the work could be done in a shorter time, at less cost, and that all practical needs would be met. The Gatun Dam

A. 

Courtesy Canadian Pacific Railway 

A huge steamship in a lock of the Panama Canal on its way from the Pacific to the Atlantic Ocean. The gates of the next lock are being opened to admit the ship. Point to each gate. See also the electric tow cars used for hauling the ship into the lock. was built to turn the valley of the Chagres River into a large lake. This in itself was a great piece of work. By using locks the largest ocean ships are raised to the level of this lake. They sail on the lake part way across the isthmus, and are lowered again to the level of the ocean by locks near the other end of the canal. 

Ships are towed through the locks by electric locomotives running on tracks along the sides of the locks (A).

At the Gatun Dam a hydroelectric plant has been built that uses water from the lake to run its generators. Enough electricity is generated to furnish the power for the electric locomotives, to operate the gates, and for other purposes.

Use of the Canal. -The Atlantic end of the canal is farther west than the Pacific end, so that a ship sails southeast in going toward the Pacific Ocean (map, page 272). The canal is fortified by the

United States but in times of peace it is open to the ships of all nations. Ships must pay toll for the privilege of using the canal. Traffic through the canal is very great and is increasing yearly. It is interesting to know that many ocean routes have been greatly shortened by the building of this canal. In the old days the distance from New York by water through the Strait of Magellan to 

San Francisco was 15,126 miles. By the 

Panama Canal route it is 6059 miles - a

PUERTO RICO AND VIRGIN ISLANDS 

Climate. Puerto Rico is the most eastern of the four large islands of the West Indies. It lies at about 18° north latitude, and has an even, tropical climate. 

It is not excessively hot, because it is surrounded by ocean waters and is in the course of the northeast trade winds (page 

263). As the island has mountains of moderate height the trade winds are forced to higher altitudes in crossing them. 

This causes more rain to fall on the northeast side than on the southwest. In parts of this island irrigation is needed at some period of the growing season. 

People and Industries. The area of 

Puerto Rico is about three fourths that of

Connecticut. The population is nearly equal to that of Connecticut. About three fifths of the population are white and two fifths are Negro. The island was long under the rule of Spain, but was ceded to the United States in 1898. The A. 1998

A modern school system is being developed. Roadways, including railroads, are being constructed, along with telegraph and telephone lines. Sugar is the chief product, and the amount produced has grown much larger under American rule (A). Coffee, tobacco, and a variety of tropical fruits also are raised. Vegetables are now sent in large quantities to the winter markets of New York and other northern cities. Such vegetables may be purchased in these cities within a week after being gathered from the truck farms. of Puerto Rico. San Juan, the capital, and Ponce are the largest cities.

THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS 

Out in the Pacific Ocean, about 2100 miles southwest from San Francisco, lie the Hawaiian Islands. Many of the ships crossing the Pacific between North American ports and those of Asia, Australia, and 

New Zealand stop at Honolulu, the chief port of the islands. There they are able to get fuel and supplies and to take on or land passengers and freight. It is because of the central position of these islands that they are said to be "at the crossroads of the Pacific." In 1898 the 

Hawaiian Islands were annexed by the 

United States. As you read about them make up your mind as to whether these islands are of much value to our country. 

Size and Location. The area of the group is 6449 square miles, of which the one island Hawaii has nearly two thirds (map, page 278). The area of the group is much less than that of Massa chusetts or New Jersey. The state of 

Ohio is more than six times as large.

---

THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS 

277 The more northerly islands are just to the south of the Tropic of Cancer, and the whole group is between 18° and 23° north latitude.

Formation. — The islands have been built chiefly by volcanoes that have poured out lava from the interior of the earth. They are really volcanic peaks that rise above the level of the sea, but they rest upon the ocean bed 15,000 to 18,000 feet below the surface of the ocean. 

The highest peaks are those of Hawaii, which reach nearly 14,000 feet above the sea. Mauna Loa, on this island, is an active volcano. At its top, and at another point on the east side of the mountain, are the largest craters of active volcanoes in the world (A). These craters are several hundred feet deep and two or 

U. S. Geological Survey 

A. Part of the crater of a volcano in Hawaii. three miles wide. When the lava in the craters cools, as it sometimes does, there are places hard enough to walk on, but they contain lakelets of spluttering lava. 

At certain times the lava rises in the higher crater until it runs out of some break in the side of the mountain and flows slowly down the slope. These streams of melted rock sometimes flow across the island for fifty miles or more to fall into the sea. The period between two such eruptions may be several years. 

Climate. The islands are in the belt of the northeast trade winds (page 263). 

These winds blow over the Pacific as they do over the Atlantic. As these winds are forced up into cooler heights when they cross the mountains of the islands, the rainfall is heavy on the northern and eastern sides. Not much rain falls on the southern and western parts of the islands. 

The climate is mild and even, because the islands are in the tropical part of the earth where the temperature changes very little at sea level. There are no wellmarked rainy and dry seasons, although there is usually more rain in winter than in summer. The temperature decreases about one degree with each 300 feet of elevation and there is usually snow on 

Mauna Loa and on Mauna Kea, the other great peak of Hawaii. There is little or no vegetation above 11,000 feet. 

Agriculture. The chief industry of the Hawaiian Islands is agriculture. The soil is fertile, being formed from decayed. lava. The climate is warm the year round, so plant growth is not interrupted by frosts or snows anywhere near sea level. Breezes from the ocean make the temperature much cooler than it is in tropical regions of the same elevation that are far inland. ―—

THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS 

279 

Courtesy Matson Navigation Co. 

A. - Pineapple plantation near Honolulu, in the island of Oahu. One pineapple grows at the top of each plant, only a short distance above the ground. New plants grow from shoots that spring up from the base of the old plant. 

Sugar. The greatest crop of the island is sugar cane. Soil and climate are both suited to this crop. There are great plantations in the valleys and along the coasts. Where rainfall is not abundant enough for the crop, irrigation works have been constructed. Many Americans have invested in the sugar industries of the islands, and much of the raw sugar is sent to San Francisco to be refined.

Because the growing season is continuous you can see at one time cane that is just starting to grow, cane that has been growing for some time, and cane that is ready to cut. It is not necessary to plant the fields each year, and some fields are not plowed and replanted for several years. 

Other Crops. Among the other crops grown on the islands are pineapples and other tropical fruits, rice, coffee, tobacco, figs, nuts, and dates. Great fields of pineapples (A) are found in many places in the islands, and the industry is increasing in importance. Some of the pineapples are shipped fresh to market, but most of them are canned. The tobacco is made into cigars and cigarettes. The rice is grown chiefly for home use as a food for the poorer people and field workers. 

Manufacturing and Commerce. 

There is but little manufacturing except the making of raw sugar, the canning of pineapples, and the making of cigars.

Sugar mills and canning factories have been built in the regions where the cane and pineapples are grown.

The greater part of the trade of the islands is with the United States. Only a small part is with other countries, chiefly the importing of foodstuffs from 

Japan, China, and Australia, and of fertilizers from Chile and Germany.

Government and People. The islands were under native rulers until 1893, when a republic was established. Five years later they were annexed by the United States, and were made a territory in 1900. 

They have their own legislature and send a delegate to Congress at Washington.

A. 

One of the fine Hawaiian hotels, on Waikiki Beach, Honolulu. Do you think the outrigger canoe shown in the foreground would upset as easily as our canoes? 

The original Hawaiians belong to the brown race, but they form only a small part of the present population. The people are now of many nationalities. 

In addition to the natives there are 

Japanese, Chinese, Filipinos, and Americans, as well as some Portuguese and other people from Europe, besides many of mixed descent. The English language is used in schools and in business. 

Cities. - Honolulu, on the island of 

Oahu, is the largest city, chief seaport, and the capital. It is a beautiful and modern city, and many of our people go there to spend a winter in its warm and sunny climate. There are fine business blocks, many of them owned by Americans, and large hotels for travelers and visitors to the islands (A). At Pearl Harbor, near by, there is a United States naval station where vessels of the United States Navy go for supplies and repairs. Honolulu is important as a refueling place for Pacific 

Ocean steamers. It takes three weeks or more for steamers to cross the Pacific on some routes, and it would be difficult for a ship to carry all the coal or oil needed for so long a voyage. 

Hilo is the chief city of the island of Hawaii.

THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS 

281 

THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS, GUAM, AND SAMOA 

The Philippine Islands are southeast of 

China. They lie wholly in the Torrid 

Zone, between 4° and 22° north latitude. 

Of what value are they to our country? 

Physical Features. There are over 

7000 of the islands, with a total area of about 115,000 square miles. Of the larger islands, Luzon in the north is the largest, with 41,000 square miles of surface, and Mindanao in the south has 

37,000 square miles. Much of the land | is hilly or mountainous, and there are many volcanic peaks. Earthquakes are not uncommon. The higher peaks are from 8000 to 10,000 feet in altitude. 

Climate. The climate is warm, and the rainfall is heavy, especially on the northern and eastern mountain slopes.

The prevailing winds are from the northeast. In crossing the warm waters of the ocean they have picked up water vapor which falls as rain when the winds cool as they cross the mountains. The winters are dry, and the summers wet. The soil is deep, and the ground is shaded with a dense growth of plants. In many regions the ground is usually damp and often flooded. Houses are raised above the ground to be above the mud. They are small and light and built chiefly of bamboo (A). Fierce storms called typhoons blow across the islands at times and do much damage. Many of the small native houses may be blown down by such storms. Roads and trails are often impassable, but some good roads are being built. From the United States government weather bureau at Manila, storm warnings are sent out and daily weather reports are issued.

L. Green from  

A. Native houses in the Philippines, made of bamboo and roofed with thatch. Compare them with houses of our country and account for the differences.

History and Government. - These is lands were discovered by Magellan in 

1521, in the first exploring expedition that went around the world. Magellan himself was killed here, but the islands soon came under Spanish rule.

The islands were transferred to the control of the United States in 1898 as a result of a war with Spain. They contain over 12,000,000 people. Of these, a small number are Americans and Europeans, 50,000 are Chinese, and a smaller number are rather tiny black men known as Negritos; but most of the people are of the brown race, and are called Filipinos especially the majority who are Christians.

Chinese immigration is now forbidden, as it is in Hawaii and in the main part of the United States. 

Much exploration and surveying have been done by the American army and by men of science since 1898. The United 

States Coast Survey has charted the dangerous seas in and about the islands.

The governor general and a few other officers are appointed by the President of the United States. A Philippine legis lature is elected by the people. An excellent system of education has been provided. Most of the teachers are natives, but the English language is generally used in the schools. 

Forests and Minerals. As in most warm and wet countries, the forests of these islands are very dense. Many kinds of trees are found, including more than fifty kinds of hardwoods. Some of these are heavy and take a fine polish, and are therefore used for fine woodwork. Some are so hard that an ordinary saw will not cut them. The top of a large dining table is sometimes made from a single slab of native wood. There are forest districts and stations, all in charge of expert foresters. In this new care of the forests, as well as in the agricultural experiment stations, in the educational system, and in the charting of the coasts, the good work of the American government is seen.

The bamboo and rattan are put to a variety of uses by the natives, especially in making tools, domestic utensils, and the houses of the poor. The well-to-do 

Filipinos have homes of comfort and elegance. The poorer people and the savage tribes often live in huts of poles, roofed with a thatch of boughs or of grass. The abaca plant is grown for its fibers, called Manila hemp. In preparing the hemp for market, the plants are cut down, the layers that form the main stalk are taken off one by one, and the pulp removed by scraping. The fibers remain. 

These are washed and dried and are used in making rope or are shipped to other countries for that use.

Soft coal is found, and nearly all the important metals are known to exist in the Philippines, but as yet little mining has been done.

Agriculture. The resources of the islands are very large, but are not yet well known and are little developed. The soils are very deep and rich; in many places they are from volcanic rocks that have decayed and have been fertilized by the decaying plant growth of which there is so much in a moist, warm region. 

Very important industries are connected with the raising of coconuts. The white meat of the coconut is crushed and pressed to get an oil used in food products and in making soap. When the coconut meat is dried it is called copra, and much A.

THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS, GUAM, AND SAMOA 

A. Plowing with a water buffalo. of it is shipped out of the islands to our own and other countries. Coconut meat is shredded and used in the manufacture of candy and in puddings and cakes. 

Raw cane sugar and tobacco, as well as refined sugar and cigars, are among the exports sent to the United States. 

Rice is the main food crop, but it is not sent to other countries. At times not enough is grown for home use. More and more of the forest is being cleared for crops, and in some valleys narrow terraces on which rice is grown have been built on the hillsides almost to their very tops. 

Corn, bananas, coffee, spices, and small fruits are raised. Farming methods are crude. The water buffalo, used in tilling the soil (A), is slow and unruly, and requires a frequent plunge in mud and water. 

This habit fits it, however, for use in the rice fields, which must often be flooded.

Commerce and Cities. Much of the surface is covered with a jungle, but the muddy trails are giving way to good roads, several thousand miles of which have been built. These roads make it possible to reach the soils, forests, and minerals of the lands in the interior.

Several railroads have been built during the recent years of American occupation, 

283 and there are now in the islands more than 6000 miles of telegraph lines. There is ocean cable service to Asia and to the 

United States.

The chief city is Manila, the capital, which has a population of about 330,000. 

The second city in size and importance is Iloilo, on the island of Panay. 

Guam. A few hundred miles east of the Philippines is the small island of Guam. 

The United States took Guam from Spain in the war of 1898. It is useful as a fueling station for vessels visiting the United 

States, Hawaii, and the Philippine Islands.

Samoa Islands. -The island of Tu tuila and a few smaller islands of the 

Samoan group belong to the United 

States; the others are controlled by 

New Zealand. Tutuila is a mountainous island, with the excellent harbor of Pago 

Pago. A United States naval station is maintained there.

The American flag has also been raised over a few other small islands in the 

Pacific Ocean (map, page 278).

Canada is one of a group of countries that make up the British Commonwealth of Nations. It is under the British flag but it is in most ways entirely independent. 

You remember that you read earlier in this book about the finding of Puget Sound by Vancouver and of the Columbia 

River by Captain Gray. You remember, too, that for many years England and the United States claimed that part of our continent. People of both countries made settlements there. They did not go to war to settle the question, but finally agreed in treaties that the parallel of 49° north latitude should be the boundary from the Pacific Ocean almost to the 

Great Lakes. In the same peaceful way, by arbitration, or the decision of a committee, the boundary between our state of Maine and Canada was fixed, and also the line between Alaska and Canada.

We have much trade with the country that is so close to us on the north, on the north, and many of you who have never seen any other foreign land have been in 

Canada. You will now want to learn about the country itself, its people, and their resources and industries. Make a list of the lakes and rivers that are on the boundary between Canada and the United 

States. What parallel of latitude is used as the boundary between Canada and our states of New York and Vermont?

Regions and Provinces. The most southern point in Canada is in about 42° north latitude, on the shores of Lake Erie, not far from Detroit. The northern parts are on the Arctic Ocean, only a few hundred miles from the North Pole. 

Like the United States, Canada has low mountains in the east, high mountains in the west, and broad plains lying between the two highlands. 

Southern Canada may be divided into four regions. four regions. On the east are Nova 

Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince

Edward Island, which are often called the Maritime Provinces. An old name for the region is Acadia. Here are the only ports of eastern Canada that are free from ice throughout the year. The most important ports are Halifax, St. 

John, Sydney, and Charlottetown. The surface is low and nearly flat in Prince Edward Island. The surface in the two other provinces is higher and much more hilly. It is much like the surface of parts of New England. 

The second region consists of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. These lie along the St. Lawrence River and the

Great Lakes, and extend northward into a wilderness of rocks, hill lands, and forest. Northern Ontario and Quebec border Hudson Bay, and Quebec has a long shore line on the Gulf of St. Lawrence. 

The lowlands along the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes have rich farms and the largest cities and densest population of the country. Some of this region is hilly, but in southern Ontario there are lake plains like those of western New York. 

North of the St. Lawrence Valley and the lake plains is the region known as the Laurentian Plateau. It includes most 285

in Quebec and Ontario. of Quebec, crosses Ontario, extends into | Keewatin. In the southern part of this 

Manitoba and Saskatchewan, borders region are forests, and in the north are Hudson Bay on the west, and reaches the treeless tundras (page 269). In this re- 

Arctic Ocean. Only a part of this area is gion are Great Slave Lake and Great Bear 

Lake, and many other large lakes whose outlets lead to Hudson Bay or the Arctic

Ocean. The Yukon Territory is moun tainous and continues the highlands of 

British Columbia northward. A part of northern Canada is often called the

Barren Lands. Some of these lands are free from snow in summer and are brilliant with flowers. They are visited by countless numbers of wild fowl. 

The third region includes the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, whose northern boundary is the parallel of 60° north latitude. It consists of prairie and dry plains, and, at the south, is like the plains of North Dakota, Nebraska, and Montana. This region has in it Lake Winnipeg, and much of it drains by the Red River, the Saskatchewan, and other streams, through the Nelson River into Hudson Bay. It is the most important part of Canada for the raising of grain. A part of the province of 

Manitoba borders on Hudson Bay and is similar to northern Quebec and Ontario.

The fourth region is the province of British Columbia, which also has as its northern boundary the parallel of 60° north latitude. Through it the Western 

Highlands extend from the United States on the south. They also reach over into western Alberta. On the east are the "Canadian Rockies," and on the west is the northern continuation of the Cascade Range of Washington. The glaciers in these mountains of Canada are larger and there are more of them than in western United States; but there are not so many of them, nor are they so large, as those of 

Alaska. The southern parts of British 

Columbia are drained by the Columbia and Fraser rivers, and the northern parts by branches of the Mackenzie, which flows into the Arctic Ocean, and by smaller streams flowing to the Pacific Ocean. 

The northern plains of Canada extend to the Arctic Ocean and include the provisional districts of Mackenzie and North of the main body of the continent are many large and many small islands. 

They have much snow, and are inhabited only by a few groups of Eskimos. 

Shore Line and Scenic Beauty. 

Nearly all the shore lines of Canada are rugged and broken, with deep inlets or fiords, bold headlands, and many mountainous islands. For this reason there are good harbors in British Columbia and in the Maritime Provinces. The St.

Lawrence River is at tide level as far as 

Montreal. Along the western shore, vessels go from Victoria or Vancouver northward to Alaska in quiet waters behind the fringe of islands that border the coast. Many bays reach far into the land between high mountain spurs, or promontories. 

Hudson Bay is an inland sea, 900 miles long, lying in the interior of Canada. 

It was named for Henry Hudson, whose sailors set him adrift there to perish about three years after he had sailed up the Hudson River.

Both the eastern and western coasts of Canada are important for their commerce. 

The coast of Hudson Bay may become important; but the Arctic shores will

Visitors to Canada delight in the grandeur of the rugged mountains and the charm of the beautiful lakes (A).

- The climate of the Mari time Provinces, and of the region along the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes, is like that of New England, New York, and 

Michigan. The storms of the westerly winds pass over this part of Canada. 

Moisture from the Atlantic that comes with the east and southeast winds gives heavy rains in summer and heavy snows in winter. Southern Ontario, in the latitude of southern Michigan, is almost surrounded by lakes, and has a mild climate. Here grapes and peaches flourish, as in western New York and southern 

Michigan. Northern Ontario and Quebec are much colder.

The summers of Manitoba, Saskatche- 

Wan, and Alberta are much like those of the western plains of the United States, but as these provinces are farther north, the winters are longer and colder. Saskatchewan and Alberta, however, are warmer than the lands eastward about 

Hudson Bay. One reason is that westerly winds, called chinooks, blow across the

mountains in those provinces as well as southward in the United States. After crossing the mountains the air warms as it comes down upon the plains, and makes them warmer than they would be without this wind. The climate of western British 

Columbia is moist and mild like that of western Washington.

Indians. - Canada, with its abundant forests, rivers, and lakes, was a natural home for many Indian tribes. They could hunt in the forest, fish in the waters, and gather an abundance of wild fruits. 

Their canoes enabled them to make long journeys by water. These canoes were made of strips of birch bark sewn together with split roots of spruce, lined with thin strips of cedar, and made strong by cedar ribs. The gum of some evergreen tree was used to make the seams watertight. 

The finished canoe was so light that it could move in shallow water and easily be carried across the portages between lakes and streams.

Explorations. The first explorations up the St. Lawrence and along the Great

Lakes were made by Frenchmen, and the land was long under the French flag (page 7). The missionaries and the fur hunters went through all parts of the great wilderness. They found nothing so useful to them, for travel and for carrying their packs of skins to market, as the Indians' birch-bark canoe.

The search for fur-bearing animals really was more important than any other circumstance in the early history of Canada. 

After the English took possession of 

Canada, the hunting went

The 

Hudson's Bay Company, which had been formed long before, spread over most of the country. It held many fortified posts, called "factories," to which the pelts or skins of animals were brought by the hunters and trappers. 

Large parts of the vast Canadian wilderness are little known even yet. For many years explorers have sought knowledge of the rocks, minerals, forests, rivers, and soils, making long and toilsome journeys with canoes no larger than those used by the red men centuries ago. In this way maps are prepared, information about the country is provided, and immigrants and settlers learn where there is good land for farms. They also learn where rich masses of minerals have been found, and where to build their roads. — - 

People. The total population of 

Canada is over 10,000,000. This is about four fifths as many people as live in the state of New York. Canada, however, is about 80 times as large as New York state. Taken as a whole, the country is very thinly populated.

Most of the people live in the southern part (316 A). There are more people in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec than in other parts of the country. The western farming area has few people for every square mile of area. Why?

The sheaves are then set up in shocks until the grain is dry enough to be threshed. the customs of the early settlers are still found. Most of the English-speaking people of Canada are of English or Scotch descent, and several hundred thousand of them were born in the British Isles.

Many immigrants in Canada have come from the United States, and smaller numbers from continental Europe and from 

China and Japan.

The people of the United States and Canada have always been very friendly. 

There are no forts anywhere on the boundary between the two countries. 

The Peace Bridge (9 B), built across the 

Niagara River, celebrates the long period of peace which has existed between the two countries. 

Agriculture. In the Maritime Provinces mixed farming is carried on. Grain, fruits, and vegetables are raised and live stock is kept. Fine apples are produced in the Annapolis Valley of Nova Scotia.

The most valuable kind of live stock in 

Canada is the silver fox which is bred for its beautiful fur in fox "farms" on 

Prince Edward Island (288 A). 

Southern Ontario, especially the socalled Niagara 

Niagara peninsula partly surrounded by three of the Great Lakes, is the chief farming region of eastern 

Canada. It has excellent soils and a mild climate, and produces wheat, apples, grapes, peaches, and small fruits. Much of the butter and cheese shipped to Great 

Britain comes from Ontario. 

Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta are wheat-growing regions. The surface, soil, and methods of raising the crop are like those in the great wheat region of the North Central States. Winnipeg, the chief wheat market for the district, has a grain exchange similar to that at

Chicago. Many cities and villages on all the railroad lines have elevators to which the farmers take their wheat for transfer to the railroads. Oats are raised (A); but as the summers are short and cool, corn does not do very well. Wheat is raised, though not in large quantities, in the valley of the Peace River. Cattle and horses are raised on the dry plains, especially in Alberta.

A.-Logging railroad on Vancouver Island. Of what are the ties and roadbed made? For what use is such a railroad constructed? 

British Columbia has rich agricultural regions, though only partly developed.

They are suitable for grain and general farming, and the mild climate of the coasts and valleys especially fits these areas for fruit culture. One of the best of the fruit-growing regions is the valley of the Fraser River.

Manufactures. -The manufactures of 

Canada include agricultural machinery, vehicles, and other iron and steel goods. 

The weaving of textiles and the preparation of food products and of lumber and wood pulp are also important.
