Forests. The forests of Canada cover about 800,000 square miles, or more than one fifth of the country. In the eastern provinces there are hardwoods and pines, as well as spruces, aspens, and larches. 

More than a third of the area of Nova Scotia is covered with forest. The great lumbering region of the Maritime Provinces is New Brunswick, which has large mills at Fredericton and St. John. 

The eastern forests extend through 

Quebec and Ontario. The Ottawa Valley is important for its white pine, which, with other timber, is floated down the river to Ottawa. There large mills work it up into lumber. Much lumber is also manufactured at Montreal and Toronto. 

Many of the soft woods, such as spruce, especially the smaller and imperfect trees, are used for making wood pulp. The forests of northern Quebec have not many large trees, but the timber is suitable for pulp, railroad ties, telegraph poles, fences, mining timber, and firewood. Tree growth in the cold north is very slow, and a small tree may have required hundreds of years for its development. 

The forests of central Canada extend between Lake Superior and Hudson Bay to the northwest, across the southern parts of the Mackenzie basin, and join with the forests of British Columbia. The valleys and lower slopes of this province are covered with wonderful forests of cedar, spruce, and Douglas fir, similar to the trees of Washington and Oregon. Here is the third great center for lumbering in Canada (A). Much of the product goes to 

Vancouver and is shipped to foreign lands. 

Forest fires are very destructive, and they are started not only through carelessness of hunters and by sparks from locomotives, but also by lightning. In a

A. Asbestos mine in eastern Quebec. Although asbestos can be used in the making of a coarse cloth it is really a mineral. It will not burn and is used for fire curtains in theaters and to cover steam pipes. dry time the mossy floor of the forest, the thick undergrowth, the dry, fallen timber, and the pitchy character of many of the trees, cause a fire to spread quickly. It sometimes outruns and destroys the swiftest animals of the forest. Half of the 

Half of the timber wealth of Ontario is said to have been destroyed by fires. While the forests are one of the main resources of 

Canada, there is danger of their exhaustion, and measures are being taken for their care and preservation. 

Two regions have few trees or none. 

These are the plains west of Winnipeg and the Barren Lands of the north. On the western plains many farmers are planting trees, for windbreaks, for fuel, and for other uses. 

Mining. - One of the most important minerals of Canada is coal. There are three principal regions for coal mining in the Dominion. The first is Nova Scotia, where mining has been carried on for many years. Nova Scotia furnishes most of the coal used for household purposes and for manufacturing in eastern Canada.

The second locality is in the plains east of the Canadian Rocky Mountains. In this region the greater part of the coal is soft, and has not yet been extensively mined.

The large region between Winnipeg and the St. Lawrence River has no coal. It either imports coal from the United States, or brings it from Nova Scotia. The third region in which coal is found is British Columbia, which has large supplies like 

Washington on the south. 

Petroleum has been found in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, and in the Mackenzie district. Large beds of oil-bearing shales from which oil can be obtained are found in New 

Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Not much use has been made of these shales up to the present time.

Some iron is found in various parts of Canada, but in many cases the mines are far from coal, and the iron-smelting industry of the Dominion is not yet very large. However, iron mined beneath the sea in Newfoundland is near enough to the coking coal of Nova Scotia to make possible a large steel industry at Sydney. 

Asbestos is found in eastern Quebec, and that region furnishes most of the world's supply (A).

A. - Fishing fleet at Prince Rupert, British Columbia. 

In the province of Ontario, north of Lake Huron, are several mining centers where nickel, copper, silver, and gold are produced. Ontario is now by far the largest producer of gold in Canada, and in the Sudbury district it produces nine tenths of the nickel of the world. 

The Klondike region in Yukon territory, on the borders of Alaska, also yields much gold. The mining center is Dawson.

Another important mineral region of Canada is in the province of British 

Columbia. Mountain ranges are found in much of this region. They contain deposits of gold, silver, lead, and copper.

The value of the mineral output of Canada has increased greatly in recent years. 

Some mines, such as the silver mines of 

Cobalt, are being exhausted, but there are vast unexplored areas in both eastern and western Canada in which other large mineral areas will no doubt be found. 

Fisheries. - Canada has a broken shore line, and in its numerous bays there are found great numbers of fish. On the east, off the shores of Nova Scotia, is the shallow water of the Grand Banks of 

Newfoundland. Here and in the Gulf of St. Lawrence many fish are caught.

In all the Maritime Provinces fishing is an important industry. Cod, herring, and halibut are especially valuable. Many lobsters also are taken. In recent years the value of the lobster fisheries has been greater than that of the cod fisheries, which had always been the most important. 

Nova Scotia has the largest fishing industry in the eastern part of Canada, carried on from Halifax, Yarmouth, and other ports. Some of the geographical advantages of Nova Scotia in this industry are (1) its many protected harbors, where small fishing villages have grown up, (2) the nearness of the fishing grounds, and (3) the fact that ships to carry the dried, salt, or canned fish to market can come direct to the shipping centers. 

Canada has thousands of lakes and rivers in which fresh-water fish flourish. 

Fishing is a large business on the lakes of Manitoba, and many men are employed in it. The "catch" includes salmon,

trout, and whitefish. The salmon and | John, Quebec, and Montreal. Ships of other fisheries of British Columbia are like several lines sail from Montreal to Eurothose of Washington and Alaska. Most of the salmon are canned, and the annual product amounts to several million dollars. 

Halibut and herring also are numerous, and shellfish are gathered near the shores. 

On both the Atlantic and the Pacific sides of Canada, seals, walruses, and whales are still captured in considerable numbers. This branch of the fishing industry is smaller than it formerly was. 

Codfish from the Labrador coast are marketed in Spain, in Greece, and especially in Italy. Codfish has been called the "bread of the sea," because it is abundant, nutritious, and is easily preserved by salting, smoking, or drying. 

Parts of these fish are used for making glue, oil, and fertilizer, and in Arctic lands they are used even for fuel. One medicine, or specially valuable food, is made from this fish, namely, cod-liver oil. 

The ordinary codfish weighs only a few pounds, but large specimens weigh more than 100 pounds each. - - 

Furs. In 1670 the Hudson's Bay

Company was formed to trade in the furs produced in America, and particularly in Canada. The Dominion is still one of the leading fur-producing regions of the world. Hunting and trapping are carried on in the large areas where it is not suitable for many people to live. There are also many farms" where fur-bearing animals are raised for their skins. Foxes, raccoons, minks, muskrats, and other animals are bred for this purpose. Montreal is an important market for furs in eastern Canada. Winnipeg and Edmonton also are fur markets. 66 

Transportation by Water. The prin cipal eastern seaports are Halifax, St. pean ports, except during the winter months, when the St. Lawrence River is blocked with ice. From Montreal ships of considerable size can go to the head of the Great Lakes at Duluth or Chicago. 

They pass the rapids of the St. Lawrence

River and enter Lake Ontario by means of canals. By the Welland Canal they can reach Lake Erie. Between Lake Huron and Lake Superior the Soo Canal takes them past rapids in the St. Marys River. 

The Red River and the Saskatchewan are navigable for small boats for hundreds of miles, to Lake Winnipeg. From the lake to Hudson Bay the Nelson River is broken by difficult rapids.

The Mackenzie River and its branches are useful for navigation in northern

Canada, but not for foreign trade, as it flows into the Arctic Ocean. It serves the fur-trading posts along the river, and these have been called the outposts of civilization. For much of its length of 

2000 miles, measured to the source of Peace River, it goes through a very sparsely settled country inhabited chiefly by hunters and trappers, most of whom are Indians.

The Hudson Bay is not much used by ships, except those carrying grain of the western plains from the port of Churchill to Europe.

Cities. - Ottawa is the capital of the 

Dominion of Canada, and is an important industrial center, especially for the timber products of Ontario. 

Quebec is an old city standing on a bold promontory north of the St. Lawrence

River. It was here that Wolfe won his victory over Montcalm in 1759; and the result of the battle was that this part of America passed from the French to British rule. The dredging of the St. Lawrence has made it possible for ocean vessels to go up to Montreal, and consequently 

Quebec, though prosperous, is not relatively so important a port as in an earlier period.

Montreal, with over 800,000 people, is the metropolis of Canada (A). It is served by the transcontinental railroads, and on the south is connected by rail with 

New York, by way of the Champlain and 

Hudson valleys. 

Toronto is the largest city of Ontario, and the second in size among the cities of Canada. It has much manufacturing, is in the midst of a productive agricultural region, has many fine buildings, and is the seat of Toronto University. Kingston is at the foot of Lake Ontario.

Hamilton is at the head of the lake, and is in the midst of the fruit-growing region. 

There is an extensive development of electrical power at Niagara Falls on the

Canadian side of the river as well as on the American side (294 A).

Winnipeg is the metropolis of central Canada. It has grown rapidly on the site of one of the forts of the Hudson's Bay Company, where the Assiniboine joins the Red River. All the great railroads that cross Canada center at this market city of the prairies. Southward, railroads run to Minneapolis and Chicago. Regina and Moosejaw in Saskatchewan, and 

Calgary and Edmonton in Alberta, are railroad centers and are important and growing cities. 

Vancouver is the great Canadian seaport on the Pacific coast. Its site was a forest until 1885, and it is now a large and splendid city, the terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the point of departure for ships running to all countries on the Pacific Ocean (A). Victoria, at the south end of Vancouver Island, has a beautiful situation. It is an important port and the capital of British Columbia. 

Prince Rupert, a little south of Alaska, is another seaport on the Pacific coast.

NEWFOUNDLAND Newfoundland is a colony of Great 

Britain, but did not, like other colonies of this region, join the Dominion of Canada. 

It is nearly as large as the state of New York but has not many more than a quarter of a million people. 

Perhaps you think of Newfoundland as far north. St. John's, its capital, is in about the same latitude as Seattle, where roses may bloom until Christmas. You have been told in this book that some places are warm because they are by the sea or the borders of a large lake. Why is not Newfoundland warm? It is partly because a current of cold water from the Arctic seas flows southward along the east coast of the continent to New England. 

Steamships from Canada bound for some British ports find their shortest course north of Newfoundland. Through what strait must they go? Outside of this narrow passage, you may see icebergs which have broken loose from Greenland glaciers and set out on a long voyage southward with the Arctic current. 

The climate of Newfoundland is too cold for most crops. Oats, hay, and some vegetables can be raised, but most of the food must be imported. Much of the land is rocky or too wet for cultivation. 

There is some forest, and the trees, which are not large, are of spruce and other kinds suited for wood pulp and paper. English firms have built large mills for making both pulp and paper. 

Some useful minerals are found.

Among them are iron, copper, gold, silver, lead, and coal.

As the sea is all about, the main work of the people is in fishing. Not far away are the Grand Banks, where the waters are St. but a few hundred feet deep. The meeting of the Gulf Stream from the south and the Labrador Current from the north makes the region of the Grand Banks a feeding place for fish, particularly cod, halibut, and mackerel. 

Here many nations have fished for centuries. 

John's is the center of the fishing industry. 

Newfoundland is not far from the route taken by steamers on their way from New 

York to Europe. If from mid-ocean a passenger sends a radio message home, it may be picked up at St. John's and go the rest of the way by land wire.

Labrador belongs to Newfoundland (map, page 284). Fishing is almost the only means of getting a living there. 

What mountain in Alaska is in the same latitude as the north end of Labrador?

GREENLAND 

Greenland is the largest island in the world. It has over 800,000 square miles of surface, most of which is covered by an ice sheet. There are several towns and villages on the coast, inhabited by Danes and the native Eskimos. The island was discovered more than nine hundred years ago by the daring sailors of northern

Europe. It now belongs to Denmark. 

Furs, ivory, eider down, and seal oil are the chief products.

In the parts of North America you have already studied, except Greenland, most of the people speak the English language. 

In the province of Quebec in Canada, however, many of the people use the 

French language instead. In all the

North American countries south of the United States, except in a few West Indian islands, the main language is Spanish. You have already learned about several of these lands because they belong to our country. You are now to study the southern lands of North America that do not belong to the United States.

The American Mediterranean. Be tween the continents of North America and South America there are two bodies of water largely separated from the 

Atlantic Ocean and from each other.

These are the Gulf of Mexico and the 

Caribbean Sea (map, page 298). They are often called the "American Mediterranean." They have been given this name because they lie between the continents of North America and South 

America somewhat as the Mediterranean 

Sea of the Old World lies between the continents of Europe and Africa. You will get a clear idea of the outline of these two bodies of water by a study of the map. 

Follow with your eyes the Gulf coast from the southern end of Florida to the eastern tip of Yucatan. Look across

Yucatan Strait to Cuba and follow its northern shore until you can look northward to the southern end of Florida. shores that your eyes have followed are those of the Gulf of Mexico.

The 

From Yucatan let your eyes follow along the coast to the south and east until you see the island of Trinidad. Then let your eyes travel along the chain of islands to the north and west until you reach the western end of Cuba. You have followed the shores that surround the 

Caribbean Sea. 

Whenever you use the names of these two water bodies remember how they are separated, in part, from each other, and from the Atlantic Ocean. 

Latin America. In nearly all of the countries on our continent south of the United States, in the West Indies, and in 

South America, the explorers and settlers were either Spanish or Portuguese or 

French. Through hundreds of years these languages have been used by most of the people. All three of these languages are much like the ancient Latin language, and people have therefore for many years called these parts of the New World "Latin America." 

Until recently the Spanish language was little known in our country. Now it is taught in many schools. There is much need of it for those who travel in these southern countries or trade with their people. For many years most of this trade went to countries in Europe. Now more and more is coming to our country and there are direct steamship lines between their ports and our own. 

A number of air routes have been established between our country and the various Latin-American countries. This has been done to speed up the mail service and to help business. 299

MEXICO 

South of the United States our continent is less than half as broad as in our country; and, in general, it gets narrower and narrower toward the south. It is largely a land of mountains and plateaus. 

They are a continuation of the highlands in the western part of our own country. 

These highlands continue to the Isthmus of Panama, where they sink to much lower levels, but they rise again to great heights in South America.

The country just to the south of our own is Mexico. A part of the boundary between Mexico and the United States follows the course of the Rio Grande.

West of El Paso in Texas the boundary between the two countries crosses the land to the Pacific Ocean.

Size and Surface. The area of Mex ico is about one fourth that of the United States. Its most northern point is a little north of 32° north latitude, and its most southern point is a little south of 15° north latitude. The Tropic of Cancer crosses the country about midway between these two points. The northern part, therefore, is in the Temperate Zone, and the southern part is in the Torrid Zone. 

Using the scale of miles on the map (page 298), find the length of Mexico.

Measure from the point where the Colorado River crosses the northern boundary to the point where the southern boundary reaches the Pacific Ocean. What is the width of the main part of Mexico along the parallel of 25°?

The eastern shores of Mexico are washed by the waters of the Gulf of 

Mexico and the Caribbean Sea, and its western shores by the Pacific Ocean. On the south it is bounded by two of the countries of Central America. On the map find the peninsula of Lower California. This part of Mexico is almost completely separated from the main part of the country by the Gulf of California. 

Notice that the Colorado River flows into the northern end of this gulf. North of the lands at the mouth of the Colorado there is a region in southern California that is below sea level. Why is it not flooded by the waters of the Gulf of 

California? Read again what is said about the lands at the mouth of the 

Colorado on pages 241 and 242 if you need help in answering this question. 

Above the coastal lowlands on each side of Mexico rise steep, rugged mountain ranges. These ranges come together south of the city of Mexico. Where the two mountain systems join, volcanic peaks reach great heights. Their upper parts are covered with ice and snow even though they are in the Torrid Zone. The highest of these is Orizaba, which rises 18,314 feet above sea level. It is nearly as high as Mt. McKinley. Mt. Popocatepetl is 17,888 feet high, and several others have altitudes of from 12,000 to 

16,000 feet.

Between the mountains of eastern and western Mexico is a vast plateau opening toward the United States at the north, where it has an altitude of about 4000 feet. It rises toward the south, where it reaches a height of 8000 feet. As a whole, the elevation of the plateau increases from north to south and from east to west. The city of Mexico is near the southern narrow end of this high basin. 

Southeastern Mexico is a land of mountains and hills.

Most of the rivers of Mexico flow down the mountain slopes on the east and west.

Climate and Products. - Mexico has many kinds of climate. It extends over seventeen degrees of latitude. It is bordered by the sea on both sides. It has great differences in altitude. In most of 

Mexico there is a dry season from November to June, and a rainy season during the rest of the year. The northeast trade winds (page 263) blow across Mexico, and so the mountain slopes facing the Gulf of Mexico are wet. The coastal lowland up to 2000 or 3000 feet is known as the hot country. These hot, moist regions are very unhealthful places in which to live, especially for white people from cooler | lands. They are the region of the dreaded yellow fever. dreaded yellow fever. A large part of this region is jungle. There are no good roads or railroads, and those who wish to enter the forests must cut a pathway through the tangled undergrowth.

Farther south is the hot, dry peninsula of Yucatan. In parts of the peninsula there is enough moisture so that there are large forests. Here, too, grows the plant called henequen or sisal hemp," valuable for its fiber. (6 The higher slopes of the mountains that lead up to the plateau are temperate, but warm rather than cool. The cool zone is on the plateau. It has a temperate climate, and is so dry (A) that, in many places, irrigation is necessary for growing crops. It is in this part of Mexico that most of the people live. The southern part of the plateau is in the Torrid Zone,

A. 

Pyramid of the Sun, built by the Aztecs about 6000 years ago. It is 219 feet high, 761 feet long at its base, and 721 feet wide. It is the largest artificial mound in the western hemisphere. but on account of its elevation it has an enjoyable climate. Midday is usually hot, and at that time Mexicans close their places of business and stay indoors to avoid the hot sun. The early morning and late afternoon hours are much pleasanter, and it is then that the people are most active. The nights are cool.

The northern part of the plateau is warmer because it is much lower. It is also dry because the eastern mountains shut out the rain. It is a region of cactus and sagebrush (301 A). There are areas where cattle can be grazed, but agriculture without irrigation is impossible.

The west coast, including the peninsula of Lower California, is hot and dry like So southern California and Arizona. little can be grown in Lower California that the Mexicans call it the "fleshless arm of Mexico."

The southern and southeastern hills and lowlands are very hot, but since the distance from ocean to ocean is short there is moisture almost everywhere. The hills are covered with dense forests. 

The result of all this variety in climate is that Mexico produces the fruits, grains, and forest trees of both temperate and hot countries.

People of Yesterday and Today. 

hundreds and perhaps for thousands of years before the discoveries of Columbus there were people in Mexico who lived an orderly and settled life. These native people, later called Indians, were divided into many tribes or nations. The strongest of these was the Aztec nation. The 

Aztecs built fine temples (A) and other

MEXICO 

303 public buildings, made roads, irrigated their fields, and carried on trade. They made articles of clay, cotton, and silk, and mined gold and silver that they used for ornaments and temple decorations. 

The country was conquered by the Spanish general Cortes, and was under Spanish control for three hundred years. 

Spain was never successful in its control of other lands and people. In the years that have passed since its early explorations and settlements, Spain has lost one by one all of its foreign possessions. 

Many of them have declared themselves independent and set up their own governments. Some have passed to other nations as a result of war, treaty, or sale. 

A little more than a hundred years ago the Mexican people set up a government of their own. For most of the time since then Mexico has been a republic with a government somewhat like that of the United States. The country is made up of twenty-eight states, four territories, and a Federal District.

There are about 16,500,000 people in Mexico, including the natives or Indians, the descendants of the Spanish settlers, and the half-breeds or mestizos. The 

Indians are descended from the Aztecs and other tribes. Most of them belong to the working or serving class. They are often called peons. They buy a cotton suit for a dollar, a pair of sandals for a dime, and a blanket for a dollar and a half, and they have all the clothing that they need. They are poor, polite, and usually lazy. Although schools have increased in number in recent years, the peon class is still largely without schooling. The mestizos are descended from 

Spanish people who married natives. 

They call themselves the real Mexicans. A. 

A home-made Mexican plow. 

Ewing Galloway

Rude and simple ways of living are found side by side with those of modern life. The houses of the poor are only one story in height and are built of sun-dried brick or adobe. Straw is mixed with the clay in these mud bricks, as in ancient Egypt. Some of the farmers still use wooden plows (A), and peons carry heavy loads on mountain trails. The burro, or donkey, is much used as a beast of burden. There are, however, a number of well-equipped railroads, and the wealthier people have beautiful homes and make use of automobiles.

Beans and corn are common articles of food. The poor soak the corn, grind it, and make it into round cakes. These are baked in an open iron pan and are called tortillas. A kind of century plant, or agave, which, like many desert plants, has much juice, supplies a common drink. 

Mining. There are mines in almost every state, and the value of the silver produced has in some years amounted to over $100,000,000. There are many gold mines and many copper mines, and near Durango is a great deposit of iron known as 

Iron Mountain. Quicksilver, lead, zinc, and sulphur also are found. Among the precious stones found in Mexico are onyx, opals, turquoises, topazes, emeralds, agates, and garnets.

A.-Silver mine near Pachuca, Mexico. It is believed that silver was mined here by the Indians before the discovery of America. 

Hundreds of millions of dollars are invested by Americans and other foreigners in Mexican mines (A) and oil wells. 

Mexico was once second only to the United States in the production of petroleum. Old wells no longer yield as much as they did, and the new wells also are small producers. There are now several countries that produce more oil than Mexico. Recent laws have made the operation of oil wells by foreigners less profitable, and the production has decreased as a result. Most of the oil is sent in pipe lines to the coast at Tampico and shipped from there to 

American refineries. 

Agriculture. Corn, wheat, beans, and tobacco are raised in the cooler parts of the country. Corn is the chief crop and is the staff of life to many Mexicans. Almost all tropical fruits are grown, as well 

as sugar, coffee, cotton, indigo, rice, and the vanilla bean. Henequen, or sisal hemp, is extensively raised in Yucatan. It is sent to the United States to be used in making rope, twine, bagging, rugs, and carpets. 

Some kinds of cactus contain fibers that can be used in making paper. Many hammocks are woven in Yucatan, and some are very beautiful and costly. Mahogany, rosewood, logwood, and other tropical trees abound in the hot parts of 

Mexico, and lumber forms one of the valuable exports. 

Some rubber is produced.

Grazing. -The dry plateaus of northern Mexico, like those of western United States, furnish pasturage for thousands of cattle. 

The life on the ranches, with their cowboys and round-ups, is like that on the Great Plains of the United States. 

Some estates are very large and contain many villages and even private railroads. 

Irrigation is increasing in the states of northern Mexico. 

Cities and Routes of Trade. Mexico city is the capital and the largest city, with about 1,000,000 people. Much of it is well built, and its cathedral is one of the largest churches of the New World (305 A). The oldest railroad of Mexico is the one between the capital and Veracruz. The climb from the coast to the plateau is accomplished by skillful engineering. Main lines of railroad extend northward and connect with lines in the United States. Other lines reach

CENTRAL AMERICA 

How many countries are there in Central America (map, page 298)? British

Honduras is a British colony. The 

Panama Canal Zone, as you know, belongs to the United States. The rest of 

Central America is divided into six small republics Guatemala, Honduras, Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. 

The Republics of Central America. 

All of Central America is less than twenty degrees from the Equator, and the climate is hot. As the land is narrow and in the region of the trade winds, there is a heavy rainfall nearly everywhere. The lowlands of the coast are swampy and unhealthful. The climate of the mountains and hills on the west and southwest is more favorable for human occupation. 

There are several active volcanoes, and earthquakes are frequent.

Few of the people are educated, and the conditions of life are unsettled. As in other tropical lands, many of the houses B. 

Ewing Galloway

The 

Part of a banana plant. bananas grow pointing upward. are primitive. Coffee, sugar, rubber, and tropical fruits, especially bananas, are extensively raised and are the chief exports. All these countries are rich in cabinet woods and dyewoods. 

Like Mexico, these countries were long ruled by Spain, but became independent early in the last century. With education, with sanitary ways of living, and with the development of commerce on the isthmus, they will no doubt become prosperous. Some of the cities are well built. The largest city of Central America is Guatemala. 

Bananas. Bananas are now a common fruit which can be bought in almost any grocery or fruit store. Fifty years ago it was hardly possible to buy bananas in the United States; it is only since 1900 that they have been easily obtainable. 

The hot, wet lowlands bordering the 

Caribbean Sea in Central America produce bananas in large quantities (A). 

The thick vegetation along the coast has been cleared to make room for the banana plantations. Banana plants grow to a

CENTRAL AMERICA 

307 height of twenty feet or more in a little over a year. Then they begin to bear fruit. The bananas that are to be exported are not allowed to ripen on the plants but are picked while still green. 

The big bunches of hard, green bananas are taken by railroad or by other means to the coast, where ships built especially for transporting perishable fruit are waiting. These fruit liners have holds which can be cooled, or refrigerated, so that the fruit will not ripen too rapidly on its trip to northern markets. Great seaports, such as New Orleans, New York, Philadelphia, and Boston, receive the fruit and distribute it to inland markets.

Coffee. Coffee is raised in the uplands of the various Central American countries. Coffee requires a hot climate, but the young trees must be shaded from the very hot rays of the sun. For this reason banana plants are usually set out for shade among the little coffee trees. The trees require a great deal of moisture, and the soil must be rich and well drained.

THE WEST INDIES 

On the map, page 298, find the long chain of islands that shuts in the Caribbean Sea from the Atlantic Ocean. You will see that it is made up of two groups. 

One group is known as the Greater 

Antilles and consists of four large islands: 

Cuba, Hispaniola (often called Haiti),

Jamaica, and Puerto Rico. The other group, called the Lesser Antilles, is made up of many islands which are much smaller. They lie in a curve from a point near the eastern end of Puerto Rico almost to the northern coast of South America. 

North of Cuba and Hispaniola, and east of Florida, is another group of small islands, called the Bahamas.

Position and Climate. - The West 

Indies are in the belt of the northeast trade winds between 10° and 23° north latitude. The larger islands are in the northern part of this region and have in general an east-west direction. The highlands of these larger islands also have an east-west direction, and it is upon their northern slopes that the rainfall is heaviest. The southern and western parts have much less rain and at times need irrigation. As all the islands are south of the Tropic of Cancer, the climate is hot the year round, except as cooled by the sea.

Some parts of the year are dry and some very rainy, and the changes in seasons depend upon rainfall instead of upon temperature. Contrast such seasonal changes with the different kinds of seasons in our home state. The rainy season in the West Indies is from May to 

October, and during this time fierce whirling storms, known as tropical hurricanes, often sweep the region and do damage on sea and land. 

A. A tobacco field in Cuba. 

Ewing Galloway

Industries. The leading industry of the West Indies is agriculture, and the chief crops are sugar and tobacco (A). 

Coffee and spices, Coffee and spices, bananas, pineapples, grapefruit, oranges, lemons, coconuts, and other tropical fruits are grown. Another product is cacao seeds, from which chocolate and cocoa are made. In the forests many valuable trees are found, including cedar, rosewood, and mahogany. Lines of steamers ply regularly to many ports of these islands to carry the fruit and other products to the market cities of the United States.

Many of the islands were long under Spanish rule, though none are so governed today. Spaniards, half-breeds, and Negroes constitute most of the population of the West Indies.

THE WEST INDIES 

309 

The island of Puerto Rico and three of the small Virgin Islands are possessions of the United States about which you have already learned.

Population. 

The white population of the West Indies is not large, but it is the whites who own most of the plantations, orchards, mines, and factories. The vast majority of the people are Negroes who are laborers. For these Negroes, life is rather simple. They must do a certain amount of work in order to live, but they do no more than they must. Their homes are small, very cheaply built, and used chiefly as places in which to sleep and as a protection from rain and the heat of the midday sun. Fires are not needed, so there is no coal to purchase. Clothes are not necessary to keep them warm, and so a few very simple garments are all they need. Shoes they do not wear. They are happy in their care-free life, although most of them have no schooling and know little about what is going on in the world. The younger generation, however, benefits from the schools that have been built in some of the islands, espe cially in Cuba and Puerto Rico. 

have come from other countries as government officials or as managers of estates, find life in the islands very lonely. They look forward eagerly to the coming of the steamers that bring mail and supplies from the outside world. Three things that help to keep these lonely people in closer touch with the world are (1) wireless telegraphy, (2) radio broadcasting, and (3) airplanes.

It gained its independence with the aid of the United States in 1898, after three centuries of Spanish control. Under the rule of Spain the resources and industries of the island were largely undeveloped.

Cuba, near the chief eastern port, Santiago de Cuba. Havana at 23° north latitude is only about 100 miles from the southern tip of Florida. It is the capital and the largest city, with a very large and well protected harbor. It was cleaned and freed from yellow fever by sanitary engineers employed by the United States.

Curaçao and several smaller islands form a Dutch colony. 

Relations with the United States. — 

For many years our country has carried on trade with Cuba and other islands of the West Indies. They have found in the United States markets for the products of their fields and mines and forests. 

We have imported a vast amount of sugar, much tobacco, many cigars, and great quantities of winter vegetables and tropical fruits, especially bananas. We have taken much of their iron and copper and such timber as cedar and mahogany.

To them we have sent cotton goods, machinery, furniture, and a great variety of manufactures. We have sent them such foodstuffs as cereals; dried, salted, and canned meats; and codfish. All of this is in the way of ordinary trade. Our relations with the people of the West Indies have been much more important than as buyers and sellers of goods. 

We have helped them in their problems of government and in their problems of sanitation. We have invested money in their industries and helped them to increase the yield of their crops and the quality of their products. 

Bahama Islands. The Bahamas are a group of many small islands north of 

Cuba. They belong to Great Britain.

They are low islands, largely of coral origin. It was on one of them that 

Columbus made his first landing in 1492.

Sponge fishing is one of the industries of these islands, and Nassau is the principal city. Most of the people are Negroes. 

The Bermuda Islands. One other group of islands may be mentioned here, although they are not really a part of the 

West Indies. They are in the Atlantic 

Ocean east of Charleston, South Carolina (map, page 298). They belong to Great

Britain, and a naval and coaling station is maintained there. They are far enough south to have a warm winter climate, and many of our people go there for the winter. 

The chief crops are onions, potatoes, and winter vegetables, most of which are sent to the United States or Canada.

NORTH AMERICA AS A WHOLE 

And so you come to the end of the story of the countries, large and small, that occupy the continent of North 

America and the islands near it. North

America is the larger of the two Americas and the third in size among the continents of the world.

Most of it is in the temperate and cooler parts of the earth. It is in such temperate and cooler regions that the great nations of our modern world are found. 

Surface. The relief and drainage of 

North America are easy to remember.

Along the west is a great mass of mountains and plateaus. The eastern coast is low, but a short distance inland there are other mountains. They are lower, shorter, narrower, and less rugged than those of the west, and they are a less serious trade barrier. The great heart of the continent is a lowland, with some minor elevations, that extends from the 

Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean.

The drainage of the continent follows the slopes of the land. In the southern part of the central lowland the plains slope to the Mississippi and with that river from north to south. In the northern part of the central lowland (A) the 

Mackenzie basin drains to the Arctic, and its drainage area slopes as the river flows. 

The lands around Hudson Bay drain into it and slope toward it. Another great drainage system of the continent is that of the St. Lawrence. This includes the

Great Lakes. Parts of Canada and the 

United States slope to its waters. The remainder of the continent is drained by shorter streams except the basins of three great rivers of the west that flow out of its plateaus and mountains. The Yukon flows into Bering Sea, the Columbia into the Pacific Ocean, and the Colorado into the Gulf of California.

Countries. How many countries of 

North America can you name? Remember that Canada is the largest but that the United States with Alaska is almost as large. Mexico is much smaller than either, but it is also much larger than the group of small countries to the south of it that make up Central America. 312

On the north of the continent there are Arctic seas icy cold from year's end to year's end. At the south the waters are always warm, sometimes almost hot. 

The warm waters of the Gulf Stream flow from Florida to the northeast, off the east coast. This warm east-coast current is matched in the northern Pacific off the 

Aleutians and the Panhandle of Alaska by the warm drift of the Japan current.

Winds blowing inland from the Pacific, the Atlantic, or the Gulf are cooled as they cross the mountains or as they get into higher latitudes. Industries. 

the chief industries of the people in the different parts of the continent and think of them as connected with one or more of the larger natural regions.

You should remember | in the southeastern and southern part of the United States, is raised also in irrigated regions farther west. Sugar cane is grown in Louisiana and Florida, and rice in Louisiana, Arkansas, Texas, and California.

There is fishing in coastal waters, in the deeper seas, and also in the Great Lakes, in smaller lakes, and in many rivers. 

Cod, salmon, halibut, mackerel, bluefish, weakfish, and many others are caught for sale. The chief cod-fishing grounds are the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, and the chief salmon fisheries are in the waters of the northwest from Oregon to Alaska. 

Shellfish such as lobsters, crabs, and shrimps are taken in large numbers. 

Agriculture is one of the greatest industries. Fruit raising, dairying, and grazing are found in many parts of the continent. In the east there is truck farming and market gardening along the coastal lowland from Florida to Maine. 

Oranges, grapefruit, and lemons are raised in Florida, southern Texas, Arizona, and California. Peaches are grown in 

Georgia, Maryland, New Jersey, New

York, and Michigan. Among the famous apple-growing regions are those in Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New 

York, Missouri, Oregon, Washington, and

Nova Scotia. 

Mixed farming has long been followed in the northern part of the Atlantic 

Coastal Plain, on the Lake Plains, and in

New England. It is now becoming more and more common farther south. Special crops also are grown in the eastern region, such as potatoes in Maine, cranberries in Massachusetts and New Jersey, and peanuts in Virginia and farther south.

Among the chief crops of the central lowland are cotton and food crops for men and animals. Cotton, grown chiefly 

Wheat and corn are grown in many parts of the United States and to some extent in Canada and Mexico. Unless you remember where these producing regions of our country are, you should study again the maps in this book showing where these crops are raised. In studying the wheat map, remember that it is spring wheat that is grown in northern United States. Winter wheat is grown farther south. Don't forget the wheat-growing region of eastern Oregon and Washington.

In the corn belt and farther south the corn is raised as a grain, and the ears or kernels are fed to hogs, cattle, sheep, and poultry to fatten them for market.

In the dairying regions the whole plant is cut before the ears ripen. It is then chopped up and stored in silos for use as a winter food.

Much hay of different kinds is raised, and many cattle and sheep feed upon the native grasses in various parts of our continent. Among the hay crops there is one that grows so rapidly that it is cut several times a year. This is alfalfa, which will grow in regions of less rainfall than many other hay crops. 

Remember the two special methods of farming that are in use in dry regions: dry farming and irrigation. If you need to review them, find the right pages by consulting the Index.

These regions include not only the great highlands in the western part of the continent but also the Appalachian Because of the great wealth of natural resources it is reasonable that many people of our continent should engage in manufacture. More or less change must be made in most natural resources to fit them for man's use. The development of manufacturing has led to the growth of cities and to the building of a vast network of railroads and a greater network of highways. In more recent times these transportation routes have been supplemented by air routes carrying some freight but chiefly for the transportation of mail and passengers. Such agencies bring together the raw materials for factories, and whatever is needed by factory and other workers. They also distribute the manufactured goods through the continent or take them to ports for export.

Map Review of North America. In this book there are many maps which are useful in studying the geography of the New World. 

It will be profitable to use some of them for a review of North America. You will find a list of the colored maps on page viii and the black and white maps on page ix. One excellent way to study maps is by means of imaginary trips by airways, our newest means of transportation. Such journeys are most interesting if you consult the maps first to find out what important features you would see.

SOUTH AMERICA 

We think and speak of the United States | as our country," and of the continent of North America, of which it forms so large a part, as "our continent." Most of the people of the United States were born within its borders, but the ancestors of nearly all of them came from beyond the seas. Some few of our people have but lately come from other lands. That is one reason why we are interested in the people of other continents. 

Another reason is that we carry on trade with the people of many of the countries into which these other continents have been divided.

The continent of South America is joined to North America by the Isthmus of Panama.

The two continents were discovered and explored in the closing years of the fifteenth century and the early years of the sixteenth century and were then spoken of as the " New 

World." This name is still much used by the people of the older countries of Europe. 

In learning about the continents and oceans it is best, at first, to make use of a globe. 

This is because the forms of the land and ocean areas are shown accurately on a globe, as are also their true positions in relation to one another. In studying a globe you will find that the continent of South America is not directly south of North America, but southeast of it. You can get an idea of how far east the continent of South America lies, by making use of the meridian of 80° west longitude. Find this meridian on your schoolroom globe. Trace it southward from the North Pole, across the eastern part of Canada and the United States, into the 

Atlantic Ocean, across Cuba, the Caribbean

Sea, and the Isthmus of Panama, and on southward to the South Pole. You see that most of North America is west of this meridian, while nearly all of South America is east of it. Remember, too, that all of North 

America is in the Northern Hemisphere and most of South America is in the Southern

Hemisphere. On the globe trace the Equator from east to west across the continent of 

South America. 

North and South America Compared. - In some ways the continents of North and South 

America are much alike. You would not call them "twin continents," perhaps, but they are enough alike so you may think of them as "sister continents." Each is shaped somewhat like a triangle (V). In each, the shortest side of the triangle is on the north, the longest side is on the west, and the sharpest angle is toward the south. 319

SOUTH AMERICA 

321 The most extensive highlands in both continents are near the Pacific Ocean. Their mountain systems are among the greatest on earth; they are high and long and broad, and inclose high plateaus. There are also mountain and plateau areas in the eastern part of each continent, as well as lowlands along their eastern coasts, and interior lowlands between their two chief regions of highland.

There are similarities in the drainage of the two continents, also. In each there are great rivers that flow from the interior of the continent into the oceans, or seas, to the north, the east, and the southeast. 

In many other ways the two continents are very different from each other. Along the coast of South America there are no great indentations such as are found in the northern continent in Hudson Bay and the Gulf of

Mexico. The broad part of South America is in the tropics, where the lowlands are always hot and where, over large areas, there are heavy rains and dense forests. But the broad part of North America is in the Temperate and Frigid zones. 

Map Study. -1. You have learned that the parts of a physical map which are colored green represent lowlands. Observe how large a part of 

South America is made up of lowlands. Notice that these lowlands are drained by three great river systems, all flowing into the Atlantic 

Ocean. Name the three great rivers. Which one of them has a delta, like the Mississippi 

River in our own country? 

2. The parts of the land shown in a brown or a lighter color represent highland regions. Find the very high mountain system along the entire 

Pacific coast. What is its name? Point out the lower highland region in eastern South 

America. What is its name? Find a smaller highland region in the interior of northern South

America. What is its name? 

3. Find the Equator and the Tropic of Capri corn. The locations of these lines tell you that the greater portion of South America is in the Torrid Zone. By turning to the map of North 

America (page 6) you can see that nearly all of Canada and all of the main part of our own country are in the North Temperate Zone. Only two of the larger countries in South America lie mainly in the South Temperate Zone - Argentina and Chile. Point them out on the map on page 318. 

4. Notice that with the exception of a narrow southern extension all of Brazil, the largest country in South America, is in the Torrid Zone. 

However, the elevation of the Brazilian Highlands does much to make more temperate the climate of a large section of Brazil. Why is this so? 

5. Two great seaports on the Atlantic coast are Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires. Point out their location on the map. An important seaport on the Pacific coast is Valparaiso. Point out its location.

Making a Sketch Map of South America. 

Look at the map of South America until you have the shape of its outline so well in mind that you can draw it from memory. It will not be so hard to do this as it was to make your sketch map of North America, because the coast line of South America is much more regular. There are no deep indentations like the Gulf of Mexico or 

Hudson Bay, with resulting peninsulas like 

Labrador or Florida. Do not try to draw your first outline from memory. Keep looking at the map. Use a pencil so that you can erase the lines easily if your map does not look right. 

Do not try at first to show all the little ins and outs. Make smooth lines. Remember that your aim is to represent correctly the general shape of the continent to get right proportions in length and breadth of the different parts. 

Start at the most eastern point near Cape St. Roque and follow the coast line toward the southwest until you reach the southern tip at 

Cape Horn. Then go on up the western coast to the Isthmus of Panama. Be careful to show the bulge toward the west as you pass the middle of this western coast line. Then go on across the northern and northeastern coasts until you reach the point where you started.

Now go back over your map and locate the mouths of the three great river systems of South 

America the Orinoco, the Amazon, and the 

Plata. Later on you can draw in the main rivers, the boundaries of the different countries, and mark the location of the important cities.

BRAZIL 

Turn to the map on page 318 and find 

Brazil. You will see that it is the largest country in South America. It includes nearly half of the continent within its boundaries, and is somewhat larger than our own country.

Although the southern point of Brazil is in nearly 34° south latitude, most of the country lies within the Torrid Zone, since it is broadest in the north. Brazil includes the part of the continent that juts eastward into the Atlantic Ocean, a fact that had much to do with its discovery and early history. 

It was Vasco da Gama, a Portuguese navigator, who first sailed from Europe around the southern end of Africa to India. That was in 1498. After his return to Portugal, another expedition was sent out to India, under command of Pedro Alvarez de Cabral. 

Warned by da Gama of calms near the west coast of Africa, Cabral sailed so far west to escape them that he saw the coast of the land we now call Brazil. This land was promptly claimed for Portugal and was later settled by the Portuguese. It was for a long time under their control but later became an independent country. You are now to learn how it has added to the world's resources and wealth. 

A Trip to Brazil. - Brazil has a seacoast more than 3600 miles in length. Every one of the South American countries except 

Ecuador and Chile borders Brazil. Count the bordering countries on the map (page 

318). How many are there? 

Would you like to take a trip to Brazil, sailing from New York? As most of Brazil is in the Torrid Zone, you would probably want to be there during the cooler months of its year. Remember that countries south of the Equator are having their summer when we are having our winter, and their winter when we are having our summer. Therefore you would sail from New York in the summer. 

Suppose you go first to Rio de Janeiro, which is the largest city of Brazil. It is also the capital of the country, although Brazil has set aside a large tract of land in the interior, where a new capital sometime may be built. 

Your steamer will head toward the southeast, for it must keep to the east of the easternmost point of South America. Each day the ship's "run" for the preceding twenty-four hours will be marked on a map which every one can see. A few days out from New York, your ship crosses the Tropic of Cancer and enters the Torrid Zone. The weather becomes very hot, but beyond the Equator it begins to get cooler again.

Southern parts of Rio de Janeiro as seen from the top of the Sugar Loaf, looking west. At the right you see a small part of the great harbor. At the left are seen two beaches on the coast of the ocean. 

About 600 miles south of the Equator, your | ship rounds the easterly part of South America. Its course is changed to the southwest, following the general direction of the coast of the continent. It is nearly twelve days after leaving New York when your ship at last turns toward the coast of the continent and sails into the harbor of Rio de Janeiro - or "Rio," as it is often called. 

The Great Harbor. The harbor of Rio de Janeiro is not only the best on the coast of South America; it is one of the best in the world. Its position on the Atlantic is almost midway between the northern and southern points of the continent. To reach it you have traveled about 5500 miles. From 

London or Liverpool in England the distance is only a very little longer. 

Even by that route the distance between 

San Francisco and Rio is nearly 9000 miles.

Before the construction of the canal what route would a ship have taken between these two ports? 

As your ship nears the shore at Rio, you will notice, beyond a very narrow coastal plain, what appear to be high mountains close around the city and rising to a jagged and irregular crest line behind it. The harbor entrance, about a mile wide, opens into a great bay. The entrance is deep enough for the largest ships in the world. On the west of the entrance, a mass of granite shaped like a blunt cone, and called the Sugar Loaf, reaches a height of over 1200 feet. The bay has a width of eleven miles and extends northward between inclosing highlands for more Ships from the west coast of the United than sixteen miles. It is deep enough so the 

States use the Panama Canal route to Rio. | largest ships can move freely about in it.

Prosperous and Progressive. - That Rio is both prosperous and progressive is indicated in part by its very size. It is shown also by the beauty of its streets and of its buildings, both public and private; by the extent of its foreign and domestic commerce; and by the amount and variety of its manufactures.

There is a canal two miles in length running through the heart of the city. On each side of it there is a street bordered by double rows of royal palms. There are numerous other broad streets and avenues also, bordered by trees of one kind or another (B). When the weather is fair, many people may be seen sitting at little tables along the edge of the sidewalks in front of the more popular cafés. A. - Rio de Janeiro and vicinity. It is large enough so that all the naval vessels of the world could anchor within it at one time (A). On its southwestern shore is Rio de Janeiro.

Through the wholesale traders of Rio, both foreign and domestic goods are distributed to smaller places along the Brazilian coast and to inland settlements. Inland towns are reached by railroad lines that lead up the valleys of the mountains to the great plateau The City. Rio de Janeiro was first built on a low alluvial plain. Sea walls and harbor works since constructed have changed the old | beyond. irregular coast line into straight lines and graceful curves. Shallow bodies of water inclosed by the sea walls have been filled in. Beautiful boulevards have been built along the water front. They are shaded by magnificent trees, and made lovely with beds of gorgeous flowers. The harbor has many docks, piers, and wharves. 

There are warehouses, grain elevators, and all the modern equipment for loading and unloading ships.

Rio has a population of about 

1,500,000 people and is larger than any other city of South America except Buenos Aires. It is more than one fifth as large as New York, nearly half as large as Chicago, smaller than 

Philadelphia or Detroit, but two and a half times as large as Buffalo.

It is from this plateau region, and from coast lands to the north and south, that Rio gets most of the raw materials for its manufacturing plants. These include textile and flour mills, furniture and shoe factories, and meat-packing plants.

A large part of Brazil's foreign trade passes through the port of Rio. Much of it is carried on with the United States. In recent 

On The Eastern Brazilian Highlands. 

the map, page 322, locate the region named 

Brazilian Highlands. Notice particularly that it includes the part of the continent that juts far out eastward into the Atlantic Ocean.

Notice also, however, that along most of the coast, between the highlands and the ocean there is a coastal plain, but that it is narrow. 

For a part of the distance, even, the mountains seem to rise directly from the sea. 

Seen from the sea or from the harbor of

Rio de Janeiro, the imposing heights that border this central part of the Brazilian coast appear to be a great range of mountains. 

But after climbing to the level of the highland beyond it, you discover that it is really the seaward-facing escarpment of a great plateau.

This highland region bears many names in its various parts, and its area is more than half that of all Brazil. Its surface is rolling and varies in elevation from about 800 to 3000 feet above sea level. It is crossed by a number of mountain ridges having a general northeast-southwest direction.

Even though it lies almost wholly within the tropics, its elevation so reduces its temperature that it is a pleasant land in which white people can live and work in comfort.

Brazilian Highlands, you will notice that the prevailing winds over most of this region are the southeast trade winds. They bring moisture to the land from the Atlantic Ocean. 

Heavy rains fall along the coast and on the eastern and southeastern mountain slopes. 

Much less falls in valleys between the mountains and on the nearly level plateaus and on the plains farther west.

A. Average rainfall in South America during the half year from May 1 to October 31. 

The Rainfall Maps. The maps on this page show the rainfall in South America as it is divided between the warmer and cooler parts of the year. Notice that in most parts of the continent the rainfall in one half year is very different in amount from that in the other half year. In some places it is more. 

In other places it is less. The time in the year when the rain comes, and its amount, make a great difference in the crops that are raised in different parts of the continent, and in the right seasons in which to raise them. 

These maps do not show how the rainfall varies in amount from year to year; so you must not expect too much from them. Indeed, in using any map, be sure that you know what it is intended to show.

The falls and rapids of the Brazilian Highlands, if fully used, could develop an enormous amount of electrical power. Up to the present, only a small part of the available energy has been used.

Industrial Regions of the Brazilian High lands. What are the industries carried on in this great highland area? The mineral wealth of Brazil is found chiefly in the eastern part. Agriculture is most successful in the eastern and southeastern parts, but, with irrigation, it is possible also in the northeast. 

In the south there are large forests, and in the west there are grasslands much like those of the Great Plains of our own country. 

Mineral Resources. Both gold and diamonds are found in Brazil, but the annual production of each is small, much less than it was years ago. There are large deposits of manganese, a metal used in the manufacture of steel. It is exported to the United States and other steel-making countries. There are some deposits of a low-grade bituminous coal, but only a small amount is mined. Four or five times as much coal of a high grade is imported from the United States and Great

Britain. There are enormous deposits of a very high-grade iron ore, but as Brazil has no good coking coal, not much is mined. It is a reserve supply upon which the steel-making centers of the world may sometime call. 

Agriculture. Except for parts of the coastal plain, the agricultural areas in the eastern and southeastern Brazilian Highlands are the most densely settled sections of the Even in these sections only a country. small part of the land has been brought under cultivation. In the grasslands farther west, only a small fraction of the area is used for pasture, and the population is sparse. The most valuable of all the crops raised in 

Brazil is coffee.

Coffee Plantations. In Brazil coffee grows best on the well-drained, rolling uplands near the Tropic of Capricorn, having an elevation of from 1000 to 3000 feet above sea level (A). The land has a fine, rich, red soil formed in part from decaying volcanic rock. The most successful plantations are the very large ones. So much expensive machinery is needed in growing coffee and B. - Cultivating coffee trees. The trees stand close together in the rows, and are pruned to keep them from growing very high. preparing it for the market that men with small farms and only a little money cannot succeed in the industry.

Some of the larger plantations cover hundreds of square miles and have millions of trees. The coffee trees are planted in long rows along the slopes and across the tops of the rolling hill lands, because the hill slopes and tops have less frost than the valleys. 

On these plantations many laborers are needed to cultivate the trees (B), to plant new ones, to help in picking the fruit, and to prepare the coffee for export. These laborers and their families live in villages that have been built in pleasant places on the plantations. On each of the very large plantations there may be two or three of these villages. 

During the harvest season other laborers are brought in, as they are in the wheat fields of our own country. 

Preparing the Coffee for Export. When ripe, the fruit of the coffee tree looks like clusters of dark red cherries. Usually each one of these has two seeds, or "beans." To get them out, the fruit is crushed in a machine that tears and loosens the pulp without

A. 

Heaps of coffee on a drying platform in Brazil. On the hillside in the far distance you can see many rows of the coffee trees. injuring the seeds. From this machine the whole mass goes to another, where the beans are separated from most of the pulp. They are then scrubbed to remove any small particles of pulp that may still cling to them. 

After the beans have been cleaned, they must be dried.

The coffee crop is usually harvested during the dry season-June to September - and at that time the beans can almost always be dried out of doors in the sun. This is done by spreading them on drying platforms (A). 

The drying is carefully watched and the beans are raked from time to time so that they will all dry equally. If heavy dews are expected or rain threatens, they are raked into piles and covered to keep them from getting wet. 

Sometimes, when wet weather prevents outof-door drying on the platforms, drying machines are used. The beans are covered with a tough outer skin and a delicate inner one called the silver skin. Both of these coverings are removed from the dried beans by machines. 

When the coffee is ready to be shipped, it is put up in bags of 132 pounds each. The annual production of Brazil averages more than 13,000,000 of these bags. From most of the plantations the coffee is sent to São Paulo, and from that city to Santos or to Rio de Janeiro for export. The roasting and grinding of the coffee is done in the country where it is to be used, and usually only a short time before it is used.

Why would it not be just as well to have these things done in Brazil before the coffee is shipped? velopment of cotton growing and an increase in the growing of tobacco and sugar cane were partly due to the World War, when ships were not available to import these products. 

The increase in the production of these and other crops is due, also, to the need the coffee growers feel for other crops to raise. In some years more coffee is produced than can be sold profitably, and the plantation owners therefore do not want to depend upon that crop alone.

BRAZIL 

333 Beans are raised in the central and southern parts of the highlands, and thousands of bushels are exported. Manioc or cassava, from which tapioca is made, is also grown. 

Yet all of these crops taken together use only a small part of the highland area that is available for agriculture. If you could fly over these lands in an airplane, you would see millions of acres where there are no roads, no villages, and few if any inhabitants. It is a fertile but empty land waiting for the settlers that will some day come. 

Live Stock. In the western part of these great eastern highlands of Brazil, there are vast areas of grasslands. In the southern part of the country, also, there are grasslands which are parts of a rolling plateau much like our own Great Plains. Many millions of cattle are being raised on these pasture lands. But so vast are these grassy areas that many times as many millions could be raised there as no doubt they will be, sometime in the future. The Brazilian government is encouraging the cattlemen to improve their stock by importing fine animals from other countries.

Horses, mules, and donkeys are raised for use on the farms and plantations, for there are not many roads on which trucks and pleasure cars can be used with comfort. 

Sheep are raised for their flesh and wool, goats for their hides, and hogs for their meat. 

Modern slaughtering and meat-packing plants have been built in São Paulo and in Rio de Janeiro, and a large export trade in meat and hides has been built up. There are also plants where jerked beef is prepared for sale in the hotter parts of the country where fresh meat would spoil quickly. Jerked beef is lean beef that has been salted and dried.

The Coastal Plain. You have already learned that there is a narrow coastal plain along much of the eastern coast of Brazil. It is not of uniform width. In some places it disappears altogether, where mountains reach the coast and slope steeply down to the sea. In other places it is wide enough to include some rather large but shallow lakes. 

Parts of it are salt marsh or swamp land. 

Other parts are high enough above sea level and well enough drained to furnish excellent farm land. Among the products of the coastal plain are cotton, sugar, lumber, and cacao "beans," from which chocolate is made. 

Cacao. — The cacao tree grows best in a region of high but even temperature, where the rainfall is heavy and well distributed through the year. An average temperature of 75° to 80° and a rainfall of from 50 to 

150 inches are required for its most successful growth. The trees grow in shaded places, in a deep, rich, well-drained soil. The cacao pods are the size of a large cucumber and hang from the trunk and larger branches of the tree (A). The ripe pods, when gathered, are opened and the beans and the pulpy mass surrounding them are scooped out. The pulp is allowed to ferment and in so doing becomes hot. The heating improves the quality of the beans, and the pulp turns into a liquid that is allowed to run off, as it has no value. 

The beans are usually dried on brick or cement platforms, and are then bagged and shipped to chocolate-manufacturing countries. The United States uses about two fifths of the world's crop of cacao. Brazil ranks second among the producing nations; it is outranked only by one of the countries of tropical Africa.

Cities of the Highlands and Coastal Plains. 

You have visited three of the largest cities of 

Brazil. These are: (1) the beautiful capital city of Rio de Janeiro; (2) Santos, the coffee port, and (3) São Paulo, the city in the highlands northwest of Santos. 

Of these three cities, Santos is chiefly concerned with coffee and the coffee trade, and has but few and small manufactures. Here coffee is handled, sorted, graded, stored, and shipped. Everywhere you see coffee and smell its delightful aroma, for in addition to the large quantity prepared for shipment some is roasted for local use.

In Rio, there are large textile mills. These make use of cotton from Brazilian fields and wool from Brazilian sheep ranches, as well as of some imported wool and silk. Cattle and sheep from the grazing regions furnish the B.

Turn to the map on page 326. Follow the coast north from Rio, until you find the city of Bahia (called by Brazilians São Salvador).

It is built at the entrance of a large bay, at the foot and on the western slope of a peninsula that rises steeply from the shore. This bay is shaped somewhat like the one on which the city of Rio is located, and it forms a large and beautiful harbor.

The older part of Bahia along the water front has narrow, crooked streets, but modern wharves and docks have been built, and steamers are loaded and unloaded by machinery. Many of the old buildings are roofed with tiles, and bright tiles have been built into their walls. The modern city is on the higher slopes and is reached by elevators and steep, winding roads. The streets are wider, and the houses and other buildings are larger and much like those in our cities. 

Bahia is the port of large tobacco and cacao regions. There are many factories in which cigars and cigarettes are made for local use and for export. Other exports of Bahia are cacao, hides, tobacco, coffee, and sugar.

Turn again to the map on page 326. On the coast of Brazil, north of Bahia, find the city of Pernambuco (Brazilian name, Recife).

It is built on low land around a lagoon formed by two small rivers, and on an island between the rivers. Its several parts are connected by a number of bridges. As it is so near the 

Equator, its average temperature is high and the rainfall is heavy. These conditions and the nearness of swamp lands on the south made it, for a long time, a very unhealthful place in which to live. Efforts to improve conditions have been successful, and sickness is much less common than in former years. 

In spite of its disadvantages, Pernambuco is one of the important ports of Brazil. It is much nearer to the ports of the United States and Europe than are the other seacoast cities you have been studying. It is the outlet of a sugar-raising and cotton-raising region, and its exports include sugar, cotton, hides and skins, and lumber.

The Amazon Basin. Much of northern 

Brazil is drained by the Amazon River system. This river rises in a small lake on the eastern slope of the Andes Mountains, and flows eastward to the Atlantic Ocean. Measured along its winding course, it is about 

3500 miles long. Only the Mississippi 

Missouri River is longer, and no river in the world has a greater volume of water. 

The size of the Amazon drainage basin is enormous. It is three fourths as large as the 

United States and includes more than half of Brazil and parts of several other countries. 

What countries are these (map, page 318)?

Although the headwaters of the Amazon and of its tributaries reach back into the highlands, much of the Amazon basin is less than 1000 feet above sea level, and large areas are only a few feet above the normal level of the river. The seaward slope of the land bordering the Amazon is so gentle that for the last 2000 miles of its course there are times when the river drops only an inch in each five miles. Yet its volume is so great that its products of eastern and southern Brazil which muddy waters can be traced in the ocean are not found in the United States. 337 The steamer on which you travel will use this channel because of its greater safety. 

All the other outlets of the Amazon are more or less blocked by sand bars and swift currents, and by floating trees and island-like masses of shrubs, grasses, and earth. 

About 80 miles up the Rio Pará from the ocean, you reach the well-built and attractive city of Pará (or Belém) on the east bank of the river. Pará reached its greatest size and importance some years ago when the Amazon basin was producing most of the world's rubber. At that time it was the chief outlet for all the products that came down the river, and the place from which supplies were distributed. In recent years the production of rubber in Brazil has decreased, and as a result the commerce of Pará also has decreased. More than 90 per cent of the world's rubber supply now comes from rubber plantations in Asiatic countries. 

Even if you make only a short stay in Pará, you will find it both hot and rainy. It is built on low land only a short distance south of the Equator, and its average yearly rainfall is about 100 inches. In hot countries people usually rest during the middle of the day, when it is hottest, and in Pará it is in the early afternoon that the heaviest rainfall also may be expected. You should therefore do your shopping, make your calls, and visit theaters, parks, and museums in the late afternoon and evening when it is cooler and the rain for the day is over. 

The steamer on which you made your journey to Pará could, with perfect safety, go many hundreds of miles up the Amazon. 

But it will probably be best to change to one of the smaller river steamers for the trip.

During the rainy seasons when flood waters pour into the Amazon from its headwaters and its many tributaries, it may rise in places as much as fifty feet or more. Both the main stream and the tributaries within the rainy belt overflow their banks and spread out over the bordering lowlands. The Amazon becomes a great lake whose width is sometimes as much as 200 miles. During these flood periods, the people who live on the lower lands along the river are forced to move to higher lands or to live in boats until the flood goes down. The forest trees and the interlacing vines that bind them together rise out of the water as a wall of living green (A).

The Amazon Forests. In hot, rainy regions such as that of the Amazon, the forest areas, called rain forests, are very dense. 

They are entirely unlike those in our own country or other temperate regions where many trees of one kind are found growing close together over large areas. In the rain forests there are as many as forty or fifty kinds of trees and those of the same kind are widely scattered. Cutting trees for lumber is therefore less easy and more expensive than in the forests of temperate lands. 

To add to the lumberman's difficulties, all forms of vegetation grow with the greatest luxuriance. There are no open spaces carpeted with dead leaves, where patches of sunlight fall in ever-changing patterns, such as we find in our own forests. In the great tropical forest of the Amazon, almost every inch of soil is occupied by some plant. It is a real jungle. The trees stand close together. 

Great vines, rooted in the soil, wind their way upward around the trunks of the trees, slowly choking them to death. They swing from branch to branch and from tree to tree. 

Shrubs and other growths block the spaces between the tree trunks. Those who must 

The largest of the forest trees are tall, but they are by no means so gigantic as the big trees of California. Most of the trees of the rain forest are of moderate size. Included among them are such hardwoods as mahogany, rosewood, ebony, and Spanish cedar, and others whose wood will take as fine a polish as any of these. 

Among the trees of this vast forest, a forest that is said to be the largest in the world, are many whose wood, or bark, or sap, or fruit, or seeds yield products valuable to mankind.

Products of the Amazon Forest. The name Brazil was given to the country because a red dyewood known by that name was found in the forest. Brazil-nut trees also are found there in great numbers. You have probably eaten the delicious white meat of Brazil nuts. They are three-sided, and fifteen or twenty of them are found closely packed in the round, hard shells that grow on the trees. They are gathered in great quantities by Indians who live in the forest, and are sold to traders to be shipped to other countries.

Cacao trees (page 334) are found growing wild, especially along the lower course of the Amazon. There are other trees from which a vegetable wax is obtained. There are plants that yield long, strong fibers. Some of these fibers are as fine as silk. Today they are used by the natives in making hammocks and some other articles, but sometime they may come into the markets of the world.
