American Brazilian Association

A. Tap and cup on a rubber tree. Some of the Brazilian rubber trees grow very large. 

Of all the trees of the Amazon forest, the ones that have so far been of greatest value are those from which rubber is obtained, of which there are several varieties. They are found in flooded lowlands, and because those along the rivers are most easily reached it is from such regions that most of the Brazilian rubber comes. 

How Rubber Is Obtained. Much of the land where rubber trees grow is owned by large companies. Native Indian rubbergatherers are hired to collect rubber and prepare it for market. As soon as the season of floods is over, the rubber-gatherers go into the forest. Each one is told where to camp, and he puts up a simple shelter with open sides and a roof of palm leaves, where he and his family live during the rubber-gathering season.

As the rubber trees are some distance from each other, each man locates about a hundred B. 

United States Rubber Co. 

Rubber-gatherer on his rounds. Here he is crossing a small stream on a very simple foot bridge. trees and cuts a path from tree to tree. This path is so arranged that it starts and ends near his camp. Next the trees are tapped, by making a gash or gashes in the bark. There is a milky-white fluid, called latex, circulating through the inner bark, and it is from this that crude rubber is made. Under each cut a cup is fastened to catch the latex (A). The latex, however, does not flow for long, and a new cut is usually made each day. This is generally done by taking a thin shaving from the surface of the cut that was made the day before.

Early each morning the rubber-gatherer starts on a round of his trees, tapping them and fastening on the cups. When he returns to to camp he gets his breakfast, for he eats when he can and has no fixed hours for his meals. He rests awhile and then goes around with a pail to gather the latex from the cups on the trees (B).

SOUTH AMERICA 

United States Rubber Co. B.

A. Making rubber by smoking the latex. Compare the size of the ham just started with those in the next picture. 

When he gets back he builds a fire, using oily nuts that make a great deal of smoke. 

He pours a little of the latex on a stick, or paddle, and turns it around and around in the smoke (A). Soon the latex hardens and takes on a brownish color. More and more latex is added and smoked until it has all been hardened in this way. That gathered on following days is treated the same way until a large ball of this crude rubber has been formed. Such balls are called hams.

At the end of the season boats are sent from camp to camp, to gather the rubber hams to be shipped down the river. Not all rubbergatherers work for large companies. Some work for themselves alone, but the methods are about the same.

Rio Negro (Spanish for "Black River") on account of its dark-colored water. Find it on your map. Not far up this river, on some high land that borders it, is the city of 

Manáos. Your steamer will take you to this river port, and there your journey ends. You could sail on up the Amazon many miles into Peru, to the west of Brazil; for the river has neither falls nor rapids to interrupt steamer traffic for 2700 miles from its mouth.

The city of Manáos is not so large as Pará. 

It is a city of the forest and a center of the rubber trade (B). It was the profits on rubber that built its fine buildings and laid out its wide streets and beautiful parks. At present the rubber industry is not prosperous, and Manáos is not the important city that it was some years ago. But it may sometime become a shipping center for other forest products. 

Animal Life in the Forest. Before leav ing these forests of the Amazon, let us learn a little about the animal life. In the great river itself and in its tributaries there are large alligators and hundreds of varieties of fish. In the jungle there are pumas and

BRAZIL 

341 A. Jaguar or American leopard. This animal is larger and heavier than the leopard of Asia and Africa. jaguars, fierce cat-like animals of great strength. There are monkeys, large and small, that chatter at each other as they swing among the branches. There are snakes, the largest of which is the boa constrictor that wraps itself about its prey and crushes it. 

There is the sloth that hangs back downward from the branches, and there is the foul vampire bat. As a touch of beauty, there are rare birds of brilliant and beautifully colored plumage. 

Savannas. Read again on pages 337-338 about the northward and southward movement of the belt of equatorial calms or doldrums. On the northern and southern margins of the region over which the doldrums move, the rainy seasons are short and the dry seasons are long. During the rainy season grass grows quickly on extensive plains called savannas. In the dry season, the grass withers and dies. When the grass is fresh and green the savannas make wonderful pastures. But the dry seasons are so long, the heat is so great, insects are so annoying to cattle, and there are so many cattle diseases, that the savannas, called campos in Brazil, are not yet much used for cattle ranges. Grasslands in other parts of Brazil and in other South American countries are much more favorably located for cattle and sheep raising. 

Comparing the Mississippi and the Amazon. Although the Amazon is not so long as the Mississippi-Missouri, it is much longer than the Mississippi alone. Because of the greater rainfall in its basin the Amazon has a far larger volume of water; and it is, on the average, much wider and deeper than the great river of our continent. So vast is the volume of water carried by the Amazon that the Brazilians call it Rio Mar- meaning 

River Sea.

It is only by dredging that a depth of 9 feet is maintained in the Mississippi River as far north as Cairo. Expensive work was necessary also in order to get that same depth on the Ohio River to Pittsburgh. As a result of dredging and other costly work, ocean steamers can reach New Orleans, about 110 miles from the Gulf of Mexico. The Amazon averages more than 100 feet in depth for a distance greater than the total length of the Mississippi. Ocean steamers can reach

Iquitos, 2300 miles from its mouth. Smaller steamers can go still farther up the main stream and from 500 to 1000 miles on all the larger tributaries.

There are times when lands bordering the Mississippi are flooded. To prevent such floods, levees have been built along the river at a cost of many millions of dollars. Without the levees there would be annual floods, much of the valuable farm land could not be used, and the Mississippi basin, which now has a population of nearly 50,000,000, would be far less densely peopled. The Amazon and many of its tributaries have annual floods when their waters spread out over vast areas. areas. No attempt is made to control them. 

The whole basin, nearly twice the size of the Mississippi basin, has a population of less than 3,000,000, and no industries of sufficient value to make a control of floods necessary. 

On maps, pages 320, 322, find the Guiana Highlands, and see which part of that area is drained to the Amazon. These highlands have an east-west direction, and when

SOUTH AMERICA 

the doldrums are farther south the northeast trade winds blow across them. The northern and eastern part of the highlands have heavy rains, but the southern slopes and the lower lands just to the south have much less.

The People of Brazil. There are about 

40,000,000 people living in Brazil. That is a small number for so large a country. How does it compare with the number living in our own country? If the population of Brazil were spread out evenly over the whole country, there would be only twelve people in each square mile. The map on this page shows how the people really are distributed. Notice the large part of Brazil where the average number of people is less than two for each square mile. Notice also the denser population in the southeastern part of the country, and in the coastal regions near great cities. 

When the settlement of Brazil was first undertaken by Europeans, they found Indians occupying parts of the country. Most of the early white settlers were from Portugal, but some were from Spain. Later, Negro slaves were imported from Africa.

Transportation. The railroads of Brazil 

The railroads of Brazil (maps, pages 326 and 346) are few and short. 

Most of them lead inland from coast cities.

In the whole vast basin of the Amazon there is but one short road. This was built, at great cost, around the falls of the Madeira 

States. This change was natural.

The people of the United States now use more coffee, rubber, cacao, and hides and skins than are used by the people of any other country. Brazil ranks first in the production of coffee and second in cacao. Its animal industries furnish an enormous number of hides and skins, and although its rubber production has greatly decreased, fine 

Pará rubber is still the world's best. 

In exchange for what we get from Brazil, we send foodstuffs, textiles, coal, gasoline, machinery and tools, automobiles and trucks, and building steel.

SOUTH AMERICA 

Brazil is largely in the Torrid Zone. Our country is in the Temperate Zone. Naturally the two countries will always have products to exchange, and trade between them should increase. Brazil has enormous empty spaces suitable for agriculture and grazing. It has great wealth of iron ore, but little coal. The value of its forests cannot be told, because there is now no way by which those in the Amazon Valley can be cut at a profit. Yet with an increasing population, the empty lands will be occupied. 

Some day the iron ore will be needed. Some of it may be sent to steel-manufacturing countries, and coal brought back as a return cargo. The same sort of exchange is made between the Lake Superior iron region and the Pennsylvania coal regions. The world's need of timber may sometime become so great that a way will be found to use even the forest trees of the Amazon basin. When these changes come, let us hope that both our own country and Brazil will be benefited by them.

ARGENTINA, PARAGUAY, AND 

URUGUAY Go now from Brazil to the more southern part of South America, east of the Andes

Mountains (map, page 346). There you will find three countries Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina. 

Which of the three is the largest? Argentina is about a third as large as Brazil and more than four times as large as Texas (Tables 1 and 2, pages 389, 392). The size of Paraguay may not be given accurately, as that country and Bolivia disagree as to the boundary between them. If the disputed territory is divided equally between them, Paraguay will have an area one tenth that of Argentina, or two and one half times that of New York. Uruguay is about one and a half times as large as New York. It is the smallest of the South American republics. 

This group of countries lies between 21° and 55° south latitude, and mostly in the South Temperate Zone - except that a small part of Argentina and a large part of Paraguay are north of the Tropic of Capricorn in the Torrid Zone. 

Five Natural Regions. This group of countries may be divided into five natural regions whose boundaries are based largely upon differences in climate (map, page 322). 

These are: (1) the Gran Chaco, a semitropical region of forests and savannas, where the climate is hot and moist; (2) the temperate, rolling grasslands of Uruguay; (3) the

Pampa, or Pampas, a plains region between 30° and 40° south latitude and extending west from Uruguay and the Atlantic Ocean almost to the Andes; (4) a semi-arid region west of the Pampas and east of the Andes; (5) the bleak, wind-swept, treeless region of Patagonia, between 40° and 55° south latitude, partly plains and partly plateau.

Of these five regions the one that is most densely populated, with the largest and bestdeveloped industries, is the Pampas.

Courtesy Bence Tourist Co. 

A. 

A large flock of high-grade sheep in Uruguay. 

The Pampas. The Pampas region is a nearly level, almost treeless area about one fourth the size of Argentina. Its eastern part is a region of fine and fertile soils. Farther west and nearer the mountains, the soil is somewhat coarser. You remember that our Great Plains increase gradually in elevation toward the Rocky Mountains. In the same way the Pampas rise gradually toward the Andes.

The average annual rainfall is nearly 40 inches along the Atlantic Ocean, but this decreases to less than 16 inches along the inland margin of the Pampas about 400 miles farther west (maps, page 328). There are few streams and none of them are large. The rain that falls sinks rapidly into the earth except when there is an especially heavy downpour. Then a thin sheet of water, like a very shallow lake, may spread over the surface, but it disappears in a short time. 

The whole of the Pampas region is used for grazing, dairying, or agriculture, and it raises a great surplus of food to be sent to other countries. Grazing is the oldest of these industries and the most profitable.

Animal Industries of the Pampas. - The early Spanish settlers brought their farm animals with them to this new country. The lands upon which they settled were unfenced, and some of their cattle, horses, and sheep wandered away on the Pampas. As snow seldom falls there, and the temperature never drops to zero, these wanderers were able to live without shelter. The native grasses furnished plenty of food, and within a few years there years there were great numbers of wild horses, cattle, and sheep roaming the plains. 

They were hunted like other wild animals. 

Horses caught alive were tamed for use or for sale. Wild cattle were killed for their hides, and sheep for their skins and wool. 

Later, a jerked beef industry and the manufacture of beef extracts developed. 

The breeding of fine horses and the better kinds of sheep (A) and cattle (348 A) began in the latter part of the nineteenth century. 

It was then that the owners of the great ranges or estancias began to fence their pastures. tures. High-grade animals, for which very high prices were paid, were imported from 

Europe and the United States.

A. Cattle-raising regions of South America. 

At the same time the cattlemen began to plant alfalfa on former pasture lands to take the place of the native grasses. Alfalfa 

Alfalfa grows rapidly and makes an excellent pasture. From fields that are not pastured, it can be cut for hay several times during the growing season, or it can be put in a silo to be fed as green fodder. Alfalfa is used in 

Argentina to fatten cattle for market, as corn is used in the United States. 

Study map A. How many cattle does each dot represent? You can see that there are more cattle in northeastern Argentina, in Uruguay, and in southern Brazil than in other parts of the continent. In Argentina the number of cattle decreases toward the south and west, where there is not enough rainfall for good pastures, and toward the north, where it is too hot and moist. Study also map B. You will notice that the greatest B. 

-Sheep-raising regions of South America. 

number of sheep are in the cattle district of Argentina and Uruguay, but that many are raised farther south. raised farther south. This is a region of poor pasture, where sheep can find food but cattle cannot. 

Beef cattle and sheep that are fat enough to be slaughtered are sold to great meatpacking plants, most of which are owned by the meat packers of the United States. Find the cities of Buenos Aires, La Plata, Rosario, and Santa Fé in Argentina; and Montevideo and Paysandú in Uruguay. There are packing plants in all of these places. Most of the beef is chilled and then sent in refrigerator ships to eastern United States and to countries in Europe. Some beef and nearly all the mutton are frozen and sent abroad in ships that keep the meat frozen during the voyage. At the end of the trip it is stored where it can be kept frozen until it is sold.

SOUTH AMERICA 

A. Cows and calves on an estancia in Argentina. 

The flavor of frozen beef is not so good as that of chilled beef, but freezing does not seem to injure the flavor of mutton. Transportation by water is so much cheaper than transportation by rail, that meat from Argentina or Uruguay can be sold in eastern United 

States for less than meat from the packing plants of central United States. 

Dairying is increasing in both Argentina and Uruguay, especially in those parts of the country reached by railroads; and both butter and cheese are exported. Other animal products that are sold include (1) much fine wool for clothing, (2) hides and skins to be made into leather, (3) fats for making tallow, soap, and candles, and (4) bones that are used for a variety of purposes.

Very few of the great land owners live on their estancias, which are left in charge of trusted managers. Under the managers, gauchos, or native cowboys, care for the cattle.

Crops are raised and alfalfa planted chiefly by tenant farmers, many of whom are Italians. Contracts are made with these tenant farmers for a period of years. The farmer agrees to plow the pasture and to cultivate the soil to get rid of the native grasses. 

He also agrees to leave the land planted to alfalfa at the end of the contract period. 

He must then move to another location on the estancia perhaps many miles away or to another estancia. 

Most of the wealthy land owners are unwilling to divide their great estates into smaller fields for careful cultivation, being content with the income from the sale of the animals that are raised. They are equally unwilling to sell their land. Tenant farmers and immigrants find it almost impossible to buy farms. 

As tenants they will not build roads, or put up schoolhouses for their children, or good homes for themselves. They know that in a few years they must move to a new location

and leave behind whatever they have built. 

All this makes them discontented and unhappy. In

In the United States things are very different. Farms average about 150 acres in size. 

Most of the farmers own their farms, live on them, and do much or all of the work, hiring additional help only as it is needed. many cases farms that are for sale are purchased by tenant farmers or immigrants. 

In most of the northern regions there are churches, schools, stores, and railroads in near-by villages which can usually be reached over good roads.

How the Land of Argentina Can Be Used.- 

A study of the best use for the land of Argentina has been made. It shows that nearly one third can be used for crops, and a slightly larger amount for grazing. Nearly one fourth is covered with forest or can be used for orchards. Less than one tenth is waste. 

Of the land on which crops can be raised, only one fourth is now being cultivated.

Most of the cultivated farms are large, and the best of modern agricultural machinery, imported from the United States, is in use. 

The chief crops are alfalfa (page 347); cereals, especially wheat and corn; and flax. A.

The Corn Lands. When you were studying the corn belt of central United States, you learned that corn needs more moisture than wheat. In the United States, a large part of the corn raised is used to fatten hogs and cattle. 

In Argentina, the raising of hogs has not yet developed into a great industry, and most of the cattle are fattened on alfalfa (page 347). 

As a result, most of the corn raised in Argentina is exported. 

Flaxseed. You probably know that flax is raised in Europe for its fiber, from which linen is made; and that much flax is raised in certain of our North Central States for its seed. This is becoming a great industry in 

Argentina also. Most of the crop is exported, a large part of it coming to the United States. 

The flaxseed is used in making linseed oil.

Cotton. In some parts of the Gran 

Chaco, cotton is now grown (332 A). The soil is fertile, there is enough rain and it comes at the right time, and there is a dry harvesting season. The industry is prosperous even though it is difficult and expensive to get the cotton to market. The yield is large, labor is cheap, and the boll weevil is not known.

Much of the cotton grown is used in Argentina mills, but some is exported. 

In the forested region of the Gran Chaco, the most valuable trees are the quebracho, the Paraná pine, and the small maté tree. 

Quebracho. Quebracho is an extremely hard and very heavy wood. The name means "ax-breaker." The heart wood of this tree is rich in tannic acid used in tanning hides to make leather. Other Forests in the Plata Basin.- Much 

Much of the region that you are now studying is drained by the Paraguay, Paraná, and 

Uruguay river systems. Find them on the map, page 346. Their waters finally reach the broad bay that is named Plata River. or on their western slopes. After these winds have crossed the mountains they have very little moisture left, and much of Patagonia has less than 10 inches of rainfall annually (maps, page 328). Some snow is blown through mountain valleys to melt on the eastern slopes and furnish moisture for a few short mountain streams. There is enough moisture, especially toward the south and in the southern islands, to permit a scanty growth of grass. growth of grass. Several million sheep are raised, some for their wool, others for mutton. 

This region is as dry as the sheep-raising regions in Australia and in North America.

A Great and Beautiful City. - On the south shore of the Plata River, about 155 miles from the open Atlantic, is the city of Buenos Aires. It is the capital of Argentina, the largest city in South America, the largest city south of the Equator, and the largest city in the world whose people speak the Spanish language. On the maps of three continents, notice that this city is in about the same latitude as Cape Town in 

South Africa and Sydney in Australia. 

Nearly four fifths of the trade of Argentina with the rest of the world is carried on through the port of Buenos Aires and its outer port, La Plata. At almost any time of the year, ships from many parts of the world may be seen loading or unloading at the wharves or piers there.

A. The Christ of the Andes. This statue stands on the boundary between Argentina and Chile. 

All of the leading railroads of Argentina center in Buenos Aires. Most of them are owned and operated by English companies. 

Two lines cross the Andes Mountains. One of these is the Transandine Railroad from Buenos Aires to Valparaiso in Chile. It is about 900 miles in length. In the high mountains it has been necessary to build many miles of snow sheds over the track, so that trains can run during the winter. 

At a high point in the Andes, just above the tunnel through which the railway passes, stands a famous monument. It is a statue of the Christ (A), put up as a pledge of peace between the two countries. 

Another railroad from Buenos Aires to the

Pacific passes through Rosario and Tucumán to La Paz in Bolivia. From La Paz there are three lines to ports on the Pacific Ocean. 

Most of the other railroad lines of Argentina are much shorter and serve the wheat, corn, flax, and cattle regions, and the dairying districts. In the plains of Argentina there are no hills to be cut through or tunneled, and few streams to be bridged. So level is the land that one railroad has 175 miles of track without a curve. Several air lines carrying mail and passengers are in operation from Buenos Aires as a center. 

The chief manufacturing industries of the city are those that have developed naturally out of the resources of the country. They include huge meat-packing plants, flour mills, creameries and cheese factories, tanneries, and shoe factories.

SOUTH AMERICA 

The People of Argentina. You learned that the population of Brazil includes many people of the white race but also many Indians, Negroes, and people of mixed blood. 

In Argentina, however, almost all the people are of the white race. Among them are many of Spanish or Italian descent, and some other 

European people.

In most of Argentina the climate is like that in other temperate parts of the world, where we find the greatest civilized countries of the present day. White people can work there in comfort and with energy. 

Most of the European immigrants of recent years are industrious and thrifty. Some of them have been able to purchase land or to enter into business and have prospered. The government of Argentina now requires each immigrant to prove that he has good character and good health, and that he is willing to work. It is only people of this kind who are wanted in Argentina, even though many millions more can find homes there before it is as densely populated as our own country. 

Mineral Resources of Argentina. It is probable that Argentina will always be largely a farming and grazing country. However much the country may have in the way of mineral wealth, no great mineral deposits of high value have been discovered either in the Andes or elsewhere. Small quantities of gold, silver, copper, lead, and zinc have been found, and some mining of these metals is going on. Petroleum has been found in the northwestern part of the country and in southern Patagonia, but the chief producing area is near the coast about 900 miles south of Buenos Aires.

Deposits of low-grade coal and some lignite have been located, and iron-ore deposits are reported from several places in the northcentral part of the country. The development of manufacturing on a large scale depends to a large degree upon cheap coal and iron. The fact that in Argentina there are no profitable mines of either being worked, means that the machinery and the coal for manufacturing plants must be imported.

Manufacturing in Argentina is chiefly directed to the preparation of foodstuffs and other raw materials for export. Most manufactured goods for use in Argentina are imported from other countries (page 355).

A Land of One Industry. — The single great industry of Uruguay is grazing. Great herds of cattle and enormous flocks of sheep are spread out over the rolling grasslands, which are not so nearly level as those of the Pampas in Argentina. These pastures of 

Uruguay are a southern continuation of the hill lands of southeastern Brazil.

The native grasses are so good, and the rainfall is so abundant and well distributed, that much less land has been planted to alfalfa in Uruguay than in Argentina. Agriculture has developed very slowly. The soils are fertile and the climate ideal for raising cereals, flaxseed, and fruits and vegetables, but the people of Uruguay prefer the freedom of life that the grazing industry gives.

It passes through Mendoza, surrounded by its irrigated vineyards, and climbs the eastern slopes of the Andes. 

Through tunnels it reaches the western slopes of the Andes, and drops down to the plains of Chile and the sea.

The ocean route may be around the islands at the southern end of the continent past 

Cape Horn, or through the Strait of Magellan.

This strait was named after a Portuguese navigator who was the first to discover this winding channel from the Atlantic to the Pacific. He was in command of three ships, one of which was the first to sail around the earth, although Magellan himself was killed when his ships stopped at the Philippine 

Islands. Magellan's new route from the 

Atlantic to the Pacific grew more and more important as the New World was settled. 

Parts of the channel, however, are narrow, and shifting winds and changing currents make careful steering very necessary (A).

Southern Chile. Much of the Pacific coast of southern Chile is bordered by islands the peaks of sunken mountains. This is the latitude of the "Roaring Forties"so named because of violent winds and sudden storms met with in the latitude of the westerlies by early navigators. Between the islands and the mainland there is an "inside passage." There are also narrow bays or fiords leading back into the mountains that rise steeply from the sea, as they do in 

British Columbia and the Panhandle of southern Alaska. 

Dense evergreen and hardwood forests cover the rain-soaked and mist-shrouded western slopes of the mountains of southern Chile. The trees are not as large or as good as similar forests in our own country, and the finest lumber must still be imported. 

Coal. Chile is fortunate in having coal deposits of considerable size. They are probably the largest in South America. The chief deposits and the mines now operating are on the coast between Concepción and Valdivia, where the coal veins extend out under the sea. About 1,500,000 tons are mined annually, most of which is sold to 

Chilean railroads. The lack of good coal in most South American countries has retarded the development of manufacturing, even where raw materials are available. 

The Central Valley. Spanish explorers sailing southward along the desert coast of western South America found a break in the coastal mountains. At this point they were happy to discover a green valley that led into the interior. They called it " Valley of Paradise." In Spanish this is Valparaiso. 

The name has been kept as that of the chief seaport of Chile, from which railroads and highways extend eastward to the Central Valley. On the west, between this valley and the Pacific, are the coast ranges. On the east are the snow-covered Andes Mountains towering thousands of feet above the level of the valley and stretching on and on toward the north and the south. Toward the north the snow line rises on the side of the mountain because of increasing warmth. 

Toward the south it sinks nearer and nearer to sea level as the temperature decreases. 

One of the peaks in this part of the Andes is Mt. Aconcagua the highest in the New 

World. Its top is about 23,000 feet above the level of the sea. 

Heavy rains and melting snows furnish water for many mountain streams, some of which as they reach the valley form beautiful lakes. In the northern part of the valley, where the rainfall decreases, the water of these streams is used for irrigation. On a | number of these tumbling mountain torrents

A Land of Large Estates. In the early days of settlement in Chile, large grants of land were made to some men, and in this way great estates were created. Many of the largest holdings have been more or less split up through sales or their division among heirs. Even at the present time, however, nine tenths of the land in the Central Valley is held in estates of over 500 acres (A). The number of small farms is increasing, and this leads to a more careful cultivation of the land. In Chile, as in Argentina, many of the owners of the great estates live in the cities and leave the management of their land to others. 

Principal Products. Among the crops grown in the Central Valley, wheat ranks first. It is raised in all parts of the valley (map, page 349), and more than half of the land under cultivation in Chile is devoted to this crop. The demand for wheat bread is so great that less than one tenth of the crop is exported. Smaller amounts of barley, oats, corn, and rye are raised.

Parts of this valley are so well suited to the raising of fruits that it has been called the "California of South America." In the warmer northern part oranges, lemons, figs, and olives are raised. In the more temperate region berries and such orchard fruits as apples, peaches, pears, plums, and cherries are grown. There are many vineyards (map, page 352) in the valley, especially in the northern irrigated portion. A large winemaking industry has developed, and some of the grapes are made into raisins.

Nearly every variety of vegetable can be grown, and in regions where the cold season is very short two or three crops may be raised in a single growing season. The building of the Panama Canal greatly shortened the sea voyage between Chile and the cities of eastern and central United States.

Two Important Cities. The two largest and most attractive cities of Chile are Santiago, the capital, and Valparaiso, the chief seaport. Santiago is in the Central 

climate so mild that flowers bloom in parks and gardens at all times of the year. Yet peaks of the Andes within sight of the city are capped with snow from year's end to year's end. There are fine public and private buildings, well-paved and well-lighted streets, excellent shops, and many rather small factories. The main north-south railroad of Chile passes through the city and it is connected by an electric railroad 117 miles in length with Valparaiso to the northwest. 

Valparaiso is the largest seaport on the 

Pacific coast of South America. The harbor is not naturally so well protected as is that of Rio (page 324) or those of our own ports of 

New York and San Francisco. It has therefore been necessary to build breakwaters to protect shipping in the harbor from storms.

A. Principal mineral products of South America. 

Northern Chile and the Atacama Desert. 

Northern Chile is in the region of the southeast trade winds (diagram, page 263), and is dry. The winds usually blow along the coast or down from the mountains, and from cool to warmer regions. They bring little or no rain to northern Chile. Winds that have crossed the continent from the Atlantic have lost their moisture on their journey and bring none to these western coasts. Some rain or snow falls on the cold upper parts of the Andes. Small streams tumble down the mountain sides but only one of these reaches the Pacific. The others dry up or are lost in the sands of the desert.

Some trees and grass grow along the banks of the small mountain streams or where they sink into the desert. Elsewhere, for miles and miles on end, no living thing can be seen. It is a cruel region in which to live and work, as day after day passes with a cloudless sky and a burning sun overhead, and hot sand under foot.

The Desert of Atacama, named after Indians who once lived in that region, includes a large part of northern Chile. It is one of the most desolate regions in the world. 

The Atacama Desert, however, and other desert areas farther north in Chile, are so rich in minerals that thousands of men are employed in the mines there, and many, many millions of dollars have been invested in the mining properties and machinery. Railroads have been built from mines and refining plants to seaports along the coast, and to connect with the main line to Santiago and Valparaiso. At the ports there are houses for the workers who help to load and unload steamers by using smaller boats. The larger ships must stay well out to sea to avoid being dashed on shore in time of storm. Water is brought to the camps from high up in the mountains, and food, machinery, and other supplies must be brought in by railroad or steamer. A large part of the meat supply, however, comes from Argentina. The cattle are driven across the Andes and slaughtered after they reach the mining settlements. 

Nitrate. -The most valuable of the minerals found in this desert region is a salt called nitrate of soda, or nitrate of soda, or "nitrate." It is found mixed as a kind of cement with rock material, and forming layers so hard that they must be broken up by dynamite. 

The nitrate areas are scattered through the desert from 19° to 27° south latitude.

Some of the layers may have as much as 40% of nitrate, but most of them have much less. Some layers are only a few inches thick; others may be several feet thick.

Some are found on the surface, others are buried to a depth of many feet beneath materials that contain no nitrate. 

Rock material containing a valuable amount of nitrate is crushed and then put into tanks of boiling water. The water

From the tank the water with its dissolved nitrate is run off into pans, where the water is evaporated, leaving a mass of white nitrate crystals. As soon as it is dry enough, the nitrate is packed into bags and stored, or sent to the ports for export. In refining nitrate some borax and some iodine, a drug used in medicine and surgery, are obtained. There are also old lake basins whose deposits contain borates from which borax is made.

Nitrate is used chiefly in the manufacture of fertilizers and explosives. Before the explosives. Before the discovery of methods by which nitrogen can be taken from the air and used in the manufacture of nitrates, most of the world's supply came from Chile. Enormous amounts were exported yearly to the United States and

European countries. Some of these countries are now manufacturing nitrate to meet a part of their needs, but Chile still exports large amounts, which vary from year to year. 

Iquique and Antofagasta are the chief ports for the shipment of nitrate, although several other smaller ports are used.

The government of Chile raises a part of the money to meet its expenses by taxes on exports. In years when much nitrate is exported, from one fourth to one half of the money needed has been raised by the tax on it. The government of our country, under the Constitution of the United States, has no power to tax exports. 

Years ago parts of northern Chile belonged to Bolivia and Peru. Bolivia had a seacoast and harbors, and Peru a longer coast line than it now has. Then came a war between those countries and Chile. Chile won, and its boundary has been established where it is shown on the map (page 346). The lands formerly belonging to Peru and Bolivia now yield much of Chile's supply of nitrate. 

The railroads of Bolivia connect with those of Chile to reach the sea, and, under a treaty between the two countries, Bolivian exports and imports are handled at the ports of Chile. This arrangement, however, is not quite satisfactory to Bolivia. It would prefer, as would any other nation, its own seacoast and harbors. In that way it could more freely carry on its trade with the rest of the world. 添​喜

Other Minerals in Chile. There are several copper-producing regions in Chile. 

The largest of these is in the Desert of Atacama, about 160 miles northeast of the port of Antofagasta. It is a mountain of ore that is mined by blasting off the face of the mountain and using power shovels (A) to load the trains that take the ore to the smelters. It is a low-grade ore that could not be mined profitably until large-scale operations by modern methods (B) were put in use by the United States company that now owns the mine. There is another coppermining region in the Andes of central Chile. 

The output of these and other mines makes Chile second among the copper-producing countries of the world.

Two large bodies of high-grade iron ore are known in Chile. One is in Atacama but this is not now being worked. The other, not far from Coquimbo, is owned by a Pennsylvania steel company. An electric line has been built from the mines to the coast, where modern ore docks, like those on Lake Superior, have been constructed. The ore is sent to the United States for smelting, while Chile imports manufactures of iron and steel. 

For many years Chile was a large producer of silver, but in recent years the amount has greatly decreased. A small amount of gold is obtained in the refining of copper and silver ores, and some lead, zinc, manganese, and sulphur are obtained.

The chief exports of Chile are its minerals.

The People. -The people of Chile are descended from Spanish and other European peoples, and from mixed marriages between these settlers and the Indians. They are progressive and industrious, and proud of their nickname of "Yankees of South America." For the most part, the Indians of 

Chile were a more sturdy, powerful, and independent people than those of countries farther north. In the edge of the forest between southern and central Chile are the remnants of a very proud Indian race called Araucanians (A), who maintained their independence until about fifty years ago.

THE WEST COAST DESERT 

369 

A. Square in the center of Lima, the capital of Peru. This city is in a rich irrigated district. Compare the buildings with those in Santiago (362 A). The statue is of General San Martín, the George Washington of Peru and Chile. 

THE WEST COAST DESERT 

You have learned that much of northern

Chile is a desert, rich in minerals, but having no forests or well-watered fields. Even the higher Andes there have so little rain or snow on their western slopes that only one of the mountain streams crosses the desert to the 

Pacific Ocean. The Atacama Desert of northern Chile is part of the West Coast

Desert region (map, page 322). 

If you could fly from Chile northward over the coastal region of Peru, you would find that it also is, for the greater part, a barren waste. Yet there would be one very noticeable difference. There are more streams coming out of the mountains, they extend farther into the desert, and more of them reach the ocean. Why is this so, and how has it influenced the distribution of people and the nature of their industries? 

Winds and Rainfall. The West Coast

Desert is in the region of the southeast trade winds (page 263; see also the maps on page 328). Winds from the Atlantic Ocean 

cross the continent and are cooled as they are forced into higher altitudes, up the eastern slopes of mountains. On these eastern slopes the rainfall is very heavy, and on their higher parts there is snow. Winds blow through passes in the eastern ranges, and bring some rain and snow to the tops of the western Andes. At times, storms and heavy fogs sweep in from the Pacific and bring moisture to the western Andes of Peru. 

Irrigation. In your flight over the Peruvian coast lands, you would notice that the streams reaching the lower lands are used for irrigation. Water is taken from the rivers at some high point and spread over lower-lying fields through a network of irrigation ditches. Where this life-giving water is brought to the fields there is no more desert. Instead, there are fields of cotton, sugar cane, and rice, and orchards and gardens. Every river that comes out of the mountains is made to yield its precious water to the fields. There also you will see pleasant cities (A) or villages with homes and shops and market places.

Reproduced from G. R. Johnson: Peru from the Air, American Geographical Society's Special Publication No. 12, N. Y. Cuy 

The port of Callao, Peru, showing the new breakwater and within it the mole, part of which has been in existence since 1865. Railroads connect it with the shore. The harbor is part of a somewhat open bay. 

The Peruvian cotton has a long fiber with a natural crinkle that makes it especially valuable to use with wool in the manufacture of textiles. The sugar cane is very rich in its sugar content. 

Petroleum. There is a petroleum region in northwestern Peru, on the ocean shore near the boundary of Ecuador. The oil is of high quality. Among the South American countries, only Venezuela and Colombia exceed Peru in the output of oil. 

The Smaller Ports. In flying along the coast of Peru, you would see hill lands, sand dunes, bare rocks, and cliffs. Then you would catch sight of a curving coast line that partly incloses a bay. Its waters are sheltered enough from storms so that steamers lying off shore are more or less protected. 

A pier runs out into the water. Here boats can be loaded and unloaded, and boatmen transfer goods between the pier and steamers anchored in the deep water of the bay. 

Among the sand hills at the shore end of the pier are the mud huts of the laborers and 

boatmen. It is a poor place in which to live and in sharp contrast with the pleasant villages in the irrigated valleys. Such small ports are to be found at many places along the coast. From them are shipped the products of irrigated fields and orchards. 

Cities of the West Coast. 

On the map, page 368, find Lima, Callao, and Mollendo.

Lima is the capital, largest city, and chief business center of Peru (369 A). It is well back from the coast and is surrounded by irrigated fields from which much of its food supply comes. Its chief manufactures are cotton goods, woolen goods, and shoes. Lima is connected by railroad with the mining regions in the mountains, and with Callao (A), a near-by seaport that has the only good natural harbor on the 1400 miles of Peru's seacoast.

This long coast line of Peru is equal to the distance from Key West to New York on our 

Atlantic coast, or from San Diego to Vancouver on our Pacific coast. To the wharves and docks of Callao come ships from many countries, bringing goods from all the world

A Story of the Past. The shores of 

South America were discovered by Christopher Columbus, and by other explorers and adventurers from Spain and Portugal.

As a result these two countries gained control of almost the whole continent. They found, everywhere, native Indian people as other explorers found them in North America.

Some of the Indians were savages roaming wild in the forest where their descendants HIGHLANDS OF PERU AND BOLIVIA may be found today. Others had reached 

To understand what you will find in the highlands of Peru and Bolivia, you should know about the people who lived there before 

Spanish explorers came to the New World.

In those highlands, many thousands of feet above the level of the sea, there are the ruins of cities, temples, and palaces. Even so late as the latter part of 1932, some explorers stumbled by accident upon the ruins of a great city unknown before then. What is the story of the people who lived in these ancient cities? a high degree of civilization. They tilled the land and used the water of the mountain streams to irrigate their fields. They built wonderful stone buildings and good roads. 

They had an orderly government. 

The natives who had made the greatest progress in these arts of civilization belonged to the empire of the Incas. Their capital was Cusco, an ancient city among the mountains of Peru. The lands that were controlled by the Incas are largely in Peru and Bolivia, but extend also into Ecuador on the north, and Chile on the south.

SOUTH AMERICA 

A. Llamas in a residential street of La Paz, Bolivia. 

Notice that there are packs on the backs of some of them. 

The Incas, and the tribes ruled by them, mined much gold and silver, and used those precious metals in decorating their buildings and in making ornaments of various kinds. 

They were experts in agriculture. Along the coast they constructed irrigation works, and cultivated fields along the rivers, as you have learned is being done today. In the mountain valleys they made terraces on the steep slopes by building walls to hold the soil in place, and raised potatoes, corn, and cotton. 

They found potatoes and corn as wild plants and developed them by cultivation, giving to the world two most important food plants. 

They used the llama (A) as a beast of burden. 

The Spanish explorer Pizarro, with a small party of soldiers and adventurers, invaded the country in 1532. By the use of firearms, the Spaniards captured and later killed the king of the Incas, and conquered the land for Spain. It remained under Spanish rule for nearly three hundred years. 

you

Two Independent Republics. 

- As know, Bolivia has no coast lands (page 365) and you have studied those of Peru as a part of the West Coast Desert. Two parts of Peru and Bolivia remain to be studied. 

One of these is the region of mountains and plateaus. The other is a lowland east of the 

Andes, a part of the great interior lowland of the continent. Each of these countries has boundary disputes about the extent of its lowland area (map, page 318).

It is in these two countries that the Andes - here often called "the roof of the Western 

World"- reach their greatest width and nearly their greatest height. The average elevation of the eastern and western ranges of the Andes is almost twice that of our Rocky Mountains, and the great peaks of Illimani and Sorata (map, page 368) reach heights of more than 21,000 feet. Compare them with 

Mt. Whitney, the highest peak in the United 

States (14,500 feet), and Mt. Marcy, the highest peak in New York (5344 feet).

The eastern and western ranges of the Andes spread out to inclose a great plateau with an average elevation of about 12,000 feet, and, farther north, numerous shorter and lower ranges. Between those shorter ranges are mountain valleys with bare slopes. 

Farms and Grazing Lands. - The people of the plateau and valleys are chiefly Indians and mestizos. Most of them are farmers and have a great affection for their small holdings. 

In the mountain valleys where there is enough rain, or where irrigation is possible, the floor of the valley and its terraced lower slopes are cultivated. Being near the Equator, the lower valleys are warm, and the crops of warm regions are grown there. These include corn, beans, some orchard fruits, and vegetables. In the higher valleys the crops are those of cooler lands-wheat, barley, rye, and potatoes. The plateau is bare, windswept, and rocky. Comfortably warm when the sun is shining, it is cold at night; frosts are frequent, and the growing season is short. 

Some crops are grown, but grazing is more common, although common, although the grass is poor and scanty. In the summer the shepherds drive their flocks up the mountain slopes almost to the snow line.

A.-Part of the Central Railway of Peru, on which you see a train carrying copper bars from a Cerro de Pasco smelter. 

On the lower slope there are some terraced fields. 

Some large grazing areas are owned by men who live in the cities. The herds and flocks of such an owner are left in the care of a mestizo manager and the Indians he employs. 

The beef animals are generally poor and their meat tough. The sheep are small and the wool is of various colors and of poor quality. 

A demand for better meat and a better kind of wool has led to attempts to improve the breed of the animals.

Two Valuable Animals.-The llama (372 A) 

is small but strong for its size, and very surefooted. It belongs to the camel family and can travel long distances if necessary without much food or water. Llamas are the pack animals of the Andes mountain trails. Each animal will carry about 100 pounds, but if overloaded it will lie down until a part of the load is removed. The alpaca, which belongs to the same family as the llama, is raised for its long, fine wool.

A Famous Mine in Peru. The Central 

Railway of Peru (A) and the Southern Railway of Peru connect the coast with the mining and agricultural regions of the Andes.

The Central connects the port of Callao with Oroya, on the eastern slope of the western range of the Andes. Its construction was difficult and very expensive. Part of the road bed was blasted out of the mountain side, and passengers look down into gloomy gorges. There are many tunnels, bridges, and switchbacks. The grades are steep, and where the railroad crosses the western range its pass is 15,680 feet above sea level— the greatest height reached by any railroad in the world. A railroad from Oroya goes to one of the world's great copper mines at 

Cerro de Pasco (map, page 368).

The Cerro de Pasco mines and a great smelting plant at Oroya are owned by an American company. The same company

A.

The volcano El Misti towers above the city of Arequipa, which lies at its base. Arequipa is about sixty miles inland, on the railroad from Mollendo to Lake Titicaca and Cusco. owns other mines not far away. It mines nine tenths of the copper of Peru. Some gold and silver are obtained from the same ore as the copper. Men sent from the United

States manage the mines and the smelter, but the hard work is done by Indians who have always lived in these high altitudes. 

Vanadium and lead also are mined in small quantities, and some coal from which coke is made. Vanadium is used in making certain kinds of hard steel. Peru produces more than half of the world's supply. From mines not reached by railroads, ore is brought out by llamas or donkeys. The metals are shipped, and supplies for the mines are received, at Callao. 

From Mollendo to the Bolivian Plateau. —

The Southern Railway of Peru connects the port of Mollendo with Arequipa and Cusco, once the capital of the Inca empire. From From Mollendo it crosses the desert and winds upward more than 7000 feet before reaching Arequipa. This city (A) is the center of the wool trade and has some manufacturing. For over 35 years (1891-1927) Harvard University, of Massachusetts, had an observatory near Arequipa. The air there is usually clear and the night sky cloudless. Although the 

North Star and others near it cannot be seen there, most of the stars can be seen very well, including the Southern Cross and all other stars that cannot be seen in our country.

After crossing the western Andes the railroad continues to Lake Titicaca (375 A). 

Steamers on this lake, the highest navigable body of water in the world, are owned by the railroad and connect with a short line to La Paz. This is the least used of the Bolivian railroads.

La Paz is the largest city of Bolivia and its chief financial and business center. It was built in a valley below the level of the plateau to protect its people from the cold biting winds and dust storms that sweep across the higher land. Because La Paz is a railroad center and Sucre, the legal capital of Bolivia, is not, most of the government business is done in La Paz.

A. A small native boat on Lake Titicaca. Both the boat and the sail are made of reeds tied together. 

The Mines of Bolivia. The richest mineral region of Bolivia is in the eastern Andes, where tin, silver, gold, copper, and lead are found. Only the tin is mined in large quantities, and Bolivia now produces about one fourth of the world's supply. The amount of silver mined is now small, although the silver mines of Potosí were once the marvel of the world. Gold is found in the ores of copper and silver. The copper mines of Bolivia produce much less than those of 

Peru and Chile.

The chief railroad serving the mines is the 

Antofagasta-Bolivia Railway (page 368), although many of the mines are at some distance from it in the mountains. Donkeys and llamas are used to carry the ore down the mountain trails.

Another railroad from La Paz - and the shortest route to the sea- goes to the port of Arica. Its mountain section has steep grades and is expensive to operate. Most of the freight still takes the longer route to 

Antofagasta. A railroad connects that route also with the railroad system of Argentina and gives an outlet for Bolivia on the Atlantic at Buenos Aires. Bolivia, as you know, is in the unhappy position of not being able to reach the sea except across the territory of neighboring countries.

EASTERN PARTS OF BOLIVIA, PERU, ECUADOR, AND COLOMBIA 

You turn now to the study of the eastern parts of Bolivia and Peru and a similar region in eastern Ecuador and Colombia. The greater part of this area is a lowland included in the basins of the Paraguay, Amazon, and

Orinoco rivers. But it includes also the the eastern slopes of the Andes Mountains and the foothills that lead down to the plains. 

This region is very unlike the coast lands to the west of the Andes in Bolivia and Peru.

A Lonely Land. - Find this region on the maps. Ecuador was given its name - the 

Spanish word meaning "Equator"-because it is crossed by the Equator. The whole region that you are now studying is in the Torrid Zone. Over much of it the doldrum belt, with daily rains, moves north and south with the changing seasons (pages 

337-338). Almost all of its plains and mountain slopes have dense forests (A); although there are savannas in southern Bolivia and in Colombia. How different it is from the

West Coast Desert and the treeless valleys and plateaus of central Peru and Bolivia!

Yet it is a lonely land, a land in which few white people live or would care to live.

It is shut off from the Pacific Ocean by the Andes and it is hundreds of miles from the Atlantic. It can be reached only by mountain trails from the west, by river trips many days in length from the east, or by the manmade bird, the airplane. Trails across the mountains to the plateau or the sea are steep and difficult. Loads going west are carried by Indians, llamas, or donkeys. The river routes to the east are long, and most of the few native Indians in the region are unfriendly and unwilling to help. Air service is limited and too expensive except for mail, a few passengers, or goods of high value. 

Whatever is grown or found within this region can reach world markets only by one of these routes, except for the small area that is served by the railroad from La Paz to 

Buenos Aires.

BOLIVIA, PERU, ECUADOR, AND COLOMBIA 

377 

A. 

Indians at work on a terraced mountain side east of the high Andes. The plants are coca shrubs. Your dentist sometimes uses cocaine, a drug obtained from this plant, to deaden the pain while he pulls a tooth. 

Industries and Products. As in other 

As in other parts of South America, large estates, some of a half-million acres or more, are owned by rich men who live in the cities. On most of these a small part of the land is in use by Indians or mestizos who send some products to market over the mountain trails to the west.

Some parts of the mountain slopes have been terraced, for growing the coca shrub (A). 

From its leaves is made the drug cocaine, used in medicine and surgery. 

Southeastern Bolivia is a part of the Gran

Chaco (map, page 322). Some of it is scrub, a part is grassland, and another part is forest. 

The population of this area is small. Potatoes, cereals, fruit, sugar cane, rice, and coffee are raised, but there are no industries that send important products to world markets.

The forested lowlands of the Amazon and Orinoco basins are inhabited chiefly by Indians who live by hunting and fishing. 

Not many years ago the Indians in this area gathered the latex from wild rubber trees and prepared "hams" of crude rubber (page 340). So much plantation rubber is now produced in the Far East that the wild rubber industry of South America is no longer very important.

Iquitos, the largest settlement in the whole area you are now studying, was once a famous rubber-shipping port on the Amazon in eastern Peru. It can be reached by goodsized steamers, but with the falling off in rubber production its commerce is dwindling.

Another forest industry once very important, especially in eastern Ecuador, has been almost destroyed. Quinine, a drug much used in medicine, is made from the bark of the cinchona tree. the cinchona tree. These trees grow wild in the forests of the eastern Andes, where the natives strip the bark from the trunks and branches. The industry is declining because many of the wild trees have been killed, and because of the cinchona plantations in the 

Far East.

SOUTH AMERICA 

In Colombia, some cattle are pastured on the savanna lands along the Orinoco, but to get them to market they must be driven into the highlands. Even at the start of the drive they are generally in poor condition, and when they reach the highland markets their condition is worse. The meat is stringy and tough and brings a low price, but their hides have some value.

The Future. This part of South America 

(eastern Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador, and southeastern Colombia) has great forests that could yield an enormous amount of lumber. There are grasslands on which millions of cattle could find pasture. It has a fertile soil and abundant rains where tropical products can be raised almost without limit. 

There are many streams whose waterfalls and rapids could furnish all needed power. 

Yet much of this region has a population of less than one person per square mile. When will it be developed? So far as can now be seen that time will not come until some energetic people can clear parts of the forest, control the river floods, and build railroads that will carry goods cheaply to market.

The population of the world must grow much more dense than it is now before any nation will seriously attempt to do these things.

Products and People. - Find the Gulf of Guayaquil. On a river flowing into this gulf find a city of the same name. It is the largest city and chief port of Ecuador. Near it are large cacao plantations. At one time 

Ecuador was the leading cacao-growing country in the world. Now the Gold Coast of Africa and near-by islands produce over twelve times as much, and Brazil three times as much (page 334).

Ecuador is losing its cacao industry as it has lost much of its cinchona and rubber industries. One reason for this is that the population of this west coast region is made up chiefly of Indians, Negroes, and mestizos who do not like to work. Nearly all of them suffer from hookworm disease, which makes them tired and weak, but which can be cured. Until a few years ago yellow fever, one of the most deadly of tropical diseases, was found here also. American army surgeons in Cuba discovered that yellow fever is carried from person to person by one kind of mosquitoes. Methods of killing off these mosquitoes were worked out, and with the help of American sanitary officers many

South American cities have been freed from this disease- including Guayaquil. Malaria, also caused by a mosquito, is another disease from which the people of Ecuador suffer, but it too can be controlled. 

White managers can now live here in safety. When there is more labor and the natives are able and willing to worknative laborers do on plantations in other parts of the world - many tropical products as

On the coastal plain of both 

Ecuador and Colombia the tagua nut is gathered. It is called vegetable ivory because it is hard and white like ivory. Millions of pounds of these nuts are used each year in making buttons. Fine light straw hats, made from the 

fibers of a small palm, are woven by the natives. As they were sold through Panama for a long time they are called Panama hats.

Two Precious Metals.-In western Colom- 

In western Colombia there is much placer mining for gold and platinum along the streams that flow out of the Andes. Natives, using the same methods that were used in placer mining in California, wash these precious metals out of the river sands and gravels. In some places dredges are in use also. The whole region is, unfortunately, very unhealthful, and any great development of the industry must wait until sanitary conditions are improved. At the present time the mining region can be reached only by footpaths through the forest jungle or by canoes on the streams, yet Colombia produces nearly half of the world's platinum. A.

NORTHERN COUNTRIES OF SOUTH AMERICA 

The northern part of South America is bordered by the Caribbean Sea and the 

Atlantic Ocean. It includes the northern part of Colombia, and all of Venezuela, British Guiana, Surinam or Dutch Guiana, and French Guiana. Southeastern Colombia has been studied as part of a larger region including similar areas in Ecuador, Peru, and 

Bolivia; and southwestern Colombia has been studied as part of a tropical jungle bordering the Pacific (pages 376-380). 

The northern countries of South America are in the Torrid Zone, and the prevailing winds there are the northeast trade winds. 

What does this region produce that is of interest to the people of the United States, the nearest of the great trading nations?

Caribbean Colombia. - In Colombia, the northern Andes divide into three great ranges that extend from south to north. 

Between these ranges and along their sides are the cool uplands where most of the white population of the country live. On the coast the land lies close to sea level, and it is hot and damp. Bananas, sugar cane, and rice are grown there. In the cooler uplands the crops are corn, wheat, cotton, and the fruits and vegetables of temperate lands. 

Out of one of the mountain valleys, the Magdalena River flows into the Caribbean Sea through swamps and over sand bars. 

It is the outlet of a rich agricultural and mineral region. It is about 1100 miles long and is navigable for a part of its lower course, but not all of the way to the sea. 

Its chief port, Barranquilla, is connected by rail with the seaport Puerto Colombia, and by airplane routes with Bogotá, the capital, and with Buenaventura on the Pacific. 

The mineral resources of the Colombia mountains and valleys are not yet fully known. Gold is found in the mountains as well as in river gravels (page 379), but the

Bogotá is the chosen home of much of the white population, and a trading center for the surrounding country.

Colombia and Venezuela follows a lofty range of the Andes. East of this range, notice a lowland surrounding an arm of the Caribbean known in part as the Gulf of 

Maracaibo and in part as Lake Maracaibo.

East of this lowland, another range of the Andes extends northeast and east along much of the Venezuelan coast. 

South of the range just mentioned are the grassy plains of the Orinoco River-the llanos, a broad, low, featureless region of savannas. South and east of the llanos are the 

Guiana Highlands, a region that extends eastward into the Guianas and borders the 

Amazon basin on the north.

Over all of this northern part of South 

America blow the northeast trade winds, bringing rain to the northern mountain slopes. From parts of Colombia the rain is shut out by the mountains that these winds cross. This is also true of the grasslands of the Orinoco, except when the equatorial belt of rains, in moving north and south with the seasons, crosses these plains.

The northern slopes of the Andes and the Guiana Highlands have dense forests. The plains of the Orinoco have a rainy season when the grass grows rapidly and the river overflows, flooding large parts of the plain. 

This is followed by a dry season when the grass withers and dies. If it catches on fire at this time, it burns over enormous areas. 

Products of Venezuela. Crops of tropical lands are grown along the Caribbean coast and in the lowlands around Lake Maracaibo.

Here are the chief sugar-cane region and a cacao-growing district. In this same lowland, much petroleum has been found and many wells have been drilled. 

In the highlands west and south of Lake 

Maracaibo, coffee of an excellent quality is raised, and the industry is increasing. Cotton and corn also are grown in this region. 

There are minerals in the highlands and mountains of Venezuela, and some gold and copper are mined.

On the llanos, cattle raising is at present the only possible occupation. This is handicapped by a long dry season, by flooded plains during the growing season, by distance from a market, and by the lack of labor. 

The Orinoco is navigable for a long distance, but there is not enough traffic to make river transportation profitable. At the mouth of the river is a great delta much like that at the mouth of the Mississippi.

The Guiana Highlands have but a small native population, and no industries of importance. 

Cities of Venezuela. La Guaira, at the base of the mountains that border the 

Caribbean, is the chief port of Venezuela.

Through it most of the commerce of the country is carried on, although there is another shallow port at Maracaibo.

From La Guaira, a railroad climbs the mountains to Caracas, the capital, which is about 4000 feet above sea level. Although 

La Guaira is less than 7 miles from Caracas the railroad between the two cities is 23 miles in length. It is a very picturesque route. Caracas (383 A) is high enough above sea level to have a comfortable climate. 

Venezuelans are proud of their capital and speak of it as the "pearl of the Andes."

The Guianas. The Guiana Highlands extend east from southern Venezuela into 

British, Dutch, and French Guiana. As their names indicate, each of these three small countries belongs to a country in Europe. 

All of the rest of South America is occupied by independent republics.

The northeast trade winds bring heavy rains to all the Guianas. Their coastal lowlands are hot, damp, and unhealthful, especially for white people. They are frequently flooded during the very rainy season, and no period of the year is entirely free from rain.

Caracas is a beautiful city with well-kept squares and public gardens. Clouds often conceal the tops of the near-by mountains.

The chief crop-growing regions are on the lower lands near the coast, and in the river valleys where there are fine soils and fertile fields. Sugar and rice are the two most important crops, but other food crops for the people include yams, corn, bananas, and other fruits. Cattle are raised on grasslands near the coast, only to meet the needs of the people. The only product of value obtained from the forests is balata, used to cover (insulate) electric wires.

In each of these three countries some gold is mined in French Guiana by the forced labor of convicts. More diamonds are found in British Guiana than in Brazil. Much bauxite is mined, and is sent to the United States for manufacture into aluminum. 

Most of the people of British Guiana are Negroes, descendants of slaves; laborers from tropical islands of southeastern Asia; and mestizos. All of these can live and work there in greater safety and comfort than white men could. In French Guiana, the population has been increased by its use as a colony to which many of the worst criminals of France have been sent.

Agriculture has been more successful in Surinam or Dutch Guiana because the Dutch settlers built embankments to keep their fields from being flooded. fields from being flooded. Pumps also are used to remove any surplus water that gets on the fields. The same is true of agriculture in part of British Guiana which was once owned by the Dutch.

When you began the study of South America, you learned that in some ways it is much like North America, and in other ways it is very different (pages 319-320). You found that South America is southeast of our continent. If you use the meridian of 74° west longitude the meridian of New York

City - in the same way as you did the meridian of 80° west (page 319), you find again that most of North America is west of it and nearly all of South America is east of it. 

Before you leave the study of South

America, you should gather together some of the facts that you have learned about the different countries. 

Size. On the map, page 320, use the scale of miles to find how long South America is from its southernmost point at Cape Horn to its northernmost point on the Caribbean 

Sea. Find the latitude of each of these points, and, taking 70 miles as the length of a degree of latitude, find the length of the continent. How do the two results compare?

What continents are larger than South 

America? What continents are smaller? (See Table 1, page 389.)

Lands That Cannot Be Used.-The greater part of South America is in the Torrid Zone and, as the map on page 320 shows, most of the continent is less than 1000 feet above sea level. Much of the Amazon basin is less than 500 feet above sea level (map, page 326). A region in the Torrid Zone only a little above sea level is hot. In this tropical part of South America, the prevailing winds are the northeast and southeast trade winds. 

They meet in the equatorial calms that move north and south with the seasons, and there are daily rains. A large part of the Amazon basin therefore is hot and rainy, and dense rain forests cover much of it. Up to the present time, this region has yielded few products for the use of man. 

The most important one has been rubber, but now the production of rubber there has greatly decreased. Some day, perhaps, the world will need the products of tropical lands now overgrown by rain forests, and they may be cleared away. In the Amazon lowlands not only must that work be done, but vast floods must be brought under control. To do all this calls for earnest and intelligent labor, and much money, and both are now lacking for this task. The future of this region cannot be foretold, but at present it is not bright. No area of rain forests anywhere near as large as the Amazon lowlands has ever been cleared, although some jungles have been cut down and converted into plantations. The flood waters of some rivers, like those of the Mississippi, have been held within artificial banks, but this has never been done for a stream carrying even half as much water as the Amazon. 

Jungle lands along the coast of the Atlantic 

Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and for some distance south along the Pacific Ocean are also largely waste. They produce but a small part of the crops that could be grown there. 

Some are not used because not enough labor is available or the laborers are not intelligent, others because diseases drive laborers away. 

There are deserts that cannot be irrigated, such as some of those along the west coast. 

There are lands that are too cold for crops, such as the plains of Patagonia. There are snow-covered mountains, too cold and bleak for crops or man. There are lonely forests on plains and mountain slopes, too far from the markets of the world to be of commercial value. Neither the timber that is now growing there nor the crops that could be grown could be sold at a price that would pay for necessary labor.

What may be done to change these conditions, no one can say. South America is a land of the future.

Natural Resources not Fully Developed. 

In the agricultural and grazing sections of 

South America, a full use of the land has never been attempted. Land is held in great estates; most of the labor is hired (A). 

There is hardly any careful mixed farming by the owners of small farms, as in our country. 

In regard to the mineral resources of South America, the case is much the same. Many mineral regions are known, some of enormous extent, of which a number are being worked. 

Other deposits are known that are not being worked because they are hard to reach and cannot be mined at a profit. Many parts of the continent where minerals may be found have never been explored. Most of the mines now being operated have been developed by companies in the United States or Europe.

Manufactures, using the raw materials of the country, have been started in several of the more progressive cities. The growth 

MO NW-22 of manufacturing, as well as the carrying on of large-scale mining, requires much coal. But not much coal has been found in South America, and most of the little that has been found is of poor quality. 

The best mines are so located that mining is difficult and expensive. In most places it is cheaper to import better coal from the 

United States or Europe. To a small extent, electric power plants have been built to furnish electricity to cities and manufacturing plants. But here again a limited supply of skilled labor has made it necessary to use imported machinery and foreign mechanics, machinists, and managers.

Those parts of South America where the most rapid progress may be expected in the arts and industries are the A B C countries

A. - Puerto Colombia boasts the longest pier in the world, 4000 feet long.

The future there should bring a better use of land, an increase of manufacturing, more more educa- tion, and more orderly and settled governments.

Many of the cities in South America have gained in trade because of the growing industries of the surrounding regions. In 

Brazil, Rio de Janeiro, Santos, and São Paulo have grown in size and commerce because of coffee; Bahia because of cacao; and 

Pernambuco because of sugar. Buenos Aires and Bahía Blanca in Argentina, and Montevideo in Uruguay, have grown because of the surplus wheat, corn, cattle, sheep, wool, and hides that they ship to Europe and the 

United States. Valparaiso in Chile, Callao in Peru, and Puerto Colombia in Colombia (A) are other ports that are increasing in size with an increase in the industrial importance of their hinterlands.

Education has been largely confined to the wealthy and to the white population of the more progressive countries.

For most of the poorer people there have been no schools at all. Even for the wealthy not much technical education has been provided. Not until more people receive an education, and technical training is more generally given, will skilled native laborers be available. 

At present, most of the Indians and Negroes, and many mestizos, cannot read or write.

A study of the map on page 

342 will show that most of the people of the continent live near the oceans. The interior of the continent has very few people, and almost all of them are Indians or Negroes.

Transportation and Trade. - Railroads and good roads are very limited in South America. The railroads that have been built are chiefly short lines extending back from the coast, or connecting a few of the larger inland cities with near-by ports. 

Only two lines, built at enormous expense, cross the Andes. Not many of the railroads of South America have ever paid a fair return on the money invested. In most of the continent there are too few people to pay the cost of good highways. It is only in recent years that the more progressive cities have paved their streets. 

Fortunately, South America has thousands of miles of navigable waterways reaching into many parts of the country. Air routes also are developing, both for travel in South America and for travel between the two 

American continents.

SOUTH AMERICA AS A WHOLE 

387 The great highway of world trade is the ocean, and the countries of South America are kept in touch with world markets through their seaports. Most of the trade of South

American countries is with the United States or Europe. The goods, however, must be carried long distances, because the greater part of South America is in the Southern Hemisphere. The meats shipped must be kept chilled or frozen during the long voyages. 

The expense of transportation by steamers, though less than it would be for an equal distance by railway, is nevertheless higher than it would be if the distances were shorter. 

Because of differences in products and needs, the commerce between North and South 

America is constantly increasing. Because such products as corn, wheat, and meat find a better market in Europe than in the United

States, a large part of the commerce of some South American countries is with Europe. 

Pan-American Union. In the city of 

Washington, there is a beautiful building that is the home of the Pan-American Union. 

The members of this Union are the republics of North and South America. It was formed so that through meetings and the exchange of information the people of the member countries can know more about each other. This has brought about better understanding and more friendly relations.
